en: Preface to the *Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School*, composed by Feng Zizhen, Court Gentleman and Vice-Director of the Academy of Scholarly Worthies.

Regarding the *Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School*: it was compiled by the śramaṇa Puhui of Qiantang, based upon the teachings of Master Faying of the *Treasury of Jewels* (Baojian).

[The] Compiler: This is the direct voice of the ancient virtuous ones, like a cough. Each of these karmic conditions (*nidāna*) supplements what already exists and fills what has not yet been recorded.

I have therefore engraved them upon woodblocks to summon Zen travelers. One day, as I was about to finish reading the small preface for the first volume—which seemed to vie for primacy—I offered this praise: "Is this not supreme mastery? Is this not the fulfillment of all wishes?"
"Maṇiye. Is this the "linked pearl" (lianzhu) produced by the masters of this assembly? Is it not like the one Xiwangmu personally obtained from the Red Water?
At another time, when the merchants of Xiyu arrived with their laden pack animals and the bearded traders of Xianyang gazed upon its value, they stood in their stalls with high noses and azure eyes;
yet whether those two arms held up what was truly the jewel or not, the raw gem of Mount Jing was cast away upon the blind pavement.
"My feet were amputated twice due to illness; how could I have shed blood and wept in your presence to explain myself? Someone said: "Those who wander in my garden behold the sumanā flower;
those who ascend to the stage of enlightenment realize the āmra fruit. That flower is not perceived by waiting for the eye to grasp it, but is instead apprehended within the heart.
The fruit does not require item-by-item enumeration to reach its marrow and essence; this is what is called true awakening and true realization.

To peruse it superficially or taste it only momentarily, failing to discern with certainty what it truly is in a state of haste, is merely the common, reckless practice of wearing coarse cloth socks and blue traveling shoes.

I say that because there are degrees of sharpness and dullness in wisdom, there are differences in the speed of understanding; and because there are depths and shallows in insight, [the results differ].
In discernment there is skill and clumsiness. It is like the fragrant grasses at the edge of the world that pass before the eyes of a prince:

everyone knows their splendor flows and turns, never touching the sandy wastes; yet, among the lush and tangled thickets, only he can look upon them and name them—whether they be *quian*, *heng*, *zhi*, or *li*.
This is what is called the true appreciation of the "six harmonies" within the single expanse of the wilds. Is it not so?

However, while the tip of the nose may universally scent all manner of pure fragrances and the complexion of the cheeks may slightly improve, this is ultimately not yet the true essence of having eyes beneath one's feet as described in the commentary to the *Li Sao*.
Nevertheless, "Makhadeva [the Buddha] covered his tongue," for the characteristics of discrimination are empty; "Vimalakīrti remained silent," for the path of language is cut off.
"The Venerable One had nothing to say, and I had nothing to hear. On another day in the Zen grove, we shall present it face-to-face and exchange it.

The down payment and the family treasures are secretly present within you as you turn your head; with a single shake beneath the patched robe, the jewels of the Sangha are poured out in full, each person becoming a pearl from the sea of Canghu.
What need is there for further connection? I have written this to serve as the preface.
Preface to the Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School:
Now, when the Patriarch came from the West, he did not establish written words, pointing directly to the human heart alone.

Yet, at that time, his disciples already had what was called "not clinging to written words, yet not departing from written words," taking them as the functioning of the Way; this had already entered the secondary level of teaching. Therefore, there arose...
“You have received my seal of the ‘skin’; it is indeed true that the Way does not reside in words. The disciple asked, “What do you think of this? He replied, “It is not so.
Although the Way does not reside in words, if one’s words are appropriate, even speaking all day long—what harm would that do to the Way? Otherwise, even a single word may be considered superfluous.
It was from the blooming of a single flower that five petals came to share in its fragrance; thus has it been transmitted through the ages.”
The two lineages branched out and flourished; the kōans and opportunities for practice shone like the five lamps of the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.

As the various patriarchs succeeded one another, there arose both "Nian-gu" (Selections of Ancient Cases) and "Song-gu" (Verses on Ancient Cases). The Nian-gu is seen in collections such as the *Bafang Zhuyu Leyao* (Essential Pearls and Jade from the Eight Directions).
As for the Song-gu, there was Master Baodian, who during the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty resided at Ba’en Temple in Chiyang and compiled the records of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Regarding the机缘 (ji-yuan) at Chaling, there are three hundred and twenty-five cases of *songgu* (verses on ancient precedents).
One hundred and twenty-two masters contributed two thousand one hundred verses, which were titled the *Chan-zong song-gu lian-zhu* (The Linked Pearl Verses on Ancient Precedents of the Chan School).

This work was highly esteemed within the monastic community, yet its woodblocks were nearly worn away. Consequently, I reflected that from the Chunxi era until now, nearly two hundred years have passed; during this interval...
Greatly renowned and venerable masters are as numerous as stars scattered across the heavens; their verses on ancient cases (*songgu*) are no less than those of the former sages.
Alas, however, their linked compositions (*lianjizu*) are lacking. I have long felt ashamed to have been unworthily included among the ranks of the Zen school for many years.
Having realized nothing in Zen and attained nothing in the Way, I would begin a work only to stop again, faltering repeatedly. In the year of Yuanzhen Yiwu (1295), I was...
At the Yiwu Puzhi Mountain Monastery, my affairs were simple, so I immediately continued my draft of writings. I managed to recover only one or two pieces.

Following the traces of my drifting life—whether in public or in seclusion—I recorded whatever I encountered as I went along. Over twenty-three or twenty-four years, these have gradually formed a sequence.
For those karmic conditions that arose first, I appended verses; for those not yet present, I added them along with the circumstances. Furthermore, there are four hundred and nine [verses].
In thirteen fascicles, this work contains the verses of four hundred and twenty-six patriarchs, totaling three thousand and fifty stanzas.

It is titled *The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls: Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School*. Intending to solicit funds for its publication so that it might be shared with later students who are still deluded, [the compiler] declared:

"The Way does not reside therein. From the plucking of the flower and the smile, to the three prostrations and the transmission of the marrow—originally, there was not a single word given to them; yet [this collection] illuminates...

It was manifest within the space between my heart and mind; the Way spread boundlessly. How could there have been, as there is today, the practice of harmonizing phonemes and manipulating words and phrases like a harp to deceive the ears?
To cause later generations to abandon the root and pursue the branches is truly lamentable. I smiled and did not answer.
After a long while, he sang: "Within the shadows of five clouds, a divine immortal appears; In hand he grasps a red silk fan to shield his face. One must quickly fix one's eyes upon the immortal;
Do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand. Thereupon, he said to him: "What you have discussed is the fan in the hand.
Is that which I have compiled truly contained within the fan? Alas! Let those who understand me or condemn me judge this."

This is the preface, compiled here. On the first day of the sixth month of the Wumao year of the Yan’you era, the śramaṇa Puhui of Qiantang, formerly residing at Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery in Shaoxing Prefecture, wrote this for himself.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Comprehensive Collection of Linked Verses on the Ancient Cases of the Chan School*:
The entanglements of the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot be rotted by water nor destroyed by fire; their branches link and their vines proliferate, spreading forth without end.
The *Chanzong songgu lianzhu tongji* (Comprehensive Collection of Linked Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School) was compiled by Master Huì of Lúān.
It has long been carved into printing blocks and circulated throughout the world. Recently, due to certain circumstances, those blocks were scattered among the populace.

In the summer of the Jisi year of the Hongwu era, fearing their loss, I entrusted a fellow practitioner to redeem them and enshrine them at Huànjū on Mount Dàcí. This occurred on the twentieth day of the sixth month.
It was the eighth day. The following day, at the place where the old woodblocks had been stored, a fire broke out with fierce winds, and the flames spread to over a thousand households.

Alas, this too is extraordinary! Yet, is it that the "entanglements" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs possess such spiritual efficacy? Or is it that divine beings have protected them so that this came to pass?
With deep reverence, I have donated my own funds to employ craftsmen to repair and complete them, so that they may circulate widely and the wisdom [of the Dharma] be perpetuated forever.
I have recorded the extraordinary circumstances regarding how these woodblocks were obtained. This is merely to mark the date and month.
Written in the second month of spring in the Ren-shen year of the Hongwu era by the śramaṇa Jingjie, resident monk of Zhongtianzhu Mountain.
[This concludes] the Preface to the *Chanzong songgu lianzhu* (The Linked Pearls of Chan School Verses on Ancient Cases).
Composed by Zhang Lun, Military Commissioner of Ningwu Army, Director of the Yulong Wanshou Palace in Longxing Prefecture, and Marquis of Kuo State in Wugong Commandery.
The Western Sage appeared in the world for the sake of the great causal event; subsequently, by means of the Eye of the True Dharma...
It was entrusted to Kāśyapa and transmitted through twenty-seven generations until Bodhidharma entered the Middle Kingdom.

There he administered the great medicine of the Dharma and opened the gate of ambrosia, directly guiding those of superior capacity without relying on written words. From that time until now, more than six hundred years have passed.

Those who have attained Bodhi are beyond counting. Although their minds transmit through non-transmission and their Dharma is taught through non-teaching, the verses and gāthās arising from the conditions of various capacities have gradually increased over time;
these jade-like phrases and golden chapters are fully present in the recorded sayings (gong’an).

The Great Master Faya of Ba’en Baojian in Chizhou, during the leisure moments following his delight in Chan practice, compiled and gathered three hundred and twenty-five recorded encounters (*jīyuán*) from the time of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, down to the masters of antiquity and the present day, as well as one hundred and twenty-two verses on ancient cases (*sònggǔ*).
He entitled this work the *Cánzōng Sònggǔ Liánzhū Jí* (Anthology of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases from the Chan School); it may truly be called the treasury of Vairocana.
Within, it fully encompasses all treasures; within the sandalwood grove, there are none that are not fragrant trees.

To open up awakening and insight for the benefit of future generations—by carving this into wood and circulating it, how could this be considered a minor contribution? Having long admired the vehicle of the patriarchs and delighting in promoting the gift of Dharma, I was requested to compose this preface.
Unable to refuse my firm refusal, I have written this on the eleventh month of winter in the year of Tuiwei Dayuanxian during the Chunxi era.

Preface to the Old Collection of the String of Pearls Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School, composed by Dharma Master Fasheng, the Great Master of the Dharma-Jade Mirror at Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty.
In the past, I, Fasheng, traveled south to seek the Way. During the intervals between Chan sessions and banquets, I collected various verses on ancient cases and consulted with spiritual friends.
According to what he heard and retained, he engaged in discussion with his fellow students;

over more than thirty years, he selected and verified three hundred and twenty-five cases of karmic conditions and composed two thousand one hundred verses concerning one hundred and twenty-two patriarchal masters.

These have been compiled into fascicles and titled *The Linked Pearl Collection of Zen Verses on Ancient Cases*. It is my wish that they be shared with all Bodhisattvas throughout the world who study Prajñāpāramitā.
Although the wondrous essence not transmitted even by Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot be captured in words or names, it has never originally possessed written characters;
how then could there be secret teachings? Pointing directly at the opportune moment, nothing is concealed, so that one may see through to the original face of the person themselves.
For this reason, the Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
Through parables, words, and teachings, they reveal and instruct, desiring to lead sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*). How could this be in vain?

The lay devotee of Chiyang gathered gold to carve woodblocks, so as to broaden what is seen and heard, providing a gift of the light of the Great Dharma. The twelfth month of the second year of Chunxi, Year Yiwei.
The eighth day. Recorded with reverence by Bianci.

*The World-Honored One’s Occasions for Inquiry*.

When the World-Honored One Śākyamuni was first born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward the earth, walked seven steps, and looked around in the four directions, saying: "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am honored.
Later, Yunmen said: "Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to a dog, just to ensure that heaven—"
Lower Tàipíng: Lángyá Jué said, "One may truly say: 'To take this profound mind and serve every dust mote and land'—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. The verse says:
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha’s birthday, he pointed to heaven and pointed to earth, declaring himself the foremost.
Nine dragons sprayed water to bathe his golden body. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. (Dongshan Cong)
Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth, his words ring out clearly. Passing on words and transmitting messages from the painted hall;
the messenger still possesses great spirit, and the host must surely be extraordinary. (Quán Dàdào)
When the jeweled palace and dragon towers suddenly descended, he walked seven steps and his brows cleared with joy. His words were no mere words, for there was no room for humility;
in all of heaven and earth, who else could surpass him? (By Yuan Zhen of Yexuan).
The former kings labored to establish the foundation and initiate the enterprise; the later emperors sit upright with folded hands, maintaining the fullness of their reign.
Swords and halberds have all been converted into farming implements; at such a time, who could proclaim the sounds of Great Peace? (Foyin Yuan)

As soon as he descended into the royal palace, he revealed his primordial nature; walking seven steps in every direction, he proclaimed it once more. Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, no one could comprehend him;
alone he thundered with the sound of a dragon, pervading the great trichiliocosm. (Seal of the Ocean-Print)
Before chaos was divided, no one understood; once heaven and earth were split apart, all matters were fully revealed.
Heaven-endowed skill is truly strange; in the end, he puts on a performance for others. (Baoning Yong)
Walking seven steps and pointing toward heaven—under the blow of the monk’s staff, life is hard to preserve. What was accomplished after emerging from the mother’s womb?
How does that compare to the time before descending upon Jambudvīpa? (Zhang Wujin)
He took seven steps and immediately proclaimed himself Honored One. How could one dare let family disgrace out the door?
Having finished saving sentient beings while still in his mother’s womb, he too must have had a mark for every blow. (Changling Zhuo)
As soon as he was born, he could walk; he was immediately brilliant and spiritual. Among heaven and earth, I alone am honored. It is laughable how he looked only ahead and not behind;
who would have known that after his passing there would be Yunmen? (Cao Tang Qing)
A single fire casts the golden ball; its perfect roundness costs nothing in tongs or hammer.
Picked up and cast from the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom peak, it strikes down the white phoenix from the heavens. (Cishou Shen)
Born with his full body beneath the Ashoka tree, he took seven steps in a fresh and unprecedented manner. Meeting him, they said, "Who would have thought you would rise so early?
Who knew there was yet another traveler on the night road? (Nanhua Ying)
The Old Barbarian could not avoid emerging from the womb; he also knew how to appear thus before people. Pointing to the earth, pointing to the heavens, he claimed to be number one;
yet for sentient beings, there was disaster for forty-nine years. (Gushan Gui)
As soon as this old fellow was born, he was already in a hurry; taking seven steps, he acted like one demented.
He has deceived countless foolish men and women, opening his eyes wide as he enters the boiling cauldron. (Jingshan Gao)
With hands of *tūla* cotton, he points to heaven and earth; with deep blue eyes and double pupils, he gazes upon the four quarters.
Walking seven steps, he proclaims, "The whole world belongs to me. All his life he has been a child playing with toys. (Fodeng Xun)
Before black and white are distinguished, the whole body is wondrous; as soon as patterns and colors appear, it becomes discordant. From this, the family style has been leaked far and wide;
the nostrils of the descendants in the final age are crooked. (Yue’an Guo)
As soon as he emerged from the womb, he transcended all; he walked seven steps and alone was called Honored One.
Had he encountered Old Yunmen at that time, we would not be burdening our descendants as we are today. (Sushan Ru).
[Continued Collection] The Old Barbarian displayed all manner of empty airs; with one finger he pointed to heaven and another to earth.
At that time, everyone thought he alone was honored; today, reflecting back, who is not so? Every person is already within the radiance;
when encountering this text, there is no need for further avoidance. (Yuwang Da)
A stone tiger of a thousand years gives birth to a qilin; with its single horn, its entire body shines with five colors.
It completely snaps asunder the golden locks and jade gates, raising clouds of dust within the realm of Vairocana. (Xuedou Zong)
Her beauty is like that of Xi Zi when she left the Golden Palace; her charm resembles Yang Guifei descending from the Jade Tower.
Still holding the lute to half-conceal her face, she becomes all the more elegant and graceful so that others may not see her fully. (Fujian Qín)
Within the Vairambha Garden, his good reputation was lost; parting from him was in vain, only to spread a foul name. It is certain that not a single word could be stolen [from him];
until now, he has falsely been made out to be an unvirtuous man. (Xiatang Yuan)
A single arrow of tussilago from the Five Indias stirs up a million troops of China;
had it not been for Yunmen’s execution of the true command, one would have nearly mistaken the zero point on the scale. (Shichuang Gong)
Wandering everywhere and looking in all four directions, he alone claims supremacy. On level ground, there is no wind, yet ripples rise.
While it may still be bearable that the calamity reaches one’s own household, who would have known it would bring disgrace to descendants for a thousand ages? (Lan’an Xu)
Turning over the earth’s axis, heaven and earth grow narrow; Shifting the celestial wheel, the universe expands wide. One must display one's skill among the strong;
Smash through empty space and look upon the beginning of the kalpa. (Zhengtang Bian)
Slaves and servants, nine times born and ten times dead; their inner selves are not upright, and they are driven by those on the outside.
Even if they open their mouths, they speak beyond the mark; they cannot avoid rolling their whole bodies in mud and water. (Yuedang Chang)
Bathing an infant beneath the *aśoka* tree; at the clear dawn, the rosebush opens with dew.
Turning past the place where monks meet, the donkeys and horses emerge from their wombs in the back stable. (Tiantong Jing)
The herb has no cause for being brought forth; adding further commentary only makes one more deluded. Who in the Western Heaven or this land knows this?
At midnight, the udumbara flower blooms amidst the flames. (Ying’an Hua)
Stepping out the gate, the wind is in harmony with the surroundings; east, west, south, and north, there is no one else. One cannot find the Old Man of Shaoyang upon inspection;
his descendants cannot avoid stirring up the dust of worldly guests. (Huikan’s Verse)
Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth—nowhere to hide. "Gautama, Gautama! What kind of nose are you looking for? (Moon Forest Guan). "I say to myself that I rise early at the fifth watch;
who knew there were still travelers on the road at night? The gentle breeze and heavy rain are not as they were of old;
Yao and Shun wear their robes with ease while the ten thousand nations pay them homage. (Yuan’an Yan).
Never having entered the womb of Māyā, his two hands know not where he is placed;
emerging from her right flank, he manifests within the realm of Māra—fit only for lamentation, unfit for gazing upon. (Tianmu’s Homage).
With a single "wa" sound, he immediately utters "ta-li. Suddenly emerging is such a great icchantika. From this land and the Western Heavens, calamity and harm arise.
Stately and majestic, he washes the earth until it becomes no more than mud. (Bejian Jian)
Walking seven steps, he still seems like a mere semblance; pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, he is not clear.
Once right and wrong have fallen upon the ears of bystanders, even if one were to wash them until the year of the donkey, they would not be clean. (Xutang Yulu)
With two fingers pointing to heaven and earth, he takes many more steps around; how pitiable is the Yellow-Faced Old Man, like a crab falling into a boiling cauldron. (Xiyan Hui)
Since birth, I have regretted being of the same lineage; my heart and liver would surely melt even if cast of iron.
You alone are honored within the three realms—what can be done as today passes into tomorrow? (Jiakuan Zhen)
A monk asked Jiufeng Qian, "I have heard it said that you, Master, remarked: 'The various sages who appear from time to time are merely messengers.

Is this true? The Master said, "It is. The monk said, "When the World-Honored One pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth, saying, 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored,' why did you, Master, instead call them 'messengers'?"
The messenger said, "Master, it is precisely because he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth that he is called a 'messenger'. The verse says:
The wondrous marks are perfectly luminous and cannot be grasped; the slaves and servants are merely diligent in their service.
Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, they claim to be honored and great—yet they too are merely messengers transmitting words. (Danxia Chun)

[Added for inclusion: Before the World-Honored One had left Tuṣita, he had already descended into the royal palace; before he had even emerged from his mother’s womb, his work of saving sentient beings was already complete.

The verse says: The Great Elephant has originally no form; reaching the ultimate void, it encompasses all things. At the very end, he has already gone too far; facing south, he gazes at the Northern Dipper.
From the Tuṣita Heaven in the royal palace to his birth from the womb—the beginning and end form a single thread, with no coming or going from the start.
Traces are swept away, footprints extinguished, and the very root eradicated; lotus flowers bloom everywhere amidst the fire. (Yuánwù Qín)
This is not about casting one's body across the sea; it is about walking with ease amidst packs of jackals and tigers. Do not bring right and wrong to judge me;
throughout my life, my piercing investigations have remained unrelated [to such concerns]. (Gushan Gui)

A sharp blade may have honey upon it, yet there is no need to lick it; do not taste the water from a household where there is *gudu* poison. By neither licking nor tasting, one avoids transgression entirely;
composed and robed in brocade, one returns to one’s own home. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
Originally departing from Tuṣita to descend into the royal palace, he then proceeded to the mountain of blades and entered the cauldron of boiling oil.
In a casual moment, he seized the white-handed thief; his eyes are filled with nothing but exposed loot. (Xiatang Yuan)
Dangling a hook is not like a traveler lost at a ford; casting a net is truly not the act of one waiting for a rabbit.
Where has the black chicken gone at midnight? At dawn, it swallows the Jade Qilin. (Zhengtang’s Discernment)
The skin and bones were once starkly exposed; today the face has gained a thousand layers of thickness.
To head-butt and tail-sweep is surely to be further punctuated by the bell after the *kalyāṇamitra*’s midday meal. (Oran’s Verse)
[Added for inclusion: On the eighth day of the twelfth month, at the moment the morning star appeared, the World-Honored One suddenly said: "How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them. The verse says:
When Gautama lost his eyes, there was but a single branch of plum blossoms amidst the snow;
now, thorns grow everywhere, yet he laughs at the spring wind for its chaotic blowing. (Huitang Xian)
The Yellow-Faced Gautama is no great man; where the morning star appears, he only smears himself with filth.
Now is the time to seek out a live snake to play with, lest his descendants be left stranded halfway along the road. (Fuxincai)
Upon seeing the morning star once, the dream was immediately over; a thousand-year-old peach pit grows into a green plum.
Though it lacks the flavor for seasoning soup, it has once served to quench the thirst of a general. (Xuedou Zong)
Having emerged from the mountains, it was already late; yet one seeks advantage in the world.
Even if you were to transcend the three realms in a single thought, I would still strike you with my fist right across the face. (Fozhao Guang)
This old man has always boasted in vain; For no reason, his diseased eyes see flowers in the sky.
If only he could transcend the three periods of time right now— Upon closer inspection, it turns out he has not yet arrived home. (Wuyongquan)
Six years in the wild grass as a fox-spirit; leaping out, his whole body is nothing but tangled vines. Having lost his eyes, there is nowhere to seek them;
he deceives people by stubbornly claiming to have realized the Morning Star. (Tiantong Jing)
Two thousand years ago, the Yellow-Faced Old Man raised his head; was it not upon seeing the morning star? Vast and boundless is the universe, with countless people;
how many sons of men possess eyes that truly see? (Kentang Chong)
The Snowy Peaks are rugged and the years have passed deeply; when have you ever seen the morning star at midnight?
How pitiable are those whose karmic consciousness is vast and confused—they have missed the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma. (Miaofengshan)
When the morning star appears at midnight, the mechanism before one’s eyes is clearly and utterly lost.
To say that all the marks of a Tathāgata are fully present is but an empty fist deceiving a small child. (Wan Shi Kong)
For six years I remained hidden in the Snowy Mountains, my head covered in ash and my face smeared with dust, feeling ashamed of my own countenance.
This morning, suddenly beholding the appearance of the morning star, I finally realize that until now I have been deceived by my own eyes. (Iron Mountain Ren)
Six years he buried his body in the grass; at that time, though he had eyes, they never once opened.
Indeed, he beheld the appearance of the morning star, yet before reaching the gate, it was cold as ashes. (Jieshi Peng)
Six years of ascetic practice on the Snowy Peaks; this morning, the true Master was struck down. Nowhere in the heavens or across the earth can he be found;
these ten billion emanated bodies are but empty fabrications. (Tianmu Li)
Before the Mountain of Perfect Enlightenment, one loses one’s eyes; whether ordinary or sage, all are born blind.
To this day, every night when the morning star appears, who is willing to walk where it walks? (Chijue Chong)
The morning star appears at the third watch of the night; each one’s eyebrows arch above the eyes. An old man with a yellow face builds a mound on level ground;
what a pity for this one who tells dreams within a dream. (Da Xie Qian)
The moment the bright star appears, the eyelids are pierced. Myriad thousands of Chinese and foreign words are spoken.
Beggar, you who have suddenly grown rich—do not speak such dreams; whose hearthfire has no smoke? (Amitāyus).
The golden bell strikes through the night at the ninefold city walls; returning after six years, my emaciated form has been transformed.
Waiting until the eyes and minds of sentient beings are awakened, the Snowy Mountains remain as ever, their blue peaks towering and majestic. (Xutang Yu)
Light as a golden wheel, yet heavy upon the grass seat; exchanging a golden ball for a man, a clay pellet for a pearl.
Sentient beings of the final age possess clever eyes and minds; the morning star shines empty, the Snowy Mountains are cold. (Xianji Yun)
The moon fills the vast sky, the stars fill the heavens; as soon as Gautama saw this, his eyelids were pierced through.
Countless are the people in the marketplace of Chang’an—how can they compare to every household staying awake until nightfall? (Qianfeng Wan)
One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. As soon as the assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:

"Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The verse says: The Dharma-King’s Dharma is like this: Observe it with clear discernment. As soon as the words were spoken, he descended from the seat; The sound of the gavel still resonates through the ten directions.
His voice shakes the great trichiliocosm; dragons and tigers submit. No one can match the talent of the Dharma King. To understand immediately upon hearing his words is still dull-witted;
the thousand eyes of the sudden teaching open all at once. (Mingzhao Qian)
Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel to inform the assembly: "The decree of the Dharma King ought to be thus.
If there be any *siddha* guests within this assembly, they need not wait for the radiance of the hair-tuft between his brows. (From the Beita Zu)
Only those among the assembly of successive sages would know this; the Dharma-king’s decree does not go like this.
If there were a *śrāmaṇera* guest within the assembly, why would Mañjuśrī need to strike once? (Xuedou Xian)
A million numinous mountains are like reeds and hemp; they gather like wind and clouds, completely surrounding him.
Had it not been for the old Mañjuśrī at that time, Śākyamuni would have surely scattered sand once again. (Foyin Yuan)
The various eminent ones, like qilin and dragons, were all deceived at that time in one fell swoop. The true son of the Dharma King strikes the *ghanṭā*;
even until now, it serves as a source of laughter. (By Zhengjue Yi)
Before the signs have appeared, it is already two or three steps too late; after the white mallet has struck, how much more unbearable!
Had there been a guest of the immortals at that time, we would not have come to this present day of forced pointing south. (Haiyin Xin)
A single blow from the Teacher of the Seven Buddhas turns the goose-king into a duck and the turtle into a tortoise. The dragons and elephants at the full banquet all lean their ears;
they laugh themselves to death at the ancient adept of Vulture Peak. (Byuexuan Zun)
The towering form of the crown-mark is ultimately difficult to behold; its unfolding and rolling back is like a flash of lightning.
Had there been people of this present age at that time, they would have discerned the needle and thread beneath Mañjuśrī’s hammer-stroke. (Baizhang Yuanwen)
Contemplate deeply the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the nature of the Dharma King’s Dharma. The reflection of the jade wheel falls upon coral branches;
a single gust of pure wind stirs heaven and earth. (The grace of Kṣitigarbha).
The moon in the heart of the waves is thoroughly cold; its clarity surely allows no dragon to coil there. How many unreturned travelers are there across the Five Lakes?
Yet they are caught by those on the sidelines grasping their fishing rods. (Shangfang Yi)
Mount Sumeru rises from the sea, spanning across the heavens; north, south, east, and west, its limits cannot be seen. Not a single bolt of plain silk could capture it;
people vie with one another to transmit it throughout the world. (Da Hong Su).
Sitting upright with a fixed gaze, the words have not yet formed. With one direct blow, how clear is the meaning!
If you entrust yourself to this command turned upside down, boundless pure winds will arise and stir the earth. (Mengan Xin)
Do you see this fragment of true wind? The primordial matrix of transformation employs the shuttle of principle; it weaves an ancient brocade containing the image of spring.
Alas, what can be done about the Lord of the East leaking its secrets? (Tiantong Ju).
A single bright moon reflects upon the heart of heaven; the living beings of the four seas are indebted for its illuminating presence. Why need the western wind shake the vermilion cassia tree?
Across the azure void, it once again sends forth its sound through the ninth month of autumn. (Fujian Qín)
How could one repay the decrees of the Dharma King? Old and decrepit Mañjuśrī forces his head out.
It might still be bearable to bring trouble upon Śākyamuni, yet to this day, for a thousand ages, there is nothing but clamor and noise. (Longmen Yuan)
The silver hare is so pure and bright it cannot be imitated; it was only forced to be smeared with paint by Mañjuśrī.
For a thousand ages, descendants have had no place to find it; beneath the three wooden rafters, its beak is utterly mute. (Yu’uan Guo)
The shadow of the golden mallet stirs; the light of the precious sword is cold. A multitude of a hundred thousand gaze with eyes fixed in unison.
(Chu Anfang). Gautama presses his finger; Mañjuśrī relies on the command. The celestial mechanism is leaked; one blow strikes it right. (Nanhua Bing).
[Continued Collection] The true command is entrusted to the total grasp; there exists no device of ordinary or sage. The secure barrier is shattered into a hundred fragments;
like sparks from flint and flashes of lightning, it shines forth. (Nun Wuzhuo’s General Summary).
The ancient sovereign’s former transformation transcends all proclamations; the seal of the wordless is clearly inscribed.
If a monk of the present day were to face this directly, often those who would number a thousand would become but five hundred. (Zhengtang Bian)
The Dharma King’s decree has extinguished all obstructions; a single expanse of empty stillness, utterly free from flaw.
Beneath the hammer, the eyes of all sages remain unopened—how many fine steeds have been exhausted by the salt cart? (Lingyan An)
Do not be overly preoccupied with calculating your livelihood; if you try to analyze it too closely, matters will only go further astray.
If one is a cub of a man-eating lion, why must one add fangs upon fangs? (By Yue-lin Guan)
When the Way prevails and times are clear, men of talent are honored; when the family prospers and the state is wealthy, even children are pampered.
Were it not for the early blooming of flowers along the purple roads, how could one see the yellow orioles alighting upon the willow branches? (Muan Yong)
The World-Honored One was asked by a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā): "The Buddha possesses six supernatural powers;
I possess five. What is that one power? The World-Honored One called to the seer, and the seer responded.
The World-Honored One said, "That one power—you ask me about it. The verse says:
The Immortal’s single question was fully answered; yet Gautama has not a single thing. Having summoned the rabbit, he lets it go as before;
how many mountain ghosts call out to one another in the dark? (Foyin Yuan)
That one question you asked me makes Śākyamuni, the Old One, feel ashamed. He knows only how to tread step by step upon red lotuses;
he does not realize that, in his confusion, he has entered the wild weeds. (Zhengjue Yi)
Never encountered throughout immeasurable kalpas; how could you remain unmoving and yet reach its center? Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is but a trifle;
what is this single penetration of the most wretched Gautama? (Baoning Yong)

Question: How did the Buddha manifest that single penetration? The World-Honored One pointed directly at the face to reveal the traces of delusion. Auspicious clouds gathered thickly as a gentle rain fell;
the great thunderous sound of his voice was like a wind sweeping across the earth. (Yunxi Gong)
"You ask how this question is direct: the mountain plum and the river willow share the fragrance of spring. There is no need to search for one who carries stolen goods;
they have already revealed their own identity in the hall. (Changling Zhuo)
[Continued Collection] You ask me about that one call. At the pivot gate, a hairless lock is turned inward.
At any moment, with a single pull, it can be opened. Three wives sit facing one another—*tok!* (Duanqiao Lun).
That one stroke—you ask me of it. The mouth is the gate of calamity; it summons causes and carries their fruits.
The Great Dharma King of Shame and Compassion: Bing-Yi-Li-Ren does not belong to Fire. (Bao Ye Yuan).
The World-Honored One was asked by a non-Buddhist practitioner: "I do not ask about speech regarding existence, nor do I ask about speech regarding non-existence.

The World-Honored One remained seated as he was. The non-Buddhist praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away my clouds of delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way].
Having paid homage, he departed. Later, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What did the non-Buddhist realize that led him to say this?"
[The monk] entered. The World-Honored One said: "It is like a fine horse of the world that moves at the mere sight of the whip's shadow.
The Verse says: "The whip's shadow is distinct; I point it out to you. With a flash of insight from much learning, the spirit is refreshed.
Fenyang reports to you, his fellow Chan practitioners: Pick it up with your own hand; do not loathe the dust. (Fenyang Zhao)
The pivot-wheel has never yet turned; once it turns, it must run in both directions. When the clear mirror suddenly confronts the stand, one knows beauty and ugliness in that very moment.

Once beauty and ugliness are distinguished, the clouds of delusion disperse. Where could dust arise at the Gate of Compassion? Thinking thus, I recall the fine horse that caught the shadow of the whip;
though it had already galloped a thousand li, its wind-like speed was summoned back. (Xuedou Xian)
The double blades cover and protect, yet both are shattered; from this, the clouds of delusion suddenly part.
Having recovered the bell-handle from the beginning of the kalpa, a gentle shake stirs the thunder and clouds. (Tianyi Huai)
Ten thousand fathoms of cold pool, bottomlessly clear; At night’s stillness, the jeweled fish swim toward the light. With a single pull of the rod, they follow the hook upward;
The vast expanse of water scatters the moonlight bright. (Baizun Yuan)
Having passed through the night and stayed overnight in the wild grasses, when he opened his eyes, the sky was already bright with dawn.
With an empty stomach and bare feet, he returned singing; the travelers on the road were already quite numerous. (Baoning Yong)
Making a special effort, he earnestly asks whether it exists or not; through the wind, one should respond without expending labor.
Even if the clouds of delusion are cleared away to allow entry, one cannot avoid lingering laboriously halfway along the path. (Jingzhao Zhen)
Snow covers the lofty forest, all of one hue; pure light, above and below, contains a void-like azure.
A woodcutter stands at the cold river crossing; his gaze reaches the full moon—white for whom? (Cheng Kumu).
The non-Buddhists are coarse-minded and accustomed to both the perilous and the level; the Old Barbarian’s whip-shadow reveals his needle and awl.
The traveler picks up the hare of the East Gate—who cares if the hound Han-ku is exhausted by his efforts? (Chang Lingzhuo)
The World-Honored One is like a bronze mirror; hung in the void, it is as still as the autumn moon.
Without partiality inside or out, it makes one’s gallbladder shiver with awe; high and low, everything is reflected therein. (Fujian Qín)
The bright sun shines across heaven upon both being and non-being; who would say that the Sugata sits in the full-lotus posture?
If you wish now to see the events of those years, know that the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox has always lain halfway along the path. (Longmen Yuan)
Without asking whether existence or non-existence prevails, words fall first; the bright mirror upon its stand illuminates both simultaneously.
The clouds of delusion disperse and the morning sky is vast; the brilliant sun is round and red as fire. (Fóxìng Tài)
Revealing his shadow while concealing his body, he questioned the World-Honored One; Gautama’s single stroke required no further embellishment.
From this point, the clouds of delusion unfurl and roll away; one’s spirit, though tenfold, loses eight parts. (By Fodeng Xun)

Delusion and enlightenment leave their tracks before the skull; why trouble yourself further by raising the whip? Merely observing the precepts of chickens and dogs, you do not study the Chan of the Patriarchs. (Gushan Gui)
The two gates of confinement are struck and cannot be penetrated; a speck of dust unmoved, one naturally departs from the source.
Suddenly, the karmic mirror shatters into a hundred fragments; the Yellow-Faced Gautama loses his trace. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] A non-Buddhist came with great earnestness to question the Buddha; some spoke of questioning, others of not questioning, and still others of silence.
The Great Hero did not expend the slightest effort; why ever was a whip used for a fine horse? (Zhaotang I)
The World-Honored One’s single eye penetrates the three realms; the heretics’ pair of eyes pierce the five heavens. The intention of the flower is at its peak as the peach-cheeked face smiles;
the springtime radiance does not reside merely upon the tips of the willow branches. (Xuechao I)
Regardless of whether words are spoken or not, he speaks of seeing the shadow and seeing the whip;
the pillar has its mouth hanging on the wall, and the lantern retreats three thousand paces. (Xiatang Yuan).
The tiger-trapping mechanism is installed in two places; a single cut in the rushing current dries up ten thousand sources.
A swift steed catches a glimpse of the whip’s shadow; its frosty hooves and hair stand cold with awe. (Nirvāṇa-Asanga).
Hunting through the vicissitudes of prosperity and decay is not yet remarkable; in the end, who is truly a renunciant? The native land lies vast and distant with no news;
only occasionally does a solitary cloud return from beyond the ridges. (Zhengtang Bian)
The crimson sun shines through the void, illuminating the great thousandfold world. Both Buddha and Mara are exhausted; their heads transcend beyond.
Do not idly discuss matters on the path; bare your chest and look closely. (Daimpō Chi)
Before asking whether it exists or not, one has already fallen into error. The ancient mirror of Xuanyuan suddenly confronts the dais.
Although it distinguishes beauty from ugliness in the present moment, the clouds of delusion remain as impenetrable as ever. (Kentang Chong)
Holding a brick yourself, you toss it into the air; inevitably, you strike your own head with it.
It is truly painful and difficult to describe; rub your own wound and go back home—enough! (Duanqiao Lun).
Whether there is no word or there is a word, do not ask; sit and observe the success or failure, and you will naturally remain at ease.
When Śāṇavāsī suddenly realized his fall from the source, who would say that the World-Honored One had ever raised his whip? (Fundamental Enlightenment I)
[Added from another source] Once, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma did you teach yesterday? He replied, "I taught the Dharma of certainty.
Again he asked, "What Dharma did you teach today? He replied, "I taught the Dharma of uncertainty," and so forth. The verse says:
The ancient mirror has from the start been free of even a speck of stain; it distinguishes beauty and ugliness before one’s eyes. Now that the mirror is shattered, there is no light or shadow;
the wind rolls the waters of the Chang Jiang until their color becomes turbid. (The Poison-Coated Whip)
Yesterday and today, speaking of the definite and the indefinite: the Emperor’s decree within the realm, the General’s command beyond the passes.
When the outsider entered the dream-world in those days, he has yet to awaken even until now. (Gao’an Wuzhuo).
Yesterday was fixed; today is not fixed. Once the true command has been issued, all follow that truth. Beneath the table, Mount Ling’s black standard is planted;
the hundred-thousand banners and troops all beg for their lives. (Shantang Chun)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Once, because Devadatta slandered the World-Honored One, he fell alive into hell.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to inquire after him, saying, "Are you at peace within hell? He replied, "Though I am in hell, it is as joyful as the third dhyāna heaven.
The Buddha again ordered Ānanda to inquire, "Do you still seek to escape? He replied, "I await the World-Honored One."
As soon as he arrived, [the monk] came out. Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the Three Realms; how could he have any portion of entering hell?
[The monk] replied, "Since the Buddha has no portion of entering hell, how could I have any portion of leaving hell? The verse says:
It is laughable that Devadatta entered the Naraka hell for ten small kalpas, yet attained the wondrous bliss of the third dhyāna;
he blew on his robe’s hem and had to return to the bird’s nest (Zantang Zhun).
The great hermit dwells in the marketplace; the small hermit dwells in the mountains. Each finds their proper place and attains peace and leisure according to their lot.
Why need there be further discussion of coming and going? Wherever one lives, there is abundance of joy. (Clouds on a Remote Peak).
Hell and heaven are laid open with eight characters; who would have known there is neither going nor coming?
If you say you have already attained the bliss of the third dhyāna, you have not yet escaped burying yourself alive. (Songyuan Yue)
Having risked everything at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one knows not where to seek a whole corpse.
Blown up by the winds of karma, one revives and awakens; yet one asks: what time is it now? (Xutang Yu)
[Added from another source] Once, when the World-Honored One was about to engage in a debate with the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, they made a prior agreement, saying:
"If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head as an apology. The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine?

The Brahmacārin replied, "The fundamental tenet of my doctrine is 'non-acceptance of all things. The World-Honored One asked, "Do you accept this view? Thereupon, the Brahmacārin flung his sleeves and departed.
He departed. When he reached the middle of his journey, he attained a realization and said to his disciples, "I shall return to cut off my own head to offer thanks to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "It would be fortunate indeed to achieve victory before the assembly of devas and humans;
why then would you cut off your head? Zhizhi replied, "I would rather cut off my head before one who possesses wisdom than before one who lacks it."
Having previously attained victory, he then sighed and said: "My doctrine has fallen into defeat in two places.

This view is coarse where it accepts the point of defeat, yet subtle where it does not accept the point of defeat. No humans, devas, or followers of the Two Vehicles can know where my doctrine has fallen;
only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas know where my doctrine has fallen. He then turned back.
Upon arriving before the World-Honored One, he said, "My doctrine has been defeated at two points; therefore, I shall behead myself as an apology.
The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such matter. You should turn your mind toward the Path.
Thereupon, together with his five hundred followers, he simultaneously threw himself before the Buddha, left the household life, and realized arhatship. The verse says:
If this view were to accept [the truth], it would destroy the family lineage; if this view does not accept [the truth], with whom could one debate?
The eaves collapse and both ends snap off; within a single hair-tip, the universe appears. (Tianyi Huai)
Rejecting everything, he displays his family style; with a single word, he shatters both sides at once.
Having seized the red banner at the place where light returns, one finally believes that even before words are spoken, one has fallen into one's own school. (Fundamental Enlightenment I)

When seeing this, it is like receiving dust upon the eyes; even if one does not accept the matter as it appears, the situation remains discordant. The thief’s body has already been exposed, yet he vainly turns his head back;
with a ghost’s face and a god’s head, they are buried in one place—utterly useless.

[Added for inclusion: Once, when the World-Honored One was present as the Gandharva King performed music, at that moment the mountains, rivers, and great earth all resounded with the sound of the lute.
Kāśyapa rose and danced. The King asked, "Is Kāśyapa not an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted?
How can he still have residual habits? The World-Honored One said, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma. The King [said, "I understand"].
Again, as the king played the lute three times, Kāśyapa likewise danced three times. The king said, "Kāśyapa has danced; is this not so?
The World-Honored One said, "In truth, he never danced. The king said, "How can the World-Honored One speak falsely?
The World-Honored One said, "I do not speak falsely. When you played the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all plants and trees all danced."
"The sound of the lute—is it not so? The King said, "It is. The World-Honored One said, "Kāśyapa was also like this; he truly never performed a dance.
Thereupon, the King believed and accepted [the teaching]. Master Xiushan asked Chan Master Chengyuan:
"When the Gandharva King plays music, it causes Mount Sumeru to tremble and the waters of the ocean to surge in waves. What did Kāśyapa do?"

"How do you understand this dance? Yuan said, "Kāśyapa was once a musician in a past life; his habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated. Xiu asked, "What about 'Mount Sumeru towers aloft and the waters of the sea surge with waves'? Yuan then desisted. Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying, "That is precisely his habitual tendency. The verse says: Mount Sumeru towers aloft, The waters of the sea surge with waves. If one does not know how to turn it around, One will surely fall into the pit of habitual tendencies. If one can turn it around, It is like a flower blooming in the sky. Even if one were to speak for a thousand eons, How could one ever exhaust its meaning? If you wish to see the Buddha’s original face, Look directly at the tip of your own nose. When the moon is bright, the water is clear; When the moon is dark, the water is turbid. Do not ask others to tell you— Look at yourself right now! If you can understand this, Then you have truly seen the Buddha. The true Buddha, unconditioned, dwells within my own body; three calls and three responses—how profoundly awake!
If a person does not awaken to this fundamental source, they will wander through vast eons of dust and kalpas, identifying with consciousness and spirit.
[Added for inclusion] One day, the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; enter the city with your alms bowl. Ānanda responded, "Yes.
The Buddha said, "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual of the seven Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda then asked, "What is the ritual of the seven Buddhas? The Buddha called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "Take the bowl and go."
Mimian said: "The Great and Small World-Honored Ones were lightly nudged by Ānanda;
they could not help but call a bell a jar. The verse says:
From the ritual protocols of the seven Buddhas of the past, what has Ānanda ever lacked? How laughable is the Yellow-Faced Gautama, for no reason at all.
He performs a circumambulation. (From *Dun’an Yǎn*). [Added from another collection.

Once, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

By means of their supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛty-abhijñā*), each of them individually beheld their past lives. They saw... that they had committed killing in the past.
One who has committed patricide, matricide, or other grave offenses harbors doubt within the heart and is unable to enter into the profound Dharma.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, grasped a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop, stop! You must not commit an act of parricide. Do not harm me; I am certainly [to be spared]."
"Mañjuśrī, to be harmed while practicing goodness means that from the very beginning there has been no self or person;
it is only because of the internal mind perceiving a self and a person that when the internal mind arises, the 'self' is necessarily harmed—this is precisely what is called 'harm.

Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized for themselves that their original mind is like a dream and like an illusion, and that within this dream and illusion, [there is no such thing as a self]."
"There is a self and persons," up to "the parents who give birth and are born. Then, five hundred bhikṣus praised him with one voice, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Wisdom, has profoundly penetrated the very source and bottom of the Dharma. You yourself took a sharp sword in hand and pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata;
yet the sword and the Buddha were likewise identical—of one single characteristic, without duality, and without characteristics."
There is nothing that arises; how, then, can there be killing within this? The verse says:
For the sake of the irrigation channel, he stirs up dust along the way, Causing the entire mechanism to sever the clouds. When the Buddha and the sword are both forgotten, where has he gone?
Returning home, the melody of the tune is once again fresh. (Xiang Tianqing)
From the very beginning, Buddhas and Patriarchs have always been at odds. Where the electric mechanism turns, it is straight as a bowstring.
If the Golden-haired Lion could understand the pressure of this harmonious sound, the Qilin in the moon would laugh until it pierces the heavens. (Xiatang Yuan)
When Mañjuśrī confronted the Tathāgata that very day, the eyes of the five hundred śrāvakas were suddenly opened wide. To understand the Buddha as the Tathāgata is likewise so:
within the casket of the blue snake, wind and thunder roar. (One Primordial Awakening)

[Added for inclusion: The World-Honored One struck a skull and asked Jīvaka, "In which realm was this person born? He replied, "Born into the human realm. He struck another and asked, "In which realm was this person born?

He replied, "Born in the heavens. He struck yet another; Jīvaka was at a loss. The Verse says: The World-Honored One strikes the skull, asking about the path of birth; Jīvaka replies with the human and the heavenly realms. When the third skull is struck, he is utterly bewildered; The ancient mirror shines forth, revealing the true source.
The Tathāgata’s single blow is known by few; directly beneath it, clearly revealed—who is this? Limitless moonlight follows the water away;
a fragment of cloud turns back toward its old mountain. (Tudu Ce)
The Old Barbarian’s single blow—who could have known? In the great furnace, a red cauldron, flakes of snow fly. They cannot remain among the green grass of the tomb;
White clouds look back toward the old mountain to return. (Xiatang Yuan)
[Added for inclusion: When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

Upon seeing the place where the hair had been spread, the Buddha signaled for the assembly to withdraw. He then pointed to the ground and said, "In this very spot, a Brahma-shrine (a Buddhist monastery) should be established."
At that time, there was a wise elder who held up a banner and, inserting it at the point where [the finger] had been, declared: "The construction of the Brahma-shrine is now complete.
Then the devas scattered flowers and praised him, saying: "This younger son possesses great wisdom! The verse says:
Upon the tips of the hundred grasses is boundless spring; Picking it up with the hand at random, one uses it with intimacy.
The sixteen-foot golden body is a mass of merit; Casually waving the hand, one enters the red dust. Able to act as master amidst the dust, One naturally welcomes guests from beyond transformation.
In every place, one’s livelihood is sufficient according to one's lot; One need not begrudge that one’s skillful means are not inferior to others. (Tiantong Ju)
With a single branch of tall bamboo, he established a monastery; the wind swept a gnat into the South Sea. When the foul water was splashed on him, it became the second;
those of dull faculties miss the mark when asked about the first three. (Zhang Wujin)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Once, when the butcher Guang'e was slaughtering a thousand sheep daily, one day he went before the World-Honored One, cast down his butcher's knife, and said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas. The World-Honored One said, "So it is, so it is."
The verse says:
"In the past he was the sword, today he is the Buddha; this morning as Buddha he can be the sword.
Being able to be the sword and being able to be the Buddha are without distinction—thus one beholds the white jade tuft between his eyebrows. (Yuǎnwù Qín)

At the place where the butcher’s blade was laid down, a blow from the staff could not turn him back. The clouds depart for the imperial capital; the waters flow back to the Yangtze and Han rivers. (Tuan’an Xiu)

[Added from a supplementary collection: Once, when King Prasenajit questioned the World-Honored One, [the King] asked: "In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), does conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) exist?
If one says it does not exist, then wisdom would not be one; if one says it does exist, then wisdom would not be two.
What is the meaning of this 'one' and 'two'? The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Nāgaprabha, you once asked this very same question."
Meaning. Now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and hearing is called the single meaning and the double meaning.
The verse says: The place of questioning is extraordinary;
The place of answering is transcendent. Regarding the single and double meanings of the Truth (Satya), The horn of the black dragon is broken. (Zhenru Zhe)
No hearing, no speaking—the mind is inexhaustible. Through the iron wall and silver mountain, a single thread passes through. Where is the true Holy Truth of this one?
Last night, the autumn wind reached the wutong trees. (Donggu Guang)

[Supplement] In the past, when the World-Honored One arrived before the Many-Sons Stūpa, he commanded Mahākāśyapa to share his seat with him and sit down, then surrounded him with his *saṃghāṭī* robe.
He then declared: "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I transmit it secretly to you."
"You should protect and uphold this. Transmit it to future generations so that it does not become severed.
The verse says: "The secret transmission shared half the seat; It is precisely right to spit right in the face. If it were not so, one might let it pass;
But descendants cannot avoid meeting with calamity. (Haiyin Xin)
A monk asked Xinghua, "Before the Many Sons Stupa, what did they discuss together? Xinghua said, "One person transmits the false;
ten thousand people transmit the real. The verse says:

In the Way there is nothing to be realized; only then does one traverse the path of the myriad dharmas. Whether walking in light or in darkness, neither being heedful nor guarding oneself—when the moon comes, the color of the pines grows cold;
when the clouds depart, the green mountains are revealed. Across the Bridge of Tiantai, through all antiquity and the present, how many people have been able to cross?
(Touzi Qing). [Added from the Supplementary Collection.

Once, when the Brahmin Kṛṣṇadanta employed his supernatural powers, he took two *saṃhāra* and *pīpal* trees in his left and right hands and went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to offer them to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Brahmin! The Brahmin responded, "Yes. The Buddha said:
"Let it go," [the Buddha] said. Zhi let go of one branch with his left hand. The Buddha said again, "Let it go.
Zhi let go of one branch with his right hand. The Buddha said again, "Let it go. Zhi said, "Both my hands are now empty."
"Unsure of what more you could put down," the Buddha said, "I am not instructing you to discard that flower.

You should discard the six internal sense organs, the six external sense objects, and the six consciousnesses in between. When there is nothing left to discard, that is the place where you escape birth and death. Zhi suddenly attained great enlightenment. The verse says: The six roots, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses— When all are cast down, they are all gone. If you wish to transcend birth and death, There is nothing at all to be grasped.
"O Brahmin, who knows of your transgressions? King Yama’s karmic mirror reflects all without partiality. By this means you have seen the Buddha and become an Arhat;
only now do you believe that within the alchemical vessel there is another heaven. (Nantang Xing)
Held up with both hands, he was told to let go; standing there empty-handed, one still doubts and hesitates.
Where the realms of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness cannot be found, thank the spring breeze for blooming in profusion. (Xinwen Ben)
The path across a thousand cliffs is cut off; before the wind, one’s livelihood is new. Who would have known that beneath this straw hat lies none other than a man of former sorrows? (Wuji Pai)
[Added for inclusion: As the World-Honored One was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Mañjuśrī requested that the Buddha turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"In the forty-nine years I have dwelt in this world, I have never uttered a single word.
You ask me to turn the wheel of the Dharma again—is it that I have ever turned the wheel of the Dharma? The verse says:
For forty-nine years he struck out and circled about; in the end, he let out a great lion’s roar.
Although he never began to turn the wheel of the Dharma, in the final analysis, his distinctions were made spontaneously. (Wuji Pai)
In the past, Ma Shang never turned the Wheel of Dharma; now to turn it again is but a wearying of the spirit.
Travelers on the road do not know that day has dawned, yet they still clutch their talismanic seals in search of night-light. (Beijian Jian)
Throughout his life, this old fellow has been far too full of empty talk; taking what is non-existent for what is existent, he deceives the blind and the deaf.
Only at the final moment does a single word prove true—this too is like the "bell after the meal" for the *jiaoli* (Dharma teacher). (Bieshan Zhi)

what, then, is there to transform? At that moment, the celestial maiden used her supernormal powers to transform Śāriputra.
