Śāriputra replied in the form of the goddess, "I do not know by what means I might have transformed into this female body.
The goddess said, "Śāriputra, if you could transform this female body, then all women..."

A person should likewise be able to transform. Just as Śāriputra was not a woman yet manifested in a female body, so it is with all women; though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. He immediately withdrew the body of Śāriputra, restoring it to its former state, and asked: "Where now is the physical form and appearance of a woman? Śāriputra replied: ... [The remainder of the passage follows] ... Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, this is the power of the Buddha’s majestic virtue. It is not that I have transformed myself into a woman. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is because you have long cultivated the roots of goodness that you are able to transform yourself at will.

All women are also like this: though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. Why? Because their minds are fundamentally free from the characteristics of a woman. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a man who has cultivated the roots of goodness for many kalpas were to manifest in a female body, would you consider him a woman? Śāriputra said: "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "All women are also like this. Though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women. Why? Because their minds are fundamentally free from the characteristics of a woman. Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know that all dharmas are devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self. They are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, and without intrinsic nature. Why? Because all dharmas are originally quiescent and ultimately extinguished. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "The Dharma-body of the Buddhas is pure and free from defilement; It is neither male nor female, transcending all forms. If one can understand the true nature of all phenomena, One will realize that there is no distinction between male and female. Just as the moon appears in the water, Though its reflection is seen, the moon itself does not move; So too are all phenomena—though they appear, Their essential nature is eternally quiescent. If one realizes the emptiness of all things, One will transcend the marks of male and female. This is called the supreme liberation; It is the path of the Tathāgatas. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard these verses, attained the stage of non-retrogression. All the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. Thus ends the "Chapter on Transforming the Female Body" from the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Śāriputra said: "The physical form and characteristics of a woman's body neither exist nor do not exist.
The goddess said: "All dharmas are likewise; they neither exist nor do not exist. The verse says:
Śāriputra has already perfected the untainted seeds; having changed his physical form, nothing remains known of him. A single thread runs through all paths, not a separate thing:
at midnight, the barbarian monk walks through the snow on his way home. (Zhengtang Bian)

When the Venerable Piṇḍola went to the great assembly at King Aśoka’s palace, the king, during his turn to distribute incense, paid his respects and asked, "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha;
is this so? The Venerable One raised his eyebrows with his hand and asked, "Do you understand?
The king replied, "I do not understand. The Venerable One said, "The Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta invited the Buddha."
[The Master] was observing the fast. At that time, I was also included among their number. The verse says:
Lifting his eyebrows to show King Aśoka, At that moment, both ordinary and sage were beyond discussion.
From the beginning, it has been difficult to gather when facing the assembly; Upon the eyes, as before, two tufts grow long. (Foyin Yuan)
A single film over the eye causes empty flowers to fall in confusion; meeting on a narrow path, it is difficult to avoid.
Great King, do you recognize this old monk? His snow-white eyebrows hang long, trailing upon the ground. (Fohuiquan)
Our Buddha personally beheld Piṇḍola: his eyebrows were long, his hair short, and his brows thick.
King Aśoka still harbored doubts; Oṃ maṇidhari śrī sulu (Bao Ning Yong).
[Continued Collection] The ancient style of the assembly on Vulture Peak has been cast off; from now on, its momentum shall be inexhaustible.
Before Mount Jindou, it is once again leaked forth: do not mistake aconite for *tianxiong*. (Zhengtang Bian)
The Venerable One personally beheld the Buddha come; his double brows were raised and his smiling countenance opened. Between ancient and modern times, there is not a hair’s breadth of separation.
Who in heaven or on earth can accompany him? (Fozhao Guang)
Raising the eyebrows with one’s hand—thousands of sages have never recognized this. At Vulture Peak, the assembly remains solemn;
what need is there to speak of today or yesterday? (Yuelin Guan)
Raising his eyebrows, he answered the point of the question; having personally seen the Buddha, he did not deceive. To this day, he continues to receive offerings throughout the four worlds;
spring rests upon the plum branches, cold with lingering snow. (Tiantong Jing)
The Venerable One personally beheld the Buddha at that time; his eyebrows were raised with an air of dignity. At the crown of his head, he possessed the wide-open *vajra*-eye.
His kindness was so great it could hardly be repaid, as vast as rain and dew. (From the *Kuchan Jing*)
With thick eyebrows and a towering, imposing countenance, he has never actually seen the Buddha.
Meeting him at Mount Nanyue and Tiantai, he is called by others a "monk who catches alms. (Yi’an Shen)
He raised his eyebrows to show King Aśoka; the Buddha’s countenance was clearly revealed, majestic and grand.
To this day, the waters of Lake Anavatapta flow down into the human world, moistening the eight wildernesses. (Tianmu Li)
A single word from the Sovereign issues forth like silk threads; the Venerable One’s eyebrows part in eight distinct strokes.
The winds clear and the misty waves stilled across the four seas, the azure sky is boundless and the waters have no shore. (Wuzhun Shanfan)
The Venerable King Ch’oe-mi did not meet [him]; the ancient style of the lands of the ten directions is pure.
Having personally participated in the Buddha’s supreme assembly of offerings, he was no ordinary monk of gruel and rice. (Hyonghwan Gung)
Before Aṅgulimāla had left the household life, he served non-Buddhist teachers and received their instructions.
Desiring to ascend the throne as King Kośika, he used the thumbs of a thousand people to fashion a flower crown; he had already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine.
He was lacking only one finger. He then intended to kill his mother to obtain that finger. At that time, the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
observing this with his divine eye, he manifested as a śramaṇa before Aṅgulimāla. Aṅgulimāla then released his mother, intending to kill the Buddha instead.
The Buddha walked slowly, while Aṅgulimāla ran after him in haste but could not catch up. He then called out, "Gautama, stop! Stop!"
The Buddha told him, "I have dwelt here for a long time; it is you who have not dwelt [in the Dharma]. Upon hearing this, Aṅgulimāla’s mind suddenly attained awakening.
He then cast away his blade, went forth as a monk under the Buddha, and the Buddha immediately conferred upon him the tonsure and the robes.
The verse says:
Yangxue is fierce and bold, just now surging with vigor; Gautama, stop, stop! Let the wind and waves subside. To kill a man and make him a Buddha—this is the point where one is pierced at the head.
To overturn rain and turn clouds occurs in a single kṣaṇa. (Shushan Ru).
Hastening yet walking slowly, with no before or after; one simply treads the single road of Chang’an. When Yang Qu returns his head, he knows his dwelling place;
then he can ascend to the clouds on level steps. A flower crown requires no fingers born of a mother; beard and hair need not trouble one’s effort to shake them.
It is well that when flowers are moved, butterflies arrive along with them; in buying stones at ease, one gains an abundance of clouds. (Fodeng Xun)
[Continued Collection] "I have dwelt here for a long time; you do not dwell here. If you were to dwell here, your nostrils would be pressed together.
Without moving a step, you travel throughout the entire world. A nun is ultimately nothing but a daughter. (Yunju Wu)
Seeking from others brings nothing but weary toil; the fault lies in the proliferation of mouths.
Having slaughtered your entire family, you now kill yourself as well—whom can you possibly hope to withstand? (Byunyun Nan).
When Yaśas, having gone forth as a śramaṇa, entered the city with his alms bowl and arrived at the house of a certain elder, he encountered the elder’s wife in the throes of childbirth;
the mother and child had not yet been separated. The elder said, "O disciple of Gautama, you are considered a most holy one.
What dharma do you possess that can relieve the difficulties of childbirth? Yaśas replied, "I have only just entered..."
The Daoist did not know this Dharma and said, "I must go ask the Buddha and return to inform you. He hurried back to the Buddha and reported the matter in detail.
The Buddha told him, "Go quickly and tell her: 'Since I followed the noble and holy Dharma, I have never killed a living being.
When Yang Kui went to deliver the message, the woman heard it and was immediately released from her predicament; both mother and child were saved.

Peace and security. The verse says: The Noble Dharma has never killed since its inception; fundamentally, there is no birth or killing, only pervasive clarity and brilliance. All these persons and selves are empty in nature;
all enemies and kin are merely provisional names. When the nectar of immortality first moistens one, it removes the heat of affliction. [The golden seed of the jade lotus—] two...
In full bloom. (Juehai Yuan). Within the moon, Lady Heng does not paint her brows; she uses only clouds and mist as her silken robe.
Unaware that her dream has followed the blue phoenix away, she still returns with a flower branch held over her face. (Gushan Gui).
Before the mountains of Huayin lies a well a hundred feet deep; within it flows a cold spring that pierces the bones. Whose daughter comes here to reflect her image?
She does not look at anything else, but gazes upon her tilted neck. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] Not a step behind, not a moment too soon. How can an enlightened monk understand this? "To grind one's bones and crush one's body would not suffice as recompense;
a single phrase, when clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. (By Nun Wuzhuo Zong).
Throughout kalpas of sages and saints, never before has one killed; now, with this single stroke of the blade, rest.
Truly, it falls upon the chest of Ge-dan; it makes the old bhikṣu of Vulture Peak laugh to death. (Mianjie)
"One does not gain a single bit of wisdom without experiencing a single event. Having never killed a living being, he is utterly without inhibition;
conveying words and delivering messages, he acts with effortless grace. When he picks up his mouth, he loses his nose. (Muan Yong).
Among the worthy and holy ones, one does not kill; the family, father and mother, are naturally complete. The transformations of yin and yang leave no initial trace;
the spring blooms upon the flower branches, suddenly exquisite. (Tianmu Li)
Colorful banners and divine flags chase the morning breeze; the cock-crowers urge the drumming of the drums, *dong-dong*.
The bronze urns measure the long watches—when will they cease? Being thus hurried along, one becomes an old man. (Nansou Mao)
Without food, hunger cannot be cured; without medicine, illness cannot be healed. The yellow-faced old Gautama knows the nature of all sentient beings. (Bao-ye-yuan)
"I, Gautama Buddha, possess perfect and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The separation of mother and child occurred only at that moment" (Hengchuan Hong).
As for Prince Nanda, he sliced his flesh to return to his mother and sliced his bones to return to his father;

only then did he manifest his true body and, exercising great supernatural power, preach the Dharma for his parents. Foyan Yuan said: "The flesh has already been returned to the mother; as for the bones..."

He returned the collection to his father. What do you take as your body? If a student can see through this point, they will sweep away the five aggregates and swallow up the ten directions. Thus, he spoke in verse:
The bones return to the father; the flesh returns to the mother. What, then, is this body? Listen clearly: the mountains, rivers, and the lands appear as its entire form;
the worlds of the ten directions exist within it. Through myriad kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no coming or going. What the mountain monk says here is not mere speech.
Flesh and bone have all been returned to their parents; one does not yet know which among them is Nanda.
With a single flip of the body upon the tip of a hair, every single hair-tip is perfectly exact. (Jingshan Gao)
[Continued Collection] The Original Body of Prince Nanda: Stands tall and independent, untainted by the dust of the world.
Clouds disperse and waters flow; heaven and earth are still. Amidst the fence, the yellow chrysanthemums vie for the spring. (Zidehui)
The bones are analyzed back to the father, the flesh back to the mother; one does not know which is the Nātha. Deep in the night, he loses his footing beyond a thousand peaks;
for all eternity, the long wind blows as the crescent moon slants. (Muzhou of Shaoshi)
The bones return to the father, the flesh returns to the mother. The sun sinks in the west, the waters flow east. (After a long pause) Dew. (By Jian of Beijian).

After the rain has dispersed and the clouds have gathered in, there stand some dozens of towering peaks. Though Wang Wei possessed a nimble hand, it would be difficult for him to capture their traces with his brush.
(Wuzu Fan). Seven virtuous noble sisters were traveling together through the Śītavana charnel ground. One sister pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here;
where is the person? As the sisters contemplated this intently, they all attained enlightenment. This moved Śakra, the Lord of Devas, to respond.
The Rain of Flowers offered this praise: "I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas. Seeing that you sisters have awakened to the Way, I have come to make offerings.
What do you sisters require? I can provide whatever you need. The women replied, "In our home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided.
We require only three things: first, one rootless tree; second, [a second item]; third, [a third item]."
There was a place where yin and yang did not reach, a valley where the three essentials were called for but no response came.
Śakra said, "I possess everything that is required; however, as for these three things, I truly have none.
The woman said, "If you do not have these, how can you hope to save others? They then went together to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "My disciples do not..."
To explain this meaning: only the bodhisattvas can understand this meaning. The verse says:
Suddenly encountering him within the charnel ground, Śakra’s practice of giving was already too late. Where could the three items he sought have been found?
Yet it causes all the sisters to knit their brows. Whether Kauśika knows or not, he offers again three or two sprigs of celestial flowers.
(The Buddha’s Wisdom Spring.
The corpse remains here, but where is the person? A swift thunderclap splits the mountains, the wind shakes the seas; clouds fly and rain disperses—thus we meet.
At that time, the eyes of the skull emit a brilliant light. (Lungya Cai).
The Imperial Son wanders in springtime, not following others; he invites his sisters to enter the Śītavana cemetery.

Within the heap of the dead, he reveals the path of one’s own origin—do you see him stirring up the dust and smoke? For those of keen intelligence, no more is required: turn your head and you will tread upon your own home.
Deep in the clouds at the bottom of the abyss, the old smoke and vines remain. (Fodeng Xun).
[Added later] To discuss the profound and the subtle is truly worthy of praise; as soon as Śakra heard it, he rained down flowers. When the occasion arises, one must seek three things;
look, look—Śakra Kauśika is brought to despair. Through kalpas, never once has he turned his back; clearly, ask him!

Yet it is all-encompassing. (Daguai Zhi) On the ground where there is neither yin nor yang stands the rootless tree; the valley’s echo need not be met head-on. The seven treasures are arrayed, dense within the great void;
the earth shakes as flowers rain down in immeasurable numbers. Śakra Devendra and the Seven Virtuous Maidens clearly point out the true gold.
The locus: non-arising, the dharma-less, the fundamental suchness. This very moment is beyond words (Yuánwù Qín).
On the ground where neither yin nor yang exist, a cry meets no echo; on the rootless tree, everyone grasps.
The Seven Sage Maidens were too coy and foolish, painting their brows with red powder. Kauśika has not these three things; how could he be stirred by celestial flowers?
Flying wildly. (Fujian Qín). Branches and twigs accumulate upon the rootless tree;
in the mountains and valleys, silence is the closest phrase. A vacant field where yin and yang do not reach;
fruits form and flowers bloom, each blossom fresh. (Zhengtang Biàn).
Looking at it, it cannot be seen; listening for it, it cannot be heard. Within the home are three kinds of treasures, whose wealth and honor surpass heaven and earth. (Yue’an Guo)
A single tree of rootless seeds; the mountain elder does not trouble himself with weeding or hoeing.
Having smashed a peach pit from a thousand years ago, there is no need to seek fish by climbing a tree. (Mongan Yue). (3)
A single expanse where neither yin nor yang exists; clearly and brightly, it sells the expensive and buys the cheap. There is no place for a corpse to be buried alive;
three heads and two faces are laid bare.
It does not belong to a single mountain valley, yet it penetrates a thousand gates and ten thousand doors. At the clear dawn, a single cry of the cuckoo exhorts people.
Better not to go back.
What basis is there in a realm where neither yin nor yang exists? The rootless tree withers people to death; though one calls out, the mountains and valleys do not echo.
Maheśvara has three eyes—what is to be done, what is to be done? By turning misfortune into fortune, he vexes Kauśika. Great!
Laughter turns into weeping. (Tu’an Qi) The seven treasures and eight jewels are at your disposal as you require; yet the three things have never existed from the start.
If you can extract them from within this non-existence, there is no need to see a Buddha to ask what it is like. (Tianmu Li)
[Added from another source: Formerly, there was an old woman to the east of the city who had been born at the same time as the Buddha, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him; nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, she saw nothing but the Buddha.
He then covered his face with his hands; within the palms of his ten fingers, they were all entirely Buddhas. The verse says:
At the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment, an old woman with hair as white as fluff possessed great spirit. Born at the same time as the Buddha, she loathed seeing him;
what can be done about a hateful person? What can a hateful person do? (Xiaoweng kan).
With eyes open, it is there; with eyes closed, it is there. There is no way to avoid it; take the wrong for the right.
A majestic qilin has but a single horn. (Closing the room, opening the gate.)
To the east of the city, the Holy Mother sits upon a lotus pedestal; the true eye of all sentient beings in the great earth is opened.
Born together with the Buddha, yet she detests seeing him; one body cannot become two Tathāgatas. (Xutang Yu)
In my whole life I never wished to meet the Buddha; yet at the tips of my ten fingers, his azure countenance appears.
Along the roadside, after the wind and rain have passed through the peach blossoms, there is nowhere for the horse’s hooves to avoid the lingering red petals. (Shishihui)

The Great Being Shanhui of the Twin Trees was invited by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty to lecture on the sutras. As the Master ascended the seat, he struck the lectern once with a ruler and then descended.
Emperor Wu was astonished. Master Zhigong then asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not. Zhigong said, "The Great Being has finished his lecture on the sutras.

The verse says: The Great Being ascends the seat; A single strike upon the table. The Emperor is left staring in wonder; Zhigong asks, "Do you understand? "I do not," the Emperor replies. "The lecture is now complete," Zhigong says.
He did not entrust this body to the Twin Sala Trees, but instead stirred up dust and ashes in the land of Liang.
Had he not encountered the Elder Zhizong at that time, he too would have been a sorrowful exile from his native land. (Xuedou Xian)
The long parting from the Twin Śāla Trees had its cause; the enlightened sovereign of Jinling yearned for the Benevolent Man. How excellent was the ascent to the High Seat!
With a single strike, the Great Trichiliocosm transcended the dust of the mundane world. (By Zhengjue Yi)
When has this Great Being ever lectured on the sutras? Master Zhigong used skillful means to assist him. With a single stroke, everything on the desk was rendered useless;
it left the King of Liang with eyes bulging in rage. (Baizhang Yuan).
When the Great Being preached the sutra, he struck the desk to form annotations; a single pill dispels myriad ailments, requiring no donkey-load of medicine. (Cishou Shen)
A single sound from the desk, *míng-míng*. Already, layer upon layer of footnotes have been added. Why does King Liang not turn his head?
Master Zhigong takes what is wrong and makes it even more wrong. (Fujian Qín).
[Continued Collection] He personally receives the title of Lord of the Three Assemblies under the Dragon Flower Tree; he hammers open the nine-layered city of the Phoenix Hall.
King Liang has toppled the Diamond Buddha—furthermore, how can one ask him not to preach the sutras? (The Daoist who bears the tally).
Two mouths, clearly, yet neither has a tongue; born together and dying together, I resolve this for you. Nalaka eats thorns upon his crown;
blood flows from beneath Vajra’s feet. (Dongshan Kong)
The Great Being misinterprets the commentary; Master Zhigong misinterprets the commentary. Stinking meat accumulates at the butcher’s gate;
it is laughable that no one buys it. (Fan Wuzhun)
The Great Being of the Twin Trees was truly without precedent; he again revealed a model to the Liang dynasty. Before the meaning of the scriptures was discerned, the profound path was cut off;
with a single stroke upon his desk, he moved the Emperor’s countenance. (Ge Lu Tan)
When Master Fu saw Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and did not rise, the ministers asked, "The Master sees the King;
why does he not rise? The Master replied, "If the ground of Dharma moves even once, all things will be unsettled. A verse says:
The state of Liang causes distress to the Wei; crossing the river or plunging into the water, one follows the current in darkness.
Although not an inch of land remains where one dwells, how can one resist the autumn wind blowing through half a tree at the Twin Groves? (Touzi Qing)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] One day, Master Fu Da-shi, wearing his patched robe, cap, and sandals, went to have an audience with Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. The Emperor asked, "Are you a monk? Fu pointed to his cap. The Emperor said, "Are you a Daoist? Fu pointed to his sandals. The Emperor said, "Are you a layman? Fu pointed to his patched robe. Fenyang Shanzhao provided this verse in his place: A monk, a Daoist, a layman— Three paths, one road. The Great Master’s three fingers Point directly to the source. If you wish to see the Buddha, Look at the tip of his nose. If you wish to see the Patriarch, Look at the back of his head. If you wish to see the Layman, Look at his feet. If you wish to see the Three Jewels, Look at his whole body. If you wish to see the Three Realms, Look at his face. If you wish to see the Three Vehicles, Look at his eyes. If you wish to see the Three Bodies, Look at his heart. If you wish to see the Three Worlds, Look at his mind. If you wish to see the Three Karmas, Look at his actions. If you wish to see the Three Times, Look at his past, present, and future. If you wish to see the Three Truths, Look at his emptiness, conventionality, and middle way. If you wish to see the Three Mysteries, Look at his silence. If you wish to see the Three Insights, Look at his clarity. If you wish to see the Three Liberations, Look at his non-attachment. If you wish to see the Three Vows, Look at his commitment. If you wish to see the Three Roots of Goodness, Look at his compassion. If you wish to see the Three Jewels, Look at his faith. If you wish to see the Three Refuges, Look at his reliance. If you wish to see the Three Gates of Liberation, Look at his non-conceptualization. If you wish to see the Three Bodies of the Buddha, Look at his manifestation, enjoyment, and reality. If you wish to see the Three Treasures, Look at their inexhaustibility. If you wish to see the Three Virtues, Look at their perfection. If you wish to see the Threefold World, Look at its emptiness. If you wish to see the Threefold Nature, Look at its suchness. If you wish to see the Threefold Reality, Look at its ultimate truth. If you wish to see the Threefold Dharma, Look at its teaching. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-going, Look at its lack of destination. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-abiding, Look at its lack of location. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-resting, Look at its lack of support. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-grasping, Look at its lack of attachment. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-releasing, Look at its lack of letting go. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-binding, Look at its lack of fetters. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-liberating, Look at its lack of release. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-obstruction, Look at its lack of hindrance. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-penetration, Look at its lack of piercing. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-perception, Look at its lack of cognition. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-conception, Look at its lack of thought. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-mind, Look at its lack of consciousness. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-self, Look at its lack of ego. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-person, Look at its lack of individuality. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-being, Look at its lack of existence. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-non-being, Look at its lack of non-existence. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-birth, Look at its lack of arising. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-death, Look at its lack of perishing. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-life, Look at its lack of vitality. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-decay, Look at its lack of aging. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-sickness, Look at its lack of affliction. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-suffering, Look at its lack of pain. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-happiness, Look at its lack of pleasure. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-empty, Look at its lack of voidness. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-form, Look at its lack of shape. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-sound, Look at its lack of noise. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-smell, Look at its lack of fragrance. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-taste, Look at its lack of flavor. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-touch, Look at its lack of sensation. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-object, Look at its lack of phenomena. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-subject, Look at its lack of self. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-knower, Look at its lack of subjectivity. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-known, Look at its lack of objectivity. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-seer, Look at its lack of vision. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-seen, Look at its lack of sight. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-hearer, Look at its lack of hearing. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-leaving, Look at its lack of exit. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-entering, Look at its lack of entry. If you wish to see the Threefold Non-opening, Look at its lack of expansion.

The Great Being possessed many abilities. The Fifth Patriarch Ji said, "It makes all bystanders laugh to death. Fuxincai said, "Do you wish to recognize the embodiment of the sages of the Three Teachings?
Realize it at the point where [the Emperor] questioned Emperor Wu. Do you wish to recognize the function of the sages of the Three Teachings?
Take it up at the point where the Great Being pointed. Even if one clearly distinguishes between essence and function, [one must still go further].
"In the school of the patch-robed monks, it is a great distance away. The verse says:
"The Daoist caps, the Confucian shoes, and the Buddhist *kāṣāya*— The three traditions are harmonized into one family.
Forgetting the path to the Tuṣita Heaven, He sits upright at the Twin Trees awaiting the Nāgapuṣpa. (Hu Yinzhi)
Clad in tattered rags, as cold as a fragment of drifting cloud; feet in morning boots, head crowned with a hat.
To make the three schools follow the same track—though one may knead sand, it will never form a ball. (Xiaowenkān).
Sealed with clay, the three imperial edicts emerged from the mists and clouds; they reached the palace of the sovereign in Jinling. Since antiquity, who has been able to equal such versatility?
The Way crowns the head, Confucianism adorns the feet, and the Śākya robe is worn. (Bao Ye Yuan)
Neither Confucian, nor Daoist, nor yet Chan; his fabricated practice is truly pitiable.
He has wasted a lifetime with three matters unresolved, even now more than eight hundred years have passed. (One Robe Precept)
[Added for inclusion] Master Fu’s verse says: "Night after night one embraces the Buddha in sleep; Day after day one rises together with him.
Whether rising or sitting, he is always in attendance, Like a form and its shadow, they are inseparable. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, It is simply this very sound of speech."
The verse says:

Who has a single ruler to discipline them? Exchanging it for a city of illusory silver. (After a long while: Having once suffered the bitterness of snow and frost, they are startled even by the falling of willow blossoms. (Tianyi Huai).
When it is time to sleep, one sleeps; when it is time to rise, one rises immediately. Washing the face, the skin glows; sipping tea, the beak is moistened.
The great ocean gives birth to red dust; level ground rises in waves and billows. He-he, a-ha-a; ra-li-li, ra-li.
(Baoning Yong). [Added by Zeng] Master Fuda’s verse says: "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe; walking, I ride a water buffalo.
A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not. The verse says:
On the sixth month, the upper day of fu; on the eighth month, the mid-autumn day: when people are at peace they do not speak; when water is level it does not flow. (Xinwen Ben).
When fish swim, the water becomes turbid; when birds fly, feathers fall. The Great Being lays his body across [the path], yet he does not suffer the blows of the axe or chisel. (Muan Yong).
The dog runs, shaking its muzzle; the monkey worries, scratching its head. Outside the gate of Ruiyan, the water has flowed westward since ancient times. (Duanqiao Lun)
[Added from the Supplement] Master Fu’s Verse says: “Mount Sumeru is the father of the mustard seed; The mustard seed is the grandfather of Mount Sumeru.
The mountains and waters are level and plain; I strike the ice to come and brew tea. The Verse says:
It is no easy matter for Mount Sumeru to contain a mustard seed; yet it is as simple as a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru. When the great river is churned, it becomes ghee and curd;
with a light blow, one penetrates the barrier of the Patriarchs. (Yuánwù Qín)
[Added for inclusion] Master Fu’s Verse says: “There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; Formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast.
It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, Yet does not wither along with the four seasons. Wuzu Yan said: “The ancients spoke thus;
it may be called ‘adding flowers upon brocade. It is indeed extraordinary. But how do you all understand this? Bailian [responded].
Today, in accordance with the capacities of those who follow after, I have not spared my eyebrows. I shall also express this in verse:
Existence within existence; non-existence within non-existence; The subtle within the subtle; the coarse within the coarse.
With earth on his face and ash on his head, he is unstained by dust; in the flower-lined streets and willow alleys, he delights in the true nature of heaven.
As the golden cock crows at dawn, the dream of the jade tower ends; beneath a single tree, flowers bloom for the spring of vast eons. (Zu’an Jian)
The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Verses on the Ancient Cases of the Chan School, Volume Three.
The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Verses on the Ancient Cases of the Chan School, Volume Four.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Temple in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty.
The śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery during the Yuan Shaoxing era compiled this continuation of the Bodhisattva’s机缘 (jiyuan/encounters).
The Baguāng (Buddhabhadra) Upāsaka frequently stayed at major thoroughfares. Someone asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am waiting for someone."
A man came. [The Master] said, "Come! The man replied, "I am coming. The Master said, "You are not this person.
Alternatively, he untied a cloth bag containing all manner of objects and scattered them down, saying, "Look! Look! Then, picking each one up one by one, he asked the man, "What is this called?
Alternatively, he reached into the bag and offered a fruit to a monk. As the monk was about to take it, the Master withdrew his hand.
Handan said, "You are not this kind of person. When he saw a monk passing by, he struck him on the back once.
The monk turned his head; the Master said, "Bring me a coin. At other times, he would lean against his bag and sleep soundly all day long.
Sometimes he would go out into the marketplace, where children would clamor and chase after him. Sometimes he would play with the children, holding a staff or a rosary.
Once, a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Thereupon, the Master set down his cloth bag and stood with palms joined.
The monk said, "Is there anything else besides this? The Master picked up the cloth bag and placed it on his shoulder.
He took it and departed. The verse says: Maitreya is not he;
the hemp sack is not it. When both right and wrong are forgotten, gold is born from the Li River. The supreme treasure fills the sack.

Buying high and selling low—if you understand this through deliberation, there is no need for three prostrations. Chuan’s commentary on the *Mahāyāna-arthaviniścaya-sūtra* is like the glow of a firefly in the moonlight or a lamp beneath the sun.
With a cloth bag as a pillow, one sleeps a single sleep; leaning against the mountain, the mountain colors are layer upon layer of azure.
(Ya Xuan Zun): Pick it up and you walk; let it go and you rest. That drowsy master—his cleverness turns into clumsiness. How could he know the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
His skirt and tunic are patched a hundred times over. Sometimes standing alone, who is there to understand him? Return! Go back!
Ah! A single sky of bright moonlight (Fohuiquan). Tired, he comes with his bag and remains silent;
those watching by his side are all filled with doubt and suspicion. Unable to avoid opening it up for everyone to see, what a set of worn-out household utensils!
Do not be surprised that his clothes are tattered; entering the marketplace, he has no sense of inhibition. He stands across the path, blocking the way.
Such people as these know how to circle and draw the patterns (Yunfeng Yue).
Of the thousand ways and myriad forms, who can truly comprehend them? This old monk, though prone to dozing, has packed his bags full; his mind is free from all sensations.
The Samādhi of the Place of Touch. At the ends of alleys and the corners of streets, buying high and selling low (Yuantong Xiu).
It is all just a single cloth bag; what marvel can be found within? When weary, it serves as a pillow;
carrying it along causes no hindrance. Sometimes opened in the bustling marketplace, it is mostly one’s own goods for sale (Baiyun Yuan).
"Ha! This foolish skin-bag. With coarse brows and large eyes, he spends all day on the street, yet there is no buying or selling in the marketplace.
Aha-ha! Go back! Return! Pay back the money you borrowed! (Baoning Yong)
Dividing his body into ten billion forms, he mingles with the dust; his appearance is simple and guileless, beyond all conjecture.
Carrying a single bag, he goes wherever he pleases; scattering a thousand things, he gathers them back again. He displays himself among humans and in the heavens;
at market ends and street corners, he sleeps and then returns. Though one waits for such a time, it is not yet found; even now, he remains the Old Huangmei. (Foguo Bai).
Heaven cannot cover it; earth cannot support it. It encompasses both heaven and earth, all returning to the cloth bag.
At the crossroads of the street, he opens it wide; lifting up everything, he lets people take what they like. (Lingyuan Qing)
He does not cultivate the three thousand codes of dignified conduct at all; he pays no heed whatsoever to the eighty thousand subtle practices.

It is only because he waits for someone in the bustling marketplace that people call him a "down-and-out. Having long abandoned the inner court of Tuṣita Heaven, even if he were to return, he would forget the path by which he came.
I bow my head to the World-Honored One Maitreya, who possesses such a broad heart and great capacity. (Jingshan Gao).
[Continued Collection] Next, one and a half more. Having sought out three or two coins, who would have known that within this tattered cloth bag there are so many Maitreya Buddhas? (Xiatang Yuan).

Patting backs to seek money is a mere farce; turning one’s head and shifting one’s brain, one remains oblivious to the true mechanism. How pitiful that no one in the bustling marketplace recognizes it;
empty-handed, one returns home with a cloth bag slung over the shoulder. (Fozhao Guang)
A wind-crazed fellow on the banks of Changting; dragging his staff, he turns his head—waiting for whom? He says:
"That person has never been there from the start; you must know there is a time to turn back. (Tianmu Li)
To turn one's head is already late; it is just as it was before one had turned their head. Having failed to find even a single coin, there is no place to reach;
yet you still labor in vain—deceiving whom? (Beijian Jian)
When meeting people, he begs for a single coin; yet the bag within him is richer than a rival state. It is not that his descent into this world was late;
it is that he detested the Buddha and refused to become one. (Huanxi 1)

[Supplement] Venerable Baṭa, while discussing the collection of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) with Master Sheng, said: "The lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the subtle particles of form is called emptiness.
Master Sheng replied: "You have only clarified that form is empty within the cause; you have not yet clarified that form is empty within the fruit.
The Master asked: "What is the emptiness of form within the fruit? He replied: "Because a single particle is empty, the multitude [of particles] is empty."
The emptiness of atoms. Because the collection of atoms is empty, a single atom is empty. Within the emptiness of a single atom there is no collection of atoms;

within the emptiness of a collection of atoms there is no single atom. Master Yanguan said: "The emptiness of form in the cause and the emptiness of form in the fruit—this is all dreaming within a dream. The verse says:
Numinous light fills the eyes, clustering mountains and rivers; within this illusory realm, phenomena abound. Having realized the wondrous essence, one knows that conditions do not obstruct;
yet clinging emotions are worn away by the objects themselves. (By Shuangquan Qiong)
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form. The pass of Tongguan is blocked and the road is impassable.
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, even the finest hair is consumed; yet the green mountains remain as before amidst the white clouds. (Tianyi Huai). (2)
East, west, south, and north—throughout the hundred thousand and eight thousand [miles]—emptiness arises where there is nothing to grasp. A lotus grows within the fire;
majestically, within form there is no mark of emptiness. Radiant, within space there is utterly no form or shape.
Directly beneath, form and emptiness are not two distinct things; the name "form" originally does not belong to me. (Lingyin Edition)
[Added for collection: The Layman Vimalakīrti manifested illness in the city of Vaiśālī. Thinking to himself as he lay upon his bed, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate;
will He not deign to show His pity? The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, that superior man is difficult to approach..."

He was eloquent in response, profoundly penetrating the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma. His eloquence was unimpeded and his wisdom unhindered.
He fully understood all the methods and regulations of the Bodhisattvas and entered every secret treasury of the Buddhas.

He subdued all Māras and sported with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*). Having already attained mastery in both wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he nevertheless remained [in this world] to receive [the teachings].
The Buddha’s holy intent was to go there to inquire after his illness. A verse says:
"Alas, this old Vimalakīrti! Born of compassion, he suffers in empty vexation. Lying ill in the city of Vaiśālī, his entire body is utterly withered."
The Seven Buddhas and the Patriarchs arrive; with a single stroke, all are swept away. He asks about the Gate of Non-duality, and at that moment, he collapses.
Not collapsing? A golden-maned lion has nowhere to be found. (Xuedou Xian)
The Buddha’s illness and the Dharma’s illness are the most difficult to cure; only the *Zazamo* (Miscellaneous Mo) is truly marvelous.
Mañjuśrī bows his head and praises the layman: "He has lost the golden-haired lion cub. (Tianyi Huai)
In the city of Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti knew whether [Mañjuśrī] had ultimately penetrated through or not.

Before the golden-maned lion had even arrived, the single room was cleared out and the secret was already leaked. When it came to the inquiry regarding the Gate of Non-duality, he pushed forward a lump of solid, hole-less iron.
He was only just barely struck by Mañjuśrī’s single blow; for a thousand years and ten thousand ages, it remains indented. (Dahong Su).
Sitting coldly in the city of Vaiśālī, a hundred ailments broke out all at once; unable to have Mañjuśrī come, he was on the verge of being killed by them. (Jingshan Daokai)
A thousand men and ten thousand people shoot at a single wild goose; each one has a hand skilled in the art and an eye for discernment.
A sweeping west wind makes the goose’s shadow strange; alas, every arrow is released from the bowstring. The general with monkey-like arms looks up;
as the bow opens, the autumn moon’s reflection is perfectly round. A single shooting star flies off toward the heavens, while its scattered feathers fall before his eyes. (Guangjian Ying)
The suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of parting from those one loves. Let us set aside Gautama for a moment—what a chaotic mess! (Zhengtang Bian).
When he manifested illness in the chamber of Vimalakīrti, even Mañjuśrī found it difficult to draw near. Looking at it now, there is no medicine that can cure him;
the best course is simply to avoid food. (Zhe’ung Yan).
Feigning illness has been incurable from the start; Mañjuśrī specifically applied his needle and awl. The matter was stripped away, leaving but a mouth three feet long;
when questioned, it remains as before, like a drumstick. (Wuzhun Fayan).
A single sick Vimalakīrti stirs waves without a breeze; the wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few, while the poor resent having even one body too many. (Hu Yinyi)
[Added for inclusion: Sudhana first went to the Śāla grove to visit Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī directed him to travel south to the kingdom of Suprabha to pay homage to the bhikṣu Meghashvara.
Proceeding in succession, he reached the terrace of Maitreya and returned outside the city of Samantamukha.
There, reflecting and standing still, he desired to have an audience with Mañjuśrī. Then Mañjuśrī extended his hand across...

One hundred and ten *yojanas*. [The Master] rubbed his crown with his hand, whereupon he immediately saw as many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as there are motes of dust, and he immediately received and practiced their teachings.
A monk asked Chao Yin of Shanglan: "After Sudhana saw Mañjuśrī, why did he instead go to the south?
The Master said: "Learning depends on entering the inner chamber; knowledge leads to universal penetration. The monk said: "Upon arriving at Su..."
Macheng asked, "Why did Maitreya instead send him to see Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "The Way is vast and boundless;
it is inexhaustible when encountered in others. Touzishan Qing said, "Indeed, the Way is neither delusion nor enlightenment; its realization arises through the teacher."
Not abiding in the sublime practices that adorn the noble or the mundane, Mañjuśrī sent him away to ascend Mount Sumeru;

on the seashore he encountered his teacher, and in the marketplace he paid homage to his friend. At times he was at the mountain of blades, in brothels, in the fetters of punishment, or within royal palaces;
at other times he was among young girls and boys, or with Gopā, the noble queen. Maitreya snapped his fingers, and Samantabhadra beheld him face-to-face—thus he saw him again.
What further matter is there for Mañjuśrī? One must trustfully know that he understands all directions and knows existence;
the Way is vast and boundless, yet its luminous traces are not obscure. Having exhausted the ultimate and reached the subtle, you worthy ones, do you still know?
Why is it that Sudhana does not visit another person? Tell me, who is this person? (After a long silence, he said: "With a head full of white hair, he departs..."
Through crags and valleys, at midnight he pierced the clouds to pass through the marketplace. He further composed a verse:
"The sun rises into the sky, high and low it employs its light; The source of Kunlun flows into the rivers and streams. Clouds linger on the spring mountains as the wind is inexhaustible;
Geese depart for the south, and heaven and earth turn autumnal."
Fifty-three people point the way; following them, one drifts through over a hundred cities. What is gained by wearing out straw sandals?
How does this compare to returning home and putting an end to asking for directions? (Tieshan Ren)
Vastly wandering through dreams to travel south, fifty-three visits originate from the fingertips. The Great Being’s arms are long while his robe sleeves are short;
Sudhana’s feet are thin while his straw sandals are wide. (Dachuan Ji)

[Added for inclusion: Sudhana went to Mount Supratiṣṭha to visit the bhikṣu Meghashvara. After searching in the four directions for seven days, he finally saw him walking slowly in circumambulation upon a separate peak.

He prostrated, heard the Dharma, and entered the realm of the Buddhas, attaining the "Dharma-door of Recollecting All Buddhas and Universally Perceiving" and realizing the stage of *prathamacittotpāda*. The verse says:
Seeking a spiritual friend atop the peak of Mount Sumeru, one gazes toward the south, north, east, and west—how far does the horizon extend? Deokyun comes from afar across distant mountains;
how precious are his manifestations, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, and ten millions. (Yeon-gyeong Jung)
The lush, verdant grass atop the peak of Sumeru follows step by step, yet no trace is seen.
If you say it is another mountain meeting face-to-face, the single sail has already passed to the east of Haemun Gate. (By Byeosan Ji)
Thin mist shrouds the land where the grass grows lush; for seven days I lingered, yet no news was passed.
A single step on the tip of the staff—a slight misstep—and the sea gates roll up with waves as white as the wind-blown duckweed. (Ji Tianxin)

[Added for inclusion: Sudhana went to the country of Nalasa and visited the seer Vimalacāra. After immeasurable seers had praised him with one voice, he descended from his seat and took [the seer’s] hand.
Buddha-fields appeared before him; he awakened to true, pure wisdom, attaining mastery over its contraction and expansion.
He attained the Dharma-door of the "Incomparable Banner" and realized the stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūmi). The verse says:
The Rishi Vimukta descended from his jeweled couch; he rubbed [the Emperor’s] head, took his hand, and beheld the extraordinary auspicious signs.

The realms of the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared simultaneously; the myriad phenomena of the universe suddenly and fully manifested. The peerless and wondrous couch radiated auspicious colors; the Vairocana-scripture-treasury revealed its numinous light.
He returned to his original seat to seek the ultimate truth, yet he felt that his lifelong understanding had been shallow all along. (From the *Foguo bai*).
Walk straight along the ancient path; do not take detours or be negligent. A clear moon and a cool breeze stir through the ten directions of space.
This was the very business of Vimalakīrti and Sudhana that day—it is as good as Pan Lang riding backward on his donkey. (Huigan)
[Added for inclusion: Sudhana went to the assembly of the Buddha and visited the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. He saw him seated upon a red lotus throne atop a white elephant king;
with single-minded devotion, he drew near to him and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. His wisdom and compassion were perfected, and his practices and vows had reached fulfillment.

One immediately attains the virtues of a Buddha, manifesting as identical to the ocean of fruition, and obtains the dharma-gates of samādhi, numbering as many as the atoms within the fruits of all Buddhas. The verse says:
"One hundred and one *yojanas* away, he returns with his head anointed; With a single thought, he beholds the Master Samantabhadra. Majestic and imposing, he is present now upon the red lotus."

Seated, he stands out with crystalline clarity like a white elephant; when the wisdom and compassion of kalpas are finally fulfilled, and when the vows as numerous as motes of dust are perfectly rounded, the ocean of the Buddha’s merit is proclaimed once more. Alas, to see the waves turning vast and boundless! (Buddha-land White).
Beating the drum and playing the lute, he returns to his own home. The wooden boy can clap his hands; the stone woman knows how to brew tea.
Clouds disperse to reveal the moon at the edge of the sky; spring arrives and flowers bloom upon the trees. When Sudhana has finished his pilgrimage, the black bean has not yet sprouted.

(Yanqing Zhong). [Added by Zengshou] Sudhana traveled through one hundred and ten cities and visited fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Later, arriving before the Vairocana Pavilion, he said:
"This is the dwelling place of those who have realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness" (and so forth). He saw...
The gates of the pavilion were closed. Sudhana briefly concentrated his mind and said, "O Great Compassionate One, I pray that the gates of the pavilion open so that I may enter.
Immediately, Maitreya, leading his retinue, arrived before Sudhana.
With a snap of his fingers, the doors of the pavilions opened. Sudhana entered; once he had entered, they closed again.

He saw hundreds of thousands of millions of pavilions, and in each pavilion was a Maitreya leading his retinue, with a Sudhana standing before him face-to-face. Maitreya snapped his fingers again and said, "Son of good family, arise."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus. The verse says:
"The Youthful Child of Wondrous Intellect gathers all at the end; Sudhana reaches this point and ceases his southern journey.
Suddenly and abruptly he enters the treasury of Vairocana; He regrets having gone to other mountains to see monks. (Zhang Wujin)
On the solitary peak of Wondrous Summit, there is no teacher; wandering through over a hundred cities, Sudhana has lost his way.
If the pavilions appear again at the snap of a finger, though one possesses clear eyes, they have never been opened. (Oran’s Verse)
Fifty-three people strung together by a single thread; though the child is small, his courage is like heaven’s. Vast and boundless mists and waters beyond counting;
he has purchased the splendor of the scenery for no price. (Beijian Jian)
The question is clear and the answer is direct; they are like two swords leaning against the cold sky.
Since the gates of the pavilion were opened, one’s face is filled with shame and there is nowhere to rest. (Zhe-weng Yan)
The wisdom of Master Zeng Shen is fifty-three; pure gold has finished its hundred refinings, free from hammer and tongs. Turning the head, the mist and clouds of ten thousand ravines disperse;
at midnight, the light of the moon drenches the azure pool. (Tandang Yuan)
Having traveled through many clouds and mists in the south, he has gathered rare and precious goods to fill his ship. With a mere snap of the fingers, the wind-driven sails reach the shore;
in an instant, they are all transformed into great coins of light. (Wuzhun Shanfeng)
[Added for inclusion: When the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai was reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* on Mount Nanyue, he reached the "Chapter on the Medicine King Bodhisattva," which states:
"This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. Thereupon, he awakened to the *Lotus Samādhi* and attained the *Pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*.
He beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, solemnly and without dispersal. The verse says:
The World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi; the Master realized the diligence of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
While those on Vulture Peak had not yet dispersed, who would have known it were not for Nan-yueh? (Yang Wuwai)
Where the mountain stream ends, the evening sun slants low; upon the river, the winter wind fills the sands with snow. This is the old road I once traveled in Jiangnan;
through the mist and across the water, I see the plum blossoms. (Luoyue Ying)
He exhausted his family’s wealth and his own possessions, offering only the True Dharma to the Tathāgata. Where is that original path now?
Everywhere one looks, the Spirit Mountain rises in a lush expanse of green. (Tianmu Li)
It is well to offer the True Dharma to the Tathāgata. Flowers bloom in secluded crags and perilous places;
one night a wild wind blows them nearly all away, and countless fallen petals dot the moss and lichen. (Xutang)
When the mind is deluded, every thought revolves around the Lotus Sūtra; when the mind awakens, at every moment one turns the Lotus Sūtra.
Who would know that the guests of the hundred thousand Vulture Peak mountains are all but grains of sand in the eyes of Tiantai? (This mountain should respond).
[Supplement] Master Zhigong of Jinling, also known as Baogong, sent someone to deliver a message to Dashi of Nanyue, saying:
"Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings? Why do you always gaze at the clouds and sky? Dashì replied:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed by me in a single gulp; where else could there be any sentient beings left?"
Dù. The verse says:
In one gulp, he swallows the Buddhas of the three periods; His teeth are like sword-trees, his eyes like bells. To repair a broken string, it need not be with *luánjiāo* glue;
One only requires a true connoisseur to listen with ears pricked. (Xūtáng Yú)
The Buddha and sentient beings are swallowed in a single gulp; not even a hair’s breadth remains, and only then does the Way exist.
When the sun and moon are just lifted upon the tip of the staff, the three thousand worlds and the mountains and seas are stirred into darkness. (By Nianlin Ying)
Gazing at the misty heavens, reclining upon white clouds; unaware that beneath the mountains lies the world of heaven and earth. From where could there be further sentient beings to deliver?
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time swallow them all in a single mouth. (Original Awakening, One)
At this time, Qingxiu sings a song of Great Peace: "A single hair enters the great forge's red furnace.
If one tries to pick out the ashes from within, the crimson flames already surround the heavens. (Mongan Yue)
Master Zhigong said: "All day long they pick up incense and choose firewood, yet they do not know that their own bodies are the site of enlightenment. Xuansha said:
"All day long they pick up incense and choose firewood, yet they do not know that this is truly the site of enlightenment. Xuange questioned them, saying:
Regarding these words of the two Venerable Ones, is there any distinction between intimacy and distance? Xuedou Xian said: "A pair of unperforated iron hammers.
Wenyuan Qinq said: "All day long he picks up incense and chooses firewood, yet he does not know how to pick up incense or choose firewood.
Tiantong Jue said: "How extraordinary! An eighty-year-old patriarch taking the stage."
This is no child’s play. Tell me, where does the point of benefit and harm lie?
Whether one has wisdom or lacks it makes a difference of thirty li. The verse says:
Within the ancient Buddha-hall atop the mountain of the five aggregates, lift the incense and choose the fire to receive it properly.
Why need one seek sages and saints outside? From morning till night, everything is the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*). (Benjue I)
The Title of a Mahāyāna Sūtra Verse:
The Character [米-木+八] (Mi-ba). Formerly, there was a monk who asked Master Dizang Chen:
"The character is not formed; it is not the character 'eight' (八). I wonder what kind of character it is? Dizang said: "Look at the commentary below."
Regarding "Jiao," there was another who asked Biyun Ji. The Master answered with a verse:
"The character 'yi' (以) is not it; it is not formed of eight strokes. The myriad phenomena of the universe are clarified herein.
Even if one were to skillfully explain a thousand kinds of wonders, it is neither the *upāya* nor the sūtra."
The eight non-attainments are right before one's eyes; they are not recognized in the sutras, so look in the commentaries. Out of compassion, do not seek extensive knowledge and understanding;
what is essential is to investigate the profound mystery and reach the original source. (Fenyang Shanzhao)
The characters do not form "Eight," for it is not so. When the title of the scripture is lifted up, everyone hesitates. Let the annotations at the bottom be as you will;
yet, upon entering the gate, one first asks for the name. (Foyin Yuan).
The characters are not formed without the eight strokes; the wind and waves at the Dragon Gate are as bitter as thunder.
How many swimming fish lose their way? As before, they fall with the rain into the vast ocean. (Fohuiquan)
The ocean of meaning in our Buddha’s golden words is deep; opening and forbidding depend solely on awakening to the true mind.
The primary aim is to strike at the head with precision, secretly causing the clay ox to low through day and night. (Yunju You)

Picking up the title, one cannot grasp its essence; yet, look at the annotations below. Once the meaning of the characters is clearly understood, the Great Canon flows through both the extensive and the concise (the grace of Kṣitigarbha).
Because characters do not form it, the eight strokes are not it. The Dharma-body sleeps soundly, with nothing to obstruct or close off.
When a patch-robed monk faces it, he does not know its name; before a hundred thousand people, it cannot be called forth. (Juefan Hong)
It cannot be formed by characters; it is not eight characters. The Buddhas of the ten directions study it together; the Tathāgatas of the three periods follow its path together.
Even Ānanda, with his vast learning, could find no way to grasp it; Śāriputra, with his supernatural powers, could not emulate it.
Were it not for the golden-colored Dhūta, how could this intent have been secretly transmitted? (Min Gufo)
The characters are not eight; the non-eight is not [a character]. Filling the entire collection of scriptures, there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference.
Reaching this point in reading the sutras, you must open your eyes: the jade rollers clearly bear inscriptions on both sides. (Lohan Nan)
The titles of the sutras fill the eyes—who knows their origin? Every stroke and dot is distinct; the meaning of every phrase is complete.
If you wish to know the greatness of the power that assists the state, Xiao He was originally a sage of the Han dynasty. (Shushan Chang)
Because the characters do not constitute "eight," they are not formed; the Silent Boy laughs with joyful delight. The udumbara flower appears in the world of men;
his nostrils pierce through to heaven, yet he does not smell. (Kaifu Ning)
Not formed by characters, it is not the eightfold path; the Śakrāloka eye cannot peer into it.
From atop a single hair-tip, it is brought forth once more; the wrathful Nanda loses his majesty. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
The Dragon Palace and the Ocean Treasury have never contained it; even seeking it through Sanskrit and Chinese translations is in vain.
It was needlessly leaked by the Patriarch, and the reason for his missing front teeth is precisely this. (Lingyan Yin)
[Continued Collection]: Bird tracks are half-revealed amidst the gray moss; tadpoles swim together in the spring waters.
If you do not believe, accept, and practice this, you will inevitably rise from your seat [to leave]. (Shiming)
Do not seek the original truth in the title of a sutra; what is the use of searching for the body of the Dharma King amidst a pile of paper?
If you can take responsibility before the palm-leaf volumes are even opened, you will avoid becoming one who merely traces the lines and counts the characters. (Jue'an Xiang)
I ask you, Kṣitigarbha, do you know or not? There are ten thousand myriad footnotes beneath. Counting grains of sand and pouring them into the sea is but weary toil;
it is better to let him understand what is right before his eyes. (Hengchuan Hong)
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The Buddha told Ānanda: "When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?
If you see that which does not see, it would naturally not be the characteristic of that non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it would naturally not be a material thing; how then could it not be you? The Verse says:
The whole elephant and the whole ox—their meaning is no different. From of old, all masters have shared this as their model.
If you now wish to see the old Gautama, he is already halfway there in every land and every speck of dust. (Xuedou Xian)
The majestic pillar has long been pregnant; at last it gives birth to a child, truly remarkable. Before he can even speak, he composes a rhapsody;
with a single stroke, he wins the honor of top scholar. (Baizhang Yuanwen).
The Old Barbarian’s thorough, grandmotherly heart / Was for Ānanda’s increasingly deep intent. / Han Gan’s horse neighs across the fragrant grasses;
/ Dai Song’s ox lies down in the green willow shade. (Zantang Zhun)
The clouds have gathered up and the vast sky is like water; the moon carries Chang’e as it flows across the four seas.
How shameful, the old man of the Cowherd Star, still clinging to his foolish love at the head of the Magpie Bridge. (By Fuxincai)
It is said that by departing from the hundred negations, one preserves the rules of conduct; yet it is stated that not even a single dharma remains, for it is like casting away the fishing trap.
Vimalakīrti remained silent, long keeping his mouth sealed; in Magadha all was still and quiet, the gates forever closed. (Fujian Qín)
[Continued Collection] When first learning to sell flowers, one covers the teeth with a bashful smile. By the time the countenance grows old, it is stripped bare with nothing left to hide.
Yet one laughs at the white clouds as they disperse of their own accord; who knows whose house the bright moon has fallen upon? (Chongjue Kong)
Through the forest, one faintly hears the sound of looms; one knows there must be people living in the misty heights.
Yet when one enters the gate and sees for oneself, it turns out to be nothing more than children at play. (Jiandang Ji)
When seeing, one does not see; non-seeing does not see. Neither seeing nor non-seeing is altogether neither. The Weaver Girl’s loom and shuttle are tossed in disarray;
the cowherd boy’s whip and rope are brandished at will. A single cry from a hidden bird startles the universe;
by the emerald bend of the stream, green willows hang down. (Ding of Daitang).
Smooth stones are not jade; clear waters are not gold. Great Yu channeled them westward, while Bian He wept as they sank into the earth.
How beautiful and how vast! They were mistaken for antiquity and ground down by the present age. (Xutang Yu)
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "If you can transform objects, you are identical to the Tathāgata.
The verse says: "If one can transform objects, one is the Tathāgata; When spring comes warm, mountain flowers bloom everywhere.
I have a pair of hands for the ultimate poverty; They have never easily performed the 'Three Platforms' dance. (Baiyun Shan)
If one can transform objects, one is immediately the Tathāgata; at every gate, Sudhana is revealed. Amidst the flowered willows and the alleys, he performs his dance and play;
upon the nine thoroughfares, he lies drunk upon the towers and terraces. (Zhenru Zhe)
A single hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. Heaven and earth, the great world—all return directly to the same source.
The One Breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms; where do the myriad spirits go to thank its impartiality? (Fuxincai)
"If one can master things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. "Alas, Gautama! You deceive and delude the ignorant!
(Jingshan Gao) [Continued Collection] Rainy colors mingle with mist, pervading the four quarters; With eyelids yet unopened, how could one peer?
In a casual glance, one pierces through the adamantine limit; Vast and open, there is no cause for laboring on the path. (Huan'an Ti)
Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others walk, I do not walk. It is not that I find it difficult to dwell with others;
rather, it is simply that the monastic and the lay must remain distinct. (This mountain should [be so]).
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "When the seeing sees, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
Seeing is already apart from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. The verse says:
Where the vision does not reach, mountains and rivers fill the eyes; there, not even a speck of red flowers or green willows is seen. Where white clouds arise, they are originally without mind;
the surging tides of the oceans—how could they ever swell or ebb? (Haiyin Xin)
At the tip of the staff there is no hole; even the great chiliocosm is still considered too small.
Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon it long ago, yet until this very day he has not attained the wondrous. (Gushan Gui)
When spring arrives, flowers bloom of themselves; when autumn comes, leaves fall again. Old Gautama with his yellow face—cease wagging that three-inch tongue! (Jingshan Gaofeng)

[Continued Collection] Form and emptiness, light and darkness—originally they have no cause. The "seeing of seeing" has from the beginning misled people. If one does not perceive it when the time is right, one has not yet glimpsed it;
how could one know that the calamitous specter is one's own kin? (Yuan of Dun’an).
On the zither without strings, there is no private melody. One tune played, the wheel turns. On the broken cliff where the water flows, few are those who understand.
Six times six does not equal thirty-six. (Miaofengshan)
Leaning on a slender cane, he ascends into the wind and mist; He begs the traveling folk for a broadened field of vision.
One does not know by how much that field of vision has been broadened— The white birds have flown away, and the azure sky remains. (Pak Ong-hyeon)
Rain-washed, the tender peach blossoms are pale red; wind-swayed, the slender willow filaments are light green. Within the shadows of white clouds, strange rocks are revealed;
amidst the luster of green waters, ancient trees are serene. (Qian’an Guang)
Seeing the horn over the wall, he mounts the ox; mounted, he rides into the bustling marketplace. Having roamed everywhere, he returns to lie down in the pen.
At the third watch of the night, his traces are lost. (Xue’an Jin)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: Investigating the Mind in Seven Locations. The Verse says:
Investigating the mind in seven locations, the mind was not found; Poor Ānanda, he did not yet perceive the ground.
Even if one were to investigate until seeing that there is no mind, It would still be like washing clods of earth in the mud. (Xi Yu-duan)

The interrogation of the mind at the seven locations is thus completed; through exhaustive investigation and pursuit, the truth is clearly established. It is all because the "house-thief" is difficult to guard against;
once the chaos is dispelled, heaven and earth witness the arrival of Great Peace. (Wan’an Yan)
Winnowing the chaff only to find it clinging to the grain; it turns out to be a case of acting in vain. Without encountering a single matter, one does not grow a single bit of wisdom (Beijian Jian).
He interrogated him at seven locations, from the heavens above to the heavens beyond; a beam of light shot directly onto Ānanda’s shoulder.
Gautama was far too overprotective of his son, pressing him until the eel climbed up the bamboo pole (Jue'an Xiang).
[Added for Collection] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: Distinguishing Vision through the Eight Returns. (Verse says:
The teaching of the eight returns has been handed down for a long time; since antiquity, the patriarchal masters have each analyzed it.
Even if you could achieve the state where there is nothing left to return from, you would still be like a shrimp unable to leap out of its basket. (Xi Yu-duan)
Brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness cannot be returned; that which cannot be returned is beyond all climbing and grasping.
It carves out the void of space to form its boundaries, with one layer of water separating one layer of mountain. (Wan’an Yan)
Form is empty; brightness and darkness do not know one another. When walking, you reach the end of the water; when sitting, you watch the clouds arise. (Beijian Jian).
Returning, returning, after returning there is nothing more to return to. A single idle man between heaven and earth. Last night, a tiger was caught by a leopard.
Bite. The fur and skin fall away, revealing the original speckled body.
(Jue'an Xiang). [Added from the collection] *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Ānanda and the great assembly attain their fundamental, wondrous mind. The verse says:
Searching east, west, south, and north through empty space, news cannot be conveyed from the ends of the earth to the furthest horizons. Strength is exhausted and spirit is weary;
there is nowhere to find it. Yet the ten-thousand-year-old pine remains upon Mount Zhurong. (Wan’an Yan)
"It accords with what I formerly wished for; now it is already fulfilled. This jade is truly marvelous;
I only fear it may not be true jade. (Beijian Jian)
[Added for inclusion] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva accomplishes the thirty-two manifestations and attains the fourteen fearlessnesses. The verse says:

How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Turning back the hearing, one is liberated from sound. The barking of dogs and the braying of donkeys—whether they cease or do not cease—the mundane and supramundane worlds are as lively and agile as ever. (Xiatang Yuan)
The thirty-two manifestations are inconceivable; the fourteen fearlessnesses are like flowing water.
When entering meditative absorption within a male body, one emerges from absorption within a female body. (Wan’an Yan)
Joining the ranks to choose the Perfect Penetration, you needlessly took your stand downwind. At that time, you gave a confession of death, mistakenly claiming it was within hearing. (Beijian Jian)
[Added for inclusion] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names and forms.
The verse says: "One coin as capital, ten thousand coins in profit; The wealthy are not enough, while the poor have a surplus.
A small dose of medicine that transforms the bones and seizes the womb— I must concede to him, Pān Láng, riding his donkey backward. (Wàn'ān Yán)
The golden platter cannot be moved; it rolls and turns, difficult to still. After waiting for a long while, it is perfectly bright and as clear as dew. (Beijian Jian)
[Added for inclusion] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "All things that can be returned naturally do not belong to you. That which cannot be returned—if it is not you, then who is it? The verse says:
The sun is warm and the breeze gentle; the scenery is even more extraordinary. Flower upon flower, grass upon grass, the entire mechanism is revealed.
A gust of fragrant wind rises from the wisteria, drawing the wandering bees to fly everywhere. (Xinwen Ben)

The birds have vanished from the thousand peaks; human tracks are cut off across the ten-thousand-li expanse. An old man in a small boat, clad in raincoat and straw hat, fishes alone amidst the snow on the cold river. (Kentang Chong)
Who is it that does not return? A lingering trace of red petals flows upon the fishing rocks. The sun slants and the wind has stilled, yet no one sweeps them up;
swallows carry them away as they fly toward the water’s edge. (Tianmu Li)
[Added for collection] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "When the six are liberated, the one perishes. The verse says:
Roots and objects, bondage and liberation, originally share the same source; In one place they cease, and the six functions are abandoned.
Holding a single strand of red thread, The nostrils of one's mother-born self are pierced all at once. (Wan’an Yan)
The six senses are of no use and faith does not penetrate; all at once, it is entrusted to the spring breeze. A single curl of incense smoke lingers idly through the clear day;
though the hundred birds do not come, the flowers are naturally red. (Beijian Jian)
Bondage and liberation are not distinct; existence and non-existence have no basis. Let us inquire into the fundamental source:
who bound you in the first place? [Added from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If this wondrously bright, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally all-pervading and perfect, then even down to the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and sentient beings..."
The primordial *tathatā* (suchness) is precisely the true body of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood.
Since the Buddha-body is truly real, how can there further exist the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals? The verse says:
Before the ancient temple ruins at the Double Sword Peak, the Celestial Honored One was originally a single Muni. In times of difficulty, one can only share the incense and lamps;
do not listen to idle people speaking of right and wrong. (Wan’an Yan)
Three snakes and nine rats; on a plot of land the size of one *mǔ*. Carrying a bamboo pole wherever you go, perform the play upon meeting the stage.

(Beijian Jian). [Added by Zengshou] *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Buddha said to Ānanda, "These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity.
This is entirely due to following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. On the contrary...

These three types further give rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. That which is termed "existence" is the realm of ghosts; that which is termed "non-existence" is the celestial realm.
Through the mutual inclination between existence and non-existence, the nature of saṃsāra arises. The verse says:
One deluded mind is scrutinized across seven points; furthermore, it follows the three karmas of killing, stealing, and lust. Body and mind are no longer idle furnishings.
The first arrow was still light, but the subsequent arrows are deep. (Wan’an Yan)
Ten autumns have passed since I stayed in an inn in Bingzhou; My longing for home day and night recalls Xianyang.
Without cause, I have once again crossed the Sanggan River; Looking back toward Bingzhou, it is now my native land. (Bejian Jian)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not allow the demon of the mind to give rise to deep calamity. The verse says:
Gautama’s thorough, compassionate heart— Seeing light and colors arise, the principle is hard to bear. Entering the village, he conforms to custom;
in the *nāga*-samādhi, Buddhas and demons alike sink into total stillness here. (Wan’an Yan)

to capture the rebel, first capture the king. (Beijian Jian)

Pure and fundamentally radiant, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, the mountains, rivers, and great earth all appear therein.

Pervasive and pure, it admits nothing else within; mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena are all contained therein.
(Beijian Jian). [Added from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "If that which is able to investigate is your mind, then you are mistaking a thief for your son.
Master Xiu Shan said: "If that which is able to investigate is not your mind, then you are mistaking a thief for your son."
The verse says:
"As one examines now, he is both son and thief; buying a hat to match the head, eating fish while removing the bones. (Tiantong Jue)
