Sitting coldly and desolately, he could not find peace. Carrying a single shoe in his hand, he returned to the Western Land. (Fayun Xiu)
Ordinary and holy entangled, emotions not yet forgotten; when it is vast and empty, with no sage at all, one is immediately startled into madness.
His Highness King Liang lacked strategy and was needlessly thrown into chaos by the barbarians. (Quán Dàdào)
Vastly open, a single arrow pierces the heavens; unaware, he strikes again with the chisel. The Emperor of Liang does not know where he has gone;
for ten thousand ages there has been no news. (Zhengjue Yi).
Vast and empty, transcending the sages—this is still but a skillful means. Not recognizing the Heavenly Countenance, now it is right before one's face.
Failing to attain realization while facing it, one crosses the Long River; heading north to Shaolin, one feels only lingering attachment. (Juehaiyuan)
With one arrow, he usually brings down a vulture; adding another arrow, he has already shown his forbearance. He returns directly to sit before the peak of Shaoshi;
let the Prince of Liang cease his efforts to summon him further. (Baizhang Yuan).
Refined until glowing red, struck with a single hammer-blow; countless sparks fly about on all sides.
A perfect ten-part diamond of adamant—spread out before the gate, to whom shall it be sold? (Baoning Yong)
Vast and empty, there is no sage; there is no need for inquiry. The phrase that follows penetrates all capacities—this is the eye.
Do not be surprised that we do not dismount upon meeting; it is because each has their own path ahead. (Yunhan Gong)
The primary meaning is vast and empty, transcending even the Emperor of Forms; one does not consult the almanac for many years.
How could one dispute the equinoxes of spring and summer? The white crane of Liaodong has departed without a trace; three mountains fall halfway beyond the blue heavens. (By Yishang)
The Gate of the Supreme Meaning of the Noble Truths is vast and empty; who is there to be honored as a sage?
It is truly laughable that within the second month of Jiangnan, the partridge cries out amidst the village of a hundred flowers. (Tàipíng Gǔ)
Leisurely taking a bolt of Qin-chuan brocade, I cut it to fashion a garment for a clever woman of the world. How many times has she worn it to display her skill?
Yet few know the subtle melody hidden within the dark. (Cheng Kumu)
Far-faring across the whale-waves, he enters the Great Liang. Vast and empty, with no "sage" to face the Sovereign.
Pitiful that his inch-square path finds no mirror; He remains hidden, just as once was Ziangru. (Fuxincai)
Not knowing how to be a guest, he troubles the host; his face shows no shame, with little joy and much anger.
(Changling Zhuo) At first, a single bell tolls at the Aru Pavilion; the sun is warm, and the Azure Dragon sleeps most deeply. Again, the drum is struck atop the Phoenix Terrace;
at midnight, the auspicious phoenix has not yet begun its dance. The imperial foundation is as eternally firm as a boulder; the barbarian monk has spent his efforts in vain.
The power of life arises; pointing back to Shaolin, he says, "Come, let us return. A spring breeze sweeps through, leaving the flowers in disarray.
(Fojian Qín). Unfurling the ranks and raising the banners, one seeks victory; yet who knows that the Imperial Chariot does not personally lead the campaign?
Holding fast to the glistening banners, they withdraw their formation, heading straight for Xiongpíng Mountain without dispatching an army. (Fodeng Xuán).
At that time, Bian He personally presented the jade; though it met no one, he tried again and again in vain.
To cross the river by breaking reeds, the waters of the Yangtze flow on through ancient and modern times, their color as deep as indigo. (Mengan Xin)
The butcher’s son from the Western Heaven possessed a fierce and heroic spirit; he oppressed the land of China, and his crimes could not be escaped.
Emperor Wu of Liang pressed him directly with a sudden thrust, and indeed, he raised the sword that gives life to men. (Xuetang Xing)
Vast and empty, there is no sage; his entire body is revealed. To present face-to-face is already to be separated by a ford. Do not ask of the courts of Liang or Wei;
with one flower and five petals, spring comes naturally. (Yunyan).
[Continued Collection]: The Central Asian Monk addresses the Han Ruler with the words, "Vastly empty, there is no sage. He further says, "I do not know him.
His divine steed fails to catch the mouse; the clear radiance of a thousand miles is utterly lost. (Shi Ming)
A golden chisel, a white jade mallet—chiseling open the cavity of primordial chaos, they reveal the mechanism of the Mysterious Origin.
(Zhengtang Bian) The Old Barbarian never actually crossed the Yangtze River; who says he ever used a single reed to ferry across?
It is laughable that the events of the "Ordinary Era" have long been misconstrued by his descendants. (Kentang Chong)
Treading upon the earth’s axis, the earth does not move; pushing down the celestial pivot, the heavens grow higher.
Steadily navigating the iron boat back to Shaoshi, even today the world rises with wind and waves. (Xue’an Jin)
A powerful general does not know how to pucker his lips or gnash his teeth; how could barbarian speech ever confuse the Chinese?
If old Xiao’s skin still had blood in it, he surely would have driven them across the shifting sands. (Tianmu Li)
Once a word has been spoken, even four horses cannot overtake it. Fortunately, he encountered King Liang, who let him go. At the head of the Yangtze River, he steered his boat by breaking off reeds;
how can the danger of the waves compare to the peril of one’s own questions? (Pak Ong-hyeon)
The five petals of fragrance unfold from a single flower; no one has yet depicted the vines or pruned the roots and sprouts.
Had he not been forced to set foot upon the soil of Jinling, I would still regret that Xiao Liang had not yet become a master of his craft. (Beijian Jian)
The golden crow flies up onto the jade balustrade; the black-lacquered Kunlun Mountain faces one directly. Ultimately, these things cannot be transmitted;
falling flowers and flowing water are utterly groundless. (Tiantong Jing)
Raising the first mallet of Mount Sumeru, the jade gate and golden locks are difficult to strike open. To apply the heavy back-stomp again is but a labor spent in vain;
one should regret having come from ten thousand miles away. (By Chidu Ying)
The jade flute has been blown to its end atop the Phoenix Terrace; the ancient halls lie deep and silent, unopened even at dawn.
Fallen petals cover the ground as spring has already passed; verdant shadows vainly lock away the old moss and lichen. (Xu Tang Yu)
Ten thousand waves and a thousand ripples, a single reed-raft crosses them. That solitary, fluttering figure is truly pitiable.
Old Xiao, if you understand the phrase of cutting through the current, I shall let you go at the head of the Yangtze River. (Shixi Yue)
A single reed cuts across the current; its profound intent is unfathomable. While the land of Liang enjoys great peace, the state of Wei harbors rebels.
(Xuewu Ke) Traveling ten thousand *li* to reach China, there was not a path through the clear waves, only a single stalk of reed.
Those who now face Yue from Yan—do you recognize me when I stand before you? (Deyan You)
Vast and empty, there is no sage—this is the word of truth. "Who is it facing me?"—the mind has not yet ceased. Original radiance blazes forth, illuminating the ten directions;
having come through immeasurable kalpas, it arrives at this very day. (Hengchuan Gong)

The ten-thousand-mile road from the West stretches far and wide. When the mirror of wisdom faces the window, no shadow can escape. The waves of the four seas are stilled and the dragon sleeps soundly;
the clouds of the nine heavens are clear and the crane soars high. (Xueyan Qin)
[Added for inclusion: When Great Master Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly at the human mind to see one’s nature and attain Buddhahood. The verse says:
Casting a straight hook into the heart of a rushing current, Fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs are all caught at once.
The patriarch’s livelihood is nothing more than this; Yet the spring wind that disturbs it never ceases. (Songyuan Yue)

Master Bodhidharma traveled from Liang to Wei and arrived at Shaolin in Luoyang, where he sat facing a wall for nine years before finally transmitting the Dharma to the Second Patriarch. The verse says:

Having first been exposed by King Liang, he then sat alone at Shaolin. He vainly claimed there was a "separate transmission outside the teachings," yet how could he fail to recognize this? (Baizhang Yuan).
A hundred thousand paths reach their end at Liang; the King of Liang’s words do not accord with reality. At Shaolin, no reliance is placed on the power of the Eastern Lord;
the five-petaled flower blooms, its fragrance shaking the earth. (Foguo Bai)
If your diligence turns instead into indolence, do not cling to dull meditation or sit in vacant stillness.
Shao-lin’s nine years of facing the wall were already thoroughly exposed by King Liang (Zu-yin Ming).
The Six Patriarchs tamed [beings] as they came from the East; the five petals of the Dharma-blossom spread open in China.
Sitting coldly for nine years, no one recognized him; carrying his single sandal, he returned empty-handed once more. (Cangtang Qing)
The ship sails abroad from Liang’s Putong era; with one blow, all conditioned efforts are shattered.
In vain do they speak of facing the wall and remaining silent—how can they deny that the teeth at the gate reveal the wind? (Fóxìng Tàiyī)

Sailing across oceans and climbing mountains—what was the purpose? Wandering through Liang and traversing Wei—what intent did he transmit? For nine years facing the wall, his compassion was most earnest;
Yet he was stubbornly called "Chan" by people of the time. (Tàipíng Gǔ)
Nine years at Xiong’er, leaving behind but a single shoe; one flower and five petals, the spring breeze rises from all four directions.

(Master Min, the Ancient Buddha) — Bodhidharma’s coming from the West is not worth boasting of; at Shaolin, he pressed his eyes shut and forced flowers to bloom. Distinguishing between "attaining the skin" and "attaining the marrow" is mere conceptualization;
the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and fundamentally without error. (Shushan Ru)
Before Mount Shaoshi, the wind passes by the ear; for nine years, human affairs have followed the flowing stream.
If you are not one who can play amidst the rising tide, you must by all means refrain from entering the surging waves. (Gushan Gui)
A single pull of the golden tortoise dries up the vast blue sea; In vain one drifts aimlessly upon a small boat. Today, amidst the misty waves, there is nothing to fish for;
There is no need to fashion a new moon into a hook. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] The Patriarch faced the wall for over nine years. This was the ultimate function of the teaching brought from the West; it remains even today as the guest of the world.
Yet people forcibly take these words and phrases to act as their own deeds. (By Provincial Hall Master Nanshan).
Seeking a kindred spirit through thousands of villages and ten thousand miles, a single word at the critical moment did not accord with Liang.
Facing the wall for nine years dwelling at Shaoshi, he sought the mind for a thousand ages, exhausting his spiritual radiance. (Tiantong Jue)
A single expanse of empty stillness— Neither brush nor ink can paint it. Sages and worthies find it hard to speak;
Buddhas and patriarchs force names upon it. (Zhengtang Bian)
The Patriarch came from afar to the Eastern Land; he sat facing the wall at Shaolin for nine years. The Second Patriarch transmitted the mind and personally attained the marrow;
calculating it back, he was already the predecessor. (Gao'an Wu)
He squandered his family’s wealth until nothing remained; with no foundation to rely upon, he killed a man with empty hands, committing sins that fill the heavens.
(Muan Yong) Crossing the river on a single reed, the wind and waves were fierce; for nine years at Shaoshi, he sat in vain facing the wall.
He mistakenly revealed the "peace of mind" through a single kōan; to this day, flowers lie scattered and disarrayed across the earth. (Wanshan Ning)
Failing to harmonize with King Liang, he crossed the river in secret; with no place on earth to hide from shame and fear, what was accomplished by facing the wall for nine years?
He has only deceived ordinary people into falling into the boiling cauldron. (Huyin Ji)
For nine years he faced the wall; when he turned around, he had no stratagem. Suddenly, there was someone who exerted the strength of one arm (Yuepo Ming).
When Master Bodhidharma was about to return to the Western Heaven, he said to his disciples, "The time has come;
why do you not each speak of what you have attained? At that time, the disciple Dao Fu said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters."
"It is not by departing from words that they serve as the function of the Way. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my skin.
Nizi Tongchi said, "What I now understand is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha: having seen it once, one never sees it again."
The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu replied, "The four elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist;
as for my perspective, there is not a single dharma to be obtained. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bone.

Finally, Huik'e came forward, prostrated three times, and stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow," and thereupon transmitted the Dharma and entrusted him with the lineage.
The Robe. The verse says:
Divine light; three prostrations; withdrawing and standing back. Before the waterfall on the cliff, the water flows long and swift.
Displaying perfect penetration at the Śūraṅgama Assembly, It causes Old Lu to shed double tears. (Tianyi Hui)
Shao-lin Zhen-si selects those of complete talent; his many disciples return with their foreheads marked. Do not say that robe and Dharma are easily obtained;
they once relied upon three prostrations as the auspicious matchmaker. (Zhengjue Yi)
Before the gate, the various sons stand in rows; each displays his heroism, surpassing even the King of Wu.
How is it that there is but one who remains silent? He sits, cutting off Vairocana, utterly unassailable. (Baoning Yong)
In the four quarters, above and below, all obstructions are severed; an icicle-vessel surges forth, sealing the azure sky. Within the unperforated flute lie the six musical scales;
a single note startles the fishing boat from its moorings (becoming a withered tree).
Shenguang bowed three times and stood in his place; the entire assembly forgot their understanding, for it was not yet definitive. When skin and hair have fallen away, who is near and who is distant?
Who says that "attaining the marrow" can cause the emotions to cease? (Yuantong Xiu)
When the front teeth were exposed, it was truly laughable. He sat facing the wall in silence for nine years.
Having distributed his skin and marrow bit by bit, he returned to the Western Heaven as before, full of shame. (The kindness of Kṣitigarbha).

Who has passed through the Shaolin barrier? Three prostrations and returning to one’s place; standing in the snow to settle the mind, forgetting the physical form and willingly severing an arm. (Zuyin Ming)
The toothless barbarian monk arrived in the Great Tang, yet stubbornly divided skin and marrow;
after nine years of fumbling and blundering, he returned empty-handed, adding only a few more occasions for the Chinese to laugh. (From *Foguo bai*).
[Continued Collection] The younger brothers each display their own prowess; only the elder brother is bone-deep poor.
Rising from three prostrations, he says not a word; his nostrils hang down, covering his lips. (Xuedou Zong)

Ever since the three prostrations were performed, for a thousand ages the transmission has been erroneous. Through eternal days no one has arrived; there is only the whistling wind through the cypresses and junipers. (Longmen Yuan)
Village dances and folk songs bring laughter that kills; riding oxen and carrying ducks, they move in throngs. Having finished three cups of wine, they return home;
only the pig's head remains, obstructing and annoying people. (By Zhengtang Bian)
A concave mirror reflects a person as thin; a convex mirror reflects a person as fat. It is better to smash the mirror and restore my original face. (Lan’an Shu)

Squeezing one's eyes produces flowers; thus he establishes the opening of the question. Having obtained its skin and marrow, he is nonetheless deceived by it. How many such blind fellows can there be!
To say it is cold when there is no frost in the sixth month—(Jian’an Qing).
When death comes, all must testify with one voice; when circumstances are exhausted and principles reach their limit, it is ultimately difficult to find room for compromise.
If one were to judge superiority and inferiority by comparing skin and marrow, how could one see the five petals of the flower blooming in crimson? (Gao Feng Miao)
[Added for inclusion] Master Bodhidharma said: "My Dharma, three thousand years hence, shall not have shifted by even a single hair's breadth. The verse says:
East and west, the eyes gaze upon the vastness of heaven and earth; Jade dew clarifies the autumn, and the spirit soars high. The mountains are mountains and the waters are waters;
How could there ever have been the slightest shift or change? (Ge Lu Tan)

[Added for inclusion: After Master Bodhidharma had been interred at Mount Xiong’er, three years later, Wei Songyun was returning from a mission to the Western Regions when he encountered the Patriarch on the Pamir Mountains.
The Patriarch was walking alone with a light step, carrying a single shoe in his hand. Songyun asked, “Where is the Master going? The Patriarch replied, “I am going to the West.
He further said to Songyun, “Your sovereign has already grown weary of the world. When Songyun heard this, he wept.

He departed from his master in bewilderment and traveled eastward until he returned with his report; by then, Emperor Ming had already passed away. When the tomb was opened, it contained nothing but an empty coffin and a single pair of leather sandals.

The entire court was struck with amazement and sighed in wonder. By imperial decree, the sandals were taken and enshrined for veneration at Shaolin Temple. A verse says: The Master departed in bewilderment, Traveling east until his mission was fulfilled. By the time he returned, the Emperor had ascended to the heavens. Upon opening the tomb, there was only an empty coffin, With but a single pair of leather sandals remaining.
The whole court was moved to astonishment and sighs. By imperial command, the sandals were taken And enshrined for offerings at Shaolin Temple.
The Master Xiong’er was buried at Luoyang; the Son of Heaven of Longcheng wept a thousand rows of tears.
Returning with his single sandal on his shoulder to Mount Cong, he startled to death both King Liang and King Wei (the Daoist Ke Fu).
The Master’s eyes were deep; the Master’s nose was large. The Master’s ears were pierced; the Master’s tongue was swift. The Master’s body was ink-black; the Master’s mind wore its burden high.
Carrying a single sandal in his hand, he returned to the shifting sands. The stone pagoda at Xiong’er Mountain remains even today. (Jue of Langya)
The Patriarch left behind a single sandal; it has been circulated among people’s ears for a thousand ages and ten thousand years.
One may carry it on one's shoulders and walk barefoot in vain, but when has one ever stepped upon that which belongs to oneself? (Wuzu Yan)
The mountains and rivers of Liang and Wei were originally at peace; for no reason, this old fox-spirit was allowed to remain. After nine years, his skin and marrow were completely exhausted;
now his single shoe and empty coffin further deceive the people. (Dongshan Kong)

The entire nation found it difficult to pull him back; he departed westward, carrying only his single sandal. It must be that the moon over Mount Xiong will alone cast its cold radiance for ten thousand ages. (Huyou Long)
Climbing mountains and crossing seas from the West—who would say the King of Liang’s eyes were not yet open?

With a single casual phrase, he was thoroughly exposed: nine years of sitting upright, cold as ashes. When he came, he knocked out the teeth right before the gate; when he departed, he left behind only his left shoe.
To the very end, his coming and going involved no affair at all; as before, he returned empty-handed with but a single sandal. (Kai)

The virtuous patriarch sailed eastward across the ocean; the clever son fell into a trap. Seeking the Dharma and searching for people, he brought upon himself deep calamity. Fortunately, he encountered King Liang, who was a master of the craft.
Though there was justice and a clear teaching, there was no place to clear his name. Eventually, with a single sandal, he returned west to the Pamir Mountains. There was—
Dignified and grave, leaking or not leaking; clear and distinct, yet skillfulness turned into clumsiness. (Nirvāṇa for the Ni-assembly). Casting down a single sandal:
clearly revealed, nothing hidden. As soon as the descendants set foot upon it, the ground is filled with swords and spears.
(Miaofeng Shan): Having sat in cold meditation for nine years, he failed his test; returning to the West with a single sandal, he was merely practicing deception.
The descendants of later generations harbor empty delusions; the partridge cries not because of the spring breeze. (Xue’an Jin).
Even in death he would not submit to burial; he stealthily carried off his single sandal and returned to the West.
Not captured and defeated by Song Yun, where could the authorities find his corpse? (Deep in the solitary peak.)
[Supplement] Heishan Fang said: "The late master Sīxīn would frequently cite the story of the single sandal returning to the West to question his monks, yet it was truly difficult to clarify.
Various quarters have either called it 'hidden and manifest,' or 'there cannot be two,' or 'this alone is the one reality.
If one understands it in such ways, one has not yet grasped the intent of the Patriarch."
"Do you all wish to see it? He then uttered this verse:
"Pure within the turbid, turbid within the pure; Do not say that the qilin is born with but a single horn. Traveling westward or heading eastward, the path does not err."
In every great function, head and beak meet like a chick pecking and a mother hen tapping. Do not hesitate;
this profound and essential spiritual mechanism is beyond all calculation.
*Chanzong songgu lian zhu tongji*, Volume Six. *Chanzong songgu lian zhu tongji*, Volume Seven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Faying of Baoen Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou, Song Dynasty;
continued compilation by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery, Yuan Dynasty. *Ancestors’ Occasions for Inquiry* (*Zushi Jiyuan*).

Among the various patriarchs of the Eastern Land, the Second Patriarch, Great Master Huik’e, first went to Shaolin to attend upon Bodhidharma. Standing in the snow and severing his own arm, he sought the Dharma with tears of sorrow.
Bodhidharma, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way..."
Fawang said, "You have now severed your arm to seek [the Dharma]; it may indeed be found. The Patriarch asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas?
Mozhao said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another person. The Patriarch said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind.
Mozhao said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you. The Patriarch said, "I have searched for my mind and cannot find it."
"Nothing can be attained. He said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. At this, the Patriarch attained realization. The Verse says:

Nine years facing the wall, awaiting the opportune moment; Standing in the snow reaching his waist, yet not unknitting his brows. With reverence, he sought the Dharma of the ground where the mind is settled;
Finding no mind to be found, only then was there no doubt. (Fenyang Zhao)
Severing one’s arm is easier than standing in the snow; when the mind is found nowhere, only then does the heart find peace.
Who would have known that within this landscape of ten-thousand-acre reeds, every single fisherman holds his fishing pole? (By Zhengjue Yi)
Searching from beginning to end for the mind, nothing can be found; in the vast silence, not a trace of the Shaolin man is seen.
The old snow fills the courtyard, its chill known once more; the nostrils remain, as ever, tucked above the lips. (Baiyun Yuan)
Seeking the mind, it cannot be found; everywhere one encounters those who know it. With no need for a pair of eyebrows, one transcends ten billion worlds together with them. (Yunju You)
What was accomplished by standing in the snow with it reaching his waist? What was gained by severing one’s arm with a blade? Those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure;
cease clinging to the old, ancient sage who came from the West. (Dizang En)
What is the use of deliberation in seeking peace of mind? To seek peace of mind is to weary the body.
At the place where one once stood amidst three feet of deep snow, who can be said to be the person within the snow? (Foguo Bai)
Shaolin’s wall-gazing was too much talk; he received a disciple with a full arm. In Jing and Luo, three feet of snow remain to this day;
how could the cold have ceased since the Putong era? (Yang Wuwai)
Seeking the mind, one has no choice but to settle it; the butcher shop and the brothel continue the legacy of Shaolin.
Yet how can descendants bear such directness? Everywhere they go, they bitterly search for the five flavors. (Zhang Wujin)
Severing his arm to seek the mind, he could not find it; Seeking the mind and finding nothing, he finally set his mind at rest.
Once the mind was settled, in the snowy courtyard of the late night, The jade flowers filled his eyes, yet nowhere could they be sought. (Cao Tang Qing)
Seeking the mind, it is not found; three prostrations are offered as a mere gesture. The spiritual flame blazes ever more intensely, and with a nod, one knows for oneself.
Turning back to observe where the Dharma-seal is fully manifest, the river moon and pine wind both enter the subtle. (By Fuxincai)
The father’s wealth is used by the son; the father uses the son’s wealth. Seeking the mind, there is no place to find it; the eye of the mind opens of itself.
(Changling Zhuo) If even a thread or a speck of dust were handed over to another, how could the Master have attained his complete body?
In the human realm and the heavens, wherever one meets in delusion, eight *liang* have always been but half a *jin*. (Longmen Yuan)
Three prostrations of diligent toil, snow reaching his waist; seeking the mind, finding no place, he forces himself to endure. As the divine light falls cold upon the earth, he reflects deeply;
only then does he realize that spring has arrived and the snow melts of its own accord. (Fodeng Xun)
The Second Patriarch established himself at Shaolin in those days; snow accumulated in the courtyard deep as his waist. With hands crossed over his chest, there was not a single thing;
he neither sought nor searched, nor did he settle his mind. (Gushan Gui)

Seeking the mind, there is nowhere it can be found; what more could one rely upon? Chewing to pieces a glowing red lump of iron—though one were to open their eyes with prideful spirit, how could that compare to not being deceived by the Old Barbarian? (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection]: Without waiting for the sevenfold refutation, one does not see [the self] from the very outset.
A monkey swings on a swing over the water; the Prince of Silla fires an arrow. Keep your eyes wide open and clearly see it: he pierces through the face of the Persian. (Shi Ming)
Standing in the snow with it reaching his waist; severing his arm with a precious blade. Without wavering in expression or spirit, he sports throughout the ten directions.
(By Baiyang Shun). The Second Patriarch, for no reason, went to Shaolin; he stood in the courtyard until the snow reached his waist.
Even if one were to find the mind that does not exist, one cannot avoid having one’s entire body sink into the mud. (By Shui'an Yan).
Bending one's knee to follow the elder is a great sacrifice. Amidst snowdrifts, he severed his own arm, gazing upward at the lofty heights. The iron ox is whipped into motion beneath Bear Peak;
with a single draught, the Yellow River is dried to its very bottom. (Huian Ti)

Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years amidst the deep snow; he attained one thing, attained another, and split open the myriad phenomena of the universe in equal measure. (Nun Wuzhuo’s Summary).
Brandishing a blade to sever his arm, he reveals the complete reality; one forgets the person who seeks peace of mind at the bottom of the heart.
Had he known the sensation of pain at that moment, where could the old barbarian have placed his whole body? (Wuji Pai)
In the deep night of Chang’an, the snow falls vast and white; Seeking peace of mind, I find only greater unrest.
Even if one could open the living eye before a word is spoken, How could one know they have already been deceived by the Old Barbarian? (Xian-an Guan)
On level ground, a heap of bones rises without cause; one carries this living body to be buried in the snow.
Even if you were to find the Dharma for settling the mind, bring me back my mother-born arm. (Yinshan Can)
Seeking it oneself, one cannot find it; the face is expressionless, yet flushed red. Turning over, one takes a tumble;
both hands feel at empty space. (Xue’an Jin).
Amidst deep piles of snow, a limb was severed; the Old Barbarian suppressed his full tenfold majesty. At that moment, one should have overturned it all;
had he not arrived, one would have been forced to treat a dead horse with medicine. (Shishi Hui)
The Second Patriarch was no true man of stature in his day; he divided skin and marrow only to be smeared with it.
Piteously seeking the Dharma of "settling the mind," he has remained without even one arm until this very day. (Duan’an Chang)
Seeking the mind, there is nowhere to find it; at that very moment, the mind is at peace. Had I known early on that ice is water, my two arms would surely have remained intact. (Shitada Kūn)
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, was a man of unknown origins; he did not disclose his name or lineage.
As a layman, he visited the Second Patriarch and said, "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment. I pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will grant me absolution for my transgressions.

The Patriarch replied, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall absolve them for you. After a long silence, the layman said, "I have searched for my transgressions, but they cannot be found. The Patriarch said, "I [have absolved them]."
"I have finished confessing your transgressions with you. You should now dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. He asked, "I now see that the Preceptor is the Sangha;
I do not yet understand what is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma'. The Patriarch said, "This very mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Dharma."
"The Dharma-Buddha is non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. [Huike] said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-Dharma—they are non-dual.
The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure. His name should be Sengcan. He then attended him for two years.

Dazu then entrusted him with the robe of faith of Bodhidharma and the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, reciting a verse as a secret injunction to protect and uphold them so that they would not be severed.
Thereafter, he resided at Mount Qianwan in Shuzhou or at Mount Sikong. A verse says:
The waters of Qianxi Creek are swift and the Tianzhu Peak is high; all is luminously clear, without the slightest obstruction.
From of old, one’s livelihood has been as level as the palm of a hand; yet descendants in later generations play with the ocean tides. (Yang Wuwai)
The offenses have no root; the nature is already empty. Where the wind arises, no wind is produced.
To this day, the waters of the mountains and valleys flow as a single stream of pure water into the sea. (From the Buddha-land, white).
He confessed his transgressions before the Master and requested their purification; with the offense forgotten and the mind extinguished, both were as suchness.
Who knew that Chan was a treasure among the Sangha, coming and going while dwelling beneath Mount Siguang? (Cangtang Qing).
Half-awake, half-drunk, lying on the street; suddenly awakening, one realizes that the karma of the entire body is fundamentally non-existent.
If samādhi were obtained from another person, how would mimicking their expression differ from further smearing it with mud? (It becomes a withered tree.)
A holeless flute and felt clappers—within these, the five notes and six scales are all universally present. People of this age do not recognize the yellow Tibetan *chao*;
they laugh at me, saying I am ascending the jeweled throne. (Wuzu Yan)
The wind-ailment entangles the body; though one seeks the offense, it cannot be found. Over ninety thousand *li*, the wings are spread toward the clouds (Min Gufo).

The Third Patriarch used offense to repent of offense; the Second Patriarch took error and made it right. A gust of pure wind strikes the face, and the flowers of offense and the fruits of karma both wither away.
A single grain of elixir possesses divine power; to cure the illness, there is no need for donkey-load medicines.
(Fojiàn Qín). [Continued Collection] My whole body itches; I ask another to scratch me. Scratching down to the very bone, my body is already weary.
With one stroke, he has scratched right to the mark, and all the places that have itched throughout my life are instantly gone. (Shuǐān Yī).
The Second Patriarch sought peace of mind; the Third Patriarch repented his offenses. Chasing evil and following deviance, they form gangs and bands.
Only the Old Barbarian may know; the Old Barbarian may not understand. (Tu’an Qi)
Heaven-filling transgressions have no gate through which to repent; red and festering, they pervade body and world, beyond all healing.
Already the four corners are all trampled underfoot—leave it to future generations to poke and prod with their needles and awls. (No Gate opens).

Throughout one's entire life, the nature of sin is sought but leaves no trace. It is as if the great earth and the heavens have become empty. Yet heaven and earth remain as they were, towering and abrupt;
a single stream from the hidden valley flows naturally toward the sea. (Chijue Chong)

The wind-illness entangles his body and life, beyond the reach of medicine; his home is poor and beset by robbery—how more pitiable! Who would have known that when seeking the culprit, there is nowhere to be found?
This is precisely the moment the thief returns to an empty house. (Great Rest and Humility).
Sins as vast as the heavens—beg for their confession and removal. When looked at, they seem to exist; when sought, they are nowhere to be found.
Even if one were to utterly exterminate the Hu tribes in a single word, coldly reflecting upon it, one is no true man. (Shishi Hui)

The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, was originally a śrāmaṇera. At the age of fourteen, he paid homage to the Third Patriarch and said, "I pray that the Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me.
The Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Thereafter, he served his master with diligent labor.
After nine years, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him. He resided at Mount Pòtóu in Qí Prefecture, where disciples gathered like clouds;
he restrained his mind so thoroughly that he did not sleep, his side never touching the mat. One day he told the assembly: "During the Wǔdé era, I traveled to Mount Lú."
Ascending to the summit, he gazed toward Mount Pòtóu and saw purple clouds like a canopy, beneath which white vapors divided into six horizontal paths.
"Do you understand? he asked. The assembly remained silent. Huìróng said, "Could this not be the Dharma-branch that will emerge crosswise after the Master’s passing?
The Master replied, "Excellent. Emperor Tàizōng of the Táng dynasty was moved by the Master's Way and issued three imperial summons.
He did not go. He was subsequently granted the purple robe. A verse says:
"The Stupa of Compassionate Clouds, the Master of Great Medicine— Behold him, look up to him; the two peaks stand towering high.
Lanrong could not obtain the bowl from the Western Heaven; It was bestowed directly upon the child on the road to Huangmei. (Yang Wuwe)
Meeting the Master outside the island, I was released from my bonds and returned. Beneath the Double Peaks, I alone am secluded and extraordinary.
Yet I take this robe and bowl as a worldly matter, begging them for that little boy at Huangmei. (Foguo Bai)

The Way emerges from heaven and earth; its movement is supreme. Flying clouds, summoned three times, do not leave the mists. Seeking a successor for the human realm, he finds the son of the Zhou house.
Gazing afar at Oxhead Mountain, the purple qi divides. (Cao Tang Qing)

Cease clinging to fame and reputation, for they can obstruct the Way; I only fear that the lineage of one’s teacher may also burden the person. You who inquire about the Dharma, novice monk, do not be so loquacious.
This hundred-year journey as a guest is but a matter of sharing in the common dust. (Juefan Hong)
Neither bound nor liberated; the side never touches the mat. Separating them reveals the single thread; two sets of five hundred (Master Min, the Ancient Buddha).
Before the Ox-head [monastery] was founded, the plum had already ripened. Strolling through the human world, the pond is formed beneath the moon.
The imperial summons arrived three times, yet he was too lazy to open his eyes; atop the White Lotus Peak, the lights shine upon one another (Yunyan Yuan).
[Continued Collection] Firmly declining the imperial decree of purple clay from the Phoenix Palace, this ancient adept brought disgrace upon the ancestral style.
Having cut off the two peaks so that not a blade of grass remains, he spared the pine tree only for its branches that obstruct others. (Wumen Kai).
Overturning liberation, one dismantles its very nest; from this point, a vast net is spread across the heavens.
Deceiving the small child is still tolerable, but when a single branch protrudes sideways, the clamor becomes even more confused. (Chijue Chong)
Who binds? There is no one to bind. Why then seek further liberation? It is not necessarily the geese of the Right Army General that are the cranes of Master Zhi Lang. (Shitain Kū)
Purple clouds fly from the peak of Pòtóu; three times he declined the celestial decree while aging in the emerald heights.
Although his lingering debt has no further use, it should not be handed over to a small child. (Mù of Shàoshì).
The Great Master Wuzu Hongren, in his previous life, was planting pine trees on the western mountains of Qizhou when he encountered the Fourth Patriarch, who told him:
"I wish to transmit the Dharma to you, but you are already advanced in years. If you come again, I shall still wait for you.
The Master gave his word and subsequently entered the womb of a woman of the Zhou family. Because of this, he was cast into the Zhugang River by a deity.
The object [of his care] was protected until he reached the age of seven, at which time he became a youth.

One day, the Fourth Patriarch encountered a young boy of extraordinary and refined physical features while traveling through Huangmei County. He asked, "What is your surname? The boy replied, "I do have a surname, but it is no ordinary one.
The Patriarch asked, "What is this surname? The boy replied, "It is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The Patriarch asked, "Do you have no nature? The boy replied:

Because his nature was empty [of inherent existence], the Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma; he immediately had an attendant lead him away to become a monk, later transmitting to him the robe and the Dharma.
He resided at Mount Dongshan in Huangmei. The verse says:
Why are the planted pines so old, and why are those who receive the robe so few? Previous and subsequent lives are but one dream and two awakenings.
White lotus flowers bloom at the mountain peak; the bright moon shines coldly for a thousand years. (Yang Wuwai, No. 2)

Rising at sunrise, they go forth to work; planting pines is their joy. How many were planted in the past? Now they fill the crags and valleys. The white-haired man has gone and the young child returns;
he brings laughter to the thousand-year-old cranes upon the treetops.

In the realm of sacred authority, no one in the world can judge; how could the secret transmission on the Twin Peaks be a hollow claim? His former incarnation has grown old and can no longer pass the bowl;

it was only upon returning to take up residence that he first succeeded to the lamp. The fame of his past planting of pine trees still resounds today; as for his vow to repay his mother through a thousand spirits, how much more has it increased!
Now the wind of the school pervades the land within the seas, solely because he was chosen from among the springtime seedlings. (Baizhang Yuanwen).
Hanging down, my white hair descends from the green mountains. Returning after seven years, it has changed my former countenance. While people have become youthful again, the pines are already old.
From now on, right and wrong shall fall among the common folk. (By Foguo Bai)
Who is the former body? Who is the latter body? In vain do you compare names for their newness or antiquity. Do not ask the neighbor about matters of coming and going;
I am neither the person of old nor someone other than that person. (Zuyin Ming)

No father, no elder brother—cut off right and wrong. Who can discern the time of the current flowing upstream at the heart of the river? Having attained the Dharma on West Mountain, he hides away on East Mountain.
This matter is taught only for those who are capable of knowing it. (Cao Tang Qing).
The turbid stream flows on, cutting off all divergent paths. With a turn of the body, one drives out the stake from mid-air. White lotuses bloom toward the heavens;
from this point, the celestial mechanism is entirely revealed. (Min Gufo)
The persimmons of Huangmei ripen; the white lotus flowers bloom. I ask: the Buddha-nature is the same substance, yet its form differs from that of the ordinary.
The robe was passed to the man of Nanling; the pines grow old on West Mountain as I return once more. Borrowing two skin-bags for what end?
A single pitcher of wind and moon, profound and free of dust. (Tiantong Jue)
The eldest son is unfit for use; having departed according to appointment, he returns again. Within the stretching and contracting of his feet, he greedily hastens on his journey—how swift!
He has the face given by his mother but lacks the surname of his father; he catches the five petals of the *dharma-flower* as they bloom. (Fodeng Xun)
The incense and offerings have continued for five hundred years; lone monkeys and wild cranes dwell atop ancient pines. It is said that the wondrous Way returned to the Southern Ridge;
I pay homage to the stupa toward the mid-heavens. The true body, past and present, has no place to be found; yet the sacred traces of antiquity remain as they were.
If anyone asks me of the affairs of the Eastern Mountain, there is a white lotus in the pond upon the peak. (By Baiyang Shun)
The assembly at the Dharma Gate of Dongshan numbered more than seven hundred; those who were truly capable took the Master as their model.
While the turbid stream flows on, the pure remains in abundance. On the road to Huangmei, people travel north and south. (Yunyan).
[Continued Collection] One goes and one comes; one old and one young. Two mirrors suspended facing each other, light and shadow are both reflected.
Even if you exhaust all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), you have not yet clarified the single upper orifice. (Nun Wuzhuo Zong).
An old man who went away to plant pine trees returns to transmit the joy of the Dharma to the youth. He has a mother-born face but no father’s surname;
this numinous sprout beyond the kalpas does not succumb to spring. (Shui-an Yi)
Originally a monk from the old days of Huangmei, serving his master until old age, his spirit grew ever more robust. Turning his body, he cast down the mattock for planting pines;
shifting his step, he came to divide the lamp that illuminates the world. His dharma-bag was entrusted to a woman by the stream; his robes and bowl were passed to Neng of Lingnan.
His excellent reputation remains widespread and enduring; after the rain has passed over the Huai mountains, they stand green in ten thousand layers. (Huyin Ji)
With a head full of white hair, he dwells by the crags; He is too weary to plant ten thousand more pines. His leather bag burdens the lady of the Zhou clan;
His traces are hard to find as he departs and returns. (Tianmu Li)
What a fine "Pine-Planting Wayman" he is! In his old age, he recklessly wanders the wilds, failing to recognize his own biological parents and bringing shame upon the young lady of the Zhou family.
The muddy stream could not drown him; instead, it nurtured him into a crafty rogue.
He incited seven hundred monks at Huangmei to fall into a pack, vying with one another for robes and bowls. (Master Puk-ung Hyeon)
The green pines were not yet planted when the nose reached the vast heavens; once the green pines were planted, half was lost.
To bring shame upon the Zhou family is still tolerable, but to come back again is not worth even half a copper coin. (Xiaoweng Kan).
Pine trees planted, filling the mountains; turning over in the dark. Though you have obtained the robe of faith, when have you ever known your father’s face? (Shitennō Kun)
For many years his livelihood has been by the mattock; ten thousand pines lock in the azure mist. The dream is shattered at Caoxi and heaven and earth are vast;
returning again, he is not worth half a coin. (Muzhou Daoming of Shaoshi)
The planted pines are fortunate indeed to have grown; they were merely forced to follow others into the fire-pit. Having exchanged their skin-sacks, they hurriedly turn their heads back;
as before, their nostrils do not dispute by even a hair’s breadth. (Shishi Hui)
The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was originally surnamed Lu. His family was poor, and he sold firewood to support his mother.
He went to the Fifth Patriarch to seek the Dharma. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan. The Patriarch asked, "What do you wish to seek?"
Huineng said, "I only wish to become a Buddha. The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature; how can you become a Buddha?

Huineng replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could the Buddha-nature be like that? The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and rebuked him, saying, "Go and work in the wine vats!
Huineng then prostrated at his feet and withdrew, entering the rice-hulling workshop where he performed labor with the pestle and mortar.
At that time, because the Fifth Patriarch addressed the assembly seeking a verse, intending to transmit the robe and the Dharma, the Senior Seat Master Shenxiu presented a verse, saying:
"The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror stand. At all times diligently wipe it clean;
Do not let dust collect upon it. The Master (Huineng) responded with a verse, saying: "Bodhi originally has no tree; The mirror of the mind..."
Nor is it a stand. Originally there was not a single thing; why borrow a whisk to sweep away dust? The Patriarch recognized this in silence.

At night, he called [Huineng] into his room, secretly revealing the heart-essence of the Dharma-eye, and transmitted to him the robe and bowl, ordering him to cross the river and pass over Mount Dayu to return south to Caoxi and open the Dharma-gate of Dongshan. The Verse says:
Now and of old, the single stream of Caoxi has been cold; with your arrival, Master, you have caused waves to rise. Carrying their bags, people at Yuling pursued you in vain;
carrying stones, the multitude at Huangmei found it difficult to recognize you. (Fohuiquan)
A stone falls at his waist, and the mortar and pestle ring out. Old Lu finds heaviness burdensome and lightness no relief.
Though he inherited the robe and bowl of Huangmei, he remains dozens of stages away from Caoxi. (Yang Wuwai)
When seven hundred eminent monks were in their dreams, he returned south alone under the moon at the third watch. Selling firewood and husking rice were his domestic affairs;
what matter was it that he personally transmitted the robes of the six patriarchs? (Foguo Bai).
A single verse strikes the vital point, and the entire assembly is subdued; A hundred birds carrying flowers fly away in pairs.
Remembering the path back to the mountain home, At midnight the robe was passed across the Nine Rivers. (Zuyin Ming)
The Sixth Patriarch was no hero back then; he asked another to write on the wall for him and then plastered it over.
Clearly there was a verse stating that "there is nothing," yet he accepted a bowl from that other man. (Sixin Xin)
From among seven hundred monks, one was chosen. Originally possessing nothing, they were immediately in harmony. At night, he passed on the robe and bowl to depart for Caoxi;
the iron tree blooms in the spring of the second month. (Cao Tang Qing)
[Continued Collection] A fellow from the village who carries firewood and sells fire; his tongue flows like a surging tide, and there is nothing to be done about it.
He says himself that he had no mouth when he first came, yet he can stir up wind and waves on level ground. (Jingshan Gao).
On the Huangmei dais, those present were as numerous as hemp seeds; yet how lamentable that their capacity for response was revealed within mere words.
"Directly, there has been nothing from the beginning"—even the clear blue sky and bright sun are obscured by clouds. (Xita).
A verse written on the wall says: "There is nothing. Know that the power of this waist-stone is more than sufficient. Do not say that the Lazy Old Man has no skill;
from within the husks, he pounds forth a pearl that rolls out of the basin. (Shui-an I)
Bodhi has no tree, and the mirror is not a stand; this foul mouth was clearly split open by a ghost.
Fortunately, he is but a rustic wood-seller with nothing to do, yet he stubbornly brought this calamity upon himself. (No gate opens.)
Casting down the axe for gathering firewood, he enters the mortar-house directly to pound rice. With one foot treading to the very bottom, the message of Huangmei is communicated. (Fozhao Guang).
One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere; at a single stroke, the great earth, mountains, and rivers sink away. From this point, one opens up another world entirely;
in the New Province, a bundle of firewood is as precious as gold. (Poban Xian)
The four-line gāthā cannot be deciphered; three times it was transmitted, yet it was originally non-existent.
Thorns grow upon the path of Caoxi, reaching all the way down to the present day—halfway along the road. (Miaofeng Shan)
A rustic like this is nowhere to be found in all the world; he sells firewood all day long, rushing along the weary road. Though there is a path to Huangmei, he has never reached it.
Who says that the robe and bowl were personally entrusted to him? (Shaoshi Muzhou)
Huangmei handed it over; Taicang was in a flurry of haste. In the dead of night, they crossed the river in the midst of a desolate chill.
Thinking no one would know their destination, the thief’s own body has already been exposed along with the stolen goods. (Xin’an Chou)
One does not become a woodcutter nor a miller; one simply uses the strength of one’s feet to test for fineness or coarseness.
To know whether he has trodden upon it or not, both the rice and the bran arrive in the alms bowl. (Xiyuan Hui)
With a deluded mind, he covets another’s broken bowl; with idle talk and long-winded speech, he begs others to write for him.
He knows only how to slip away in secret at midnight—has he ever even dreamed of the meaning of the Patriarchs? (Shishui Hui).
The meeting of teacher and disciple has its origins; a bright mirror is not a stand—words cast blindly into the dark.
Ruining the livelihood of Shaolin, the sound of the oars shakes the moon as it passes over the blue seas. (Ge Lu Tan)
The Sixth Patriarch, having received the Dharma, took leave of the Fifth Patriarch and was instructed to remain hidden between Huaiji and Sihui.
Upon arriving in Nanhai, he encountered the Dharma Master Yinzong at Faxing Temple. One evening, as the wind blew the temple banner, two monks were heard debating:
one said the banner moved; the other said the wind moved. As they exchanged arguments back and forth, neither reached a point of accord.
The Master said, "Can one allow those of worldly station to rashly participate in such lofty discourse? It is simply that the wind and the banner do not move; movement arises from the mind alone.
Upon hearing these words, Yinzong was struck with awe and marveled at him. He then inquired into the origins of this teaching, and the Master told him the truth.
Thereupon, Yinzong assembled the congregation and requested that the Dharma-gate of Dongshan be opened; the Master then shaved his head.
He donned the robes and received the precepts at Tianning Temple in Guangzhou. A verse says: "It is not the wind or the banner that moves;
it is only the mind that moves. This has been transmitted from antiquity down to the present day.
If those who wander as water and clouds wish to understand this hereafter, The Patriarch was truly one who knew how to appreciate the sound. (Ruilu Xian)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. A black-and-white cat with a speckled face. The traveler at night covets only the bright moon;
unaware that his clothes are soaked as he crosses the cold water. (Fachang Yu)
"It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. These words have already spread throughout the human world.
To understand the essential meaning of Old Lu, look at the ten thousand layers of mountains at Tiantai and Nanyue. (Tianyi Huai)
Vast and wide stretches the imperial post road; morning and night, it has never barred the passage of people. It is not that my entire household lacks the will to advance;
it is simply that thorns have grown before our gate. (Baoning Yong)
"It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. To understand this clearly is difficult for the awakening mind. Cease seeking in foreign tongues or Chinese speech;
look at ease upon the tip of the flagpole. (Yuantong Xiu)
East, west, south, and north—there is no empty space; above, below, and in the four intermediate directions, they are raised according to their respective parts.
All kinsmen have come to rest within a single body; having traveled to the ends of the earth, there is no companion. (The Three Patriarchs).
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. White clouds still cover the green mountains. Having grown old in recent years, I am utterly devoid of strength;
I have stolen a moment of leisure from the midst of my busyness. (Xuefeng Yuan)
It is neither wind nor banner. Why does the clear sky shake the lapis lazuli? In these enlightened times, there is no need to debate the way of public justice;
there are naturally those who look upon it with the eyes of an impartial observer. (Yuantong Xian)
It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind; along this distant path, there is nothing to pursue. White clouds originally leave no trace;
they fly and fall upon the precipice, deeper and deeper still. (Cao Tang Qing)
In the past, Old Lu leaked the celestial mechanism; he pointed directly at the wind and the banner and spoke to him: "Is it the wind? Is it the banner? It is you, indeed.
To the left and to the right, it has never been apart [from you]. (Huangbo Sheng)
The wind and the banner do not move; the beggar obtains a dream of gold, silver, and precious jewels, joyfully making use of them.
(Ancient Buddha Min) Plunging straight down into the vast ocean to seize the dragon pearl—when face-to-face it is presented, is there anything to be seen?
If one does not open the true eye upon reaching this point, the disease of the gallbladder and vital organs will be difficult to revive. (Daochang Ru)
"It is not the wind or the banner; it is your own mind. This saying has been passed down throughout the monastic groves.
If you can tread upon the path home, even tiles and pebbles may be called gold. (Zuyin Ming)
It is neither wind nor banner; throughout the ages, all vie to gaze upon it. Only when one sees through to the end does one know there is no fixed location;
who in the ancestral hall can share the chill of the night? (Tongzhao Feng)
Pointing out that neither the wind nor the banner is [the truth], he says directly that even the movement of the mind is not it.
Last night, a single moon over the cold stream shone through and shattered my old, secluded mountain retreat. (Fuxin Cai)
"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind. How many seek the sword by marking the boat? I clearly send this word to all my fellow Chan practitioners:
from antiquity, the true seal has never been bartered for gold. (Fujian Qín)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. Those who take this to be the mind are likewise muddled and superficial.
When the wind blows the drifting clouds from the azure void, the moon rises over the green mountains as a single sphere of jade. (Shushan Chang)
They contend with one another, seeing only the wind and the banner move; they refuse to turn their heads and recognize the moving mind. From this point on, Old Lu reveals his message:
the pine-wind and river-moon are all those who know the sound. (Mengan Xin)
Dreaming my way to Mount Huading, I passed through the Vermilion Hills; treading upon the cold clouds, I leaned against a stone pavilion.
Greedy to gaze at the waterfalls cascading down the cliff walls, I did not realize I was standing by the head of the emerald river. (Changling Zhuo)
"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind. Even the profoundness of Caoxi is not truly profound.
When Nanda the Wrathful tosses them about and scatters them, they cannot be found even when analyzed down to the finest atoms. (Huanglong Zhen)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. How many people look southward from beneath the Northern Dipper? The Patriarch’s direct transmission leaves no hidden trap;
for eyes to open and skin to be pierced is not difficult. (Fodeng Xun)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner; behind one mountain range lies another. When the spring rain has passed, there is nothing left to do;
leaning alone against the precarious tower, I gaze at the stupa-pole. (By Fuxing Tai)
"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind. From of old, there have simply been few who understand.
Raising one's head beyond ten thousand miles of vast sky, one sees only white clouds and deep flowing waters. (Chu'an Fang)
[Continued Collection] It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. This talkative monk cannot explain it.
If you seek the profound realization through clever words, you will find yourself separated by a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks. (Langya Huijue)
It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is only the mind that moves. A dragon gives birth to a dragon, and a phoenix gives birth to a phoenix.
Old Lu directly revealed his total capacity; to people today, this matter appears like a dream. (Shi Ming)
"It is not the wind or the banner; it is the movement of the mind. This is like borrowing Mazu to scratch an itch. Who among the solitary luan birds beyond the heavens has attained the marrow?
Who can understand how to join the glue for a broken string? (Chongjue Kong)
"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind; the Patriarch’s true eye is right here now.
Now, if you do not recognize it, mountains and rivers create obstacles; if you recognize it now, the seas and peaks sink away. (Xuedou Zong)
The wind and the banner do not move; it is the human mind that moves. Pointing directly and clearly, do not remain in a state of blurriness.
If you attempt to skillfully deliberate with intellectual views, it is much like adding a dream to a dream. (Daopei Zhi)
"It is not that the wind or the banner moves; it is only the mind that moves. This still involves a degree of conceptual elaboration and is a forced explanation.
The great earth has never added a single inch of soil; I do not know who among you is the one who nods in agreement. (Kaifuk Ning)
The direct pointing and single transmission come from the Ancestors; it was not the movement of the wind or the banner that produced Master Lu.
If practitioners of the profound Way possess the Vajra-eye, then every land and every atom is entirely empty. (Nantang Xing)
Whether it be the wind or the banner, do not harbor doubt; take a leisurely stroll back through the thickets of a hundred grasses.
Under the Great Way’s peaceful reign, there is no cause for prohibition; playful butterflies and warbling orioles fly about the trees. (Zidehui, 2)

"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind. The patch-robed monk merely exerts himself like a needle piercing a cone. After the rain has passed from the mountain cell, the twilight smoke is still;
lying down, he listens as the cool breeze arises through the bamboo grove.
The waves are calm and the wind is gentle; it is precisely the time to look on. The autumn river is crystal clear, and the azure sky is vast.
Fishermen vie with one another to cast their silk lines; they do not see the icy moon dipping into the cold water. (Chang’an Chong)
"It is neither the wind nor the banner that moves; it is not even your mind, O worthy one. Since the time of chaotic confusion, we have been muddied and stirred up until the present day."
(Xiatang Yuan): "The wind moves, the banner moves, the mind moves. A dead snake must be kept alive by someone. A wooden horse neighing in the wind stands in the path;
a hornless iron ox enters the cave. (Baiyang Shun).
The dialogue concerning the wind and the banner reveals the total mechanism; for a thousand ages, it has stirred up right and wrong within the monastic communities.
*Du!* This wood-seller from Xinzhou—gaining the advantage is losing the advantage. (Fozhao Guang)
"It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind; do not spread these words throughout the forests of the sangha.
From of old, this single stream of celestial river water has pierced through rocks and cliffs from antiquity to the present. (Tuduce)
The great ocean’s waves surge; the waters of the thousand rivers flow backward. Within the palaces of the dragon kings, not a single person is seen wandering. (Ying’an Hua)
It is not the wind or the banner that moves; Heaven itself gave birth to the Old Lord Li. From the moment he emerged from the womb, the hair upon his head was white as silver, inch by inch.
(Snow Hall’s Verse)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. The azure sky is clear and the moon is full.
How many foolish men and women seeking cleverness still look into the jar upon their bedside. (Shui-an I, 2)
It is neither a banner nor is it the wind; the precious mirror of Huangdi emerges from within his breast. The myriad phenomena of the universe cannot escape its reflection;
the foxes clinging to their den lose their tracks.
After Zhang Qian toppled Mount Kunlun, how many have reached the source of the Mengjin? How laughable are those who do not know of heaven and earth;
even now they stubbornly claim that there is still a Kunlun and a Qian. (Kentang Chong)
It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is only the mind that moves. A poor child treading on snow—his very bones are cold.
Whether in the state of a sage or an ordinary person, who can change this? A cicada has chewed through the Iron Ring Mountains. (Jianmen Division).
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. Entering the mud and entering the water, I let people behold it. Do not bring right and wrong to judge me;
the worldly life’s forced interpretations have nothing to do with this. (Yuelin Guan)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. Where the white clouds end, one sees the green mountains. How pitiable are those countless men of heroic spirit;
with eyes wide open, they solemnly enter the barrier of death. (Chuan’an Jing)
It is not the wind, nor is it the banner. Clearly, ten thousand layers of barriers are shattered.
Who would have known that having exhausted the strength of one’s own arm, one would only invite idle fame to fall into the world? (Songyuan Yue)
It is neither wind nor banner; the General rides his horse out through Tongguan Pass. All lands from Annam to the northern frontiers have been brought under his sway;
from time to time he lights his lamp and gazes upon his sword. (Tianmu Li)
"It is neither wind nor banner"—this too is suspicious. Yet he speaks of the movement of the mind; how grand his phrasing!
That which Heaven produced and which cannot be described by form—who in all the world has ever seen it? (Pak Ong-hyeon).
A single moon over Chang’an; the sound of pounding clothes from ten thousand households. The western wind blows it on without ceasing—all of it is the longing for the Jade Gate.
(Deep in the solitary peak.)
The wind and the banner move the mind; all are led away as one form. Knowing only how to open the mouth, one does not realize the conversation has fallen (no gate opens).
The earth spirits return to earth; the heavenly spirits return to heaven. With earnest devotion they see him off, with precious horses and gold coins (Wuzu Fan).
[Added by Yǔwáng Chóngjǔ. The Monk of Bālíng said: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving.
If it is neither the wind nor the banner, where then does it reside? If someone comes forward to speak on behalf of the Patriarch, [I shall grant them my approval].

He met with Baling. Master Xuedou said, "The wind moves, the banner moves. Since it is both wind and banner, where else can they be placed? Someone came forward to speak on behalf of Baling and meet with Xuedou. The Master then offered this verse: Wind moves, banner moves; Both are wind and banner. Where else can they be placed? It is neither wind nor banner; there is nowhere for them to attach. This wind and this banner have no place of attachment. The soaring falcon in the vast sky loses its track;
the golden-haired lion crouching on the ground likewise falls into confusion. A-he-he! Whether you awaken or not, it makes one think again of Xie Sanlang:
fishing alone with a single line amidst the rain of the cold river.
[Added for inclusion] A monk asked the Sixth Patriarch, "Who will obtain the robe and bowl of Huangmei? The Patriarch said, "He who understands the Buddha-dharma shall obtain them.

The monk said, "Will you yourself, Master, obtain them? The Patriarch said, "I shall not obtain them. The monk asked, "Why not? The Patriarch said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. The Verse says: The robe and bowl of Huangmei— Who would dare to grasp them? If you wish to know the meaning, Look at the one who does not understand.
Picked up at random by the hand, one sees its uniqueness; within this, there is no effort to convey the message.
Huangmei did not permit the transmission of this principle; at midnight, he once entrusted it to Old Lu. (Da-hong En)
Decisive as a bolt of steel, great skill appears as if clumsy. Holding up a single phrase, one does not "understand" the Buddha-dharma; let the leaves fall and the flowers bloom as they may.
One does not inquire whether it is the chill of spring or the heat of autumn. Distinct and distinct! An eternally cold pool, the moon in the empty realm. (Yuánwù Qín).
I know nothing of the Buddha-dharma; I have not grasped the intent of Huangmei. The fundamental substance is spontaneously perfected;

ultimately, it is simply this. The Way has already accorded with my whole life; my feet have already trodden upon solid ground. Not a single dharma meets the mind; this is the personal transmission received at Vulture Peak.
(Fojiàn Qín): "Not understanding the Huangmei Buddha-dharma; in a dream, eyes closed yet wide awake. Here there is not even two taels of gold;
the layman sells three shēng of wine. (Xuě'ān Jǐn): [No commentary provided in source text]

The plantain tree has leaves but no sprouts. Suddenly, a gust of wild wind arises—just like the tattered cassock of Master Wang in the northeast corner of the eastern corridor of the thirty-six cloisters at the Great Xiangguo Temple in the Eastern Capital.

(Jingshan Gao). [Added by Zeng] The Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "I have an object that is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it possesses none of the characteristics of male or female."
"Is there anyone here who recognizes this? At that time, the novice Shenhui stepped forward and said, "I recognize it.
The Patriarch asked, "What do you call it? He replied, "It is the original source of all Buddhas; it is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui.
The Patriarch then struck him and said, "If even calling it 'a thing' is already incorrect, how much more so to call it 'the original source'!"
The Source of Buddha-nature. The Verse says:
To call it "one thing" is already inadequate; how much less can it be pointed out as the "Source Buddha"?
Its manifestations are pervasive and all-encompassing, yet nothing can obstruct them; its movements and functions cannot be grasped. Vividly active, dark and lustrous—ask the people: do you know it?
"I know. I shall simply wait until the future to see Maitreya" (Haiyin Xin).
"A painter uses five colors to paint empty space; one must know that as soon as the brush touches the paper, the original track is lost.
"Furthermore, there was Wu Daozi of the Tang Dynasty, who spent his entire life laboring in vain over paper" (Cishou Shen).
When a single film obscures the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion. The novice Shenhui lost his money and incurred punishment;
he saw only the square head of the chisel, but failed to see the sharp point of the awl. Great Man, Little Śākyamuni: a single strike of the iron whip shatters the coral.
(Yuanwu Qin). [Added from another collection.
The Sixth Patriarch said to his disciples, "I wish to return to Xinzhou. You all should quickly prepare the boat.
A disciple asked, "When will the Master return from here? The Patriarch replied, "Leaves fall and return to their root; when I come back..."
"No Mouth. Fayan Xiu said: "Not only was there no mouth when he came, but when he went, he likewise had no nostrils.
He spoke in verse: "Leaves fall and return to the root;
when he came, there was no mouth. The water rises and the boat floats higher; the crow flies and the hare runs. Were it not for one who dwells among the forest trees..."
A lion cub, at three years of age, can already let out a great roar.
(Seal of the Ocean-Print) A single expanse of emptiness atop the mountain of the five aggregates; when coming, there is no mouth; when going, there is no trace.
To understand the principle of leaves returning to the root, one must finally reach this school in the final stage. (One Original Enlightenment)
The Patriarch’s way of hosting guests consists simply of the everyday tea and rice of the household.
Yet nowadays, his descendants insist on rare delicacies and exotic feasts. (Yuánwù Qín)
After the leaves fall and return to their root, a single drop from Caoxi is profound. Few people reach this mountain dwelling;
truly, one must be a connoisseur to appreciate it. (Longmen Yuan, 2)

Having returned to the root and attained the essential meaning, what more need be discussed? At the mouth of the cave, the Qin man has half-closed his door. As the flowers fall, they follow only the distant flowing stream;
left empty is the gathering of vast, billowing wild clouds.
Falling leaves return to their roots; the iron ox stands blocking the road. When he came, he had no mouth; seeking salt, he got vinegar.
The golden mallet does not move, yet it falls upon all mechanisms. Amidst the assembly of successive sages, he is the sixth patriarch. (Xuetang Xing)

The clouds part and the sky naturally expands; when the leaves fall, they return to their roots. Turning my head toward the misty waves, I hear the songs of fishermen passing by the distant village. (Songyuan Yue)
Xing is in the southern heavens at the very end of the sky; before he has even set out, he has already arrived in New State. When coming, he had no mouth; when going, he has no companion.
How much more so this autumn with its rustling yellow leaves? (Village Fool)

[Added to the Collection] Venerable Prajñātāra (the Patriarch of the Formless School in India), when asked by King Hīnayāna, "What is the Buddha? replied, "Seeing one's own nature is the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see his own nature? He replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "How do you see it? [The Master replied: "I see it as neither seeing nor not seeing. The King said, "If so, why do you say you see the Buddha-nature? The Master said, "Because I do not see it, I therefore see it. The King said, "This is truly the meaning of 'seeing the Buddha. The Master then composed a verse: "The nature of the mind is originally pure; It is not produced by causes and conditions. Since it is not produced by causes and conditions, It is neither existent nor non-existent. If one perceives existence or non-existence, That is merely a deluded view. If one can transcend both existence and non-existence, Then one is called a Buddha. The King then composed a verse: "The nature of the mind is originally pure; It is not produced by causes and conditions. Since it is not produced by causes and conditions, It is neither existent nor non-existent. If one perceives existence or non-existence, That is merely a deluded view. If one can transcend both existence and non-existence, Then one is called a Buddha. Upon hearing this, the King attained great enlightenment. He then prostrated himself at the feet of the Master and became a disciple. He subsequently changed his name to Śrīharṣa. The Master then departed for the West. 107b24. The Master replied, "The nature of the mind is the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see the Buddha? The Master replied, "I see the Buddha. The King asked, "How do you see him? The marvel of the bird carrying a flower: During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Fourth Patriarch observed the atmospheric omens from afar and knew that a person of extraordinary character was present.
He went in person to seek him out and saw the Master sitting upright. The Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am contemplating the mind.
The Patriarch asked, "What is it that contemplates? What is this mind? The Master had no reply and paid his respects.
The Master asked, "Virtuous One, where do you dwell in seclusion? The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk has no fixed abode.
The Master asked, "Do you know Chan Master Daoxin? He asked, "Why do you ask about him? The Master said, "I have long admired his virtue and hoped to pay him a visit.
The Patriarch said, "I am that very person. The Master asked, "For what reason have you come here? The Patriarch said, "..."
"I have come specifically to visit you. Is there perhaps another place for rest? The Master led him to the hermitage, where he saw only tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
The Patriarch raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this one remaining."
The Patriarch asked, "What did you see just now? The Master was speechless. The Patriarch wrote the character for "Buddha" (佛) upon the stone where the Master was sitting.
Upon seeing it, the Master stood in awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining. The Master, not yet understanding, requested that the Dharma be preached.

The Patriarch said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates all return to the single square inch of the mind; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained therein."

Purple qi mingles and permeates through the white clouds; having met the Master of the Lineage, the path from delusion is pointed out.
