falling flowers and flowing water wind around the riverside village. (Yuet Tang Chang)

Light does not illuminate the object, nor does the object exist; when both light and object are forgotten, there remains yet another trace. The fallen flowers covering the ground have been swept away by the wind;
as before, the flowing stream winds around the solitary village. (Kentang Chong)
It cannot be described, nor can it be painted. The Sleeping Dragon is forever wary of the clarity of the azure pool.
Even if one directs the mind toward it, it remains ultimately difficult to grasp; the adept must surely be startled in the dark. (Songyuan Yue)
[Added for Collection] Panshan addressed the assembly, saying: "Virtuous Chan practitioners, training in the Way is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering height;

it is like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. To be thus is what is called 'leaving home'. The Verse says: The earth supports the mountain, yet knows not its steepness; The stone contains the jade, yet knows not its purity. If one can act in this manner, This is truly called leaving home.
Since the mountain is solitary and steep, few travelers reach it; since the jade is flawless, its authenticity cannot be discerned.
(Sixin Xin) The earth is deep and the mountains high—by what cause is this so? Within them lies a massive uncut gem, unknown for ages.
If a person maintains such a state of mind at every thought, they are fit to be a lotus in the fire of the human world. (Benjue Yi)
Mountains forget their solitary loftiness; jade forgets its flaws. Wherever one reaches, the source of the immortals is my home.
How laughable that Ge Hong never realized this, traveling far from Goulu to inquire about cinnabar. (Lil Tianmu)

[Added from another source] Panshan said: "The path that goes upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages. Ciming said: "The path that goes upward has not been realized by the thousand sages.

Yangqi said: "It is stuck on the mouth. The verse says: The path that goes upward, Has not been transmitted by the thousand sages. It has not been realized by the thousand sages. It is stuck right on the mouth.
The path leading upward from Mount Pan—what words can describe it? Rarely is a traveler seen with pierced ears. When the mouth is placed upon it, there is nowhere to bite;
only then does one know that the thousand sages could not transmit it. (Baiyun Cuan)
It is not transmitted, for it is not so. Difficult to proclaim from the mouth of the ocean, atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, one launches an iron boat.
(Jingshan Gao) Not transmitted by the thousand sages until this day, when placed upon the mouth, it has no equal.
At the foot of Mount Dongting, in the heart of Lake Taihu, travelers on the road chatter in vain. (Songyuan Yue)
[Added from another source: As Panshan was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Is there anyone who can capture my true likeness?
The assembly presented the portraits they had painted, but none met the Master's approval. Puhua stepped forward and said, "I have captured it. The Master said:
"Why do you not present this to the old monk? Huaihua then performed a somersault and left.
The Master said, "This fellow will go on to act like one driven mad in the future. The Verse says:
The Master’s true form is so ugly and clumsy it cannot be presented; he has exhausted his body and mind, making people laugh to death.
Do not seek even a thread of meaning therein; a white-nosed Kunlun man celebrates the New Year. (Longmen Yuan)
Utterly frozen and still, no image remains; Performing a handstand upside down, it is difficult to grasp.
After the rains have ceased atop a thousand peaks following the Huangmei period, The crescent moon rises once more from the sea. (Xue’an Jin)
Clear, wondrous, and strange—a face born of a mother. How could one apply the brush of marvelous painting?
Though this fellow transmits it with tenfold likeness, he still paints a tiger and ends up with only a wildcat. (Bao Ye Yuan)
When Master Shuilao (a successor of Mazu) came to visit Mazu, he prostrated himself; as he was about to pose a question, Mazu gave him a single kick that sent him tumbling down.
The Master suddenly attained great enlightenment. Rising up, he laughed heartily and said, "How extraordinary!
How extraordinary! Hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable subtle meanings all reside within a single hair-tip."
Having realized the source above, the verse says:
A colt takes a single stride; a donkey falls to the ground. Laughing loudly, they rise up; the sheep bleat and the dogs bark. (Bye-hyeon Jun)
A single step that brings them down is enough for a great laugh; all their former skills have been in vain. Yet the snake’s head still seeks to scratch its itch;
ten thousand, a hundred thousand, emerge from a single hair. (Baiyun Yuan).
The floodwaters seize the opportune moment to penetrate the Patriarch’s intent; a colt takes a single stride and illuminates the root source.
The void collapses, leaving no idle space; one then boards an iron ship upon the vast blue sea. (Zhaojue Zong)

Chasing the galloping celestial colts across the sea, they have unexpectedly come to leap and trample, revealing their entire forms. A hundred thousand subtle meanings appear upon the tip of a single hair;
clapping my hands and laughing "he-he," I recognize him—Min, the Ancient Buddha.
[Continued Collection] The bamboo tubes must have already fermented it to maturity; I shall not decline, even if my cap tilts askew in intoxication.
The *túmí* has its own subtle fragrance, yet this is wine and was never a flower. (Lan’an Shu).
Immeasurable wondrous meanings are all encompassed; heaven and earth revolve as one unified whole.
Holding the "Smiling Blade" across the breast of the Yang, there still remains one more step to take upon the crown of the head. (Nanyuan Sheng)
It is said that spring has arrived, yet the wild winds blow with reckless frenzy. They blow the flowers away, following the current, and overturn the fishing boat. (Xue’an Jin)
[Supplement] When Shuilao encountered a monk who arrived, he drew a circle on the monk’s shoulder. The master struck it three times, then drew another circle and pointed at the monk.

The monk bowed, and the master struck him, saying, "This fellow who deceives with empty talk! Baoning Yong, at the place where the other monk had bowed, merely spat upon him and departed. He then offered this verse: A circle drawn on the shoulder, Three strikes and another circle;
The monk bows, and the staff falls— This fellow who deceives with empty talk! At the place of the other's bow, I simply spat and left.
To kick it away and bring back the fist is simply the norm. How can one avoid seeing the stars Shen and Shang?
Settling matters according to principle, without partiality—where the short is short and the long is long.

This is wrong, that is wrong—strictly avoid picking them up. The waves of the four seas have subsided; the tides of the hundred rivers have receded. The ancient strategy is loftily displayed at the twelve gates;
gate after gate has a path, yet all is empty and desolate. It is not desolate; the adept should seek the medicine for when there is no illness.
The paths of Changjing and Nanquan are not different; clearly, the principles of discourse distinguish between the intimate and the distant. Many do not need to polish the golden mirror;
the Han are simply the Han, and the Hu are simply the Hu. Pointing at the moon, one loses the way; lost in the ferry crossing, one is lost by one's own pointing.
To show you, he holds his staff as if it were nothing at all. (Fenyang Zhao)
The color and form are indeed like the real; when handled before people, it shines with even greater brilliance.
But when subjected to fire for a second smelting and test, in the end it turns out to be merely counterfeit silver. (Baoning Yong)
Whether it be so or not, if one discards medicinal taboos and intends to violate the boundaries, the entire army will suffer defeat.
From the tip of the staff emerges the ancient rhombus-flower mirror; throughout the world, the lineage flows forth from the true master. (Yuánwù Qín)
At dawn, as I departed from the capital city gates, I suddenly encountered two traveling merchants. One pointed toward the south for me; the other pointed toward the north.
To travel south, there was an official boat for crossing the river; to travel north, there was the great highway with its carriages and horses.
Although the paths to the south and north do not converge, they both lie within the single land of Central China. (Fojian Qín)
[Continued Collection] Zhenxi Tongfeng was like Zhangjing; Zhangjing was impartial, yet he drove a nail straight into his head.
That monk sought him out at Nanquan, who gave him a deep ladle-full, leaving him even more intoxicated. (By Banruo Rou)

"Is it so? and "Is it not so?"—the wondrous meaning is fully revealed. Changjing and Nanquan both suffered a defeat in this encounter. (Cangtang Qing): To say "it is" is dualistic speech; one has not yet emerged from the mud and water.
To say "it is not" is also dualistic speech; as before, one dies of oneself. Only when the staff is shaken and held upright does one stand forth resolute.
Under the bright sun and clear blue sky, the power of the wind returns to its time of decay; the great net that covers the heavens gives off a brilliant radiance.
(By Yuet Tang Chang.
Zhangjing says it is so, Nanquan says it is not; who can penetrate the waves against the current? Pity this fellow—his skin is gone.
Blood. The carriage and the blue dragon do not part; one does not dismount (Nantang Xing). "It is, it is.
He lets loose the true turtle-nosed dragon of the South Mountain. "It is not, it is not. He reins back the thousand-mile wind-chasing steed.

In the end, they meet with ruin and destruction—how pitiable! Their throats are choked so that no breath can escape; yet though there is no breath to escape, they possess the "snout" [of true realization].
Zhaozhou hangs a gourd from the eastern wall. How laughable is Vimalakīrti’s discourse on non-duality! (Qiong Gu-lian)
The mechanism of wondrous turning flashes like lightning; before one's eyes, life and death race against one another. A bright pearl has its own price as a bright pearl;
do not go to the edge of a fence to shoot at sparrows. (Muan Yong)
Magu asked Linji, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye?
Linji said, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
The Master stepped forward, pulled Linji down from his meditation seat, and sat there himself. As Linji approached him, saying, "How do you do? the Master hesitated, and Linji immediately shouted.
[The Master] pulled down the meditation seat and sat upon it; the Teacher then went out. The Verse says:
The Great Compassionate One asks about the source with his True Eye; Observe closely the mechanism of mutual exchange.
Whether one understands or not, it remains obscure and indistinct— Like a catfish climbing a bamboo pole. (Haiyin Xin)
When the Hero of the True Eye meets the True Eye, the distinctions of superior and inferior, long and short, are rendered useless.
Nanda manifests his original body; it was not produced by his parents. (Juehaiyuan)

For many years on the northern frontier, I have heard only his name; today, before the ranks, I behold him face to face. Riding alone on a single horse with a solitary lance, he fights through several bouts.
How excellent it is that, seeing the opportunity, he looses a single arrow! (Baoning Yong).
Meeting on a narrow path, it is difficult to turn back; a clash of arms in the space of a single instant.
Banners and drums flash across the field, utterly indistinguishable; tell me, who shall emerge victorious? (Puyongping).
[Continued Collection] A red-bearded barbarian with a beard like fire. The pearl rolls on the platter, the platter rolls the pearl.
Meeting on a narrow path, they boast of their skillful hands. On both sides, the snowy blades leave blood blurred and smeared. (Shitain Kū)
When the rebel bands met at midnight, they jostled for banners and seized drums to seek advantage.
Suddenly, when dawn broke and they saw one another again, their faces were covered in shame as each returned to his own place. (Bieshan Zhi)
When Mazu was visited by the Dharma Master Liangsui, the Master saw him coming and closed the door;
he then took a hoe and went out to weed the grass. Liangsui came again and knocked on the door. The Master asked, "Who is it? He replied, "It is I. The Master said, "You dull-witted monk, get out!
This happened four or five times in this manner, until Liangsui suddenly attained realization. He went back once more and knocked on the door.
[The Master] said, "Preceptor, do not deceive Liangsui. Had Liangsui not come to pay his respects, he would have been led astray by the twelve volumes of scripture for the rest of his life.
The Master then opened the door, allowing him to attain awakening, and certified him through the seal of approval.

Liangsui subsequently returned to the capital, where he dispersed his assembly at the lecture hall and told his disciples, "Wherever you people may find understanding, Liangsui has already attained it all."
[He] knew. While Liang-sui knew where [the truth] lay, the others did not. The verse says:
"The mechanism of compliance and resistance is not easily met; The great-rooted Liang-sui understood how to contemplate.
Were it not for long-accumulated matters of shared wind, How could he have been willing to turn his head and see the Dharma King? (Fenyang Shanzhao)
The Zen grove is deep and secluded; when first wandering about it, one is struck by its mystery. Tilling the weeds and closing the gate—how easy is it to look upon?
Do not say that the Old Teacher is entirely without merit; where he can deceive you, let him continue to deceive you. (Zhengjue Yi)

Shutting the door and carrying a hoe, he cultivates the most profound depths. Suddenly awakening to great enlightenment, he speaks of the original source. All his lifelong studies have been a labor in vain;
only now does he believe that the Yellow River flows on, rolling along to its end. (Haiyin Xin)
Shutting the door and taking up the hoe was already too late; to come back now is only to face further confusion.
Having long realized within the light that I had been deceived, I finally believe there is no one with whom I can leave the household life together. (Baizhang Yuan).
Shao Shi and Fen Yang were willing to grant him their approval; one who knows this will turn back and face the wind and waves.
Without ascending the mysterious pass of Magu, can you ever rest from the twelve canonical scriptures? (Zhaojue Zong)
Throughout my life, I have cast my heart and courage open to others; how many people are there who have reached this gate?
Since our parting, the old acquaintances of the capital city see the warm smoke and slanting sun as twilight falls once more. (Longmen Yuan)
Knocking on the door while the gates are closed, to whom can one speak? Upon hearing Su Gong’s words, one immediately knows where to return.
All former livelihoods have been cast aside; alas, those among the people of this age who understand are few. (Chu’an Fang)

[Continued Collection] Seeking words and chasing phrases is a manifold deception; it is simply because one has been deceived by the eyes since of old. If one can let go with a free hand, one returns to the ancestral land;
in secret thought, how many kinds of divergent paths there are! (Danxia Chun)
I personally arrived at Taoyuan, where the scenery was secluded and profound; a single jar of bright moonlight was as clear and still as autumn.
Reflecting back on the days when spring ended at the mouth of the cave, countless red blossoms were carried away by the flowing water. (Becoming withered trees.)
Magu called out in a loud voice, "Who is it?"—a single word so swift that even four horses could hardly catch up.
Thus, Master Sui shattered the cave of the spiritual essence, revealing the golden-haired lion cub. (Zhenjing Wen)

The gate is closed and one has entered the garden; it is already fully enclosed. A single call makes one turn the head and immediately arrive home. Liang-sui knew the time, yet people do not understand.
The sea and mountains are empty, reflecting the slanting rays of the setting sun. (Lan’an Xu)
To act as a human is to be thorough; to bite into raw iron, to go against the current, to drive a stake into empty space.
(Songyuan Yue) Where others know, Liangsui knows; where Liangsui knows, others do not know. Wang Wei is already dead and no one can exhaust his verse;
he leaves behind only the green mountains facing the setting sun. (Pō’ān Xiān)

Closing the door once more, I take up my hoe; the clouds are deep, and the path grows ever more winding. You must know that beyond form and shadow, I lay open my very heart and liver to you. (Xutang Yu)
Carrying his hoe, he did not look back; he simply went right on his way. Who would dare say, "You are a *zuozhu* (chairman/lecturer)"?

Chan Master Ruhui of Dongsi Temple in Hunan (who succeeded Mazu) once took issue with his disciples for incessantly reciting and memorizing the discourse "this very mind is Buddha," asking: "Where does the Buddha abide, that you say it is 'this very mind'?"
"The mind is like a painter; yet you say it is the Buddha. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way.
The sword has long since been lost, yet you are still marking the boat. A verse says:
"The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Though you may grasp this fully, I dare not guarantee it for you.
Carrying a staff and walking idly, take care not to turn your head or look back. (Zhao Tang’s one [line]).

"The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Green mountains and white clouds, falling flowers and fragrant grasses—if one is a clever master, one will never look back or turn around. (Gushan Gui)

After the rain has dispersed and the clouds withdrawn, there stand some dozens of towering peaks. Leaning on the railing, I look back again and again; turning my head, with whom can I share this? (Jingshan Gaofeng)

In times of great peace, the harvests are bountiful year after year. Travelers carry no provisions, and household doors remain unbarred. On the official roads there are no people, and the night is moonless;
singing as they go home, it is just the third watch. (Kaishan Xian)
The green mountains are not green; the white clouds are not white. The needle-point is too wide; the universe is too narrow. Sitting alone in vast silence, who knows?
A stream flows gently as flower petals drift by. The vast splendor of the scenery is not understood by men;
throughout the garden of spring, the partridges cry. (Miaofengshan)
Yesterday, as I passed west of the bamboo grove, A young child from a neighboring house cried out across the stream.
The mountains were cold and the waters solemn as half the leaves turned yellow and fell; Countless returning crows sought the trees for their roosts. (Xutang Yu)
When the sky clears and the sun rises, when rain falls and the earth becomes damp—though I have spoken my heart’s content, I fear you will not believe it. (No gate opens).
The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. A bird flies out from the forest; a startled snake enters the grass. Without a seam or crack, it is difficult to seek out.
[This] makes even the Broken Oven Abbot of Mount Song laugh to his heart’s content. (Nansou Lu).

The bright pearl of Zhènghǎi shines everywhere; from the beginning, this single jewel has been perfectly round and luminous.
When Mount Yǎng was once plundered by the Eastern Temple, he joined his palms and presented it as it happened. (Běnjué 1)

Skillfully caressing the Great A-sword, there shall surely be no injury to the hand; accustomed to weaving the whiskers of a fierce tiger, one must certainly possess a strategy for preserving the whole body.
The exquisite pearl of the ocean is skillfully displayed—seemingly detached from form, detached from sound, and detached from name. Within a sandalwood forest, one burns sandalwood itself.
A lion roars within the lion’s cave (Yuǎnwù Qín).
A lion cub within the lion’s cave, leaping beyond the herd to play with pearls and gems. When Míngzhàn of Guishān called out for him, he was utterly without a flaw;
though his principle is difficult to extend, he pierces through with the extraordinary (Nányán Shèng).
There are no words with which to respond; as soon as the mouth opens, one has already emitted light along with it. Dongsi did not know what to do with his intent;
he dug a pit a fathom deep and buried him therein. (Yunna Qing).

"Setting aside for a moment the case of having a question and receiving an answer, what is it like when there is neither question nor answer? The Master said, "I am afraid it will rot away. Baizhang said: [This refers to the Master’s response].
"I have always suspected you, elder brother. A monk asked Baizhang, "Please, Master, speak. Baizhang said, "A unified totality (yīhéxiàng) cannot be apprehended.
Later, a monk asked Changqing, who said, "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office;
yet among those beneath the forest trees, not one has ever been seen. The Verse says: [Verse omitted]

Spending his entire day discussing the treatises, he did not mark the passing years; his Zen mind was tranquil, attuned to the profound mystery. Amidst the winding white clouds, the green mountains remain;
this single Dharma, free from partiality, is transmitted through all eternity. (Da-mei Zhi)
[Added from another source: Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou (who succeeded Mazu) was once asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha?

This is precisely where all engagement ceases. The verse says:
A hundred thousand stumps of gnarled, azure-bearded pines; A few thousand uneven, jade-green bamboo stalks. The wind knocks at the moon-gate, cold as the third autumn month;
The rain beats upon the thatched hall, chilly as the sixth summer month. (Shixi Yue)
[Added from another source] Dazhu addressed the assembly, saying: "When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
when body, speech, and mind are impure, this is called the parinirvāṇa of a Buddha. Huanglong Nan said: "What a fine message!
This was an expedient means employed by the ancients to find an entryway for you all. Once you have found that entryway,"
Furthermore, one must find a way out. To climb a mountain, one must reach its summit; to enter the sea, one must reach its bottom.
If you climb a mountain without reaching the summit, you will not know the vastness of the universe; if you enter the sea without reaching the bottom, you will not know the depth of the blue ocean.
Having known both its vastness and its depth, he then uttered this verse:
One step overturns the four great oceans; one blow topples Mount Sumeru. Casting off the hand, one arrives home, yet people do not recognize it:
the magpies chirp and the crows caw among the cypress trees.

it is ever-uttering in its blazing intensity—who is there to hear it? (Fundamental Awakening, Part One).

Chan Master Weizheng of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou (a successor of Mazu) asked Nanquan, “Do the good knowledge-holders of all quarters have any teaching that they do not explain to people? Nanquan said, “There is. The Master asked, “What is it?
Nanquan replied, “It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. The Master said, “If that is so, then you have explained it.”

"You seem to have understood," [the Master] said. [The monk] asked, "I am just so; how about you, Teacher? The Master said, "I am not even a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend). How could I know whether there is a teaching that is spoken or one that is not?
[The monk] said, "I do not understand; I ask the Teacher to explain. The Master said, "I have already explained it to you quite enough. The verse says: You seem to have understood.

The Patriarchs and Buddhas have never acted for the sake of others; monks of past and present vie with one another in their headlong rush. A bright mirror stands upon its stand, reflecting myriad distinct forms;
each face looks south, gazing at the Big Dipper. The handle of the dipper hangs down, nowhere to be sought;
having grasped the nostrils, one has lost the mouth. (Xuedou Xian)
Nirvana is like the wind blowing through the old man’s sleeves; who can know the *ra-li-li-ra*?
Across the ridges, how many have misheard it, all at once calling it a *zhègūcí* (partridge song)? (Baiyun Cuan).
There is no one who does not know; when we meet, let us simply drink tea. Without seeking the path through clouds and water, how could one reach the monastery? (Changling Zhuo)
Who says that the Master has some subtle teaching? He earnestly urges others to reach the very bottom. Pressing his jade zither, he plays until dawn;
yet its sound does not enter the ears of the deaf. (Fujian Yongqin)
I turn my belly and empty my guts to speak to you; I do not know why you still hesitate.
Now is the very moment to grasp it with fierce resolve and entrust it to those in the world who have nothing to do. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] Baizhang and Nanquan discuss past and present; the dragon gives birth to a dragon’s cub—this is the grandmotherly heart.
If anyone wishes to recognize these two elders of Chan, they must know that to embroider a pair of mandarin ducks, one must have the needle. (Cishou Shen)

Luan-bird glue mends the severed strings; lion’s blood transforms donkey’s milk. From of old, he has not acted for the sake of others; throughout antiquity and the present, he has participated with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Once an arrow has left the string, there is no returning; if you wish to seize it, you must first firmly give it away. When speaking, he remains silent; when silent, he speaks.
A man came from Chenzhou and was heading toward Xuzhou. (Yuanwu Keqin).
Baizhang Zheng addressed the assembly, saying: "You all shall cultivate the fields for me, and I shall expound the Great Meaning for you."
When the communal labor for clearing the fields was completed, the assembly requested the Master to expound upon the Great Meaning. The Master extended both hands to show them.
He spoke in verse:
"I have always admired Baizhang’s skill in clearing the fields; It has been transmitted in the hands of practitioners through all time. Who says that his tongue has never moved?"
Movement. The five notes and six pitch-pipes revolve in great cycles. (Baizhang Cuan).
The Great Meaning has from the beginning been impossible to set forth; do not seek out the distant or the near beneath words.
If you now wish to recognize the Old Hero, he has produced a jade qilin with golden fur. (Foji Yu)
Opening his mouth, he spoke of the Great Meaning; later generations must not treat this lightly. Baizhang’s gate of total retention is plain yet possesses flavor. (Longmen Yuan)

Baizhang cleared the fields and expounded the Great Meaning; principle and phenomena were perfectly integrated, leaving nothing unprepared. His Brahma-voice was pure and resonant, heard throughout the ten directions;
the grasses, trees, hoes, and spades all rose up in response. At the end, he once again unfurled his two fists—dragging through mud and water, appearing as if dull-witted.
The boat drifted to the shore five thousand *li* away; to mark the boat’s side in search of a sword is but idle effort. (Fóxìng Tái)
[Continued Collection] He spread his two hands at that moment and said: "The Great Meaning circulates throughout the world;
do not say that when entering a weedy field one does not pick [the grain]. Nowhere is the grass not overgrown. (Muan Zhong).
The Great Master opened the fields and established the ancestral foundation; he clearly recorded the deeds and documents to show how they should be maintained.
His descendants refuse to leave behind the legacy of their ancestors, begging for food year after year as they toil upon the roads. (Lan’an Xu)
The labor for clearing the fields is complete; everyone is covered in water and mud.
With both hands outstretched, do not ask anyone why—last night at the third watch, the moon set in the west. (Cican Jing)
Baizhang expounds the Great Meaning; it is utterly without a handle. His entire body is nothing but mud and water;
he drowns upon level ground. (Wujie Pai).

Mazu said, "Lower your voice and come closer. The Master approached; Mazu gave him a slap and said, "Six ears do not share a secret.
Come back tomorrow. On the following day, the Master entered the Dharma Hall and said:
"Please, Preceptor, speak. The Patriarch said, "Go for now; wait until I ascend the hall, and I shall come out to bear witness for you.
The Master then attained realization and said, "I thank the Great Assembly for bearing witness. He circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.

The rooster crows at the thatched inn as the moonlight shines bright; The traveler’s dream is so deep he has not yet awakened. When his eyes open, the sky is already wide dawn;

Eighteen beauties remain unmarried; I constantly rely on matchmakers to seek them out well.
Once they have married the man from the Pan family, they immediately lose all sense of shame before others. (From *Zhuyou Jian*)

He then offered this verse: Three old men, Huddling together, Talking in their sleep. If you wish to penetrate thoroughly, You must investigate this great tiger all at once.

Without the Vajra-eye upon the crown of the head, who can discern that which transcends both the vertical and the horizontal? (Kaixian Ying)
Five times five is twenty-five. The great beast is originally a tiger; how could a dog and a cat ever speak at the same time?
Close the door at night and open it early in the morning; you must believe that its sharp fangs and claws are terrifying. Yet, from the threshold of every house, one passes through to Chang’an.
All are the paths for examination candidates ascending to the imperial court. (Fujian Qin).
Chan Master Huizang of Shigong Mountain in Fuzhou (a successor of Mazu) was originally a hunter who shot deer.
Having encountered Mazu, [Dongshan] was told to shoot himself, but he found no place to apply his hand. He attained awakening and entered the monastic life.
After receiving the Dharma and residing on the mountain, he would constantly have his bow drawn and an arrow set. Whenever he saw a monk approach, he would say, "Watch the arrow!
One day, Sanping arrived; the Master said, "Watch the arrow. Sanping then bared his chest and met it head-on, saying, "This is killing."
"The human arrow. [Zhao] Ping asked, "And what about the living human arrow? The Master snapped his bowstring three times. Ping then prostrated.
The Master said, "For thirty years I have drawn my bow and set my arrows, yet I have only managed to shoot half a sage.
He then broke the bow and arrows. Later, Ping went to see Dadian and recounted the previous conversation. Dadian said, "Since it is already alive..."
"The Human Arrow. Why did he discern it upon the bowstring? "Level, there is no counterpart. He then studied under him again.
Having attained realization, he became the successor to Duan. The verse says:
Drawing the bow and setting the arrow, he calls you back; you do not realize the Master has come with special intent. Everyone follows along, wandering in delusion and intoxication;
within the words they recognize shadows, yet those shadows cannot be opened. Sanping has still not fully grasped it;
the thunderclap resounds throughout the nine realms. (Fenyang Zhao)
For thirty years he has served a single bow; with that one bow, the bowman seeks to stabilize the world within its bounds.
How could he know that though the "Semi-Sage" (the Buddha) offered his submission, the message was not conveyed by the surrendering of jade and the leading of sheep? (By Zhengjue Yi).
Setting the arrow and drawing the bow, he used them with profound skill; throughout his life, he delighted in hitting the red heart.
Later, though he obtained but half a person, it was through the fierce fire that he became gold refined a hundred times. (Foyin Yuan)
Drawing the bow and setting the arrow is not for naught; though many may hit the mark, their lives are not preserved. When the semi-sage strikes the opportune moment, there is no other intent;
why must those of great merit be depicted in the Lingyan Gallery? (Fohuiquan)
For thirty years he drew his bow and set his arrow; though he struck, it was but three pings, incomplete. How can this compare to where ten thousand people point all at once:
a single wild goose falls into the autumn sky amidst the slanting sun? (Foguo Bai)
For thirty years he has held the bow and arrow; only when Sanping arrived did he split open his chest.
Half a sage is attained today; when will one encounter Dadian beyond the bowstring? (Chongsheng Gongsu)
[Continued Collection] In ancient times there was Master Shigong. He sat with his bow and arrows set, in this manner for thirty years; not a single person of true understanding appeared.
Sanping hit the mark, and father and son met in harmony. Reflecting deeply upon it, one realizes that he was originally just a target for arrows. (Fadeng Qin)
The arrow piercing his chest was split apart; why did only half a person remain? Because he understood the path, he could not remain whole.
(An of Lingyan in Guanzhou).
Recognizing the speckled one, he hurriedly drew his bowstring; with a single arrow howling through the wind, he went forth and startled heaven.
Drawing near, observe him closely: who could have shot through the stone of Lantian? (Xinwen Ben).
How many years has he strung his bow and set his arrow? He received from Sanping, yet his mechanism remains incomplete.
Had he been able to shoot like Hou Yi at that time, he would have avoided falling off the mark upon the bowstring. (Shuian I)
The Venerable Master Zhongyi of Langzhou (a successor of Mazu) would often see monks and clap his hands and pucker his lips, saying, "O-yeh!
O-yeh! When Yangshan arrived to pay his respects, he walked from east to west and stood there. The Master asked, "Where did you learn this samādhi?
Yangshan replied, "I learned it from Deyin at Caoxi. The Master said, "Just so, just so."
Shishan then asked, "From where did you, Master, obtain this samādhi? The Master replied, "I obtained it from Zhangjing. The verse says:

Puffing his lips, clapping his hands, and making a "ya" sound with his mouth, he directly challenged those who came to distinguish the right from the wrong. Though thousands and tens of thousands passed by, none realized it.
As soon as Yangshan saw him, he recognized him as one of his own (Fenyang Zhao).
The transmission from Caoxi was a mistaken seal; the Master of Zhangjing’s place of reception was coarse.
One might have thought the barbarian’s beard would turn the world red, yet it turns out there is still a red-bearded barbarian. (Zhengjue Yi)
Yangshan was skilled at questioning; Zhongyi was skilled at responding. Turning back and forth, every beat was a command.
(Cishou Shen) [Added by Zeng]. Once, because Yangshan asked Zhongyi, "How can one attain the vision of one's nature?
the Master said, "Suppose there is a room with six windows. Inside is a monkey. Outside, a monkey calls from the east, 'Singing-sing!'"
The monkey immediately responded. When the master called out to all six windows in this manner, each responded simultaneously.
Guishan bowed and said, "Just now, through the Master’s parable, I have understood everything. However, there is one further matter:
if the inner monkey is dozing while the outer monkey wishes to see it, what then? The Master descended from his rope-seat and took Guishan by the hand.
He performed a dance and said, "Singing-sing! I have finished meeting with you. The Verse says:
In each of the six windows, he calls out to the monkey. Having fallen fast asleep, how can one respond? I simply apply the whip to bring him to his senses;
At that time, Zhongyi was merely drifting along indifferently. (Benjue I)
Sleeping frozen in a snow hut as the night crumbles away; deep and secluded, the wattle gate does not open at night. One observes the shifting transformations of the withered gardens;
the spring breeze blows up the ashes from the *lǜ* tubes. (Tiantong Jue)
Every person has an old monkey; from evening to morning, it never ceases its antics of "four in the evening, three in the morning.
When called upon, it immediately knows where to land, rolling a golden ball across the eight-flowered tiles. (Cishou Shen)
A single room, vast and empty, facing six windows; the monkey remains, with none to compare it. When the mind is forgotten and thoughts cut off, the monkey dies;
the whole land is at peace, and the six states submit. (Nantang Xing)
A single room is desolate, the six windows are wide open. Within it, Mount Yangshang himself creates and himself arises;
he handles and plays with a single monkey, performing a thousand kinds of gestures. "Washing basin! Washing basin! I know you! (Huanshan Ning).
The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases in the Chan School, Volume Twelve.
The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases in the Chan School, Volume Thirteen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty.
Continued Collection of the Anecdotes of the Patriarchs by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery during the Yuan Shaoxing Era;
the Fourth [Section] of the Third Generation after the Sixth Patriarch (the Fourth of the Second Generation after Nanyue).
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Changer of Letan in Hongzhou (a successor of Mazu). Once, when Nanquan came to visit him, the Master was sitting with his face against a wall.
Nanquan patted the Master’s back. The Master asked, “Who is it? Nanquan replied, “Puyuan. The Master asked, “How is it?”
[The monk] said, "It is just ordinary. The Master said, "Why do you make such a fuss? The Verse says:
Facing the wall, the precarious heap allows guests to pass; When asked who it is, he asks back, "How is it? To say it is ordinary already constitutes making a fuss;
If one examines my own affairs, they are even more numerous. (Xiyuan Hui)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] National Teacher Wuye Dada of Fenzhou (who succeeded Mazu). A monk asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Do not forget your thoughts.
The Verse says: Do not forget your thoughts; This very mind is the Buddha. If you seek it elsewhere, You will wander for ten thousand miles.
The King’s majestic authority—who would dare compare themselves to it? A mere hair’s breadth of movement and the iron wheel follows.
People of the time see only the sharpness of the tip of the awl; how many can see the awl at the tip of the sharpness? (Lan’an Xu)

Wu Ye addressed the assembly, saying: "If there is even a hair’s breadth of sentiment regarding sagehood or ordinariness that has not been exhausted, one will inevitably enter the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse. Baizhang Yuan said:

"Even if every last trace of sentiment regarding sagehood or ordinariness were suddenly exhausted, one would still not avoid entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse. You blind fellows, just act this way!"
How could one understand? The verse says:
Why is there such urgency regarding "no karma"? Why is the white cloud so solitary? One might think the barbarian’s beard is red, yet there is still a red-bearded barbarian.
(Nanyuan’s Excellence):
A single path as straight as a bowstring; heart and hand in perfect accord. When the arrow pierces the shadow of the red sun, only then is one a man who shoots the eagle.
(Gushan Gui). [Added by Zeng] Chan Master Dayi of Ehu in Xinzhou (a successor of Mazu) was summoned into the palace for debate by Imperial Edict of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty.
A Dharma Master asked, "What is Chan? The Master pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master was speechless.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has expounded upon infinite sutras and treatises, yet you say that even this single point remains beyond your reach.
The Master then cited an instance: When Emperor Shunzong asked Chan Master Śrī, "How can all sentient beings in the great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood?
Śrī replied, "Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water; it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. The Master said this to the Emperor.

[The Emperor] said, "Buddha-nature is not something seen, yet it must be seen. How can one grasp the moon in water? The Emperor then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked.

The Emperor attained silent realization. The Verse says: Buddha-nature is not something seen, yet it must be seen; How can one grasp the moon in water? The Emperor then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? The Master replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked. The Emperor attained silent realization.
One falls because of the ground and arises because of the ground; to seek to arise apart from the ground is illogical.
Though one’s words may be intimate when not departing from what was asked, if one remains attached to them, it is still not it as before. (The Mirror of Withered Meditation).
Explaining principles and discussing the truth before the Purple Palace—how much toil was wasted on the Great Meaning of Geohu!
Since the Buddha-nature has always been difficult to name or fathom, how can it compare to the King’s intimate, silent realization? (Tianmu Li)
"What is that single point in the sky? Even if one were to expound infinite sutras and treatises, what can be done? It is a commodity that cannot be recognized.
Although its value is as immense as Mount Sumeru, it has nonetheless been seen through by the Sovereign. (The nun Xianlin Ying).
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Zongyin of Sanjiao Mountain in Tanzhou (a successor of Mazu) addressed the assembly, saying:
"If one discusses this matter, even to 'lower the eyebrows' is already to have missed it. Magu then asked: "I do not ask about lowering the eyebrows;
what is this matter? The Master said: "You have missed it. Magu then overturned the meditation seat.
The Master struck him with his staff. Changqing spoke on his behalf, saying, "Silent. The Verse says:
The true command is majestic and stern, allowing no admission; The stars shift and the constellations turn, yet no trace can be found.
The General reined in his vanguard horse; A chaotic miasma of killing intent rolls forth like a black wind. (Daitang Ding)
[Added for collection] Sanjiao addressed the assembly, saying: "In preaching the Dharma, one must always act in accordance with the time and the occasion.
At that time, a monk asked: "What is it like when there are four yellows and four reds? The Master said: "Carried on the tip of a staff in the third month.
The monk asked: "Why is his belly full of air? The Master said: "What can one do about a single rope? The monk asked: "How can one get out?"
The air left. The Master said, "Wait until the skin is worn through. The Verse says:

Establishing oneself on level ground, one still refuses to rest; Following the flow of time through flower-shaded groves and willow paths. Let it be released so that the belly is full of no lingering resentment;
Only then will you believe this fellow has attained true freedom. (Cishou Shen)
[Added from another source] A monk asked Sanjiao Yin, “What are the Three Jewels? The Master said, “Rice, beans, and millet. The monk asked, “What is the meaning of this?

The Master said, “The assembly rejoices and practices accordingly. The verse says: Rice, beans, and millet— The Three Jewels are thus revealed. When the great assembly hears them, They all rejoice and practice accordingly.
The three-cornered tally exchanges for rice, beans, and millet; the dragon palaces and ocean treasuries cannot contain them all. An old monk from Shushan was once questioned by one of the Empty Gate:
"He simply said, 'Nowadays, our porridge and rice are sufficient. (Da Hong Sui).
Chan Master Baoyun of Luzu Mountain in Chizhou (a successor of Mazu) would habitually turn his back to the wall whenever a monk approached.
Hearing of this, Nanquan remarked, "I usually tell the monks to try to understand [the Way] before the Buddha appeared in the world;
yet I cannot find even one or half of one who succeeds. For him to act like that—when will he ever get it? (It will take as long as a donkey's years.)
Xuánjué said, "Is this a matter of responding in song or refusing to speak?
Bǎofú asked Chángqìng, "As for Lǔzǔ’s essential point, where does it lie, given that Nánquan spoke in such a manner? Chángqìng said:
To withdraw for oneself and yield to another—among ten thousand, there is not one who does so.
Luoshan said, "If Old Teacher Chen had seen him at that time, he would have given him five strokes with the fire-brush. Why? Because he knew how to let go but did not know how to gather it back.
Xuansha said, "If I had seen him at that time, I too would have given him five strokes with the fire-brush. Yunju Xi added, "I too would have given him five strokes with the fire-brush."

Xunshan said, "If Sha, you speak entirely in this manner, do you mean they are all the same, or is there a distinct principle? If you can discern this, I will grant that the Dharma of the Venerable has a place to go. Xuanyue said, "Now tell me: did Xuansha’s five-fingered staff hit him or not?

The verse says: Xunshan’s words were like a thunderclap; Xuansha’s staff was like a flash of lightning. If you can see through them both, Then you have attained the Way. If you cannot, You are still lost in the weeds. Do you know where he went? He went straight to the Buddha-land. *Note:
This passage concerns a dialogue between Xunshan (Luo Shan) and Xuansha regarding the nature of realization and the transmission of the Dharma.*
When people come, he sits facing the wall, solemn and reverent; he does not engage in much talk or discuss points of difference and agreement.

Being intimate and direct, he does not teach others to seek outside the mind, thereby sparing them from calling out "light" and "darkness" to those who are blind and deaf. When the autumn frost spreads across the earth, cold and heat arise;
Lu Zu’s compassionate descent requires no effort. (Fenyang Shao)
The aged Chan master transmitted the lineage to Lu Zu. Upon seeing a monk, he faced the wall and personally bestowed his gaze.
If one among them is a true man, he will raise his eyebrows and depart immediately. (Foyin Yuan)
Luzu’s samādhi is the most effortless. As soon as he saw a monk approach, he would turn his back to the wall.
If one is of like mind and has realized the Way, there is no need for a raised brow to understand one another. (Liangshan Ji)
The Patriarch faced the wall and spread [the Dharma] throughout all quarters; countless Zen practitioners vainly attempt to measure it.
With nothing to do, I stand late at evening upon the riverbank; several withered cypress trees lean against the slanting sun. (Langya Huijue)
Seated, he cuts off a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks; he urges people to eliminate the difficulty of right and wrong.
Recently there has been no news from Chiyang; indeed, Guozhong did not see it with his own eyes back then. (Cuiyan Zhen)
Facing the wall, all say this is the highest capacity; yet when a monk reaches this point, where does he go?
Even if one were to cut off the waters of the thousand rivers, it would still fall under the second blow of the Chan school. (Haiyin Xin)
Luzu’s solitary wind shakes the four quarters; when monks come, he faces the wall, known by few.
Nanquan brings up an event from the age of donkeys—tell me, what time is it now? (Baiyun Cuan).
In those days, Luzu did not apply himself to effort; meeting monks, he faced the wall to manifest his family style.
If one encounters a peer of the highest vehicle—(please continue this line: Huanglong Xin).
How laughable is that old, ancient master of Chiyang! When a monk comes, he faces the wall—what does he intend to do?
For those who are naturally upright, whether man or woman, there is no need for the application of rouge and powder to achieve purity. (Cao Tang Qing)
Though not a writer, one naturally knows right from wrong in another's house. Returning a blow is like striking someone;
a flushed face is no match for straightforward speech. (Huanglong Zhen)
Before Mount Luzu, the ancient road leads through; a single, faint path vanishes east and west. Amidst the cries of the cuckoo, the spring light fades;
fallen peach blossoms carpet the ground in crimson. (Puyongping)
If there are no strings, how can one play? If there is no melody, who will listen? The gourds, earth, leather, and wood naturally harmonize with the notes gong and shang.
Throughout the vast silence of a thousand ages, the men of Shaolin also say that for nine years they transmitted this command. (By Fuxincai)
At Chi Yang, where could one even begin to grasp it? Later generations’ deliberations diverge onto different paths.
The ancients were stubbornly prone to making too much of things; let us ask: do you understand it now? (Longmen Yuan).
[Continued Collection] Tiger paths and dragon springs wind around the crags; phoenixes perch amidst frost, cranes harmonize with the cypress trees.
Who can grasp the meaning of the Patriarchal Master? To turn heaven and earth—how excellent! (The Daoist Kefu).
When Luzu saw a monk facing the wall, he said, "What prevents this principle from being direct? People of the present day must not attempt to measure it;
simply this [point] requires no expenditure of mental effort. Among those who heard this, some stubbornly claimed it was merely an act of accommodation.

They not only slandered the ancients, but also brought confusion to those of superior intelligence. If you realize the Patriarch is manifest before you, even if you do not understand, it is difficult to escape.
(Yongming Shou): "When Nanquan’s black bean had not yet sprouted, his prattling was ultimately a leaking of the celestial mechanism. Do not seek full awakening within that which has not yet arisen;
the sun rises in the east and the moon sets in the west. (Yaoshan Yu).
Facing the wall at Chiyang—who could have known? For ten thousand ages, a solitary peak faces the setting sun.
As soon as he saw him frown, he turned back; had he known earlier that this was no man of true character. (Lan’an Xu)
Luzu met people face-to-face and turned his wall toward them; being old and weary, he was too indolent to follow after them.
Later disciples could not fathom this and have consistently been like those striking tiles or divining by tortoise shells. (Shuian I)
Leaves fall by the riverbank; a single glance stretches far and wide. A few tall trees lean against the slanting sun.
Having once been where the monkeys wailed in the Ba Gorges, even an iron heart would break with grief. (Jiandang Ji)
Turning one's back to the front and facing behind, one reveals the family’s disgrace. With a thunderous voice that shakes the earth, he roars the lion’s roar.
He entrusts this to Xiantuo—do you know it or not? The Dharma-body at midnight hides within the Big Dipper. (Zuanjian)
Family wealth and possessions are all lost; not even a single thread remains. This solitary body alone is already regretted as too much.
Yet, in the deepest reaches of Chiyang, he kills people empty-handed, carrying no blade. (Shi’an Shao)
The sightless seer feels the bones; groping in the dark, he identifies kings and lords. Though the price is high, in the end no one buys it.
Let the stall cool down; there is nothing more to do but laugh it off. (Xue’an Jin)
On a warm day, a beautiful woman embroiders slowly. On the branches of the purple *zhíjīng* tree, yellow orioles warble.
If you wish to know the boundless sorrow of spring, it lies entirely in that moment when she halts her needle and remains silent. (By Nansou Long)
When people come to face the wall, what is accomplished? How can they achieve the opening of the mind and see the original source?
Before the empty kalpa, all sons of the Buddha—the *huatou* need not be raised, and it is naturally complete. (Heunggwam Gong)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Luzu, “What is ‘speaking without words’?
The Master said, “Where is your mouth? The monk said, “I have no mouth. The Master said, “Then with what do you eat your rice? The monk was speechless.
Dongshan said, “He is not hungry; why would he eat rice? Xuedou said, “A good opportunity—strike him across the back!”
"Strike! This fellow cannot close his mouth once he has opened it, nor can he open it once he has closed it.

The verse says: To gain through loss is to dwell in the extremes of being and non-being; If the root source is not severed, the branches and shoots remain linked. When there is no speaking, where is the mouth?
Once the body is turned around, it is difficult to carry down. A single sail catches the wind across Lake Dongting; One must know it face-to-face.
Already in contradiction. (Chang of Yuedang).
[Added from another source] Zen Master Datong of Ziyu Mountain in Tangzhou (a successor of Mazu) was once questioned by Prime Minister Yu Di:
“I beg the Master for a single word regarding the ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma. The Master said, “If you would ask, you must set aside all conceptualizations.
The official said, “I request it now. The Master said, “Simply ask what you wish. The official asked, “What is the Buddha? The Master called out, “Yu Ti! The official responded, “Yes.
The Master said, “Seek no further. The verse says: The call and the response— This very moment is the Buddha. Do not seek elsewhere; Right here, there is nothing more.
"What is the Buddha? Do not seek it elsewhere; we shall follow you. (The Four Continents / Moon Forest Contemplation).
[Added by Zengshou] Once Master Ziyu asked Master Yu: "What is it that 'a black wind blows its ship, causing it to drift and fall into the land of the rākṣasa demons'?
The Master said, "Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a thing?"
Yushi lost his color. The Master pointed and said, "This is precisely being blown by black winds and cast into the land of the rākṣasa demons.
Yushi prostrated himself and offered thanks. The verse says:
Attacking the person to plunder the strength of our own kind; we summoned a worthy lord whose wisdom-eye is lofty. The look of anger vanished to who knows where;
like rolling pearls and turning jade, they passed through the cloud-like robe. (Nanyan Sheng)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Yinfeng of Mount Wutai (who succeeded Mazu). One day he took his leave of Mazu. Mazu asked, "Where are you going? The Master said, "To Shitou.
Mazu said, "The path at Shitou is slippery. The Master replied, "Carrying pole and staff wherever I go, I perform my art upon meeting the stage.
He then departed. As soon as he arrived at Shitou, he circumambulated the meditation seat once and shook his staff.
[The Master] went down. [The monk] asked, "What is the essential point? The Head said, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master was speechless.
Upon returning, he related this to Mazu. Mazu said, "Go back to him again. When he says 'Heaven! Heaven!', you should then let out two sighs."

The Master went again and asked exactly as before. Tou then sighed twice. The Master remained silent once more. Upon returning, he recounted this to Mazu. Mazu said, "I told you that the path at Shitou is slippery.
Verse: The path at Shitou is indeed slippery; Even a single step can cause one to fall. If you wish to avoid such a mishap, Do not go there with your own mind.
The stony path is perilous; few can reach it. Only those who arrive know how slippery it is, like moss.
Though they stumble two or three times, drenched head to toe in mud and water, they return once more. (Xutang Yu)
Singing out the golden threads, once more blowing the purple jade flute; leaning against the tower, the person is not seen, as the wind passes and the tree-tops sway.
[Added from another source: Yinfeng, because Nanquan took the pure pitcher and gave it to the Master, saying: "The pure pitcher is an object; you must not..."
"Touching upon an object, he said to me, 'Bring some water. The Master took his *kamaṇḍalu* and poured water before the spring, then stopped.
Guizong said, 'Deng Yinfeng was also pouring it out in confusion. The verse says:
Nanquan pointed directly at the bottle; Yinfeng immediately came to scoop water. Both men were shameless, digging deep into the earth to bury themselves. (Zhaotang’s "One").

Nanquan did not point to the water pitcher; Yinfeng never once spilled the water. Let them go on beating tiles and boring through tortoise shells—the Buddha-dharma is not to be found here. (Gushan Gui)
When there is no film in the eyes, there is no need to scratch them; when there is no dust on the mirror, it need not be polished. Trusting one’s feet, step out the door and walk the great road;
slinging the staff over the shoulder crosswise, sing a mountain song. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Added from the Supplement] Chan Master Shenzang of Matou Peak in Cizhou (a successor of Mazu) ascended the hall and said to the assembly:
"To know while being without knowing is not the same as being without knowing; it is called 'being without knowing' because one knows. Nanquan said:
"If you follow the Master's words in this way, you have only spoken half of it. Huangbo said: "It is not that Nanquan was refuting him."
He concluded the previous discourse. The verse says:
Counting from the beginning, one, two, three; Counting backward, it becomes three, two, one.
Even if you were skilled at the Great Divination (Dayan) calculations, Finger-snap counting the lines would not yield the result. (Zhong’an Kong)
[Added from the Supplement] Chan Master Huilin Shanjue of Tanzhou (a successor of Mazu). When Minister Pei visited the Master, he asked, "Does the Master have an attendant?
The Master replied, "I do; however, he is not permitted to see guests. The Minister said, "What harm is there in that?"
The Master then called out, "Da-kong (Great Empty), Xiao-kong (Small Empty). Only then did two tigers emerge from behind the hermitage.
Upon seeing them, Pei was struck with terror. The Master said to the two tigers, "There is a guest here; depart now. Thereupon, the two tigers roared and left.

[The student] asked, "What kind of practice did you, Master, perform to bring about such a result? The Master held up his rosary and said, "Do you understand? [The student] replied, "I do not understand.

The Master said, "This old monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara. Verse: The Master holds up the beads and asks, "Do you understand? The student replies that he does not. The Master says: "I am always reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara."
Constantly mindful of the power of Avalokiteśvara, one subdues fierce beasts. With the path-eye clear and penetrating, how could the myriad conditions exist?
How excellent is the Great Being who constantly extends his hand! Keeping this in mind, dwelling in this, one shall enjoy peace and long life. (By Yuan of Longmen)
From Silla, Bohai, India, and this land—where the moon is white and the wind is clear, walking alone through the three realms—with no mind toward objects, taming tigers in the hermitage.
When he suddenly grasps his prayer beads, who recognizes this foremost pivot of the present? How extraordinary!
To overcome the most formidable, one must be the lion’s cub. (Nantang Xing)

[Added for inclusion: When the two senior monks Xuán and Shào visited Master Wujiu (who was a successor of Mazu), the Master asked, "Where have you two Zen travelers set out from? Xuán replied, "Jiangxi. The Master struck him and said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a pivotal function. The Master continued, "Since you do not understand, let the monk behind you respond. [Xuán then pointed to Shào. The Master struck him as well and said, "This fellow has also been here before. Shào then bowed. The Master said, "You two have come from afar; stay for a while. They stayed for several days. One day, the Master asked Xuán, "What is it like when the great matter is suddenly realized? Xuán replied, "It is like a person who has lost their way and suddenly finds the path. The Master said, "You have attained it, but you have not yet seen it. He then asked Shào, "What is it like when the great matter is suddenly realized? Yi asked for instruction, but the Master did not look at him. Yi shouted, "This ill-mannered old fellow!
Wait until I report you one by one to those with clear eyes. The Master then threw down his tea basket and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
Xuedou said, "Zechuan only knew how to hold fast to the borders; however, he was unable to die together [with the Master]."
Born at that time, he was fond of pulling off people’s head-covers (*fùtóu*). Who would dare call him Master Páng?
The Verse says:
Meeting and recognizing one another, they invite each other in vain; The clear waters and deep ravines cut across the bridge. Countless words and explanations are utterly useless.
Listen! Hurrying to bolt the doors is but a weary labor.
(Baoning Yong) Whom can one entrust with the mechanism of these two elders? The turban is pulled off and the hair hangs in disarray;
In the deep mountains, the path taken is forgotten, As if the cries of monkeys resound within the azure ravine. (Lan’an Shu)

A beauty of twenty-eight, skillfully painting her brows, pierces the curtain and enters the chamber with a mind like that of a madwoman. In vain do they labor with laughter and speech to flirt and dally;
would an old mountain elder with white hair ever deign to pluck her? (Bao Ye Yuan)
[Zeichuan was one day sitting in the abbot’s quarters when a lay practitioner (jushi) came to see him and said, “I only knew you were sitting upright in your chamber;
I did not realize a monk had arrived for an audience. At that moment, the Master lowered one leg. The practitioner immediately stepped out three or two paces and then returned.
The Master then withdrew his leg. The practitioner said, “This may truly be called freedom and spontaneity. The Master [affirmed this].
He said, "I am the host. The scholar said, "Master, you know only the host; you do not know the guest. The Master called to his attendant to prepare tea;
the scholar performed a dance and departed. Nantang Xing commented: "Excellent! Both Mazu and Pang are excellent.
Observe these two masters meeting in such a manner—it is like two dragons playing with a jewel."
Neither harms the other. This is what is called entering the forest without disturbing the grass, and entering the water without disturbing the waves.
Only upon reaching this point does one know there is a state of absolute freedom. Now tell me, what is it that possesses such spiritual efficacy?
(After a long silence) He then recited a verse:

The treasure within the patch-robed monk’s breast; the pearl in the scholar’s sleeve. When the Master walks, one follows by walking; when the Master hastens, one follows by hastening. Furthermore, the verse says:
“When the River is skilled at singing, the Layman can dance; the clouds follow the dragon, and the wind follows the tiger. The lion yawns and roars.”
The Elephant King looks back; the Dipper hides its body while the Moon Palace pursues the hare. He has worn his straw sandals through, yet he has not moved a single step.
It is better to dwell in suffering than to practice for pleasure; a poor host is better than a wealthy guest.
To advance and retreat—to speak of this principle—his sleeves dance and his song resounds as he returns. (Zhengjue Xian).
[Added to the Collection] Master Dadi of Xinzhou (who succeeded Mazu) received the essential instruction from Jiangxi. He constantly concealed his name;
whenever a student posed a question, he would only respond by striking the ground with his staff. Thus, he was known as "Master Dadi" (Staff-Striking Ground).
One day, a monk hid the staff away before posing a question; the Master simply opened his mouth. The monk—
He asked his disciples, "If someone asks me this every day, 'What is the meaning of striking the ground? what would you do?

A disciple immediately took a piece of firewood from within the hearth and threw it into the cauldron. The verse says: A single piece of wood thrown into the cauldron— The whole world is filled with its fragrance. When the fragrance reaches the nostrils, It is not something that can be grasped by the hand.
I ask my Master: all [the patriarchs] struck the ground. Although the points of inquiry differ, the principle does not; the ancients all entered through this very gate.
This was already an act of compassion performed for their sake. (By Banyu Rou)
The true matter before the Mountain of the Purple Chamber: A staff is always held in one's hand. Countless people from south and north ask for a way across;
I only strike the ground to report to the blind and the deaf. (Fenyang Zhao)
The mallet strikes the ground; only then does one believe there is nothing discarded in vain. One sees only the square head of the chisel, having lost the sharp point of the awl. (Cishou Shen)
Sitting upright as if in non-action, he strikes the ground whenever he meets someone. Startled, the Spirit of Space flees into the nostrils of the Persian. (Bǎoshòu Lè of Fuzhou).
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Master Bishu of Jiangxi (a successor of Mazu). One day, when Daowu returned from outside, the Master asked, "Where have you been?
He replied, "I went to pay my respects. The Master said, "Why do you use these two pieces of skin [your mouth]?
He replied, "I borrowed them. The Master said, "If he has them, he can lend them to you; if he does not have them, what would you do? He replied, "Precisely because..."
There was a reason for this borrowing. Later, when Caoshan heard it being cited, he said, "One son has personally attained it. He then spoke in verse:
"From the beginning, father and son have never been apart; why need the stone maiden trouble herself to ask him? Last night on the cold crag, there was no shadow."
A tree. In the depths of white clouds, a horizontal branch is revealed. (Danxia Chun). [Added from another collection.
While the Master was lying down under a *bī* tree, Daowu approached and pulled the blanket over him. The Master asked, "What is this? Daowu said, "It is to cover.
The Master asked, "Is it for one who is lying down, or for one who is sitting? Daowu said, "It is neither of these two states. The Master said, "How so?"
"What about being covered by the canopy? He said, "Do not speak in confusion.
The verse says: The *pí* tree lies down and rises; Daowu provides the canopy. A shout right before his face overturns the road-covering cloth. (Yuánwù Qín)
Meeting, we do not avoid one another; here, we play for a while. (A shout. Turning heaven upside down and earth right side up. (The Great Perfect Wisdom.
[Added by Collection] When Master Shilin (who succeeded Mazu) saw Layman Pang approaching, he raised his whisk and said:
"Not falling into Danxia’s trap—try and say a word! The Layman snatched away the whisk and instead raised his fist.
The Master said, "That is precisely Danxia’s trap. The Layman said, "Let us not fall into it together.
The Master said, "Danxia suffers from dumbness; Panggong suffers from deafness. The Layman said, "Exactly so. The Master was speechless. The Layman said, "I told you it was just a coincidence."
Thus it is. The verse says:
Carrying east, one passes west; shifting what was before to become behind. A thousand variations in the horse’s head; a hundred uglinesses on the Buddha’s face. (Yuedang Chang)
When two masters meet, there is no other principle than this: when that one shakes its head, this one wags its tail. Head and tail must correspond; one must maintain the beginning and the end.
How many contrived Chan practitioners there are who, from the very start, stir up the waves in search of water! (Fujian Qin).
[Added from the Supplement] Master Xiuxi of Tanzhou (a successor of Mazu) was asked by Gushan, "When sound and form are pure and true, what is the Way?
The Master said, "Why do you disturb the Way? Gushan then moved from east to west and stood there. The Master said:

"If it were not so, it would be a disaster. As Guishan moved from west to east and stood there, the Master descended from his meditation seat and had taken two steps when Guishan seized him, saying, "When sound and form are extinguished, what is the true reality?
The Master then gave him a slap. Guishan said, "Thirty years from now, I shall need someone like you to serve me tea."
"It is also not present. The Master said, "What do you want with this fellow from Guishan? Guishan laughed heartily. He then offered this verse:
"Before the tower, clever swallows chatter in pairs; In the woods above, lovely orioles fly in couples. Because I observed that the ancients had no fixed meaning," [he said].
Yu: "In my leisure time, I have also composed another couplet of verse (by Fojian Qin):
Two armies clash, their laughter like a frown; Their brows are arched upward, and their eyes show veins of tension. For whom are the clouds and moon over the mountains and streams a companion?
To the north, south, east, and west, there are no neighbors near. Xiatang Yuan: "..."
[Supplement] One day, when Master Fubei (who had succeeded Mazu) was sitting with Ling Xingpo, who had come to pay her respects, and they were drinking tea, the lady asked:
"To whom do you entrust that phrase which cannot be spoken even with one’s full strength? The Master replied, "Fubei has no superfluous words.
She said, "Even before reaching Fubei, one cannot help but harbor doubts. The Master said, "There is another [way]."

The master’s point of excellence was brought forth without hindrance. Baolin clasped her hands and wept, saying, "Alas! To the heavens, further misery and grievance are added. The Master remained silent.
She said, "In speech you do not know the distinction between the biased and the correct; in principle you do not recognize the upright and the perverse.
To act for others' sake is to bring calamity upon yourself. Later, a monk reported this to Nanquan, who said, "How bitter! Fubo has been caught by this old woman."
Chui-zhe went up to her once. Later, when the old woman heard of this, she laughed and said, "Master Yuanzhe still lacks a bit of a pivot.
When the Chan traveler Chengyi encountered the old woman, he asked, "What does it mean that Nanquan still lacks a bit of a pivot?
The woman then wept, saying, "How tragic! How painful! Chengyi was at a loss for words. The woman asked, "Do you understand? Chengyi joined them in weeping.
She stood with her palms joined. Ba said, "The number of dead Zen practitioners is like hemp and millet. She then cited Zhaozhou’s case:
Zhaozhou said, "If I had seen this stinking old woman, I would have questioned her until she was speechless.
Yiyun asked, "I wonder, Master, how would you have questioned her? Zhaozhou then struck him. Yiyun said, "Why did you strike me instead? Zhaozhou—
He said, "This fellow who is like a dead man—when will I beat him? I shall beat him! He struck him several times.
Upon hearing this, the old woman said, "Zhaozhou deserves a blow from my hand. Later, a monk reported this to Zhaozhou.
Zhaozhou wept and said, "How tragic! How painful! When the old woman heard these words, she joined her palms and sighed, saying, "Zhaozhou’s eye-sight pierces through all."
Poh broke up the four quarters of the world. A monk asked, "What is the Eye of Zhaozhou? The old woman then raised her fist.
The monk returned and reported this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou composed a verse, saying: "When the occasion arises, it is brought forth face-to-face;
Face-to-face, the occasion is swift. I tell you, Laywoman Lingxing, Why do you weep? What have you lost? The old woman replied with a verse:

It is said: "The Master has already understood the sound of weeping; now that it is understood, who is there to know it? At that time in the kingdom of Magadha, how many lost the opportune moment before their eyes! The verse says:
The *maṇi* jewel in the palm was never once looked back upon; who could have protected and cherished the mother-born trousers?
Not understanding the "Old Lady’s Zen" while floating the cup, one has remained stained by defilement until this very day. (Jingshan Gaofeng, No. 3)

Even lightning and sparks are still too slow; how could these dead-end Chan practitioners ever know? Turning their faces and looking back, they intend to seek it out, but the evening sun has already passed beyond the green branches to the west.
The gaze of his eyes pierces through the four continents; the old woman’s fist has no seams or gaps. How can one face this matter when it meets the occasion?
Who can mount the back of a fierce tiger?
A single movement of the strings distinguishes the melody; a falling leaf reveals the autumn. When one hesitates, it is already too late—*xiu xiu xiu xiu* (Rest!
Rest! Rest! Rest!). (Zhong’an’s Emptiness). This old nun can beat the drum of lethal poison; those who hear it from afar or nearby all tremble with fear.
Only Nanquan and Zhaozhou, sharing death and life together, pay no heed at all. *A-he-he*. These "living-dead" Chan practitioners can do nothing about it. (Buddha)
Xing Tai). In his youth, he lived in seclusion, leaning alone against the tower. A hundred families sought his daughter’s hand, yet she refused to enter the net of the drifting cup.
Looking at her reflection, she saw her hair had turned entirely white. (A laughing old man is fit.)

[Added for inclusion: The Monk of Longshan in Tanzhou (also known as Yishan, who succeeded Mazu). While Dongshan and his senior teacher, Master Mi, were traveling along, they saw vegetable leaves floating in a mountain stream.
Dongshan said, "This is a deep mountain with no people; why are there vegetables flowing down? Is there perhaps a practitioner dwelling here?
They then discussed this together and, wading through the grass, traveled five or six *li* along the stream until they suddenly saw him.
The Master, appearing emaciated and with an unusual countenance, set down his belongings and inquired after him. The Master said, "There are no paths on this mountain;
from where have you come, O Kalyāṇamitra? Dōng said, "Setting aside the matter of there being no path, from where did the Master enter?
The Master replied, "I do not come from traveling among the clouds and waters. Dōng asked, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain? The Master—
[The monk] said, "The Spring and Autumn Annals do not record this. The Master said, "The Venerable One lived here first; this mountain lived here first. The monk said, "I do not know.
The monk asked, "Why do you not know? The Master said, "I did not come from among gods or humans.
The monk asked, "What principle have you realized, Venerable One, that you dwell on this mountain? The Master said, "I saw two clay oxen fighting and plunging into the sea."
Up until the present day, there has been no news of him.
The verse says: The mud ox enters the sea; there is no news. Where in heaven or on earth can he be sought?
One might say that spring passes and autumn returns again, Yet at every step one rides upon his power. (Baoning Yong)
Parting the grass to gaze upon the wind, he roams the seas; deep within the mountainous isles, leaves drift with the current.

Together they travel until the water ends, where they truly behold an old bhikṣu with bushy eyebrows. This bhikṣu is cold and aloof; he takes the pure breeze as his line and the bright moon as his hook.
He unites heaven and earth to serve as his fishing boat and sits casting his net atop a solitary peak. This is the place of no worldly elegance.
Truly elegant! (Nantang Xing) Eyes high and low, nostrils askew;
shallow and deep, light and heavy, not much contention. Mosquitoes, gadflies, and scorpions push shoulder-to-shoulder to enter;
the phoenix and the *yuèzù* borrow paths through the roots of its teeth. He takes the long river and churns it into butter and curd; he dares to take the handle of a grain of millet and—
The stalks of grain. Hiding in the mountains is not yet the place for concealing one's person;
appearing and disappearing, let them follow the movements of the sun and moon (Xiatang Yuan).
