The Fifth of the Third Generation under the Sixth Patriarch (the remainder of the Second Generation under Nanyue):
Layman Pang Yun of Xiangzhou (who met Mazu). When he first visited Shitou, he asked, "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas?
Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, whereupon Pang was suddenly enlightened.
Later, he visited Mazu and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single mouth, and then I will tell you.
At these words, the scholar suddenly realized the profound principle. The verse says:
"Swallowing the waters of the West River in a single gulp; throughout ten thousand ages and a thousand years, not a single drop remains.
If you wish to know whether this principle is profound or not, it is simply that Mazu’s mouth was too narrow. (Baizhang Yuan).
The wind blows and the sun scorches as exposed corpses lie; weeping, one asks the immortal for a place to bury them. The old man with too many words cannot restrain his impulsive nature;
there is no place where yin and yang can be arranged. (Baoning Yong)
He drank the Western River dry and spoke to you: "The house style of Master Ma is no mere trifle. With a single oar he cut through the current, breaking the misty chill;
the heavens and waters are as clear and vast as autumn. (Tiantong Jue)
Sucking up the waters of the West River in a single gulp; the peony in Luoyang has newly put forth its buds.
Do not seek it by tossing soil and raising dust; lift your eyes and you will bump into your own. (Wuzu Yan)
Sucking up the waters of the West River in a single gulp—when you know the head, you should naturally know the tail.
How pitiful that Old Pang and Master Ma, though meeting face-to-face, are thousands of miles apart. (Fujian Qin)
"To drink up the waters of the West River in a single gulp—the Great Master had no choice but to do so.
Having been unexpectedly questioned by Pang Gong, he exerted all his strength and could only manage this much. (Wenshu said.)
I ask you, O man who walks alone through heaven and earth: You have fully raised [the teaching] and entrusted it to me, yet it is too much for words to behold.
The Western River has been swallowed up until not a single drop remains; who can unlock the throat-gate at this vital ford? (Shimen Yi)
Sipping up the waters of the West River in a single draught; the partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers.
There are those who naturally understand and smile with a nod; its arrival does not enter the ears of the deaf. (Baofeng Zhao)
Sucking the waters of the West River dry in a single gulp; the peach blossoms atop the ridge scent one’s head-wrap.
Branch after branch, leaf after leaf, all contain the spring—this too is because of me that I pay homage to you. (Gao’an Wu)
The waves of the great ocean are vast; the square inch of a small man’s mind is deep. When the ocean dries up, its bottom is finally seen;
when a person dies, their heart remains unknown. (Gushan Gui)
Sipping the Western River in a single gulp, the entire body reveals nothing hidden. Where neither sage nor ordinary person reaches, auspicious light radiates from the crown of the head. (Chuanfang)
[Continued Collection]: "Sucking the Western River dry in a single gulp; the thorny bramble kills old Pang.
If you can swallow it on the spot, you will surely be peerless within the seas. (Wenyu Qin)
Sipping up the waters of the West River in a single gulp, not a drop remains as a great wave surges forth. This colt is truly extraordinary;
he neighs to the wind and plays with his shadow amidst the setting sun. (By Baiyang Shun)
Sucking the Western River dry in a single gulp; the colt tramples old Pang to death. No need to burn paper money to summon ghosts;
naturally, the home and the realm are at peace. (Nun Wuzhuo Zong).
He drank the Western River dry; peerless in both antiquity and the present. Having passed the imperial examination, he returned home; his original surname was Páng (Pángdiǎnniúyóu).
Who could have said that Master Páng’s question was so direct? Mázǔ’s words were still stuck on his lips like mud.
Unable to withstand the drinking dry of the Western River, he laughed and turned his body within the words of the precipice. (Shuǐ'ān Yī)
Sipping the waters of the West River in a single gulp—though the flowers upon the pestle’s tip have not yet ceased to bloom. Leaf by leaf, branch by branch, they hang with rain and dew;
Mount Sumeru is hidden within the point of a needle. (Dachanming)
Sipping up the waters of the West River in a single mouth—Old Pang never clarified his own self. Drunk as mud, yet his courage was like heaven;
three spouts on a tea-pitcher from Gong County. (Songyuan Yue)
Mimdari hu. Mimdri zhi. Open your mouth and move your tongue; this is a most exquisite flavor—do not be deluded!

(Jiantang Ji): Having swallowed the waters of the West River until nothing remains, he stands forth as a truly magnificent Great Man. Everyone says that those with red beards in this world are barbarians;
who knew there was yet another red-bearded barbarian? (Miyuan Jie).
Squeezing oil from a scale-weight; enough with idle talk and long-winded speech. Wrapping a hundred thousand strings of cash around one's waist, riding a crane up to Yangzhou. (Hantang Ren)
Pure and stark naked; bright and unadorned. There is nothing to grasp; how can one know the ritual? (Retreat Hall, Xiu).
To swallow the waters of the West River in a single gulp—though the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot lift it up. A flower blooms upon the pestle’s tip;
spring days are long, and even the cat and the white ox are filled with joy. (Puan Yu).
One step higher, one step further; one stride wider, one stride wider. The colt tramples people to death. Stop! Stop! Stop! Stop! Stop!
(From *Kuchan Jing*)
[Added from another source: A lay devotee saw Danxia. Danxia made a gesture of running away. The devotee said, "That was still a gesture of casting off the body.
What is the gesture of groaning? Danxia then sat down. The devotee stepped forward and drew a seven-character figure with his staff.
Below [the character for "seven"], he drew a single character, saying: "Because of seven, one is seen; seeing one, seven is forgotten. Xufa then rose and departed.
The Master said, "Sit a little longer; there is still a second phrase remaining. Xufa asked, "Can one apply words here? The Master then wept and went out.

The Verse says: Because of seven, one is seen; seeing one, seven is forgotten. Xufa rose and departed; the Master wept and went out. If you wish to see the old man’s face, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
Because of the seven, one is seen; because one is seen, the seven are forgotten. The moon is in the center, yet the heavens have no four walls.

Throughout the ten directions of empty space, all traces are swept away and every mark is extinguished. One’s entire being is a mouth from which nothing can be spoken. Blue, yellow, azure, and green are smeared on in wild confusion.
(Aha! Nan-tang Xing.)
Because of seven [views], one seeks traces and follows footprints; seeing one, one forgets the seven—blue sky and bright day.
In the second phrase, from the ominous one gains the auspicious: "Hanging the sword in the empty hall, go back and come forth. Words of loyalty and righteousness are difficult to lose.
Alas, alas, alas! (Fang’an Xian).
[Supplement] A lay practitioner visited Danxia. He stood before him for a short while and then departed. Danxia paid him no heed. The layman returned and sat down;
Danxia then came before the layman, stood there for a short while, and returned to his quarters.
The layman said, "You went out and I entered; there was still something left to do. Danxia replied, "This old man goes out and comes in—what end is there to it?"
Yiqi said, "There is not the slightest bit of compassion. Xia said, "I have led this fellow to such a state.
Yiqi asked, "By what means did you lead him? Xia picked up the layman’s head-covering (fuhou) and said, "He looks exactly like a monk.
Yiqi took the head-covering and placed it on Xia’s own head, saying, "Now he looks exactly like a layman. Xia [laughed].
[The Master] responded with three "yes" sounds. The layman said, "There is still a trace of breath remaining.
Xiang [Yunwen] tossed down his head-wrap and said, "It looks very much like a black silk cap. The layman also responded with three "yes" sounds.
The Master said, "How could you forget the breath from former times? The layman snapped his fingers three times and said, "Moving heaven, moving earth. The Verse says: [Verse omitted]
One step out, one step in; walking slowly with measured strides. Dignified decorum and refined elegance flow forth; their graceful interchange—who can distinguish them?
Herein, the proprieties of both monastics and laity are richly fulfilled. (By Zhengjue Yi).
Danxia and Master Pang spent their entire lives manifesting spiritual powers; they traveled everywhere throughout the entirety of the universe.
The momentum of a thousand peaks ceases at the mountain range; the flow of ten thousand streams merges into the sea. (The Great Perfect Wisdom).
Burning a wooden Buddha—what heart or liver does an old thing have? The old man selling the bamboo sieve—his house is ruined and his people are scattered.

They chase one another, they pursue one another, they provoke one another, they delight in one another. Difficult, difficult! A long sword leaning against the sky, its light piercing the Dipper with cold radiance;
a blue dragon stirring the sea, yet not disturbing the waves. Look, look! Every household has a road leading to Chang’an. (Nantang Xing)
[Added for inclusion: When the Layman saw Danxia approaching, he neither spoke nor rose. Danxia then raised his whisk; the Layman immediately picked up his mallet.
Danxia said, "Is it only this? Is there more? The Layman said, "This time seeing you, Master, is not like before.
Danxia said, "It does no harm to diminish a person's reputation. The Layman said, "The original state..."
"I must bring you down once," he said. Yuanran replied, "In that case, I shall silence the natural mouth.
Yunju said, "If you silence your own fundamental nature, you will still trouble me by silencing mine. Yunju threw down his whisk and walked away.
Yuanran called out, "Master Ran! Yunju did not look back. Yuanran said, "Not only do you suffer from muteness; you also suffer from deafness."
The Verse says:
When Danxia first visited Master Pang, they faced each other clearly, yet said nothing at all. He raised his whisk simply because there was no external object;
he struck the gong—what else could it be but the Natural? Turning his head, his "suffering from muteness" was both true and real; waving his sleeves, he acted as if deaf to the outside world.
To attain the profound mystery. If you wish to reach the place where the masters met, look at the stone man’s place of walking, where laughter resounds.
(By Banyarou). The ancient’s face-to-face function: when meeting, there is nothing to be said. Raising the whisk was Danxia; striking the mallet was Pangjiao.
Turtle hair slants with every word; rabbit horns fall as one pleases. Suffering from muteness, yet suffering from deafness as well—how clear and good it is! (Fenyang Zhao).
One distinguishes the melody by the movement of the strings; one knows autumn by the falling leaves. The deaf and the blind respond to one another with mallets and whisks.
When there is spirit, one adds further spirit; even where there is no elegance, there is elegance. (The Poison-Coated Whip).
The horned antelope on the cliff has lost its breath; the sky-reaching long sword leaves no trace of use. Not a ripple stirs the reflection of the cold moon;
countless fish and dragons swallow and spit in the dark. (Zhengjue Xian)

It is said: At first, when asked, he merely took a snowball and struck him. Again, he composed a verse:
"Strike with a snowball! Strike with a snowball! Old Pang’s mechanism has nothing to grasp. Neither heaven nor earth can know it."
Cut off within the eye; cut off in the ear—utterly free and untrammeled. Even the blue-eyed barbarian monk finds it difficult to discern.
Master Pang held up the whole thing: a drop of water, a drop of ice. Layman Yaoshan’s two eyes flickered and moved.
When the pivot does not turn, it is but a weary dream. It is inherently natural; who can understand how to employ it? (Zhenjing Wen)
Chan Master Quanxi saw Pang Gong off as he was departing. Snow fell from all sides of the sky, yet not a single flake landed elsewhere.
Alas, though one has a mouth, it is like being mute. Even if you could grasp it into a single ball, the hawk would have already flown to Silla.
If you understand how to say, "Be well-prepared for the road ahead," then striking east and striking west is truly marvelous. Stay as a guest for three years; do not wait until the time of departure.
Hunger. (Above, it grows more intense).
Three feet of cold light pierce the Dipper and Ox constellations. Where the Mo-ya sword is raised, ghosts and spirits tremble with dread. The barbarians do not recognize the generals’ commands;
they have mistakenly entered the heavy encirclement, their blood flowing from their necks. (The River of Yezhu).
Vast expanse above the head, vast expanse beneath the feet. To stand firm is easy; to pivot is difficult. The Vajra-jewel sword strikes one with chilling cold.
Do not fall into the trap of viewing it outside the phrase of the critical pivot. (Shixi Yue).
[Added for inclusion] Yunju Wu said: "If someone were to ask Yunju, 'Where does it fall? I would say to them, 'It falls into the snow. Do you all understand? Verse:
If someone asks where it falls, I tell them it falls into the snow. The ten directions are all covered; How can one find a place to hide?"
Falling into the snow, one does not offend hand or foot; even with a nailed beak and iron tongue, it is difficult to open the mouth.
A palm-sweep sends a snowball flying straight at the face; it strikes the Vajra-brain from behind.

[Added from another source] A lay practitioner (upāsaka) had a verse that said: "Having sons, they do not marry; having daughters, they do not wed. The whole family gathers together in a circle, and together they discuss the discourse on non-arising. The Verse says:
Gathering the sentiments of mountain clouds and ocean moons, the body is rounded, the nose straight, and the eyes and brows arched.
With a whisk of tortoise hair and a staff of rabbit horns, he strikes the void until it rings out with a *baobao* sound. (Shixi Yue)
When spring arrives, flowers bloom; after autumn, leaves fall. Father and son sit together in harmony—what do they recognize as good or evil?
(Kuchan Jing). They say neither "yes" nor "no"; raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye is but folly within guile. With a father’s kindness and a son’s filial piety, there is nothing else:
the whole family seeks only to take advantage of one another. (Nian Lin Ying).
The man is indolent and the woman is unvirtuous; the old father is talkative and the mother has a ready tongue.
They seek every possible advantage yet remain insatiable; when have they ever known the unborn? (Xianji Yun)
[Added for inclusion] A lay practitioner’s verse says: The ten directions gather together as one; Each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the field for selecting the Buddha;
With an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. The eulogy says:
The *fuhou* hat is covered in dust, the boots and robes are torn; in the field where Buddhas are chosen, there are not two such as these.
If you say, "With a mind empty, I have passed the imperial examination and returned," a single blow upon the crown of your head shall not let you pass. (Fohuiquan)
Wind, moon, mountains, and rivers share one family; who comes to settle dragons and snakes beneath the words?
Taibai never ascended the inner palace hall, yet last night, flowers grew spontaneously from the tip of his brush. (Xinwen Ben)
Having exhausted his entire livelihood, he sells colanders; with a "white-handed" theft, he seeks advantage amidst the flames.
To look at his skill, it is nothing more than this, yet he says, "With an empty mind, I have passed the imperial examination and returned. (Fozhao Guang).
One day the Layman said, "Difficult, difficult! Ten loads of sesame oil are spread upon a tree. Baizhang responded, "Easy, easy!
The meaning of the Patriarchs is at the tips of the hundred grasses. Lingzhao said, "It is neither difficult nor easy."
When hunger comes, eat; when weariness comes, sleep. The Verse says:
The mouth chatters incessantly, never ceasing for a moment; Grasping a colander, he wanders through the fire. He has a daughter whom he refuses to marry;
In years to come, she will surely become an old spinster. (Lan’an Shu)
Enemy upon enemy; face to face, we behold one another. Playing the zither without strings, its pure sound resounds through the ages. (By Xian’an Guan)
The layman threw his entire household property into the Xiang River. His daughter, Lingzhao, would daily take a bamboo sieve to sell in the marketplace.

The Verse says: With hair bound in a topknot like piled clouds, her graceful beauty is charming; She carries several bamboo sieves balanced on the tip of her staff. Entering the marketplace—how could there be no one there?
Question: Striking upon the true lineage, one certainly will not spare them.
(Yuanzhao’s Text) "Father has cast his livelihood into the river waters; it burdens you to go along the streets selling colanders.
It is not that the family is poor and the children suffer together; how many people can truly know this mind? (Wuji’s Verse)
The father has already passed the imperial examination with an empty mind and returned home; the daughter follows his example in painting her brows like a moth.
Within this single household, there is but the business of one family; where could there be the leisure funds to buy a colander? (Amitābha).

The Layman was crossing a bridge while eating persimmons after selling his bamboo water-strainer and fence. Seeing this, his daughter Lingzhao also went and fell down beside her father. The Layman asked, "What are you doing? The girl replied, "Seeing my father fall to the ground, I am helping him up. The Layman said, "Fortunately, no one saw us. The Verse says: The Layman sells bamboo and crosses the bridge; The daughter sees and falls right beside her father. "What are you doing? he asks. "I am supporting my father," she replies. "Fortunately, no one saw us. In the end, they both fall together. The whole world is as vast as a single bowl. The Layman’s mind is like a clear mirror. The daughter’s body is like a bright moon. The Layman’s words are like a thunderclap. The daughter’s actions are like a flash of lightning. If you can understand this at once, You will see that the Layman’s heart is like a mountain. If you cannot yet comprehend it, You must know that the daughter’s spirit is like the wind. If you can discern this clearly, Then you will see that the Layman’s eyes are like the sun. If you cannot yet distinguish it, You must know that the daughter’s tongue is like a sword. If you can penetrate this in a single moment, You will realize that the Layman’s hand is like a staff. If you cannot yet grasp it, You must know that the daughter’s feet are like a boat. If you can leap over this in an instant, You will see that the Layman’s mouth is like a bellows. If you cannot yet open it, You must know that the daughter’s nose is like a needle. If you can pierce through this in a split second, You will see that the Layman’s head is like a tower. If you cannot yet ascend it, You must know that the daughter’s hair is like a brocade. If you can unravel this in a blink of an eye, You will see that the Layman’s eyebrows are like a bow. If you cannot yet draw it, You must know that the daughter’s brows are like a string. If you can harmonize these in a single thought, You will see that the Layman’s teeth are like a comb. If you cannot yet align them, You must know that the daughter’s lips are like a brush. If you can paint this in a moment, You will see that the Layman’s ears are like a drum. If you cannot yet beat it, You must know that the daughter’s heart is like a bell. If you can ring this in an instant, You will see that the Layman’s soul is like a cloud. If you cannot yet disperse it, You must know that the daughter’s breath is like mist. If you can dissolve this in a flash, You will see that the Layman’s body is like a tree. If you cannot yet shake it, You must know that the daughter’s limbs are like branches. If you can embrace this in a single breath, You will see that the Layman’s mind is like the ocean. If you cannot yet fathom it, You must know that the daughter’s nature is like the sky. If you can encompass this in a single glance, You will see that the Layman’s life is like a dream. If you cannot yet awaken from it, You must know that the daughter’s death is like a shadow. If you can transcend this in a single step, You will see that the Layman’s past is like a river. If you cannot yet cross it, You must know that the daughter’s future is like a mountain. If you can climb this in a single leap, You will see that the Layman’s present is like a house. If you cannot yet dwell within it, You must know that the daughter’s eternity is like a road. If you can travel this in a single stride, You will see that the Layman’s wisdom is like a lamp. If you cannot yet light it, You must know that the daughter’s compassion is like a mirror. If you can reflect this in a single reflection, You will see that the Layman’s practice is like a flower. If you cannot yet bloom it, You must know that the daughter’s realization is like a fruit. If you can harvest this in a single season, You will see that the Layman’s teaching is like a rain. If you cannot yet soak it, You must know that the daughter’s liberation is like a breeze. If you can blow this in a single gust, You will see that the Layman’s vow is like a mountain. If you cannot yet stabilize it, You must know that the daughter’s merit is like a sea. If you can sail this in a single wave, You will see that the Layman’s dharma is like a wheel. If you cannot yet turn it, You must know that the daughter’s truth is like a jewel. If you can hold this in a single grasp, You will see that the Layman’s path is like a bridge. If you cannot yet cross it, You must know that the daughter’s way is like a boat. If you can ferry this in a single crossing, You will see that the Layman’s realm is like a palace. If you cannot yet enter it, You must know that the daughter’s state is like a garden. If you can stroll through this in a single turn, You will see that the Layman’s body is like a mountain. If you cannot yet ascend it, You must know that the daughter’s spirit is like a bird. If you can soar with this in a single flight, You will see that the Layman’s mind is like a dragon. If you cannot yet subdue it, You must know that the daughter’s heart is like a tiger. If you can tame this in a single moment, You will see that the Layman’s life is like a spring. If you cannot yet revive it, You must know that the daughter’s death is like autumn. If you can perceive this in a single glance, You will see that the Layman’s world is like a dream. If you cannot yet wake from it, You must know that the daughter’s realm is like a shadow. If you can transcend this in a single step, You will see that the Layman’s past is like a river. If you cannot yet cross it, You must know that the daughter’s future is like a mountain. If you can climb this in a single leap, You will see that the Layman’s present is like a house. If you cannot yet dwell within it, You must know that the daughter’s eternity is like a road. If you can travel this in a single stride, You will see that the Layman’s wisdom is like a lamp. If you cannot yet light it, You must know that the daughter’s compassion is like a mirror. If you can reflect this in a single reflection, You will see that the Layman’s practice is like a flower. If you cannot yet bloom it, You must know that the daughter’s realization is like a fruit. If you can harvest this in a single season, You will see that the Layman’s teaching is like a rain. If you cannot yet soak it, You must know that the daughter’s liberation is like a breeze. If you can blow this in a single gust, You will see that the Layman’s vow is like a mountain. Pitying his child, he could not help but laugh "sha-sha. Yet on the way back, he was crushed by mud and sand.
Had the old man Huanglong seen him then, he would have struck that wretched fellow dead with a single blow. (Huanglong Nan)
The layman fell to the ground; Lingzhao helped him up. "What kind of skill does a beggar have? What point is there in seeking it? (Ying'an Hua).
Filial piety conceals the five heinous crimes; one cannot hide one's ugliness before others. This life’s close kin are, from a former existence, bitter enemies.
(Southern Old Man Mao).
When Master Pang fell to the ground, Lingzhao helped him up. To this day, though several hundred years have passed, the pure breeze has not ceased;
it has not ceased. A thousand-fathom carp from the Eastern Sea has a beak of such length. (Yi’an Shen).
While seated, the layman asked Lingzhao, "The ancients said, 'Brilliant at the tips of the hundred grasses, brilliant is the meaning of the Patriarch.
How do you understand this? Lingzhao replied, "Old and decrepit as you are, why do you speak such words?
The layman asked, "What about you? Lingzhao said, "Brilliant at the tips of the hundred grasses, brilliant is the meaning of the Patriarch. The layman [nodded].
He then smiled. The verse says:
Ten thousand miles, cloudless, the Milky Way stretches across; On the profound path of the Great Square, he walks with ease. The father’s wisdom and capacity are rare in this world;
The daughter’s halo is born upon her crown. (Or: The essence of the Hermitage).
The ancestral reputation of the Pang family endures for a thousand ages; they exchange words on the difficult and the easy. Among them, Lingzhao excels by a mere hair’s breadth;
the meaning of the Patriarchs is manifest at the tips of the hundred grasses. (Cheng Shouzuo)
As the layman was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he said to Lingzhao, "Observe the time of day and report to me when it is noon.
Lingzhao quickly replied, "The sun has already reached its zenith; there is food to be served.

As the layman went out the door to look, Lingzhao immediately ascended her father’s seat, sat with palms joined, and passed away. The layman smiled and said, "My daughter is sharp and quick-witted," and thus further extended his life.
Seven days. The verse says:
In this house there is the joy of a complete set; the newly translated melodies are different. Clearly one grieves over parting, yet it is a cause for rejoicing at meeting again.
(Xiyuan Hui): A whole family delights in a performance on a single stage; drums and music resound through the heavens as they perform at will.
Once the theatrical robes are cast off, who can know? For no reason, Huangfanchuo laughs himself down. (Beihai Xin)
As the layman was approaching the time of his passing, the Prefect Yu Gongdi came to inquire after his illness. The layman said to him, "I only wish that you would empty all that exists;

be careful not to reify what does not exist. Dwell well in this world, for all things are like shadows and echoes. Having spoken these words, he reclined upon the prefect's knee and passed away. The verse says: Empty all that exists, And do not reify the non-existent. Dwell well in the world, For all is like a shadow or an echo.

If you wish to know the place where the source is exhausted, who can point out the way for those lost? Beyond the setting sun and the chickens and dogs, peach and plum trees naturally form a stream. (Xutang Yu)

Laywoman Pangpo entered Lukmen Temple to perform a vegetarian feast. When the *vinaya-dhara* requested her to state the intent for the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), the woman stuck a withered comb behind her hair and said, "The dedication has been made. She then departed. The verse says:
Pangpo shifts the comb from the side of her topknot; a single stroke of elegance, peerless in all the world.
In all matters, let justice be decided forthwith; the rector need not write with his brush. (Cishou Shen)
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) intended to proclaim it before the assembly, yet was instead laughed at by his mother-in-law. She turned his tooth-comb back around and rebuked him for his feet;
even upon meeting, they continued their sour deliberations. (Ding of the Dumb Hall).
The Sixth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch (The Second Generation under Qingyuan, Part One):
Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Lishui (Heir to Shitou). When the Master took leave of Mazu and returned to Shitou, he said:
One day, while sitting upon a rock, Tou asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am not doing anything.
Tou said, "If that is so, then you are sitting idly. The Master said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something.
Tou asked, "You say you are not doing anything; what, then, are you not doing? The Master replied, "Even the thousand sages do not [do this]."
Shi headed the assembly with a verse of praise, saying: "Living together from the beginning, we did not know his name; Spontaneously accompanying one another, he simply goes on.
Even the sages of antiquity could not recognize him; How could ordinary people in their haste possibly understand him?
The Verse says:

The profound mystery reaches its ultimate limit, and the fundamental nature is naturally serene. If one were to say that within this interval of eighteen thousand [miles], the moon is reflected in the clear river yet the fish does not see it—why must the fisherman further cast away his trap? (Danxia Chun)
Spontaneously unknown by name, lightly cast the eye and listen. Green and lush upon the water—turns out to be duckweed. (Wuzu Yan)

Shaking off the fetters of Buddhas and patriarchs, one stands vast and free beyond the lines of the compass and square. Not performing even a single act, one attains sovereign freedom in all directions.
When the ancient mirror is set upon its stand, it clearly discerns coming and going; when the shadow of the golden mallet moves, the flowers on the tree bloom.
Let things proceed spontaneously and do not attempt to accompany them. Wherever the Dharma-clouds gather, they stir up wind and thunder. (Yuánwù Qín)

[Continued Collection] Step by step, the moon is cold and the wind is high; with every stride, the mountains are frigid and the waters deep. When meeting people, he bares his liver and reveals his gallbladder;
when encountering righteousness, he slices open his belly and gouges out his heart. (Xiatang Yuan)
Striking grass with a stone to startle the snake; secretly guarding the profound mechanism to sever all emotional attachments. A swift horse chasing the wind must discern the mark;
the report says, "The thousand sages do not know its name. (Yinjing Yan).
Sitting idly at ease or walking at leisure, a mindless cloud drifts across the mountain ridge. When both the illuminating object and the subject are forgotten, the person does not stand;
from the noon of yesterday, three watches have already struck. (Xueyan Qin)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] When Yaoshan first went to visit Shitou’s hermitage, he asked: "I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.
I have heard it said that in the South there is the 'Direct Pointing to the Human Mind' for seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood, yet I have not truly understood this."
"I humbly hope that the Master will compassionately grant me instruction. The Master said, "It is not so, yet it is also not not-so.
It is neither so nor not-so; all of these are inadmissible. What do you say to this? The Teacher was at a loss.
The Master said, "Your karmic affinity does not lie here. Go instead to the place of Great Master Ma. The Teacher received his command and paid him respectful obeisance.
Mazu again posed his previous question. Mazu said, "Sometimes I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink;
sometimes I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink. Sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are right;
sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are wrong. What do you say to this? At these words, the Master attained realization and immediately—

He prostrated. The Patriarch asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate? The Master replied, "When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito on an iron ox. The Patriarch said, "Since it is so for you, protect and maintain yourself well.

Verse: The Patriarch asked about the principle; The Master spoke of the iron ox. A mosquito upon its back— How could it ever bite? The Patriarch’s words were like thunder; The Master’s heart was as clear as water. From this day forth, he was free from doubt; He took refuge in the Buddha and became a monk.
In general, one must not be so groundless. How could a rustic old man know the vastness of heaven and earth?
Even if you count on to eighty or ninety, your home mountain remains separated by yet another pass. (Yang Woei-wei)
The smoke of war has settled across the four seas; news flows freely through the Central Plains. Lay down the three-foot sword;
cease playing with the single bow. (Gushan Gui)
What a fine point for discourse! Who can bring it forth? Even if one could bring it forth perfectly, I would not yet dare grant my approval. (Jingshan Gao).
I have emptied my belly and poured out my heart to tell you this; I do not know why you still hesitate. You should seize it with vigor right now;
do not wait until dawn when you lose the rooster. (Mongan Cong).
Layered peaks and ridges are all locked shut; who knows who has penetrated deep into Peach Blossom Spring?
The traveler sees only a single stream, flowing out with petals of peach blossoms, each one fresh and bright. (Kentang Chong)
Seated, he cuts off the path of a thousand peaks; piercing through, he opens the azure sky. How can one ask for the ultimate point?
That ultimate point lies before the skull. (Songyuan Yue)
If you act like this, you will get nothing at all. Cast off the cotton robe until you are bare-boned;
with a single blow right on the head, suddenly turning over, you will see the mouth open and the eyes turn white. (Xue’an Jin)
One mountain range passed, one layer of clouds cleared; having traveled to the ends of the earth, it became increasingly bitter and arduous.
Suddenly returning, he sits within his own house: falling flowers and singing birds are but one spring. (Xutang Yu)
The withered entrails are completely dissected; all clever devices are lost. Not a single hair or thread hangs upon the entire body. With every step, the pure breeze turns along with one’s person.
Who can divide the bright moon between the upper and lower ponds? (Gao Feng Miao)
[Added for inclusion: Yueshan attended Mazu for three years. One day, Mazu asked him, "How is your realization these days?
The Master replied, "The skin and flesh have fallen away entirely; there is only the one true reality.
Mazu said, "What you have attained may be called being in accord with the essence of the mind and manifesting it through the four limbs. Since this is so, take these three..."
"Bind your belly with bamboo strips and go to dwell in the mountains wherever you may be. The Master said, "What kind of person am I that I would dare say I will dwell in the mountains?
The Patriarch said, "It is not so. There has never been one who constantly travels without dwelling, nor one who constantly dwells without traveling.
To wish to benefit others is to have no benefit; to wish to act is to have nothing to do. You should instead become a vessel for crossing over."
Do not remain here for long. The verse says: The meeting of teacher and disciple was no light matter;

Now that the skin has been cast off, we are no longer intimate. Bound together by three strands of bamboo, we have become a mere subject of talk; To this day, we have mistaken the markings on the scale for the weight itself. The final line refers to the common error of mistaking the marks on a scale for the actual weight.*

On the Path there is a supreme treasure, peerless in saving the world. Yaoyao reveals its profound treasury, saying only: "I am not sycophantic or crooked.

To be without sycophancy or crookedness is to surpass the whole kingdom; yet though such a person offers recompense, it is not met with reciprocity. This mind stands upright like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high—its truthfulness requires no questioning of Maitreya in the future. (Yuánwù Qín)
Straight as a bowstring, clear as jade; revealing one's innermost will and heart, without any further detours or deviousness.
Even if there were gold covering the entire ground, one could not avoid being tempted by it; yet, since it cannot be exchanged, the Persian from the South Sea has a face like ink. (Fóxìng Tàiyé)
Yaoshan had not ascended the hall for a long time. The head of the monastery said, "The assembly has long been longing for the Master’s instruction.
The Master replied, "Strike the bell! As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master immediately descended from the seat and returned to his quarters.
The head followed him and asked, "Since the Master granted permission to preach the Dharma for the assembly, why did you not utter a single word?"

The Master said, "The sutras have masters of the sutras; the treatises have masters of the treatises. Why should they find it strange that this old monk [acts as he does]? (In the *Chuan Deng Lu*, this differs slightly: one day the head of the monastery invited the Master to ascend the hall.

As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master remained silent for a long while and then returned to his quarters and closed the door. The head of the monastery followed after him and said, "Master, you granted me permission to ascend the hall; why did you instead return to your quarters? The Master replied, "Head of the monastery, the sutras have masters of the sutras;

the treatises have masters of the treatises; the Vinaya has masters of the Vinaya. Why should they find it strange that this old monk [acts as he does]? The Verse says: The sutras have their masters, The treatises have their masters, And the Vinaya has its masters— Why should they find it strange that this old monk?
The Old Man of Yaoshan dispenses medicine according to the ailment. I request him to ascend the hall and strike the bell: one pill suffices, no need for a second dose, to cure his madness.
He has betrayed the Golden Immortal’s prescription for changing the bones. (By Yanxuan Zun)
The family law is simple and strict; it is neither two nor three. When the moon comes, the water becomes bright and limpid; when the clouds retreat, the cold cliffs are revealed.

The true mechanism is attained of itself; who can participate in this wondrous place? This was not merely after Mañjuśrī struck the gavel; even so, for a thousand ages, Gautama remains in a state of rightful indignation.
(Tiantong Jue): A single bright pearl, its price beyond repayment; were it not for a true connoisseur, one would cast it away in the dark. I laugh instead at Yaoshan’s wasted effort;
when the water is clear, the fish appears, yet does not swallow the hook. (Cishou Shen).
[Continued Collection] Who says Yao of Mount Yao did not ascend the hall? Day after day we meet, yet he proclaims it for us.
His solitary radiance is impartial and ever-manifest; do not mistakenly deliberate upon his silence. (It is like withered wood.)

The foolish child’s deliberate coin for silencing his crying; the fine steed chasing the wind, looking back at its shadow as it strikes the whip. Clouds sweep across the vast sky; the cranes nest in the moon.
The night’s cold penetrates to the very bones; one cannot sleep. (Tiantong Jue)
Brightly they repair the plank road; secretly they cross at Chen’ang. Not a hair’s breadth is violated, yet all are brought to ruin.
(The room is closed, then opened. The mats are spread wide—is it not seen? Why is it that those who buy are fewer than those who look on?
A perfectly honed blade that shaves a hair—treated merely as a shuttle upon a potter’s wall. (Wuzu Fan).
When the bell tolls, the assembly gathers at the abbot’s quarters. To one who faces the hardship of execution, I invite the person of the Dharma.
In every dharma, there is fundamentally not a single dharma. If you say there is no dharma, dharmas will entangle your body. (Hyōnggwon Hyong).
[Added for inclusion] While Yueshan was sitting, a monk asked, "What are you brooding over so intently? The Master said, "I am brooding over that which cannot be brooded over.
The monk asked, "How can one brood over that which cannot be brooded over? The Master said, "It is not brooding."
The verse says:
Steadfastly and persistently contemplating, there is nothing to be contemplated. In that place where there is nothing to contemplate, true contemplation truly flourishes.
At the head of Dayu Ridge, one meets the Sixth Patriarch; At the inn of Aoshan, one encounters Master Zeng (Wuzhun Shan).
[Added from the Supplement] One day, when Zun Bunan was bathing the Buddha, Yaoshan said, "This one you are bathing—you can bathe that one as well?
Zun replied, "Bring me that one! The Master then ceased speaking. Changqing said:
"Erroneous teachings are difficult to support. Xuangjue said: "Now tell me, when Changqing spoke thus, was he acting as a guest or as the host?
The assembly calls this 'the words for bathing the Buddha,' and it is also called 'the words that encompass both.
Now tell me, is it perfectly complete or not? The verse says:
Affection pours foul water over one’s head; it draws forth a pure breeze to console the solitude. Boundless distant mountains cannot be captured in a painting;
the lofty pines and tall bamboos stand cold and desolate. (Tudu Ce)
One rain, one clear sky. The eyes of the silkworms have opened; the buds of the mulberry trees are green. The magpie cries incessantly from the treetop;
the hundred-tongued thrush and the yellow oriole sing together. (Lan’an Shu)

[Added from another collection] Yaoshan wrote the character for "Buddha" and asked Dawu, "What character is this? Dawu replied, "The character for Buddha. The Master said, "A talkative fellow! Verse: The character for Buddha, written on the wall, Dawu’s mouth was too large to swallow it.
Yaoshan’s single word, "Talkative," Sealed the matter once and for all.
Daowu suddenly encountered his former teacher; the Master asked for his name and opened his fist to reveal a wondrous pivot.
To call a Buddha "truly, truly a Buddha" is to have one's belly pierced by Yaoshan (Fenyang Zhao).
Yaoshan’s question here is truly worthy of sighs; the simultaneous resonance of the chick pecking and the hen hatching is not easily praised.
To inquire of the Buddha, one must know how to present the wondrous intent; it is mostly because of this that empty flowers appear. (Yanshou Hui)
Yaoshan wrote the character for "Buddha" on his hand; he asked him, "You earnestly desire your mind to be opened. He used the character for "Buddha" alone as his reply:
"Originally, I have been observing the five precepts since the past. (Hengchuan Gong)
[Added for inclusion] During a night assembly at Yaoshan, the lamps were not lit. The Master gave this discourse: "I have a phrase;
I will tell it to you when a horned ox gives birth to a calf. At that time, a monk said, "The horned ox has given birth to a calf;
why do you not speak? The Master said, "Bring the lamp! Bring the lamp! The monk withdrew and joined the assembly.
Yan presented this to Dongshan. Dongshan said, "This monk indeed understands; it is simply that he refuses to prostrate.
He then offered this verse: A calf knows its mother well; Its two eyes are a deep, reddish-blue. Though one holds a torch to search for it, there is nothing to be found.

"Everyone, let us all go together at once to the hall for a session. (Lóngmén Yuǎn). While Yàoshān was reading a scripture, a monk asked him, "Master, you usually do not permit others to read scriptures; why then do you read them yourself? The Master said, "I am merely trying to keep my eyes from wandering. The monk said, "I wish to learn from the Master. The Master replied, "If you learn from me, you will surely end up like me. The monk asked, "What do you mean by 'like me'? The Master said, "It means you will end up reading scriptures to keep your eyes from wandering. The monk said, "But the Master’s eyes are already blind. The Master said, "Though my eyes are blind, my mind is not. The monk said, "Then what about my eyes? The Master said, "Your eyes are not blind, but your mind is. The monk said, "How can that be? The Master said, "Because you see forms with your eyes, yet you do not see the nature of form. The monk said, "What is the nature of form? The Master said, "The nature of form is not form. The monk said, "What is the nature of the mind? The Master said, "The nature of the mind is not mind. The Master said, "Not so, not so. The verse says: Autumn leaves fallen yellow, fashioned into gold coins; A foolish, crying child sees them and rejoices. The verse says: Autumn leaves fallen yellow, fashioned into gold coins; A foolish, crying child sees them and rejoices. Having caught them, they offer them to their mothers, and all say: "Look! Look
Excellent. I do not know who it is that smiles while looking on (Haiyin Xin).
One branch flourishes, one branch withers; the green leaves at the heart of the tree grow even more luxuriant. Let the yellow oriole utter its myriad songs as it pleases.
Lest bystanders shoot pellets at us. (Fohuiquan).
Applying powder, smearing clay, and wrapping the head— All depends on the pull of the master’s line. The drumhead is broken and the melody blown through;
Gather up everything and go home to rest. (Baoning Yong).

To speak of exhausting all cycles of prosperity and decay makes it even more difficult to perceive; the novice monk falls flat at the very tip of a word. The old monk points afar toward the place where the monkeys cry:
the clouds disperse into a thousand voids, and the moonlight is cold. (Dizang’s Grace)
Yunyan’s stillness is free of any fixed mold; the brilliant ancestral wind belongs to Daowu. Those of deep faith and lofty Chan understand this meaning;
whether walking idly or sitting at ease, they accept prosperity and decay alike. (Cangtang Qing)
Few can support Yaoshan’s way; it is laughable that Yunyan and Daguo still give rise to intellectual interpretations based on flourishing and decay.
How could they know that Panlang rides his donkey backward? (Chu’an Fang)

Old in years and solitary at heart, he laughs at Yaoshan; The sons sit together in a circle, forgetting even the return [to the world]. From head to toe they inquire minutely about matters of prosperity and decay;
Yet their nostrils have always been exactly the same. (Yunyan, the cause).
【Continued Collection】Three by three and two by two, they are not the same. Hand in hand, they walk and enter the grass. Turning their feet, they step in embroidered shoes;
what prevents the spring breeze from beating in the month of December? (Donggu Guang)

[Added for inclusion] Once a monk asked Yaoshan, "In the level fields and shallow grass where herds of deer gather, how does one shoot the leader of the herd? The Master said, "Watch the arrow! The monk threw himself down and lay prostrate.

The Master said, "Attendant, drag this dead man out! The monk then ran away. The Master said, "This fellow who plays with lumps of mud—what limit is there to him? Verse: The level fields and shallow grass, a herd of deer; How to shoot the leader among them? "Watch the arrow!"—the monk throws himself down.
Drag out this dead man! He runs away; the Master says: "This fellow who plays with lumps of mud—what limit is there to him?"
"Look at the lord among the *zhǔ* (deer-herders)! He lets fly one arrow and the deer runs three steps; if it lives for five more steps, it will join the herd and chase the tiger.
The true eye has always been entrusted to the hunter. The Master cried out loudly, "Watch the arrow! (Xuědòu Xiǎn).
Iron cavalry gallops across level ground; bows and arrows are not yet drawn. What a fine master among the dust! Piercing through the heart, he heads toward the roadside. (Fuxincai)
The hunter possesses a divine arrow; he shoots and captures the leader of the herd. As soon as the arrow falls, he accepts his fate and leaps forth onto the path of Caoxi.
Turning his body, he treads upon the highest pass; in a mere flash, he overcomes the victor and startles the entire flock. (Yuánwù Qín)
The colt has left the stable, yet its waist is still supple; the phoenix chick has left the nest, yet its strength is still slight. Having been born with jade hooves, it gallops a thousand li;
having been raised with golden wings, it soars through the nine heavens. (Fojian Qín)
One day at mealtime, Yaoshan himself struck the drum. Gao the Śrāmaṇera entered the hall dancing while holding an alms bowl.

Yaoshan then threw down the drumstick and asked, "Which beat is this? Gao replied, "The second beat. The Master asked, "What is the first beat? Gao went to the rice bucket, scooped out a ladleful of rice, and left. The Verse says: The first beat, the second beat— The ladleful of rice is most clear. If you wish to know the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, Look at the old fellow Yaoshan.

When the drum was struck, he danced; When the rice was served, he departed. The first beat has already been heard; The second beat is now complete. If you can discern it within this, You will see the ancient master’s true intent. If you cannot yet understand, Go ask the one who holds the bowl.
Generally, they beat drums and perform dances; this is not the same as the affairs of various quarters. "Vividly, the true sound is beyond the celestial realms;
it is certainly not a number that falls within the mundane world. (Fenyang Zhao)
Father and son meet in harmony, their essence the same; holding the bowl and beating the drum, they display the family tradition.
Although there are all manner of flavors in abundance, alas, the wind blows through a different tune. (Like withered wood.)
The drum sounds and the mallet is raised; this is the second tally. With fragrant rice in his bowl, he is sated and rests. After the eastern wind has fanned it, the spring light is beautiful;
on the distant bank, the willows drape themselves in soft, verdant grace. (Xuefeng Yu)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection: Chan Master Tianran of Danxia in Dengzhou (he was a successor of Shitou). He attended upon Shitou and served him for three years.
One day, Shitou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, you shall weed the grass before the Buddha Hall.
On the following day, the great assembly and the novice monks each prepared spades and mattocks to clear the weeds; however, the Master alone filled a basin with water and washed his head.
He knelt with his head before [the master]. When the master saw him, he laughed and proceeded to shave his hair.
He then preached the precepts for him, whereupon the student covered his ears and departed. The verse says:
Shitou clears the weeds to test the heroic; the bewildered Danxia’s eyes are not high.
Had he known how to turn his body and walk the living path, he would not have burdened his descendants to this day. (Guyuan Dao)
While at Huilin Temple, Danxia encountered bitter cold. He took a wooden Buddha and burned it for fire.
The temple steward scolded him, saying, "How can you burn my wooden Buddha? The Master prodded the ashes with his staff and said, "I am burning it to retrieve the *śarīra*.
The steward asked, "A wooden Buddha—how could it have *śarīra*? The Master replied, "Since there are no *śarīra*, take two more!"
He burned himself, and subsequently his eyebrows and beard fell out. The verse says:
Moss seals the ancient crags as cold invades the door; The birds are startled by the peril, the beasts run in confusion.
Deep in the night, the fires of the marshes burn with frosty heat; At dawn, the fisherman’s house is busy with self-doubt. (Touzi Qing)
Snow embraces the mountain gate, frozen and without spring; a single wooden Buddha is split for firewood.
Where the eyes move, the eyebrows fall—this is slandering the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma. (Zhang Wujin)
The decrepit Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard just protruded. One’s transgressions are those one has committed from of old;
who says that a thousand empties cannot be traded for a single reality? (Fodeng Xun)
Face-to-face, the upward-tending pivot is difficult to conceal; this family tradition has been bestowed upon others for a thousand ages.
Piercing through layer after layer of silver mountains and iron walls, one relies on the Abbot of Danxia to know it. (Chuanfang)
[Continued Collection] Striding along private paths, he suddenly arrives at a public banquet. His *fukuto* (head-wrap) has short ends; his waist-belt boasts its roundness.
It is not that he is a groom’s companion come to offer wine; it is merely that he has mistaken him for a youth seeking a "green mat" (official post). (Yuetang Chang)
When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, the head monk’s eyebrows and beard fell out; this was known by everyone under heaven and across the earth, yet the head monk himself remained unaware.
Originally the supreme flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), alas, it turned instead into a poisonous drug.

One must personally shoulder the karmic retribution, even though the cause of the offense was committed by another. The monastic communities debate this at great length, yet they cannot avoid measuring it with their own conceptual consciousnesses.
Yet one must consider this very self. At once, there is no need for evasion; do not further ask "how" or "what.
For now, there is no rope with which to bind oneself. (Yuánwù Qín)
Pengzu lived eight hundred years seeking to prolong his life; the First Emperor of Qin ascended the throne yet sought further immortality.
Yesterday, as I passed over Tianjin Bridge, Shi Chong was still escorting the boat of poverty. (Mañjuśrī said.)
Danxia burned the wooden Buddha in the cold; the temple steward thus met misfortune and gained blessing.
How pitiable is that improvised inspector, who does nothing but make reckless and confused divinations. (Ying’an Hua)
Dana burned the wooden Buddha; the abbot’s eyebrows and beard fell out. Drawing his bow to shoot Weichi requires a bow made of *jinyá* horn. (Wuxiangfan)
In the desolate monastery, the weather is cold; they burn the wooden Buddhas. A mass of red flames stands before a withered bed. One’s entire body is warmed through the long night;
how can the transgression be made to fall upon the abbot? (Xiangchuan Hong)
One day, Danxia visited Master Pang. Seeing a woman gathering vegetables, the Master asked, "Is the Layman at home?
The woman set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands folded. The Master asked again, "Is the Layman at home? The woman then picked up the basket and walked away.
A short while later, when the Master returned, the Layman was there. The woman recounted the previous conversation, and the Layman said, "Danxia is here."
Mo said, "He has gone. The Master said, "Red earth smeared on a cow's udder.
The Verse says: A single question from Danxia; the girl folds her hands. In the space of a moment of hesitation, the crow flies and the hare runs. Who can testify to this?
An old rustic in the mountain hut smears his ox with red earth; he says nothing of the son’s ugliness.

(The Master of the Wondrous High Terrace) reveals his head and face to offer his response: accustomed to appearing before others, he knows no shame. It is simply that this slave’s own flesh and bone are fine;
without applying rouge or powder, he is nonetheless elegant. Fair-faced youth, from of old our households have been well-matched. How pitiable!
Red earth smeared on cow udders; striking tiles and boring through tortoises with reckless measurement.
(Shangfang Yi) Thin garments, hastily adorned. Baskets left out, hands folded—of no virtue. Old Pang still has more sorrow within;
it is not until the slave-girl leaks the fragrance. (Zhang Wujin)

[Continued Collection] When the author meets the user, their application is intimate; carrying the basket back home, his intent is profound. Clouds gather and rain disperses as the river and sky are clear;
a single song from a fisherman passes by the distant village. (Miaofengshan)
The father-in-law is stubborn and the son is unreliable; the debt must be repaid to the very end. The old wife’s heart is sincere, yet she smears mud on the ox’s udder.
(Beijian Jian) Before others he sells his charms most elegantly; with a single cast, he is caught on the hook without cause.
Even if he could carry away the vegetable basket, alas, spilled water is difficult to reclaim. (Xiaoweng Kan)
Letting go or holding fast, deceiving and obstructing; a single stroke of wind and spirit flows forth from the true lineage.
Had the lacquer bucket not been broken in those days, how could one have scattered earth and cast sand? (Pong-an’s Assembly).
He bowed and asked whether the Layman was at home. The Layman set down his basket and folded his hands. "Alas! A pair of karmic enemies," he said.
"Only Pang Gong is permitted to know that there is [the Way]. (Yuan of Tui’an).
The wind carries the stench of crows; a single moth Stings the traveler into flight, making his fatherly brows knit in a frown. (Xiyan Hui)
Chattering with his mouth and beak is Danxia; folding his robes and carrying his basket, he has already answered him.
If you wish to ensure your family inheritance remains unexposed, do not speak of it upon your return to your grandfather. (Xianji Yun)

Fen asked, "Why did he not possess eyes? Fuyun replied, "Both the giver and the receiver are blind men.
Qing said, "If he had exhausted his skillful means, what then? Fuyun replied, "Can you say that I am blind?
Xuangjue questioned, "Tell me, did Changqing clarify Danxia’s intent, or was it merely using his own family wealth?"

The Verse says: Exhausting the capacity of the faculties does not result in blindness; it is like pressing down a cow’s head while it grazes on grass. The various patriarchs—four times seven and twice three—brought forth precious vessels only to incur fault.
This fault is profound and nowhere to be found; in both the heavens and the human realm, all have sunk beneath the waves. (Xuedou Xian)
[Added for inclusion] Danxia asked Layman Pang: "How was our meeting yesterday compared to today? Pang said:
"If you bring up yesterday's matter according to the Dharma, let us make it into a 'patriarchal eye' (zongyan). The Master said: "As for this patriarchal eye, can it contain Layman Pang?
Pang said: "I am inside your eye. The Master said: "My eyes are narrow; where would you find a place to settle yourself?"
The Master said, "How narrow are these eyes! How secure is this body! The Master then ceased speaking. The scholar said, "Speak one more phrase, and this dialogue will be complete.
The Master also did not respond. The scholar said, "Among all [the words], this one sentence is something no one can utter. The Verse says:
How narrow is this eye! How secure is this body! Yesterday and today—the circumstances are no different.
In Huainan and Liangzhe, it is hot in autumn and cold in spring. To understand it in such a way is quite groundless. Thirty years from now, do not let others deceive you.
(Fojiàn Qín): Yesterday and today the circumstances differ; with each cold rain comes a fresh wind. The foundation of the Great Peace clearly remains;
the sources of the mountain streams all flow toward the east. (Túdú Cè):
Meeting an opponent at the board, every move is fresh; when one finds the essence of the game, it is hard to hide the self from the eyes.
When the board is finished, one knows not where they have gone; the man who split the axe-handle laments in the empty mountains. (Fang’an Xian)
Yesterday and today are the same yet different. A fierce dragon stirs the vast blue sea; a swift falcon sweeps through the azure sky.
The eye of the lineage is as bright as the sun; the wheel of its function is as rapid as the wind. Where Danxia turns his head, the entire world searches in vain for his trace.
(Shixi Yue). [Added from another collection.
One day, Danxia was holding a rosary in his hand when a lay practitioner approached and snatched it away, saying, "If both of you are empty-handed, then let it be.
The Master said, "This jealous old man does not recognize good from bad. [The practitioner] said, "Seizing the Master’s case."
[The monk] said, "Once it has been put on, it will never be like that again. The Master said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! The monk said, "My teacher makes people afraid.
The Master said, "There are still some more blows left. The monk said, "I am old; I cannot take another blow. The Master said, "You ignorant fellow!
Even if I were to strike you, it would be of no benefit. The monk said, "And there is no skillful means for guidance here either. The Master threw down [his staff].
