Few are those who have severed the three barriers; facing the blade, who can manifest their full majesty? At the place where the willow blossoms are plucked, who beholds them?
The wind carries them across the heavens, flying like snow. (Fohuiquan)
A truly magnificent and noble man he was! Yet he was easily deceived by the sesame seeds.
Had he known how to clench his fist and display his spirit, where in this world could he have found room for him? (Baoning Yong)
The green mountains are no different; the white jade is without flaw. Vastly flows the water; in confusion, the yellow chrysanthemums.
Where there is a Buddha, not even a hair’s breadth stands; where there is no Buddha, there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences.
A traveler who has not yet returned to Chang’an, seeking the stream, naturally plucks the willow flowers. (Tiantong Jue)
Beyond three thousand li lie two layers of barriers; it is difficult for the many patch-robed monks to pass through them.
Turning one’s head toward the north and south paths of the Stone Bridge, willow catkins are scattered by the wind in a vast expanse of snow. (Puyong Ping)
Do not dwell where there is a Buddha. An iron weight for a scale has been eaten through by worms. Run swiftly past where there is no Buddha;
you will bump into the broken stove-fall of Mount Song. Do not misrepresent this three thousand miles away. Two stone men whisper to one another.
"If it is so, then one does not go. This saying has already spread throughout the world.
"Plucking the willow flowers, plucking the willow flowers. Oṃ maṇidhari hūṃ phaṭ. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] Plucking the willow blossoms, plucking the willow blossoms. Beating the drum and playing the lute. Yesterday planting eggplants;
today sowing winter melons. (Nantang Si)
Do not dwell where a Buddha resides; the spring breeze blows vast and wide, scattering willow catkins. Rush swiftly past where no Buddha dwells;
a single-leafed fishing boat cuts through the river’s surface. In the forest, crows and magpies go and come; in the garden, peach and plum trees bloom and then wither.
The *śūnyatā* spirit manifests within the vast void; the eyeless seer encounters a dark night.
(Baiyang Shun) An iron mountain collapses and crushes a silver mountain; the ball rolls upon the board, and the pearl rolls upon the plate.
Intimately grasping the mandarin ducks, he embroiders them at leisure; the golden needle is never shown to others. (Songyuan Yue)
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, one cannot abide; beyond three thousand *li*, there is nothing to rely upon.
Zhaozhou has won the radiance of his lips, yet it is this monk who knows where it truly falls. (Xutang Yu)

A monk asked Zhaozhou, "I have heard that you, Master, personally met Nanquan—is this true? The Master said, "In Zhenzhou, we grow large radishes. The Verse says: In Zhenzhou, they grow large radishes; When the spring wind blows, the fragrance fills the ten directions.
If you wish to know the source of the ancient path, Look at the moon reflected in the clear stream.
When asked about the circumstances of his initial attainment of the Dharma, he did not speak of the Eastern Land or the Western Heaven. "In Zhenzhou there is a vegetable called radish;
it has relieved the itch of hunger for nearly ten thousand years. (Fenyang Shanzhao)

In Zhenzhou they produce large radishes; the monks of the world take this as their standard. They know only from ancient times to the present, vying with one another to distinguish whether a crane is white or a crow is black.
Thief! Thief! (Xuedou Xian)—have these monks ever even grasped the nostrils of a monk?
The radish of Zhenzhou spreads throughout China and the barbarian lands; all things find their native soil most suitable. Who would say that people of that time alone cherished it?
Even today, it remains excellent for staving off hunger. (Zhengjue Yi)
Tao Qian planted only willows at Pengze; Pan Yue cultivated only flowers at Heyang.
How can these compare to gazing upon the river in the evening, where several peaks of verdant green belong to the fishermen’s homes? (Haiyin Xin)
The nostrils of the patch-robed monk are needlessly pierced; through plain and honest deliberation, one succeeds to the ancestral lineage.
Much thanks to Master Zhang’s diligent efforts, he has preserved the entire garden through the deep winter. (Fohuiquan)
"From Zhenzhou comes the great radish head; report to your lord that you must understand its origin clearly.
Most patch-robed monks merely swallow it whole; they rarely obtain its true flavor in detail. (Baizhang Yuanwen)
The radish of Zhènzhou is naturally distinct. Clearly, it speaks from mouth to mouth to people;
yet those of meager merit and icchantikas do not believe. A single one weighs three catties. (Bǎoíng Yǒng)
In Zhenzhou they produce a vegetable called the radish; later on, one reflects and finds it difficult to obtain. Old Man Wang’s descendants do not conceal anything;
whenever they meet someone, they reveal the true message directly. (Changling Zhuo)
Even the ancient Buddha Zhaozhou spoke much: "The radish grows in the fields of Zhenfu.
Many monks throughout the world gnaw at it, yet they miss Old Nanquan between their teeth. (Mañjuśrī said:)
I visited the Venerable Master Nanquan Wang: the radish of Zhenzhou has no private secrets. Held up, it blocks the mouths of right and wrong;
this "Snowy Melody" and "Springtime Song" are not the *Chuci*. (Jingshan Daoyuan)

[Continued Collection] Old Zhao’s ingenuity has neither shallow nor deep; the radish of Zhenzhou continues the tradition of the monastic groves. To reflect upon it after the fact is difficult to find;
he enters the mud and the water with the compassionate heart of an old woman. (Daguai Zhi)
"Great radishes grow in Zhenzhou; there is a reason for the harmony between master and disciple.
Maitreya is in Guanyin Temple; Zhaozhou is to the west of Dongyuan. (Gushan Gui)
Green emerges from indigo; ice is born from water. A single step cannot be taken; white clouds stretch for ten thousand li.
(Huian Ti). This little livelihood is upon the lips; once touched, it races like the wind and whirls like lightning.
In vain do you speak of the large radishes of Zhenzhou; when have you ever truly met Old Nanquan? (Shi’an Shi).
I have personally seen this eye of Nanquan; the old man’s speech was unrestrained.
It was simply because he had not removed the "vegetable smell" that he brought his descendants to the trouble of biting radishes. (Yeyun Nan)
[Added for inclusion] Once, a scholar asked Zhaozhou, "Is it true that the Buddha does not go against the vows of sentient beings?
The Master said, "Yes. The scholar said, "May I have the staff held by you, Master?
The Master said, "A gentleman does not take away what another cherishes. The scholar said, "I am no gentleman. The Master said, "Neither am I a Buddha."
The Verse says:
Where the occasion demands, he turns without hesitation; a bright pearl rolls within a lapis lazuli bowl.
Old Zhaozhou is a village schoolmaster; a single staff is carried by two men. (Shi’an Shao)
[Added from the *Zuocheng*] Once Zhaozhou went to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from Nanquan.
Baizhang asked, "What sayings or phrases has Nanquan recently used to instruct his disciples? The Master said, "A person who has nothing to do must simply go quietly.
Baizhang said, "Setting aside that 'quietly' for a moment, how would you speak the phrase for 'busyness'? The Master—
The Master took three steps forward. Baizhang then shouted. The Master made a gesture of shrinking his body. Baizhang said, "Excellent, how profoundly silent!
The Master then went out. The verse says:

When two artists meet, each finds it difficult to match the other; they are left in a state of bewildered silence. Advancing forward and retreating backward, they can neither mold nor fashion anything.
They do not travel the great highway, but instead run through the weeds. (Fojian Qín).
There is a gate within the gate, and there is one without. One does not act as Yan Ping to offend the Ox and Dipper constellations. A lion’s roar meets the howl of a jackal;
he plucks out the pupils from the eyes of Li Lou. One hand contracts, the other extends. Double Ninth is definitively the ninth day of the ninth month.
He overturns the seas and mountains to seek a true companion. His bare bones are exhausted, revealing his two elbows. (Xiatang Yuan)
[Zhaoshou] addressed the assembly, saying: "I do not like to hear the word 'Buddha'. Huan’an Jue commented:
"Everyone must take care not to understand it in this way. Since you should not understand it in this way, how then should you understand it?"
He then spoke in verse:
"The single word 'Buddha' I do not care to hear. Last year was as it is this spring. This spring a great snow has fallen;
The black basin at Lu-mu has turned into a white basin."
[Added for inclusion] Once, when the assembly was attending the evening *zanchan* (general inquiry), Zhaozhou said, "Tonight we shall answer questions;
let anyone who can ask one come forward. At that moment, a monk stepped forth and bowed.
Zhaozhou said, "I intended to throw a brick to draw out a jade gem, yet I have only drawn out a brick. Fayan asked Jue Tiezi, "What was the meaning of the former master?"
"What is it like? Jue said, "It is like the state appointing a general. He then asked, "Who could go?
At that time, someone came forward and said, "I can go. [Jue] said, "You cannot go.
Fayan said, "I understand. The verse says:
How many know the probing pole and the shadow-grass? It is just like a general’s single-sided banner. Slaying generals and pitching camp—all rests with me;
riding backward upon an iron horse, I ascend Mount Sumeru. (Cishou Shen)
"A thousand-year-old field has eight hundred owners. Who can, when the opportunity arises, discern their place of origin? Zhaozhou wished to provide an answer; he threw a brick to draw out the tiles.
Old Jue spoke of the essential point, like the ceremony of enfeoffing a general. Whether one can go or cannot go is distinguished as black or white beneath a single word.
Here, higher than ten-thousand-fathom peaks, without moving a single hair, he captures the Buddhas and Patriarchs. (Yuanwu Keqin)
Zhaozhou ascended the hall and said: "The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire;
the clay Buddha does not pass through water; the true Buddha sits within. A verse says:
The clay Buddha does not cross the water; divine light illuminates heaven and earth. If one continues standing in the snow without ceasing, who would not discern the true from the false?
The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; when people come to visit Master Hu, they see but a few characters upon his plaque. Where is the pure breeze not present?

A wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; one should constantly reflect on the story of the Broken Oven-Fall. When the staff suddenly struck it, only then did he realize he had betrayed me. (Xuedou Xian)
Setting aside the clay buddhas and the golden-wood buddhas, Zhaozhou lets loose a hawk from the vast heavens. To the east, west, south, and north, they vainly lift their heads;
through ten thousand miles of layered clouds, there is but a single sudden thrust. (Baizun Yuan).
The clay Buddha does not cross the water; before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there was once a "stop, stop.

If you examine your own retreat, it will not allow waves to rise even though they may arise. The golden Buddha does not leave the furnace; the mountains and rivers of the sea enter the painted scroll.
Though the Thousand-Handed Avalokiteśvara exerts his strength in vain, I am ashamed that Śunyata’s eyes and brows are coarse. The wooden Buddha does not pass through fire. Much...
"Master Mou once said: 'Hiding behind a blade and dodging arrows is not fit for discussion; countless heroes have missed their mark.
(Daopei Xiu) Whether golden Buddha, wooden Buddha, or clay Buddha—whether passing through the kiln, water, or fire—they all enter Zhaozhou’s red furnace of fierce flames."
Forged within the light, a single note of "White Snow" and "Yangchun"—throughout ten thousand ages, no one can harmonize with it.
(Gushan Gui) The ninety-seven kinds of wondrous marks are difficult for Gu Kaizhi or Lu Tanwei to depict in their finest colors;
Zhaozhou’s eyes were so sharp and clear he could see right into the heart, liver, and five viscera. (Jingshan Gao)
[Continued Collection] A wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; before the Terrace of Ambrosia, one meets Bodhidharma. Regretfully, the people of Luoyang have not yet arrived;
for nine years he sat in vain and coldness, facing the wall. A golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; sitting, he sighs that weary life runs along the paths.
If one does not look at it in a painting of Mount Hua, how could one know Pan Lang riding his donkey backward? The clay Buddha does not cross the water;
a single ray of numinous light illuminates heaven and earth. One can admire the old, ancient wit Xuan Sha: he did not want Nanshan, he wanted the turtle-nosed snake. (Sansheng Chang)
The forms of the three Buddhas are all not real; the pupils in their eyes are the person before you.
If you can believe in the treasure within your own home, the crying birds and mountain flowers are one and the same spring. (Yemufeng)

The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the splendor of spring fills the imperial capital. Among the young men who indulge in flowers and wine, how many can be supported as they stagger in deep intoxication?
The wooden Buddha does not pass through the fire; the Great Being is free of self and other. Yet if one’s thoughts deviate by even a hair’s breadth, one will suffer bondage for kalpas on end.
The clay Buddha does not cross the water; the bright moon shines across a thousand li. The wind is high upon the ancient trees in autumn; the bottom of the long river is frozen solid.
The golden Buddha does not cross the furnace; though one seeks its source, it is nowhere to be found. The wooden Buddha does not cross the fire; the whole mass cannot be bitten through.
A clay Buddha does not cross water; where is there that is not you? The true Buddha sits in the house; Zhaozhou says this is a calamity.
The water-buffalo knows how to plow the fields; the yellow ox can pull the millstone. (Chang’an Chong)
The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; his radiant halo dazzles the great void. If you can realize this directly and immediately, there is no need for further hesitation.
The wooden Buddha does not pass through the fire; the head monk’s eyebrows fall off. The fierce flames stretch across the sky like a rainbow, yet not a single grain of *śarīra* remains.
The clay Buddha does not cross the water; for the patch-robed monk, it is difficult to open his mouth. To hesitate is to be separated by a thousand mountains;
it is a journey of ten thousand miles. The True Buddha sits within; Zhaozhou, stop your talkative falling. To accept him face-to-face, yet as soon as you lift your eyes, you have already missed him.
The golden Buddha, the wooden Buddha, and the clay Buddha—having pierced through them and cast them beyond Jambudvīpa, he further says that the true Buddha is within;
for no reason, it has already been smeared over. (Nirgrantha Zhong).
The True Buddha sits within his house; opening his mouth, he falls into idle chatter. Fortunately, he is naturally pitiable—what can I possibly say for him? (Yuelin Guan)
Clay Buddhas, gold Buddhas, and wood Buddhas—crossing through water, fire, and the furnace—their wondrous essence is fundamentally without location.
Do not forcibly smear a false coating over the True Buddha. (Tianmu Li)

[Added for inclusion] Once, when a nun asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the most profound mystery? the Master pinched her with his hand. The nun said, "The Master still has this [duality] remaining.

The Master said, "In fact, it is you who have this remaining. Verse: The nun asked about the most profound mystery; The Master used his hand to pinch her. She said, "The Master still has this remaining"; He replied, "It is actually you who have this remaining."
Dense and profound, the meaning is most far-reaching. How many people have misunderstood it in their cold-hearted deliberations?
If the nun can understand Zhaozhou’s pinching, even an iron heart would break with grief. (Cishou Shen)
A hard, fleshy growth like cotton-wool; the elegant old Zhaozhou of Hebei. Salt where it is salty, water added where it is bland;
a laugh from the high seat that never ceases. (Zhengtang Bian)
The fierce tiger hides deep within the shallow grassy nest; several times the bright moon enters the misty vines.
Even if one possesses the Vajra-eye upon the crown of the head, one cannot avoid stumbling past him right before one's own eyes. (Gao Feng Miao)

Just so. The verse says:
The monk has gone south toward Min; the road is not far. He reports that the troops are clamoring and shouting. If one asks where the Master has retreated to avoid them, It is just so:
he sleeps peacefully as the sun is high at noon. (Fenyang Zhao)
Hearing it said that the troops in Min are numerous, I earnestly warn the traveler to avoid the clash of arms.
At the parting of ways, I point out a place of concealment; Countless valiant generals can do nothing against it. (Zhengjue Yi)
On the road back to the Seven Fujians, they vie for mastery day after day. To avoid them, one must ensure no trace is left behind.
Where is it precisely that one may hide? Beyond the green mountains, ten thousand layers of clouds. (Fohuiquan)
Once, when a monk traveling to Mount Wutai asked an old woman, "Which way does the path to Mount Wutai go?
The woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed. The woman said, "What a fine monk, yet he goes away like that.
Later, another monk reported this to Master Zhaozhou. The Master said, "Wait until I go to investigate him myself. The next day, the Master...

He went at once to ask her, "Where does the road to Mount Tai lead? The old woman said, "Go straight ahead. The Master then continued on his way. The old woman said, "What a fine monk, yet he goes away like that!

Upon returning to the monastery, the Master said to the monks, "The old woman of Mount Tai has thoroughly exposed you all. Verse: The road to Mount Tai—go straight ahead. A fine monk, yet he goes away like that. The old woman of Mount Tai has thoroughly exposed you all. How many have been deceived by this old woman? If you can discern the meaning of these words, Then you will know the true path of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
If you do not understand, then you are truly lost; In the end, you will surely fall into the pit of the three realms.
The "Wife Chan" on the road to Mount Tai: north, south, east, and west, in myriads upon myriads. Zhaozhou’s discernment is difficult for people to understand;
coming and going, his straw sandals are worn through to the very core. (Fenyang Shao)

Zhaozhou thoroughly exposed the old woman; when the leaves fall, one naturally knows autumn. How many Zen practitioners there are throughout the world, wandering aimlessly across the Five Lakes and Four Seas! (Ciming Yuan)
The numinous tortoise has not yet shown its signs; there is neither misfortune nor good fortune. Change and movement depend on the moment and rest with the diviner.
At the crossroads, who is it that asks about the broken path? Old Wang in the eastern village glares with eyes full of anger. (Touzi Qing).
Master Zhaozhou interrogates the old woman; in an era of Great Peace, he employs weapons of war. Zhaozhou has secured the Dragon-Spring Sword;
he sweeps away all smoke and dust—it is entirely his doing. (Foyin Yuan)
A monk asked about the path to You-tai. The old woman pointed directly and was not mistaken. Although she spoke with straightforward words, how many follow such a way?
Zhaozhou’s discernment brings it home; by what evidence does one who understands rely? The moonlight divides the hall at dawn; the clouds have cleared, and the mountain peaks are revealed.
(Fushan Yuan): "He who stands out from the monastic groves is Zhaozhou. The old woman’s discernment leaves no room for further inquiry. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror;
let the traveler not treat the road as an enemy. (Huanglong Nan).
Wielding the halberd and spear, Old Zhaozhou; sitting and watching the victory or defeat, he possessed a brilliant strategy.
Who truly understands how he exposed the old woman? How many practitioners of Chan have gone astray! (Haiyin Xin)
Zhaozhou thoroughly exposed the "Old Lady’s Chan"; whether speaking or remaining silent, the truth is clearly before one's eyes.
Lately, those seekers from the Five Lakes have been wandering like smoke along byways. (Jingzhao Zhen).
The old Chan practitioner is discerning within his words; he goes straight up the path to the Terrace of the Mountain without missing his way.
Having thoroughly investigated and returned, let no one question him: the boatman of Yueyang on the waves of Lake Dongting. (Yunfeng Yue)
In days of yore Zhaozhou was the chief general; when the battle with the old woman ended, who was permitted to pass judgment?
What is the matter with the road at Mount Tai today? It is instead being traversed by people in a casual and thoughtless manner. (Daguixiu)
The road to Mount Tai stretches on and on. Only by arriving there in person can one realize it is the ancient Zhaozhou.
When the old woman was seen through, she turned her head; the long river flows east as ever. (Fohuiquan)
Amidst the clamor of war, the foundation of Great Peace was established; with stony rains and gentle breezes, it surpasses ancient times.
The old woman has thoroughly scrutinized you; few know the traces of Zhaozhou. (Baizun Yuan).
What is the matter with the story of Master Zhaozhou’s old woman? Its majestic power resounds through past and present, upholding the family’s reputation.
In the high void the moon is bright while a thousand gates remain shut; on the Great Way there is no one else, and he walks alone. (Baoning Yong)
Zhaozhou’s single interrogation of the old woman—throughout the ages, his heroic spirit grows ever more precious. Those who come from the south or go to the north have yet to realize it;
from this day forth, Mount Tai shall be overgrown with brambles. (Zhaojue Zong)
"Appearing mad yet not mad—Old Zhaozhou. Whether ordinary or holy, who can discern it? Let you decide right and wrong, long and short;
the old woman was seen through by him. (Zhenjing Wen)
Zhaozhou asked the Way-seeking Woman: "Which way is it? She replied, "Go straight on like this. Everyone says she was "tested and exposed" by the old woman;
the old woman leaves you with no place to clear your name. Those who share the same path should raise this together. (Jingfu Shun).
"Whether you penetrate it or not, the old woman can bring disaster upon you. Even a person with a thousand eyes from Potalaka is but a tiger watching a water mill. (Yunju Yu)
Zhaozhou’s investigation revealed that affairs are not real; he has chased the people on the road to Mount Tai to death.
If you wish to recognize where the old lady points with her own hand, every time you raise your head, it is new again. (Dizang En)
The old woman on the road to Mount Tai was often questioned by passersby; it was only at the end that Zhaozhou knew her, and with a single word, he exposed her completely. (Yungai Zhi).
This is a traveling platform for raising questions; the old lady’s directions are all too vague and general. Piteous indeed, her eyes lack any discerning power;
she treats everyone as if they were all the same. (Foguo Bai).
The ancient master stirs up smoke and dust; sitting and watching the contest, who knows? From of old, the ancient road has been as level as the palm of a hand;
it is simply that the traveler does not see the way back home. (Yuanjueyan)
The path to Baji Terrace is unmistakable; travelers go there thus, boundless.
After Zhaozhou returned from having seen through it, the four seas and five lakes were one and the same family. (Cangtang Qing).

The road to the Terrace Mountain is straight and not circuitous; Zhaozhou went there in person to determine the wise and the foolish. Coming and going through past and present, what hindrance can there be?
If one has not yet penetrated the golden dust, it remains fundamentally coarse. (Third Patriarch’s Lineage)
The road beneath Mount Taishan is steep and rugged; how many travelers have faltered halfway?
Asking for directions by the Five-Mile Marker, they do not realize their humble steed is a dragon colt. (Shangfang Yi)
The white-haired old woman on the road to Mount Tai—how many times have countless travelers passed her by? She says directly that people do not understand the profound gate;
Zhaozhou has intentionally cut through the confusion. (Yunxi Gong)
An elder of the forest stands peerless; his majestic wind chills the four hundred prefectures.
Having once shattered the iron barrier with a single blow, his great kindness is difficult to repay even with rain and dew. (Zhenru Zhe)
Go straight ahead! Go straight ahead! Do not chase after the finger; do not travel the old path.
A man of great character strides alone through heaven and earth. (Doushuai Yue)

Originally intending to level the roads, I instead ended up adding mud upon the earth. Now, throughout the five lakes and four seas, everyone has been utterly bewildered by the words of the old woman. (Yuantong Xian)
There is a road on Mount Tai that people pass along; two by two and three by three, many stop to ask the way.
If you wish to recognize Zhaozhou’s personal penetration, his tongue has no bone—what can you do about him? (Kumu Cheng).
Highly grasping his golden whip, he emerges from the Forbidden City; The frosty wind is piercing, yet the horse’s hooves are light.
After returning with the smoke and dust entirely swept away, Travelers from the four seas celebrate the Great Peace. (By Puyong Ping)
The road to Mount Wutai enters the towering peaks; go straight ahead, and let the sound of the finger point the way for you.
There is yet another busy fellow, Zhaozhou, who upon his return says, "I have examined the old lady" (Zhang Wujin).
Who could have known that old Zhaozhou had been thoroughly exposed? With his jade whip, he spurred on the reclining golden ox.
For those who travel the road of Tai Shan through all ages, they drink the pure flavor with a smile; the style of its essence grows ever more profound. (Changling Zhuo)
Two layers of question and answer, free from confusion; within this, Old Zhao nevertheless examines the old woman.
If one does not cast one’s whole body into the tiger’s den, how can one thoroughly verify the immortal lady? (Heishan Fang)
Zhaozhou personally investigated and broke through it; at Mount Tai there are no two paths. This very old woman—few people know her traces. (Fuxincai)
In the past, there was a monk in Yan and Zhao who wandered casually amidst the thickets of war. To quell chaos, he carried no three-foot sword;
to this day, the world is free of the *chancheng* (rebellious banners). (Baofeng Xiang)
Do not let the "motherly heart" become entangled; when you meet the person on the main road, the pointing will be unerring. Do not ask about the Dragon Gate seeking transformation;
wind and thunder reside right within Ge Hong’s house. (Min Gufo)
Zhaozhou’s interrogation exposes how difficult the road is to pass. Countless ordinary people scurry back and forth like shuttlecocks.
At sunset, Mount Tai is empty and silent; even to this day, its contradictions have not ceased. (Shaolin Tong)
The "Wife Chan" on the road to Mount Tai: it directs people straight ahead to press forward. One must personally penetrate the test of Zhaozhou;
from this point on, the roads of the four seas will be level and smooth. (Yungai Chang)
The road is difficult to travel; the road is difficult to travel. What is most difficult to pass is Mount Tai. Only Master Zhaozhou possesses the official seal of certification;
with head held high and arms swinging, he is entirely at ease. Entirely at ease. Suifu produces the alms bowl. (Zantang Zhun).
"The road to Mount Tai is level throughout. It is simply that the traveler is unaccustomed to it. It is like the grievance of an ugly woman before a clear mirror;
it is the affliction of a fool regarding a wise man. (Shushan Chang)
The ancient road of Mount Tai is traveled by men; each one seeks the old woman to ask for the way. It is laughable that Zhaozhou, as soon as he was scrutinized, saw through her;
this vast emptiness throughout the ages makes people sorrowful. (Sushan Ru).
The jade flute blows forth the cry of the phoenix and the peacock. It stirs the hearts of travelers toward parting. A gust of eastern wind sweeps across the vast expanse;
in the four quarters and eight directions, few are those who understand. (Fozhi Yu)
The road at Mount Tai is level and smooth; the old woman deliberates in vain. Zhaozhou has seen through her;
a pure breeze fills the Great Tang. (Gao’an Wu)
The Chan practitioners of the world speak of "penetrating through examination. Who knows that Zhaozhou has already fallen into error? He has led his descendants to become no true men;
everyone is cleverer than they ought, lying prostrate in a cold place. (Jingshan Gao)
Three punches to the face, seven slaps on the cheeks; all the people in the great earth do not know the pain or the itch.
(Gushan Gui) On the road to Mount Tai it is difficult for people to advance; only Zhaozhou came in person.
Having exposed the old woman’s place of turning back, from then on the eyes of travelers were not opened. (Chuanfang)
[Continued Collection] The Way-Pointing Old Woman is at Wutai. When Zen practitioners arrive here, they are all rendered utterly foolish.
With a single blow, they shatter the land of Fusang; the radiant sun shines upon the nine realms of heaven. (By Guang Daozhe of Western Shu).
The wife was originally the foot of the Demon King; the three armies did not move, yet the banners flickered.
Zhaozhou’s handleless iron broom sweeps away the dust and smoke until all is empty and desolate. (Stonehead returns).
The old woman only knew how to point the way; the rooster and dog were stolen by someone.
Only after Zhaozhou had finished his investigation did she finally close her door tight. (Xi Yu Jing, Part Two)
Old Zhaozhou, in his great age, did not know how to sit in meditation in the mountains. He said he would go to test the old woman, yet he was instead exposed by her.
Skillfully binding where there is no rope; skillfully walking where there are no tracks. Not fighting, yet subduing the enemy's army; facing him directly with swift, opportune action.
The old woman has seen through Mount Wutai; who can penetrate Zhaozhou’s Barrier? (Yuánwù Qín).
Having grown old and become a perfected spirit, his transmission is unerring. Zhaozhou, an ancient Buddha, succeeded Nánquán. He lost his life seeking the image to summon back his soul;
a fine horse chasing the wind is burdened by repeated tethering. Once the "old woman's Chan" is thoroughly scrutinized, it is not worth mentioning before others.

Money. (Tiantong Jue). The thief is a petty person, yet his cunning surpasses that of the gentleman. Having committed a great falsehood, he simply snatches it away by plain hand; bold and coarse of heart.
There is no place where you can meet him; I bow my head to Zhaozhou, the Great Dharma King (who herds oxen and wanders).
His great function is fully manifested, as deep as the ocean; the armies of Māra retreat, and ghosts cannot restrain him.
Where Zhaozhou exposes the old woman’s deception, the grass bows and the wind blows—nowhere can he be found. (Nantang Xing, No. 2)
The Old Man of Zhaozhou thrusts his needle into the mire; having exposed the old woman’s deception, the entire monastic community receives this bounty.
The matron is not on Mount Wutai; for a traveler on level ground, the path is difficult to traverse.
Yet, walking straight along the easy road of antiquity and the present, one passes through Zhaozhou’s barrier with ease. (Xuedou Zong)
Go straight along Taisan Road. When Zhao La saw the old woman, he had no other words.
Having returned from this investigation, whether you know it or not, do not believe the idle people who speak of right and wrong. (Yeyu Chuan).
In the spring light of the third month, I travel to the capital; auspicious clouds and auspicious vapors gather around the Dragon Palace.
Having personally passed before the Xuande Gate, I ask the passersby once more for the way to Bianzhou. (Mañjuśrī said.)
For how many years has the old woman sought a swordsman? Zhaozhou’s discernment reveals a point of ambiguity.
To know how to employ others does not depend on inherited wealth; where is the true elegance in wearing so many robes? (Nutang Si)
One presses down as the ox eats grass; one hands the thief a ladder. Had he known early that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago. (Yuan of Dun’an)
The foundation of Great Peace lies amidst the clamor of war; it is only by not using weapons that it is attained.
Without the strength to lift a cauldron or pull down a mountain, the black steed *Wu'ei* cannot easily be ridden for a thousand miles. (By Ming Da Chan)
The four seas are one family; two mouths share but one tongue. Zhaozhou has seen through it all—whom would he have to tell his reason? (Wan’an Yan)
Squatting upon the ancient roadhead of Mount Tai, the traveling cloud-robed monks are struck by spears and halberds. Zhaozhou raises the Nala arrow;
once it has pierced through the skull, one simply rests. (By Nun Wuzhuo Zong).
The heavens are high and the earth deep; few can see them. The ocean is vast and the mountains remote; only one knows this for oneself.
Once you have scrutinized and penetrated this, turn back and do not ask further. To gain an advantage is to suffer a loss. (Mianjie)
Zhaozhou’s tongue reaches the heavens; the old woman’s eyebrows cover the earth.
Having clearly seen through this and returned, countless ordinary people fall into a deep slumber. (Nun Miaohui Jingzhi).
Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman: hitting the mark every time he shoots. He chases after a rat and breaks the oil jar.
(Fozhao Guang) The village old woman has become suddenly wealthy; she deceives and terrifies the neighborhood. Zhaozhou peddles his cleverness; it is like adding a barb to an arrow. (Huan’an Ti)
Straight on, straight on! Under the blue sky and bright sun, it has been thoroughly investigated and seen through. Not worth a single coin.
(Yuelin Guan) Originally a man of the mountains, I love to speak of mountain talk. Selling pine winds in the fifth month—fearless that they have no price in the human world.
(Meng’an Yue): On the road to Mount Tiantai, there is an old woman; on level ground, she raises a ten-foot wave without a breeze.
Having closed the sluice gates and opened the bottom valves, not a single drop reaches the Yellow River. (Wuzhun Fan).
The old woman was thoroughly exposed; her face turned green and her eyes blackened. This old fellow Zhaozhou could not deceive me. (Wenshu Ye).
Zhaozhou spoke of "breaking through the examination," yet he strikes his own forehead with his heart. How can one lack the wisdom of transformation? In vain, he seeks out an enemy.

The Way—whether you hit upon it or not—where can you grope for it? Scales on the dragon’s back; donkey’s feet before one’s face.
A somersault to turn back; a solitary cloud and wild crane. A-he-he! (Yun’gai Zhi).
[Added from another source] One day, Zhaozhou struck a fire-pot and asked a monk, "I call this fire; what do you call it? The monk was speechless.

The Master said, "Not knowing the profound principle, one merely exerts oneself in seeking stillness. Faldeng Qin offered a different interpretation, saying, "I am not as good as you. The verse says: I strike the fire-pot; the monk is silent. He does not know the profound principle. In vain he labors to seek stillness. I am not as good as you.
Zhaozhou’s eye emits light, piercing through the four worlds. A handle is attached to his alms bowl; even to this day, it remains a subject of conversation. (Old Monk Zheng).
Directly beneath, right and wrong cannot be grasped. At the place where they cannot be grasped, one must take it up with resolve. Last night, the wooden man delivered a message:
the Persian from the South Sea has passed through the Great Tang. (Yuan’an Xuan)
[Added for inclusion] Once, a certain old woman sent someone with money to invite Master Zhaozhou to recite the *Tripitaka*.
After the Master had accepted the offering, he descended from his meditation seat, walked around it once, and said, "Tell the old woman that the recitation of the *Tripitaka* is finished.
When the messenger returned and reported this to the woman, she said, "I invited him to recite the entire canon; why did you only recite a single circuit?"
Panthaka. The verse says:
He ran down from the meditation seat and walked around once; Having read the five thousand scrolls of the Tathāgata, The old woman’s years are advanced, yet her eyes are still clear;
Deep in the night under the moon, she threads her needle. (Cishou Shen)
Turning left and turning right; the vajra sword; the full treasury and the half-treasury; the arrow shot from the base;
piercing the red heart within the red heart; it startles Mount Sumeru so that its peak spins backward. (By Zhengtang Bian)
Zhaozhou’s single circuit turns the celestial wheel; the old woman’s recognition is not yet a full recompense. Universally for humans and devas he opens the true eye;
the great trichiliocosm is gathered within a single hair. (Zu’an Jian)
Unaware that sitting upright involves constant revolving, one descends the meditation seat in vain and circles it once;
turning one's back, one claims to have missed half the way—this old woman has brought her own evil karma upon herself. (Tianmu Li)
Zhaozhou’s sword-spirit pierced the ox and the dipper; the old woman’s divine talisman hung from her elbow.
One staff supported by two people—what a master among masters boasting of his mastery! (He kills Liuyan Hui.)
[Added from another source] Once, while a monk was attending to him, Zhaozhou pointed to a fire and asked, "This is fire; you must not call it 'fire.
I have already said it. The monk had no reply. Zhaozhou then poked at the fire with a poker and asked, "Do you understand?"
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "There is a Venerable Touzi in Shuzhou;
go there to pay your respects and ask him. He will surely explain it for you. If the karmic conditions accord, you need not come back; if they do not accord, then return.
The monk arrived at Touzi's place, and Touzi asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Zhaozhou. Touzi said, "Zhao..."
"What did Master Zhaozhou say? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Zen Master Linji asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not.
He requested, "Please, Master, give me instruction. Linji descended from his meditation seat, walked three steps, and then sat back down.
He asked again, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. Linji said, "Go back and report this to Zhaozhou. The monk returned and reported it to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said:
"Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "If Touzi were like this, it would not be much different.
The Verse says:
I call it fire; you may not. It has already been said: what would you call it? (By Yang Wuweï)
Zhaozhou calls it fire; his whole body enters the wild grass. I am not he now; he is precisely me now. (Yuelin Guan)
*The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls: Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School*, Scroll 18.
*The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls: Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School*, Scroll 19.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery during the Yuan Shaoxing era, this is the continuation of the Recorded Sayings of the Patriarchs,
from the Fourth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch, Part Six (the second of the third later generations under Nanyue).
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
The monk said, "Master, do not point to external objects to show people. The Master said, "I am not pointing to external objects to show people."
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Verse:
The cypress tree in the courtyard grows from within the earth; It requires no oxen or plows to till the slopes. This directly reveals the myriad aspects of the Coming from the West.
The road—dense and thick forests are its eyes (Fenyang Zhao).
"The cypress tree in front of the hall," said Zhaozhou; "the price of rice in Luling," spread by Jiyang.
Every three-year-old child can recite this; does even an eighty-year-old elder understand it? (Fushan Yuan).
Zhaozhou’s cypress in front of the courtyard: the whole world runs after Zen guests. Do not let your child grow too large;
once grown, he becomes a master thief. (Ciming Yuan)
A veteran Chan monk of seven hundred sexagenarian cycles—how settled he makes the state, yet suffering is his lot. When asked about the West, he points to the courtyard cypress;
instead, he causes the whole world to brandish weapons. (Xuedou Xian, 2)
The spiritual mechanism of a thousand miles is not easily approached. When a dragon gives birth to a dragon cub, do not be complacent. Zhaozhou seized the "City-of-Ten-Thousand-Valleys" jade;
both the Qin ruler and Liang Jiangyu lost their lives.
When entering the gate, why must one discern the incoming stimulus? These aged Chan practitioners do not know for themselves.
The cypress tree in the courtyard was pointed out in vain; it only serves to drive nails and wedges into level ground. (Yunfeng Yue)
Zhaozhou had a saying: "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Zen practitioners have transmitted it from antiquity to the present.
Though one may understand it by plucking leaves and seeking branches, one must know that a single tree does not form a forest. (Huanglong Nan, 3)

The cypress in the courtyard stands verdant, revealing the heart-mind of the Patriarchs; this story of Zhaozhou has spread throughout the monastic groves. With gnarled roots and knotted branches, it dwells in the Ground of Gold;
let practitioners cease seeking beyond the extraordinary.
Ten thousand trees wither and perish as the seasons change; the cypress in Zhaozhou’s courtyard remains ever-vigorous.
Not only does it maintain its integrity through the frost, but it frequently produces a pure resonance that resonates against the bright moon.
Zhaozhou does not employ effort at all; facing one another, how could there be subtle or coarse?
Though I show it to you in layers, you do not see it—the cypress tree in the courtyard has been non-existent from the start. (Doushuai Yue)
Deep within the courtyard, its roots coil with profound green hues; the Master once pointed this out to the stream of Chan practitioners.
Year after year, it does not alter its frost-defying integrity; when will this breeze one carries down cease? (By Zhengjue Yi)
Zhaozhou’s cypress before the courtyard: Three winters of piercing cold. Everywhere the green willows can tether horses;
At every door, one penetrates to Chang’an. (Tianyi Huai)

When someone asks about the cypress tree in front of the courtyard, I say: "I am a traveler from Lingnan. This brings to mind the winter sky of the twelfth lunar month, when plum blossoms burst open amidst the snow. (Haerin)

A monk asked about the meaning of the Westward Journey; Zhaozhou answered with the cypress tree. If there were blood beneath the skin, one would not be free from the summons of the authorities. (Cuiyan Zhen)
The lush green cypress trees in the courtyard were planted how many years ago? The Patriarch’s intent was clearly revealed to Zhaozhou.
Though the sea may turn to mulberry fields over endless kalpas, the numinous sprout casts no shadow and does not wither in autumn. (Zhaojue Zong)

The creative power of transformation is impartial and beyond thought; each and every thing is a verdant hue in the colors of the year’s end. Long and short, large and small—all are present before one's eyes.
It is laughable that people of this age cannot understand them. (Zhenjing Wen)
Zhaozhou’s courtyard cypress is a bitter affliction for the patch-robed monks; it is like a well-sweep at the mouth of a well—one cannot swallow it whole.
(By Yanxuan Zun) The cypress tree before the hall is shown to the Zen practitioners: how many have truly seen Zhaozhou? Next year there will be new branches again;
the spring wind will continue to trouble them until the very end. (By Baoning Yong)
In Zhaozhou’s courtyard, the cypresses stand dense; plucking leaves and tracing branches has continued from antiquity to the present.
If a monk with clear eyes should look upon them, the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West would surely sink into stillness. (Yang Wuwai)
The courtyard cypresses of Zhaozhou stand tall and dense; dewdrops and the clarity of the wind add to their verdant hue. One cannot seek them by plucking leaves or tracing branches;
with roots coiled through ten thousand ages, they are ultimately without end. (Daimyō Shū)
Only when one is truly startled does one recognize the startling; it is the eye of the numinous that perceives the numinous. People of this age do not understand the meaning of the West’s arrival;
they merely look at the green cypress trees in the courtyard. (Foguo Bai)
The antelope hangs its horns—doubts are utterly severed. Before the green cypress in the courtyard, he manifests the wondrous mechanism.
This Way is not to be understood through person or environment; like the bright sky, it shines everlong, day and night. (Luo Han Nan)
The old man Zhaozhou has no bones in his tongue; he speaks of it before the cypress tree in the courtyard.
How excellent is this boundless meaning at evening: "Guan, guan," the warbling birds disturb the meditation hall. (Third Patriarch’s Lineage)
When the rain clears from the ten-thousand-li expanse of the vast sky, a single orb of bright moon reflects its pure luster.
Floating clouds obscure the eyes of a thousand people; few are those who may behold the face of Lady Heng-er. (Fujian Qín)

The cypress tree in front of the courtyard—those with slight awakening transcend ordinary sentiment. After the rain, the mountains grow more verdant; when the clouds withdraw, the sun and moon shine bright. (Zhandang Zhun)
The verdant cypress in the courtyard points toward the West; Zhao’s old gate-style stands open like the characters "eight" (八).
Amidst the cold of winter, the branches hold a profound meaning; who has planted this numinous root where it takes root? (Fodeng Xun)
When asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, he pointed to the cypress tree in the courtyard. Shooting at a tiger without hitting it is merely wasting one's feathers;
to this day, there is confusion throughout the world. (Sushan Ru).

[Continued Collection] The world’s Chan practitioners gnaw on Shaolin. Zhaozhou has a saying: "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Cypress tree in the courtyard! These decrepit Chan practitioners have eyes burning red;
unable to distinguish east from west, they lose their original source. They humiliate Avalokiteśvara and turn him into a barbarian guest.
(The Fifth Patriarch’s Precept):
"The cypress tree in front of Zhaozhou's courtyard—monks of the patched robe can fathom it not. The assembly of cloud-and-water monks are all guests from the ten directions."
(Jiangya Jue). The cypress tree in front of Zhaozhou’s courtyard flashes like lightning before the eyes; many pass to and fro beyond the clouds, while the village elder’s gait is slow and feeble.
(Daowu Zhen): A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; as soon as the gray falcon sees it, he seizes it. Later hunters’ dogs lack spiritual nature;
they vainly search for it at the old spot by the withered post. (Chengtian Zong).
Su Wu did not bow; Han Xin presided over the court. If you understand it thus, ten thousand miles stretch afar.
(Manna Cheng) The cypress tree before the courtyard has roots that run deep; leaf by leaf are pearls, inch by inch is gold. Buddhas and patriarchs cannot emerge beyond this;
for ten thousand ages, it is just as it is now. (Nantang Xing)

It is easy to strike others and revile them; it is difficult to exhort others to abandon such ways. One who does not recognize the virtue of yielding to others will rush down the steep rapids. (Chongjue Kong)
Zhaozhou’s courtyard cypress—explain this to the Chan guests. A black-lacquered screen; pine and ivy clearly partitioned.
(Furi Cai) The hundred jewels’ light gathers at the invisible crown; this is the most wondrous and efficacious great divine mantra.
*Gate pārasaṃgate*. At midnight, the stone man loses his black chicken. (Zhengtang Bian)
"The cypress tree in front of the courtyard is not the Patriarch’s mind. Do not cling to a momentary vision, lest you forget the resonance of a thousand ages. (Longya said).
The cypress tree in front of the courtyard—I have clearly pointed it out to you. Great snow fills Chang’an;
the lantern swallows the Buddhas and Patriarchs. (Tudu Ce)
The ceremonial palanquin arrives amidst the sound of the still-whip. Both fists are tightly clenched and cannot be opened.
If they could be opened, where would the fragrant dust be under the heavy clouds? Amidst the sound of the still-whip, the ceremonial palanquin arrives. (Xiatang Yuan)
The ancestral meaning from the West is the cypress before the courtyard gate; nostrils vast and empty, facing the eyes.
As soon as the withered branch that has fallen to the ground leaps up, the pine and the creeper clearly separate, laughing in a surge of energy. (Tiantong Jing)
The cypress tree in the courtyard. One, two, three, four, five. Dou Ba wears a cloth robe.
Heyshan knows how to beat the drum. (Shi’an Zui)
A single word for a swift man; a single lash for a swift horse. Zhaozhou’s courtyard cypress; washing one’s feet to board the boat. (Tu’ān Qí).
[Added from another source] Chan Master Fayan of Qingliang raised the story of the "Cypress Tree" and asked Jue Tiezi:
"I have heard that Zhaozhou has this saying—is it true? Jue said, "The former master did not say such a thing. Do not slander the former master."
Yan said: "A true lion cub. The verse says:
"The cypress tree in the courtyard— Zhaozhou did not say such a thing. To receive his words, one must understand the source; Do not establish your own rules."
(Foyin Yuan). A monk asked: "The Cypress Tree in response to the West—why must these words slander Zhaozhou? They cause people to long remember the Old Man of Qingliang;
with a single phrase, he turned their heads back in those days. (Daming Xiu).
The Silla hawk soars toward the heavens; the dull-witted bird, by the fence, remains bewildered and does not fly away.
How lofty are the courtyard cypresses of Zhaozhou! Who says the former master did not have these words? (Baiyun Cuan).
Scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, a solitary, gaunt shadow; Zhaozhou once pointed to a tree leaning against the courtyard.
The old masters of Shengyuan, Daxiao, and Qingliang—did they not understand this word of the former teacher? (Zhengjue Yi)
Few know Zhaozhou’s silence; those who see it north and south of the river are rare. Where are the peach blossoms of the mountain temple now?
Meeting him, one finds nothing but the poems of Master Bai. (Da-hong Su)
"The cypress tree in the courtyard"—Zhaozhou never said such a thing. If one were a person of true substance, one would not grant it even for a moment (Zhenjing Wen).
[Continued Collection] Who says the former master did not have these words? The scorched-tail tiger was originally a panther. The hornet does not cling to its old nest;
how could a fierce general die at home? Quickly fix your eyes and look back! If you understand how to cut off the current, what need is there to go down?
A pure wind pervades the earth, rising with every step. (Huitong Dan)
Zhaozhou’s cypress tree in front of the hall; the eyes of Kunlun are like dots of black lacquer. He laughs at Fayen for slandering the former master;
Master Jue’s heart is bitter, yet his mouth is as sweet as honey. (Xuetang Xing)
No one can rival the Master of Practice; my elder sister is an even more skilled hand.
Leaping onto the hundred-foot pole, she performs a back-flip somersault. (Zhengtang’s Discernment)

Zhaozhou had a "Pine Tree" koan that has been transmitted among Zen practitioners throughout the world; yet most merely pluck at the leaves and search for the branches, unable to understand it directly at its very source.
Master Jue said, "There is no such thing as this talk"—this is truly like reviling someone with foul words face-to-face.
If a Zen practitioner possesses the eye that penetrates all quarters, they should skillfully discern the true from the false within this. (Wenshu said:)
One man, with his back turned, draws a golden-tipped arrow; another, twisting his body, draws a horn bow. North, south, east, and west, they vie to look on;
indeed, a single wild goose falls into the cold sky. (Yi’an Shen)
[Added to the Collection] Monk Xing of Ye County. When a monk asked him about the "Pine Tree" kōan, Xing said, "I do not refuse to explain it to you, but will you believe me?
The monk replied, "Since you, Reverend, have spoken with such gravity, how could I dare not believe?
Xing said, "Do you hear the sound of raindrops falling from the eaves? At that, the monk was suddenly enlightened; without realizing it, he let out an exclamation of "Aha! Xing [nodded].
[The Master] said, "What principle have you seen? The monk replied with a verse: "The raindrops at the eaves, Clear and distinct;
They shatter heaven and earth, And in that very moment, the mind comes to rest. The [Master’s] Verse says:
The cypress tree in the courtyard; the sound of raindrops on the eaves. The wind comes and the lotus stalks break. The meaning of the ten thousand ages is clear—[blank].
Drop by drop from the eaves, distinct and vivid. The blue-eyed barbarian and the yellow-headed Chinese—neither of them knows it. Whether they know it or not, it is universal.
Heaven and earth are brought into utter disorder. (Dongshan Yuan).
Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Where have you set out from? He replied, "Xuefeng. The Master said, "What words did Xuefeng use to instruct people?
He replied, "He usually says, 'The entire world of the ten directions is the single eye of a śramaṇa.'"
"Where are you all going to defecate? The Master said, "If you, O Ācārya, return, send me a spade. The Verse says:
Looking south toward Xuefeng, it is ten thousand li away; Traveling north, he has not yet crossed Zhaozhou’s Pass. He has deceived him with that one broken spade.
My son, for over two hundred years you have gone away and not returned.
(Zhengjue Yi) The path of the Stone Bridge is as slippery as moss; the winds of the Min Ridge are so high and cold they do not cease.
We meet and all speak of our travels, yet how many among us have ever reached Xuefeng? (Fohui Quan)
The śramaṇa’s single eye admits no object; the myriad phenomena of the universe emerge from it. Who among men recognizes Zhaozhou’s spade?
In letting go of this matter, one must be subtle and thorough. (Haiyin Xin)
"The great earth is the eye; where would one defecate? The world cannot do anything with this old man of Snow.
Zhaozhou sent him off with a spade, and only then did these words become perfectly complete. (Gushan Gui)
[Continued Collection] The great earth is the place where the eye disappears; when a patch-robed monk reaches this point, he becomes muddled and confused.
You must know there is another secret for establishing one's dwelling; once you understand the matter of establishing one's dwelling, there is even more. (A shout) Where is the spade placed?
(Zhao Tang says: "One.")
"Where does Xuefeng defecate? Zhaozhou sends a spade. A śramaṇa’s single eye is in such a state of disorder!
A-he-he! The drum beats in the land of Great Tang; in the land of Silla, the dance is performed with grace. (Biefeng Yin)
The great earth is but a single eye; who would dare to defecate within it? A spade was sent off, yet who knew it would reach Xuefeng? (Hengchuan Gong)
[Added for inclusion] Zhaozhou said to the assembly: "When I was traveling southward in my youth, there was a 'guestless host' koan at the hearth.

To this very day, no one has brought it up. Verse: When I traveled south in my youth, At the hearth, there was a guestless host. To this very day, no one has brought it up; How many have failed to see it?
Covering one's head, one does not notice as one snores in sleep; opening the eyes, let them be taught to blaze with a fiery red.
If you say that being "ordinary" means there is nothing to do, you must guard against beans popping from within cold ashes. (Xinwen Ben)

The meaning of the "no guest, no host" dialogue is profoundly deep; it has wandered through the monastic groves from antiquity to the present. The fire is cold and the ashes are chill, the mouth hangs upon the wall;
the patch-robed monk freezes to death, yet remains unaware of the Mind. (Shitennō Kun)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Zhaozhou ascended the hall and said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it simply dislikes picking and choosing.
As soon as there is speech, there is picking and choosing, and there is clarity. This monk does not abide in clarity. Do you still cherish [this state], or not?"
At that time, a monk asked, "Since you are not within the realm of clarity, what is it that you protect and cherish?
The Master said, "I do not know either. The monk said, "If you, Master, do not know, why are you not within the realm of clarity?"
The Master said: "If you ask about a matter, that is permissible; after prostrating, withdraw. Verse: The Ultimate Way is not difficult;

In speech and word, it is straightforward. One may have many aspects, But two are never of two kinds. At the edge of heaven, the sun rises and the moon sets; Before the railing, the mountains are deep and the waters cold.
When the consciousness of the skull is exhausted, what joy can stand? The dragon’s roar from the withered tree vanishes.
Not yet dry. Difficult, difficult! You must examine and discern this clearly for yourself (Xuedou Xian).
Most simple and most easy; coextensive with heaven and earth. To discern and clarify: why harbor such stinginess? His mouth is like a mallet, his eyes like eyebrows.
Entangled in speech and silence, the millipede pities the one-legged man. How laughable is Bian He, who thrice presented his jade—though honored, he was nonetheless crippled by having a foot cut off.
A pair of feet. (Yuanwu Keqin).
In this world there is nothing that can ensnare or confine; there is only a towering peak ten thousand fathoms high.
Suddenly, as if someone were to give it a violent shove, it leaps into the clouds beyond, leaving no trace behind. (Su’an Yuan)

The Ultimate Way is not difficult; though there be ten thousand rivers and a thousand mountains, it is only a matter of avoiding discrimination. Whether a crane is black or a crow is white, as soon as there is right and wrong, one begins to cherish and protect them.
Not understanding, one does not know that one is already fully empowered. Within clarity, it is as if letting go;
even with a girdle of gold, one still sings of the green wheat. (By Yuet Tang Chang)
Scattered wildly, bright pearls, each grain crystalline; running them on a platter, surely the sound of gold is not prized.
Whose daughter can handle needle and thread? She has strung them all through, not a single star left behind. (Wuan Quan)
[Added from another source] A monk once asked Zhaozhou, “The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it simply dislikes discrimination.
Is this the den of those who dwell in the mundane world? The Master said, “Someone once asked me this, and for five years I was unable to provide an explanation.”
The Verse says:
The Elephant King stretches; the Lion roars. Tasteless talk blocks the mouths of men;
south, north, east, and west—crows fly and hares run. (Xuedou Xian)
For over five years, he has been unable to settle his affairs; on a single-leaf boat, he carries the Great Tang.
Vast and solitary amidst the waves, who would know that there is another way of thinking? (Baizhang Yuan).
For five years they have been unable to disentangle it; there is not a single word that lacks a seam or crevice.
They only know how to pass the buck and deliberate; who would believe such a clear appraisal? Those who are clever understand it; those who are clumsy are amazed by it.
It is better to quarrel with one who understands than to speak with one who does not. (Tiantong Jue)
For five years he could not resolve the matter; instead, it often became a subject of idle talk. One must know that the Ultimate Way is not difficult;
who here knows how to find the seams and gaps? (Fojian Huiqin).

Heavenly thunder is like a drum; clouds rise and bring forth rain. When the rain clears, the clouds withdraw, leaving a single hook of the new moon. The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it is only the aversion to discrimination that hinders it.
For five years I have been too analytical, creating a separation that is far too wide. The carp of the Eastern Sea mostly have red tails;
the great tiger of the Southern Mountain has a white forehead. (Yuedang Chang)
Wind and rain swirl thickly; dark clouds gather heavily. With great effort they climb the mountain, yet the foxes enter the sea.
Following after them in pursuit, the Dragon King is not there. (Hark! Stupid Hall, settle yourself!)
The vastness of heaven and the depth of earth are but ordinary matters; the breadth of the sea and the weight of the mountains require further discussion.
With a thunderclap that shatters the lairs of mountain ghosts, he alone wields his frost-sheathed sword to settle the universe. (Wuan Quan)
[Added for inclusion] A monk once asked Zhaozhou, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. What is non-discrimination?
The Master said, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. The monk said, "This is still discrimination. The Master said, "You peasant! Where is the discrimination here?

The monk was speechless. The Verse says: Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. The peasant asks where the discrimination lies. The monk has no words to answer; He is like a wild fox seeking its own tail.
As deep as the ocean, as solid as a mountain. A mosquito or gadfly playing with a fierce wind in the void; an ant shaking an iron pillar.
To pick and choose—this is like a drum on a stand placed before the main hall. (Xuedou Xian)
The full autumn moon seals the heart of heaven. Before this very object, there is a wheel. The toad that has entered its hole has no way out;
it instead complains that the Way of Heaven is not level. (Baiyun Yuan).
The golden-maned lion opens its great mouth wide; heaven revolves and earth turns. Thunder strikes and lightning rushes; the asuras lose heart and the heretics' souls flee.
Among all sentient beings and crawling insects, there are none who do not receive this grace. (Fujian Qín)
A single pulse passes through the gate to Chang’an; the traveler sighs in vain at the hardships of the road.
This is not to boast of cleverness before others—it is the golden hammer that shatters ten thousand layers of barriers. (Wuan Quan)
[Added from another source] Once, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. As soon as there is speech, there is discrimination.
How do you, Master, act for the sake of others? The Master said, "Why do you not quote this entire passage?
The monk replied, "I can only remember it up to this point. The Master said, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination."
The Verse says: Water sprinkled does not stick; wind blows but cannot enter. Tiger-like stride, dragon-like gait; ghosts wail and spirits weep. With a head three feet long—who is this?
Facing each other, speechless, standing alone on one foot. (Xuedou Xian)
Driving back mountains and filling the seas is but commonplace; where civilization first takes root, there begins true kingship.
One sees only the imperial wind forming a single expanse, unaware of where boundaries and frontiers may lie. (Baiyun Cuan)
The skill of needle and thread enters the divine; following feelings and connecting intentions, how intimate it is! In an era of Great Peace, Hu and Yue have no boundaries;
who then is a person of the South and who is a person of the North? (Fujian Qín).
Purple silk, red brocade, and blue thread— A skillful hand weaves them into a single piece. Yet within it, seams and gaps cannot be avoided;
Alas, how can people see what they do not look for? (Longmen Yuan)
The sun is warm and the breeze gentle as the orioles sing anew; willows droop golden threads to bind the Lord of Spring.
The Lord of Spring spares not his impartial power: a single point of flower-red is a single point of spring. (Wuan Quan)

The Master said, "Which Way are you asking about? The monk said, "The Great Way. The Master said, "The Great Way penetrates Chang'an. Verse: The Great Way penetrates Chang’an; How many people know its name? If you wish to see it clearly, Look at the wall outside the gate. It is not something that can be grasped by the intellect; It is not something that can be sought through words. If you try to grasp it with the mind, You will lose it entirely. If you try to seek it through speech, You will wander further astray. Only when you cast off both mind and speech Will you see it as it truly is. Do not look for it within the scriptures; Do not seek it among the sages. If you wish to understand the Way, Just look at the wall outside the gate. If you can see it here, Then you have seen the Way. If you cannot see it here, Then you have missed the Way. The Great Way is right before your eyes; Why do you go seeking elsewhere? If you can turn back now, You will find it in an instant. If you continue on your way, You will never meet it. Do not be confused by the words; Do not be deluded by the meaning. If you can transcend both words and meaning, Then you will see the Way. This is what is called the Great Way; It is not something separate from you. If you can realize this, Then you are a true man of the Way. If you cannot realize this, Then you are still lost in delusion. This is the teaching of Zhaozhou; It is not something to be taken lightly. If you wish to enter the Way, You must first understand this. If you understand this, Then you have understood the Way. Knowing this, he returns it to the old fellow; with direct words pointing to one another, matters are urgent. Though the mountain pass road is far, one must eventually arrive;
the long, solitary path—let you traverse it as you will. (Touzi Qing)
The家风 (family tradition) of Zhao Lao is not pretentious; when asked about the Great Way, he points to Chang’an.
Who can return home by walking level on the ground? Most people laboriously create difficulties for themselves. (Shui’an I)

The Great Way penetrates Chang’an; his words are upright and his speech is likewise upright. When the winter solstice ends and the snow melts away, spring arrives, yet it remains as cold as before. (Songyuan Yue)
[Added from the Supplement] A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is it like when practitioners meet? The Master said, “Presenting a lacquerware bowl.
The verse says:
When masters meet, they present a lacquerware bowl with dignified bearing; the tortoise falls into the lacquer bucket—therein lies the primary truth.
(Nantang Xing). Water cascades coolly in the shade of ancient ravines; lofty pines a thousand feet tall retain their cold green.
One might think they merely possess the integrity that soars toward the heavens, but who would believe there is *fuling* fungus at their roots? (Nansou Long)
When practitioners meet, they ask how one has been; raising a hand for greetings and inquiries of health is already much too common. Old Zhaozhou presents his lacquer bowl;
the boatman of Yueyang faces the waves of Lake Dongting. (Shitian Xun)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when white clouds move freely? The Master said, "How can it compare to the spring breeze, idle everywhere?
Verse: How can it compare to the spring breeze, Idle everywhere, in every place?
How can it compare to the spring breeze, which is at ease everywhere? Whether flowers bloom or fall, how could they be concerned with one another?
Even the self-reliant white clouds are difficult to emulate; drifting without intention, they fill the world. (Foyin Yuan)

The bed is narrow, so one lies down first; the gruel is thin, so one sits down later. With dignified carriage and resonant steps, serene and carefree—do you wish to understand Zhaozhou washing his bowl?
Only a monk who has finished his work can consume this one portion. (Quandadao).
The plum blossoms have fallen away and the apricot flowers unfold; there is no escaping being clothed and stripped by the spring breeze. The One Breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms;
where can the myriad spirits offer thanks for its impartiality? (Baiyun Yuan).
When the gruel is finished, he orders them to wash their bowls; such coarse behavior often leads to further coarseness of mind.
Even if one reaches this point with clarity, it is still a case of being no true man throughout one's life. (Fotu Xun)
The story of Zhaozhou eating congee. He would often ask Zen practitioners: "If your heart does not betray others, you will have no shame upon your face. (Yungai Zhi)
Having finished eating the congee, he washes the alms bowl. This daily domestic routine is most harmonious. From where has the West come? Half of it has fallen away.
The Sixth Patriarch was dull-witted and did not read books. (Third Patriarch’s Lineage, Part Two)
Just upon entering the forest, one extends a single question: the alms bowl has been washed clean—what further doubt remains? The official road from of old has no detours;
for what reason do travelers not see him return?
Just upon entering the forest, one begs for instruction; the Great Gate of Giving is opened without obstruction.
Among those who received their predictions on Vulture Peak in the past, none have ever followed such a sequence as this. (Zhengjue Yi)
Having finished the gruel, one usually washes the bowl; alas, this is merely copying the gourd after the model.
When the spiritual light penetrates clearly through the river-sands of worlds, this is what is called a great man. (Yunju You)
Having finished eating congee, he washes his bowl; when has he ever pointed out the road to Caoxi? In vain he says he followed the crowd for thirty years;
he remembers spreading out his mat, but he forgets his chopsticks. (Yang Wuwe)
"Zhi-hu-zhe-re. The nostrils of a patch-robed monk point downward toward the great earth.
If you practitioners do not understand this, go ask Old Woman Wang of the eastern village. (Zhantang Zhun)
After the gruel was finished, he ordered them to wash their bowls. Zhaozhou’s words do not deceive:
"In this vast universe, people are countless; how many men among them are true heroes? (Cishou Shen).
After the congee was finished, he ordered the bowl to be washed; suddenly, his mind and ground accorded with one another.
Now, regarding those guests who have "partaken their fill" of the monastic groves—tell me, is there awakening within this? (Tiantong Ju).
Just upon entering the forest, one questions the master; from of old, withered wood has sprouted anew.
Having washed the alms bowl, they meet; once more, a cup of richly brewed tea is served. (Changling Zhuo)
The great recluse dwells in the marketplace; the small recluse dwells in the mountains. The people of the world have no way to interfere with them.
The Chan practitioners of the Five Lakes use this every morning; who can turn their heads and look closely? (Cangtang Qing).
Entering the monastic groves for the first time, one asks about their origins; having eaten and eaten, there is no fault—simply wash the bowl and rest.
When there is spirit, add more spirit; where there is no elegance, there too is elegance. (Fenning).
The Master extends his hand, valuing natural spontaneity; he refuses to engage in the artificiality of carving insects or engraving seals.
He simply, amidst the level fields and shallow grasses, casually brings forth the jade qilin. (Fóxìng Tàiyán)
Probing the principles of things, one establishes a household; meeting the opportune moment, one recognizes the mind. Much gratitude to the spring breeze, which shows no partiality;
even the peach and plum trees of a poor home now cast their shade. (Huguo Yuan)
[Continued Collection] Opening the tally and unfolding the bowl, they are always close at hand; throughout the twelve hours, the truth is everywhere present.
To directly clarify the essential meaning: within the words of Shaoyang, the whole body is revealed. (Baoning Yong)
"Have you finished eating congee yet? Who says this? Zhaozhou has an instruction. After the congee, he even tells them to wash their bowls.
I ask you all: have you realized it or not? Old Zhaozhou—whom can he be compared to? He blocks the vital passageways and the waters flow backward.
As soon as a clever monk blinks an eye, the fisherman with his boat descends to Yangzhou. (Longmen Yuan)
Zhaozhou pointed to the washing of the alms bowl; the patch-robed monks rush about, expending their efforts in vain. Not knowing how to use it in daily life, where would they look for it?
To speak of it clearly is like addressing the blind and the deaf. (Nantang Xing)
Having finished eating the congee, he washes his bowl; he has already spoken clearly to him.
Sometimes, when one reflects upon this in a state of cool detachment, there is no one in the world who can turn iron into gold. (Yuelin Guan)
Pervading the ten directions, brilliant on all eight sides; the noble steed turns to look at its own shadow, while foxes and hares hide their tracks.
(Nirvāṇa-niḥsaṅga) When the gruel is finished, he orders the bowls to be washed. An iron ship without a bottom requires someone to support it;
with a single sail hoisted high, one rides the favorable wind—crossing the sea requires a true man of great character. (Miyuan Jie)
Upon first entering the monastery, he requested the Master’s instruction. The Master held out his alms bowl and told him to go wash it.
Having traversed a thousand mountains and ten thousand peaks, he turned his head and bumped into his own home. No pointing was required; no washing was required.
A brilliant, radiant light illuminated heaven and earth. Now it hangs suspended in the void; in the chamber of Changling, he stretches out his legs and sleeps. (Wenshu said.)
Meeting you, I accompanied you with wine and song; Drunk and fallen, you asked me to carry you home. Even when carried home, you still hurled insults;
I know not what it will be like once you have sobered up. (Qian’an Ren)
Precisely because it is so utterly clear, what is attained is instead delayed. Had one known early that the lamp is fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago. (No gate opens.)

A crane stands atop the pine treetops beneath the moon; fish swim through the sky at the bottom of the water. The entire splendor of the scenery is captured entirely, without spending a single coin. (Xianan Guan)
Simply extend your request as you first enter; once you arrive at the forest of the patriarchs, your will is already high.
When the porridge is finished, wash your bowl and depart; the Master has no need for further tedious talk. (Heunggwam Gung)

Zhaozhou’s Stone Bridge originally had no stars; fish swimming in swift currents find it hard to rest.
Upon the bridge, one sees only the tracks of donkeys and horses—who would dare to walk upon the imperial thoroughfare? (Beita Zu)
Standing alone in peril, the Way is lofty; to enter the sea, one must still fish for the giant turtle.
It is laughable that the old man of Ganki, a contemporary, said that even splitting an arrow [in flight] is but a vain labor. (Xuedou Xian)
I love Zhaozhou’s elegant and spirited responses. When a monk asked whether the stone bridge could carry donkeys or horses, the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiled and nodded his head.
Aside from him, who else is a true connoisseur? (Dizang En).

The carriage of his conduct differs from the common run; his heart is true and his speech is sincere. Following the current, he attains the wondrous on his own; having reached the shore, he is not lost as to the ford.
(Lian of Tianning Monastery in Jingzhao Prefecture).

[Continued Collection] The long whale has already surged over the cresting waves; the lame turtle still churns the mud by the bridge. Whether crossing horses or donkeys, it is difficult to understand;
beneath the shadows of green willows, the paths go east and west. (Dizang En)

Zhaozhou’s Stone Bridge: One sees only a simple footbridge, crossing donkeys and crossing horses; administering medicine according to the illness, shifting steps and changing positions, enriching the wealthy and impoverishing the poor.
If you recognize it right at the head, you will ask for Qin when in Lu. (Yuet Tang Chang)
[Added from another collection] When Zhaozhou heard a novice monk shout "Assembly dismissed! (hezan), he said to his attendant, "Tell him to leave.
The attendant then told him to leave, and the novice simply said, "Goodbye" (zhenzhong). The Master remarked, "The novice has entered the gate; the attendant remains outside the gate."
The Verse says:
Having reached the gate, he stands outside. He speaks toward the person, but the person does not understand. He raises his voice even higher:
"My ears are deaf. (Gushan Gui)
The wind whistles through the pines; the rain sighs through the cypresses. A lion bites a man; a donkey from Han chases after clods of earth. (Jingshan Hongdao).
Once, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "No.
The monk asked, "From the Buddhas above down to the ants below, all possess Buddha-nature. Why then does the dog have none?"

The Master said, "It is because they possess the nature of karmic consciousness. [The monk] asked again, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "It has. [The monk] said, "If it has, why has it entered this skin bag? The Master said, "Knowing it yet deliberately committing [the offense].
