The great function, the total mechanism, attains freedom; existence and non-existence are both released and both gathered.
How many deluded consciousnesses encounter people like dogs? From this moment on, remember Zhaozhou at all times. (Foyin Yuan)
In youth, one studies and understands, yet remains dim regarding the path of the source; in old age, one relies on these [teachings] and still stagnates in being and non-being.
The ancient Buddhas were pure gold—who could discern its color? Deluded by this, those with clever intellects compete in hesitation. (Yuantong Xiu)
Releasing both existence and non-existence, yet gathering them both back; Zhao’s ancient device is peerless in the world.
Try gazing from atop the high gate of Hai—ten thousand rivers and a myriad streams all flow toward the east. (Puyongping)
Zhaozhou’s mouth contains realgar; beneath his words, who can discern their length or brevity?
How laughable are those many dogs chasing clods of earth—midnight has come, yet they bark pointlessly in the empty hall. (Cishou Shen)
There is a Way, yet there is no Way; "no" is but a redundant word. Though called a thousand times and summoned ten thousand times, he does not turn his head.
Seeking fragrance and chasing vapor, he follows after others, causing empty time to flow on and autumn to pass in darkness. (He becomes a withered tree.)

[Continued Collection]: Having Buddha-nature or lacking Buddha-nature—correctness is overturned by the inverted, and the inverted is overturned by the correct. Treading through the waters of the clear pool, the bent scale has no stars.
The fire heats the surface of the water until it turns red; a stake is driven from within the void. Those who accept this are like blind turtles chewing on dead snakes.
The two jaws are firmly clenched together. (Zhengjue Yi) Zhaozhou, the Ancient Buddha, hits the mark with every word.
Whether his words have substance or not, they are like the gold of Yan and the jade of Zhao.
Furthermore, there is the "seven-pound hempen robe," which is beyond price in heaven or on earth. (Dizang En)
The Buddha-nature is clear and distinct, transcending both existence and non-existence. Why use a gourd to hang vinegar? Thin mists and light smoke cannot remain;
the small boat has already passed beyond Lake Dongting. (Xiatang Yuan)
"The dog has no Buddha-nature; the dog has no nature, yet it exists. From the beginning, one has only wandered between these two extremes;
unable to pierce both barriers with a single arrow, the karmic consciousness continues as before to act as a dog. (One Original Enlightenment).
"The dog has Buddha-nature. Vairocana loves to drink Maitreya’s wine. "The dog has no Buddha-nature. Mañjuśrī falls drunk, and Samantabhadra helps him up.
Having helped him home, he is completely intoxicated; he speaks gibberish in barbarian and Chinese tongues, cursing his wife and servants.
(Zhengtang Bian)
There is no direct path, yet it winds and turns. On the eastern wall of Zhaozhou, as before, hangs a gourd.
There is Master Zhang drinking village wine; Master Li is drunk and does not wake. Facing south, he gazes at the Big Dipper. (Shi’an Shao)
"The dog has no Buddha-nature. On the road where one rubs the forehead, he meets Zi-hu; his karmic consciousness remains, meeting a single bite.
The entire great earth is utterly devoid of the blue-eyed barbarian. "The dog has Buddha-nature. The spring breeze stirs a thousand willow trees.
Knowing yet deliberately transgressing—how pitiable! Each and every one looks south to see the Big Dipper. (Wuan Quan)
The dog has Buddha-nature. This is the total raising of the true command. As soon as one enters the realm of existence or non-existence, one loses one’s body and life. (No Gate Opens).

Once, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? the Master said, "No. The Verse says: The dog has Buddha-nature; Zhaozhou says, "No. If you try to grasp it through existence or non-existence, You lose your body and forfeit your life.
"It is said that the karmic consciousness remains; who would say its intent is not profound? When the ocean dries up, its bottom is finally seen;
when a person dies, their mind is no longer known. (Zhenjing Wen)
Zhaozhou brandishes his sword; the cold frost glows with blazing flames. If you intend to ask further how it is, he will divide his body into several pieces. (Wuzu Yan)

Powerful in strength, advanced in years, yet his courage is even more formidable. With the clear wind following the tiger and the clouds following the dragon, there are countless snarling beasts seeking his tracks and traces;
yet the antelope hanging from its horns leaves no sign of its whereabouts. (Baofeng Xiang)
Passing before the Xuande Gate, turning one's head brings disaster. If you wish to remain free from trouble, simply return to sit within the hall. (Gushan Gui)

Someone asked about the Buddha-nature of a dog; Zhaozhou replied, "There is none. To say that he "annihilated the Hu race with a single word" still fails to make him a true man of stature. (Jingshan Daoyuan)
The dog has no Buddha-nature; its compassion is as deep as the sea. Those who seek words and chase phrases bury the mind of the Great Man. (Sushan Ru).
The dog has no Buddha-nature; the precious sword reveals its form. Falling into the general’s hands, it is held crosswise as he stands upon the path. (Chuan-an Fang)
[Continued Collection] The question is already substantial, and the answer is likewise worthy of praise. Though Luoyang may be fine, how can it compare to my own home?
Zhaozhou’s bitter mouth is far too talkative; I simply pluck the willow flowers with my own hands. (Daimpui Zhi)
Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; the seven Buddhas of the past join their palms and listen. Mount Sumeru’s jagged peaks dance the Three Terraces;
the ocean waves surge as they carry forth the True Command. (Nantang Xing)
Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; ten thousand layers of green mountains conceal an ancient mirror.
A barefoot Persian enters the Great Tang; the eight-armed Nātha executes the true command. (Chouyan Yun)
On the day of Yi-ji, the Great Man Qiu appeared; the forest became his enemy. His sharp fangs were like swords and halberds;
there was a reason for his taking life or sparing it. (Nanyan Sheng)
The Ultimate Way is not difficult: speak with integrity and act with integrity. Zhaozhou opens his mouth and reveals his very heart and liver.
(Dian Niu You) With one stroke, he cleaves both horse and man; empty space spurts with blood, surging like billowing waves.
Myriad upon myriad people gaze in wonder—whom can discern the hair on the back of their own gallbladders? (Zhong’an Kong)
An iron wall and silver mountains—a single arrow pierces through them. The decrepit Zhaozhou can bring disaster with his own mouth.
(Nun Wuzhuo Zong). "The dog has no Buddha-nature": this is the total implementation of the Magadha command. Should one even attempt to meet its sharp edge, one loses one's wretched life.
(Qian’an Guang): Poor and with nowhere to rely, my two parents struck one another; like the roar of thunder in a drought, a bolt of lightning struck the blue sky. (Huo’an Ti).
The dog has no Buddha-nature; the old oyster spits out a bright pearl. In Western Sichuan the cuckoo cries;
in Jiangnan the partridge calls. (Mañjuśrī speaks.)
Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature. Amidst the void, he digs out the mirror from the Qin era. Its radiance leaves not even a speck of starlight visible;
above, below, and in the four cardinal directions, all are completely illuminated. (Shuan-an Yan)
The dog has no Buddha-nature; when it kills a person, it must repay with its own life. Amidst myriad forms of suffering and pain, it strikes the upright because of its depravity. (Mianjie)
The Great Tamer of Persia drinks a hundred cups; he stands firm, grasping the helm as the leader of ten thousand men.
He sails against the wind past the Huangniu Gorge; he asks not of the Qutang or Yanʼyu rapids. (Dongshan Kong)
The dog has no Buddha-nature; it shatters the great round mirror. Seven times nine is sixty-three;
all-knowledge is pure. (Yian Jian)
The dog has no Buddha-nature; the Rāhu star enters its life-path. It does not kill others, yet it is certainly killed by others.
(Recorded by Nan Shuji).
The dog has no Buddha-nature; a peach-wood talisman is nailed upon the gate. A thousand evils cannot enter;
a hundred monsters are entirely eliminated. (Songyuan Yue)
The dog has no Buddha-nature; it is a clay-formed living Great Sage. It is not the man from Sizhou; even when spoken of, one cannot believe it. (Biefeng Yun).
The dog has no Buddha-nature; I urge you not to raise it up. To penetrate ten thousand layers of barriers, one must have a crossbow with a thousand-jun trigger. (Yi’an Shen)
Twenty-four states of iron are cast into a single hammer; it is flung onto the great thoroughfare, yet no one can tread upon it. (That is *ānran*.)
"The dog has no Buddha-nature"—this returns it to the great man. Though right and wrong enter the ears, the gourd hangs on the eastern wall. (Puwong Hyeon)
The single word "non-existence" has killed countless people; how many heroes lie with their corpses across the road!
(Iron Mountain Ren) A beauty of sixteen years embroiders slowly; beneath the purple *zhijing* flowers, the yellow oriole warbles.
How pitiable are these boundless sentiments of spring’s end—all contained within that moment of halting the needle and falling silent. (Aotang Ren)
With a sharp blade, he cuts off the life-root; leaping out from among the foxes and dogs, he seizes up ten thousand-forged thorns, shattering those with iron brows and copper heads. (Shi’an Shao)
Zhaozhou said, "No. The cliffs crumble and the rocks split; before he has even raised his voice, one already knows. One merely obtains a single peg (Muzhou of Shaoshi).
Regarding the dog’s Buddha-nature, Zhaozhou says "no. Master Lü holds a single medicinal gourd; bringing it forth, he heals the ailments of the human world.
Only after undergoing a great death does one truly see him (Ge Lu Tan).
The dog has no Buddha-nature; Ganjiang enters the court of Chu. With one stroke, three heads fall;
for a thousand ages, it gains a hollow fame. (Qianfeng Wan)
[Supplement] Kuan of Jingzhao asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, "It has. He asked, "Does the Monk have it or not?
The Master said, "I do not. He asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
why then do you not have it? The Master said, "I am not a sentient being. He asked, "If you are not a sentient being, [then...]"
"Is this a Buddha? The Master said, "It is not a Buddha. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "It is also not a thing.

The monk asked, "Can it be seen or can it be conceived? The Master said, "It cannot be reached by thought; it cannot be discussed through sight. This is called the inconceivable. Verse: The Buddha is not a Buddha; He is not even a thing. Thought cannot reach him; Sight cannot fathom him. This is named the inconceivable.
Set aside this monk’s question; remove the response of Jingzhao. Singing freely, he returns home; the pure breeze pervades the six directions. (Wuzu Yan)

Tearing asunder Mount Sumeru and its nostrils; treading upon the great ocean and overturning heaven and earth. The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas before one’s face are all but the children and grandchildren of my own house. (Chuanfang).

Drawing the bow with a straight posture, his shooting is difficult to withstand; the principle of the "tiger-trapping" mechanism is most profound.
Though he may covet another's single grain of rice, who would have known he would lose half a year’s provisions? (Haiyin Xin)
Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots were stolen by the old woman; having been struck, how could he have consented to let it rest? When it was necessary to act, one must act;
when there is a place to withdraw, one may withdraw. (By Yanxuan Zun)
Old Zhaozhou caught a thief; while confronting him face-to-face, he was struck with a blow in return. The thief’s crime was not punished, but was instead attributed to himself.
How many monks under heaven have understood this? (Dizang En).
When Zhaozhou greeted the old woman, Kāśyapa and Nanda both knit their brows. Yet they were struck by her with a single palm;
from the beginning, they were busy and fell into her trap. (Zhang Wujin)
From of old, the weak have overcome the strong. The thief was caught clearly, and the evidence was seen.
At that moment, he struck him with a palm; it was like a mute man eating raw ginger. (Fujian Qín).
[Continued Collection] Few reach the Demon Palace within the Tiger’s Den. When the Old Lady lost her footing, people harbored doubts.
No one understands Zhaozhou’s receiving of the slap; it has remained a source of contention until this very day. (Yudao Po of Jinling).
Departing is as heavy as a mountain; arriving is as light as a single feather. There is no separate path for going and coming;
under the overturned canopy, white-haired we meet anew. (Xiatang Yuan)

All along the way, valiant troops have violated the frontier river; smoke and dust block the roads, cutting off all passage for men. That the state remains secure depends on the presence of Zhang Liang;
from atop the city walls, the painted horns sound the "Song of Chu. (Xuedou Zong)
Hurrying on horseback and whipping it to reach the wine tower—how does that compare to sitting on the ground and watching Yangzhou?
Right and wrong, long and short, are all decisively settled; petty theft is ultimately no match for a dog’s pilfering. (Wuzhun Shanfan)
They meet face-to-face yet do not touch or clash; one grabs the other by the cheek and strikes them with the palm, refusing to let go.
One might ponder such a thing as being devoid of flavor—is it perhaps Zhaozhou’s very life-force that has been summoned? (Xianji Yun).
[Zhaoshou] addressed the assembly, saying: “Studying the sutras is within birth and death; not studying the sutras is also within birth and death.

How, then, do you all manage to escape? A monk then asked: “What is it like when neither is retained? The Master said: “If it is real, then one may. If it is not real, how could one possibly escape birth and death?”
The verse says:
Even while reading sutras, one remains within birth and death; Sitting amidst baskets of food, there is nothing to eat. Even when not reading sutras, one remains within birth and death;
Amidst piles of brocade robes, there is nowhere to wear them. Suddenly, a crow or a magpie lets out a single cry, And one leaps up with a start.
The whole household rejoices; do not hesitate to deliberate. Now cast it before the assembly; even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot lift it up.

The Linked Pearl Compendium of Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School, Volume Twenty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty;
continued by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery during the Xiaoshing era of the Yuan Dynasty.
The Sixth Patriarch’s Lineage:
The Seventh of the Fourth Generation (The Third of the Later Third Generation under Nanyue).
Zhaozhou asked a newly arrived monk, "Have you ever been here before? The monk replied, "I have. The Master said, "Go and drink tea."
He asked another monk, who replied, "I have never been there. The Master said, "Go and drink tea.
Later, the courtyard steward asked, "Why did you say 'go and drink tea' to one who had been there, and why did you say 'go and drink tea' to one who had never been there?"
The Master summoned the head of the monastery. The head responded with a "Yes. The Master said, "Go drink tea. A verse says:
Zhaozhou has this saying, "Go drink tea. Monks from all under heaven have all come here.
It is not that the Stone Bridge is originally slippery; How many monks would he have to call back? (Fenyang Zhao)
Seeing a monk being asked whether he had ever been there, one said, "I have been there, though I have not come here lately. He invited him to sit and drink tea, then respectfully took his leave.
Blue smoke shifts with time, revealing green-veined moss. (Touzi’s Blue).
Zhaozhou had the saying, "Go drink tea. All those with clear eyes have been misled by citing it; yet if they do not cite it, they are still not granted permission.
How laughable that Heyuan knew how to beat the drum! (Yunfeng Yue).
"Once arrived, it is the same as not yet having arrived; Zhaozhou continues to display his family style.
Lately, the royal decree has tightened its defenses; from now on, no human sentiments shall be tolerated. (Foyin Yuan)
Zhaozhou’s point for testing people to the very core: when he casually opens his mouth, one immediately knows him.
Had there been no "blue and white eyes" facing one another, how could the ancestral wind have reached its present state? (Huanglong Nan)
A single bowl of tea sustains the family tradition; far and near, high and low, a single path leads through.
Before the fragrant incense has been offered, who among those passing to and fro knows where the quarters lie within the western part of the monastery? (Zhaojue Zong)
Whether one has been here before or not, people go for tea out of human custom and sentiment;
yet the abbot, unaware of the flavor’s excellence, comes instead to contend over the flowers in the cup. (Foguo Bai).
The masters of the monastic groves are truly beyond compare; when facing affairs, how could there ever be any distinction?
Whether they be newly arrived or long-time residents, their earnestness is simply a single bowl of tea. (Zhengjue Yi)
In three grades he holds the bowls, the ritual propriety complete; with equal pouring for all, there is no partiality.
At the Stone Bridge and the Broken Monastery, there are no rare delicacies; simply mix the sesame seeds and fry them all alike. (Fohuiquan).
The precious casket and dragon-spring sword emit a night glow; Silently and far-reaching, they hang suspended in the empty hall.
If noble guests from the four quarters should come to visit, After the tea is finished, there is no need for weary talk of long and short. (Da-mei Xiu)

The Story of Zhaozhou’s Tea: From antiquity to the present day, the clouds part to reveal his mouth from beginning to end; yet it is difficult to preserve his heart through the winter cold. (Yungai Zhi)
Whenever they meet, everyone says, "I’ve had a cup of tea. In general, the true lineage flows through those of our own house.
Do not ask whether one has been there before or not; there are naturally travelers filling the roads with praise. (Sushan Chang)
The black pearl is free of flaws; the jade is without blemish. Carried by horse and donkey to the house of the Imperial Son.
Having once arrived, there is no longer any room for deliberation. I share with you a single bowl of tea. (Luo Han Nan)
How can one discuss the flavor within this? Fully unfolding the family style, he speaks of early spring.
Having performed his human duties three times with his mouth, this time do not say he has not tasted it. (Fojian Qin)
Zhaozhou’s single bowl of tea exhaustively examines those of his own house; though it may seem excellent for a time, how can one avoid affairs as tangled as hemp? (Longmen Yuan)
Zhaozhou’s flavor is most intimate; how many can directly accept it face-to-face?
At the point where it was personally transmitted three times, fragrance fills the mouth and the truth is complete. (Chuan’an Fang)
Receiving people with the third-grade [simplicity], his fame resounded throughout the world; testing guests with a single cup of tea, he spread his influence through the monastic forests.
Like the high mountains and flowing waters, his profound intent—who else but Ziqi could appreciate its resonance? (Yunyan).
[Continued Collection]: A visitor comes from afar; I serve him but a single bowl of tea. Human relations grow weary and thin; even kin become enemies.
How can this compare to Lu Tong, who shut himself away behind his door, brewing tea for himself until he broke into a light sweat?
All the grievances of his life were then dispersed through every pore. (Shi Ming)
Zhaozhou’s “drinking tea” is a marvel of the Chan school. Whether one has arrived or not, he is a true white-clawed thief (Huanglong Xin).
Whether you have been there before or not, simply drink a cup of tea; such is his way of hosting guests. This frugal simplicity is the way of the monk.
(Muchan Zhong). "If you have already been here, go drink tea; if you have not yet been here, go drink tea. Old Chan Master Zhaozhou—sweet in speech, bitter in heart.
The bitterness in one's heart persists until now, with no place for it to be cleared away (Cishou Shen).
As for Zhaozhou’s “I am afraid of you when you drink tea,” he is either a creditor or an enemy.
Leaning against walls and propping up pillars in great crowds, who knows who can distinguish the dragon from the snake? (Ying’an Hua).
At the top of a hundred-foot pole, a felt cloth is draped; upon it is inscribed: "Spring at the Wine Shop.
Meeting [him] and not drinking, one returns empty-handed; the peach blossoms within the cave laugh to death. (Zide Hui)
When people came to visit Zhaozhou, he would simply say, "Go drink tea. For no reason, the head monk was not alert;
Zhaozhou gave him another cup to bring him to his senses. (Benjue I)
Zhaozhou’s three times drinking tea cannot be compared to Heshan’s beating the drum. Do not seek it within words;
recognize the flavor in the mouth. If you can recognize it, Maitreya is in Guanyin Monastery. (Fóxìng Tái)
Exhausting every courtesy with frequent formalities; what need is there for bitter tea to be offered three times?
If there were a passage through the heavens within one's own nose, one would never turn back to ask another. (Mañjuśrī said.)
Whether they have been here before or not, everyone is invited to drink tea. Their mouths are as sweet as honey, yet their hearts are as venomous as snakes.
(Chuan’an Jing). Zhaozhou’s drinking of tea uproots the poisonous snake by force; empty space falls to the ground, and iron trees bloom flowers.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, Maitreya, and Śākyamuni—countless in number, changing heads and faces. Do not say that this is merely the wind of the lineage flowing through its own house. (Pu)
An-yu). Zhaozhou says, "Go drink tea.
A venomous snake lies across the ancient road; only when one treads upon it does one know it is not [what it seems].
Even a Buddha is unfit for this task. (Songyuan Yue)
The old man of Zhaozhou had a warm heart; with a single cup of coarse tea, he tested those on the path.
Turning his head toward the bridge broken by the roadside, white artemisia and red sedges reflect the slanting sun. (Zhe’ung Yan)
Zhaozhou meets people and offers them tea—who would have known that such matters arise from within the household? With his hand turned back, he creates clouds and rain;
with the wind at his back, he scatters earth and sand. This leads even Dongshan, lacking in wisdom, to ask about the Buddha and receive the answer:
"Three catties of hemp" (no Chan ability).

Tearing it apart, he once struck the ancient master; how many know the weight of the seven-pound robe?
Now cast into the West Lake, who shall receive this load of pure breeze? (Xuedou Xian)
A seven-pound robe is heavy; how could it be difficult to lift? When the sun rises in the east, it is certain to set in the west.
A single blow shatters the coral branch to pieces; thunder and rain roar through the mountains and streams. (Baiyun Yuan).
Sitting alone and walking alone, truly exhausting the measure; without rule and without standard, an old Chan practitioner.
From all four directions and eight points, who can restrain you? Who in the world can do anything with you? (Baoning Yong)
A question is asked; a friendly brocade robe is offered in response. Pointing it out, he says: "Qingzhou is where I once roamed.
The bright moon hangs in the sky, clearing the vast expanse; the leviathans have no choice but to swallow the hook. (Zhaojue Zong)
Zhaozhou’s cassock weighs seven pounds. The question is clear; the answer is intimate.
The great earth and mountains and rivers are all covered over—who is the person who cuts and sews when the occasion arises? (Mañjuśrī spoke).
A seven-pound robe, its weight utterly beyond the finest dust; what master hand could have fashioned its seams?
One must laugh at Old Wang of the Eastern Village, who enters the gate drenched from head to toe by wind and rain. (Puyongping)
The seven-pound robe of Qingzhou—exerting all one’s strength, one cannot lift it. Once the barrier of Zhaozhou is shattered, everything is simply one’s own. (Jingshan Daoyuan)
[Continued Collection] Old Zhaozhou’s response: "People find it difficult to understand face-to-face. Where does the 'one return' go? A quilted robe from Qingzhou;
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and tridacna shell. (Longya said).
At midnight, in pitch-black darkness, he caught a thief. When he lit a fire to look at him, it turned out to be Old Man Wang. (Gushan Gui).
Casually picking up the seven-pound robe—how many practitioners of Chan apply their minds to investigate it?
They all make their nests in Qingzhou, unaware that the spring colors lie in Jiangnan. (Yuan’an Yan)
In the cauldron of boiling water, there is no cool ground; the Yellow River flows with rolling depths. A vajra makes it difficult to insert a beak;
a lantern ball hangs behind the head. (Oran’s essence).
When pressed to the point of letting go over a precipice, who knows that the seven-pound robe is heavy? Through the coming of winter and the passing of summer, it is utterly useless;
it hangs between the eastern and western courtyards of Zhaozhou. (Shi’an Shao)

Addressing the situation directly before one's face; meeting face-to-face with the situation is swift. Opening one’s eyes yet remaining foolish and stubborn—this whip drives a person over the wall. (Beijian Jian)
Old Zhao’s seven-pound robe—brought forth, it fits perfectly. If you ask further how it is so, go and seek it out in Qingzhou. (Duànqiáo Lún)

[Added for inclusion] Zhaozhou was on the latrine when he saw Attendant Wenyuan passing by. He suddenly called out, "Wenyuan! Yuan responded, "Yes? The Master said, "I cannot speak the Buddha-dharma while on the latrine.

The verse says: On the latrine, he could not speak the Dharma to you; A single phrase, like a thunderclap, shakes the heavens and earth. If you can understand this at the moment it is spoken, Then the whole world is but one place of liberation.
The old monk was right on the toilet. He did not preach the Buddha-dharma for others. The stench of excrement and the fragrance of sandalwood were both revealed;
the mechanism of father and son was fully leaked. (Gushan Gui)
Zhaozhou had esoteric words; Wenyuan did not conceal them. He brought forth the teachings of the Great Canon;
his merit is truly immeasurable. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
One does not discuss the Buddha-dharma while on the toilet (dōsi). Call him over and kick him right in the face. There is no need for further discussion of repaying the Buddha’s kindness;
with this profound mind, serve every dust mote and world-system. (Wuan Quan)
Clearly and brightly the Way is not spoken; by whom can this principle be known? A gust of spring wind arrives, and flowers lie in profusion across the path. (Mongan Cong)
[Added for inclusion] Once, when Wang Gong, the Military Governor of Zhending, brought his sons into the monastery, Master Zhaozhou sat and asked, "Does Your Majesty understand?
The King said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Since childhood I have observed the fast until my body has grown old;
seeing you, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. The King treated him with even greater reverence. The following day, he ordered an attendant to deliver a message.
The Master descended from his meditation seat to receive him. An attendant said, "When the Abbot saw the Great King arrive, he did not descend from his meditation seat;
yet today, when the General arrives, why does he descend? The Master replied, "This is not something you understand.
When a person of the highest caliber comes, I receive them upon the meditation seat; when a person of middling caliber comes, I receive them after descending from the meditation seat."
When people of the lowest rank arrive, they are received outside the three gates. The verse says:
"Receiving people of the highest rank, there is no mutual yielding; Sitting upright and majestic—what is this called 'crossing over'?
If the commander and king act with lofty dignity, For their sake, he drags them down and overturns the meditation seat. (Tianmu Li)
Sitting cross-legged to welcome the honored guest, reclining on a curved bench facing the banners and streamers. This is not a matter of a different family tradition;
he dwells in a land of ritual and music. (Xiyan Hui)

A broken-legged meditation bench joined with severed firewood; it is still fit for reclining the head while greeting high-ranking guests. One clearly knows this is comparable to the earth that fills the sky with its wealth;
it is difficult to compete with the bone-deep poverty of others. (Shixi Yue)

How can a king of men compare to the honored King of Dharma? Without leaving his meditation seat, he receives those of the highest capacity. Do not say that there is still a gap between sovereign and subject;
one must first distinguish between host and guest before entering the mountains. (Yuepo Ming)
Zhaozhou’s three grades of meeting people: before he has even raised a word, the talk has already fallen. When summoned by the Prefectural Office, he simply turns his head;
this too is "a tiger looking at a water mill" (from *Kuchan Jing*).
Not descending from the meditation seat, nor raising his body; from childhood he has observed the fast until he is an old man. He has only a set of teeth fit for eating rice;
who would have known there was such a venerable Great King in this world? (Xianji Yun)

[Added for inclusion] Once, when an attendant reported, "The Great King is coming," Master Zhaozhou said, "Ten thousand blessings to the Great King! The attendant said, "He has not yet arrived. The Master said, "Then you say he is coming? The Verse says: The Great King is coming; Ten thousand blessings to the Great King! Before he has even arrived, He is already here. When the king arrives, He is ten thousand blessings. If one can understand this, One will see the ancient path. If one cannot understand this, One will fall into the weeds. If you wish to know the meaning, Look at the old master’s face. If you do not look at his face, How will you avoid being deceived? If you avoid being deceived, You will naturally be free from doubt. If you are free from doubt, You will see the ancient path. If you see the ancient path, You will see the true person. If you see the true person, You will see the Buddha-nature. If you see the Buddha-nature, You will see the Way. If you see the Way, You will see the self. If you see the self, You will see the world. If you see the world, You will see the Dharma. If you see the Dharma, You will see the Patriarchs. If you see the Patriarchs, You will see the Buddhas. If you see the Buddhas, You will see the ancestors. If you see the ancestors, You will see the teachers. If you see the teachers, You will see the disciples. If you see the disciples, You will see the parents. If you see the parents, You will see the children. If you see the children, You will see the grandchildren. If you see the grandchildren, You will see the lineage. If you see the lineage, You will see the transmission. If you see the transmission, You will see the succession. If you see the succession, You will see the continuity. If you see the continuity, You will see the eternity. If you see the eternity, You will see the impermanence. If you see the impermanence, You will see the permanence. If you see the permanence, You will see the emptiness. If you see the emptiness, You will see the form. If you see the form, You will see the mind. If you see the mind, You will see the nature. If you see the nature, You will see the reality. If you see the reality, You will see the truth. If you see the truth, You will see the suchness. If you see the suchness, You will see the thusness. If you see the thusness, You will see the awakening. If you see the awakening, You will see the enlightenment. If you see the enlightenment, You will see the liberation. If you see the liberation, You will see the nirvana. If you see the nirvana, You will see the peace. If you see the peace, You will see the bliss. If you see the bliss, You will see the joy. If you see the joy, You will see the delight. If you see the delight, You will see the rapture. If you see the rapture, You will see the ecstasy. If you see the ecstasy, You will see the wonder. If you see the wonder, You will see the marvel. If you see the marvel, You will see the mystery. If you see the mystery, You will see the secret. If you see the secret, You will see the hidden. If you see the hidden, You will see the revealed. If you see the revealed, You will see the manifest. If you see the manifest, You will see the apparent. If you see the apparent, You will see the real. If you see the real, You will see the ultimate. If you see the ultimate, You will see the absolute. If you see the absolute, You will see the unconditioned. If you see the unconditioned, You will see the uncreated. If you see the uncreated, You will see the unborn. If you see the unborn, You will see the undying. If you see the undying, You will see the indestructible. If you see the indestructible, You will see the indeclinable. If you see the indeclinable, You will see the immutable. If you see the immutable, You will see the eternal. If you see the eternal, You will see the infinite. If you see the infinite, You will see the boundless. If you see the boundless, You will see the limitless. If you see the limitless, You will see the all-pervading. If you see the all-pervading, You will see the omnipresent. If you see the omnipresent, You will see the universal. If you see the universal, You will see the total. If you see the total, You will see the complete. If you see the complete, You will see the perfect. If you see the perfect, You will see the whole. If you see the whole, You will see the totality. If you see the totality, You will see the entirety. If you see the entirety, You will see the completeness. If you see the completeness, You will see the perfection. If you see the perfection, You will see the excellence. If you see the excellence, You will see the superiority. If you see the superiority, You will see the preeminence. If you see the preeminence, You will see the supremacy. If you see the supremacy, You will see the sovereignty. If you see the sovereignty, You will see the majesty. If you see the majesty, You will see the glory. If you see the glory, You will see the splendor. If you see the splendor, You will see the brilliance. If you see the brilliance, You will see the radiance. If you see the radiance, You will see the light. If you see the light, You will see the brightness. If you see the brightness, You will see the clarity. If you see the clarity, You will see the transparency. If you see the transparency, You will see the purity. If you see the purity, You will see the stainless. If you see the stainless, You will see the immaculate. If you see the immaculate, You will see the untainted. If you see the untainted, You will see the undefiled. If you see the undefiled, You will see the unsullied. If you see the unsullied, You will see the unblemished. If you see the unblemished, You will see the flawless. If you see the flawless, You will see the faultless. If you see the faultless, You will see the blameless. If you see the blameless, You will see the praiseworthy. If you see the praiseworthy, You will see the venerable. If you see the venerable, You will see the honorable. If you see the honorable, You will see the worthy. If you see the worthy, You will see the noble. If you see the noble, You will see the sublime. If you see the sublime, You will see the transcendent. If you see the transcendent, You will see the extraordinary. If you see the extraordinary, You will see the marvelous. If you see the marvelous, You will see the wondrous. If you see the wondrous, You will see the miraculous. If you see the miraculous, You will see the supernatural. If you see the supernatural, You will see the divine. If you see the divine, You will see the sacred. If you see the sacred, You will see the holy. If you see the holy, You will see the sublime. If you see the sublime, You will see the supreme. If you see the supreme, You will see the ultimate. If you see the ultimate, You will see the final. If you see the final, You will see the end. If you see the end, You will see the conclusion. If you see the conclusion, You will see the completion. If you see the completion, You will see the fulfillment. If you see the fulfillment, You will see the realization. If you see the realization, You will see the attainment. If you see the attainment, You will see the achievement. If you see the achievement, You will see the success. If you see the success, You will see the victory. If you see the victory, You will see the triumph. If you see
The messenger has delivered his message; with palms joined and head bowed, he prostrates himself.
Facing him are a pair of clear and white eyes—yet the mountain-dwelling elder has already passed them by. (Chuan’an Fang)
The attendant came and reported to the Great King: "Zhaozhou once bowed down from his meditation seat. Out of affection for his son, he failed to notice the ugliness of the bystander's gaze.
Alas, how can one help it? His entire being remains in the Imperial Capital. (Tiantong Jue)
A single phrase of spiritual acuity is priceless; ten thousand blessings are too much for one to bear.
Observe how he takes the tail as the head, and further says, "The Great King arrives! (Chuna Xiu).
Horses as swift as the *jizi* and common donkeys fill the roads; who would dare distinguish their fineness or coarseness by their fur?
Had it not been for the discernment of Bo Le at that time, the thousand-li steed that could chase the wind would have been lost. (Cishou Shen)
Xu You came to the bank to wash his ears; Chao Fu would not drink water from which an ox had drunk.
The attendant personally entered the Imperial Capital, while Zhaozhou remained only within the weeds. (Nanyuan Sheng)
When coming, the palace follows him; when departing, the music fills the road. The attendant’s hair is white as if newly grown;
Zhaozhou meets him under a single parasol as if they were old friends. (Biefeng Yin)
Zhaozhou went to a hut master’s place and asked, “Is there any? Is there any? The master held up his fist. The Master said, “The water is too shallow;
it is no place to moor a boat,” and he departed. He then went to another hut master’s place and asked, “Is there any?
Is there any? That master also held up his fist. The Master said, “One who can grant and can take away, one who can kill and can give life.”
Huo bowed in homage. The verse says:
Question and answer have always been of one kind; At the very first stroke, do not be negligent. The General has his own fine reputation;
Failing to receive a fief is merely a matter of leisure. (By Fojie Yu)
A single horse and solitary spear, he fought at Zu Pass; life and death were but a single kṣaṇa away. Zhaozhou was most unforgiving of such fellows;
he drove home the wedge with two blows to the master’s head. (Wenshu said:)
The starless scale has equal ends; when lifted up, one must see clearly.
If you argue over fractions within it, know that you have mistaken the fixed weight on the beam. (Fóxìng Tàiyī)
The old man of Zhaozhou was fond of little and prone to much anger; he did not know how to be a guest and caused his host great trouble.
(Zhandang Zhun) With tiger-like stride and dragon-like gait, he traverses the nine realms; he knows how to raise wind and thunder from level ground.
When he casually calls forth the master of the hermitage, one sees the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward. (Foxin Cai)
An old man who established a forest monastery was Zhaozhou; holding up his two fists, he did not offer a light response.
The scale without stars is in the hands of the person present; the full weight is contained right within it. (Chu’an Fang)
[Continued Collection] The young masters of the Five Tombs vie with one another to boast of their wealth; the high monk in his hundred patches does not disdain poverty.
Lately, the ways of the world have become largely inverted: people value only the clothes they wear, not the person within. (By Sengchang of Sansheng).
The Upper Hermitage monk raises his fist; Zhaozhou’s left eye weighs half a catty. The Lower Hermitage monk raises his fist;
Zhaozhou’s right eye weighs eight ounces. Look at the Iron Ox of Shanfu—how does it compare to the Great Statue of Jiazhou?
If you say they both involve confusion, the lamp-stand and the lantern join their palms in homage. (Cishou Shen)
Passing the hand over the chest, he weeps for his lord. The coffin has not yet emerged, yet the corpse leans out.
It would be better to dig deep and bury it; one can guarantee eating tender eggplants next year. (Xiatang Yuan)
The hermitage master used it intimately back in his day; within the eyes of a monk, one must produce sinews.
Zhaozhou’s tongue held the Longquan sword; opening his mouth casually, he could kill with suspicion. (Zide Hui)
The water is shallow; it is no place to moor a boat. To be able to yield and to be able to seize is to have one’s own ground. With a single blow, both layers of barriers are shattered;
filling the ditches and blocking the ravines, there is no turning back. (Nun Wuzhuo Zong).
The Hermit’s fist raised—intimate and direct. Zhaozhou’s words point westward to Qin. True understanding does not depend on a thousand cups of wine;
even a single cup of empty tea can intoxicate one. (Zantang Shen)
Sailing with the current, steering against the wind; having fished the entire river to its depths, nothing emerges but this very thing.
(Yuelin Guan) The abbot’s fist is no different from any other; Zhaozhou makes the simple seem difficult. How many monks in the monasteries are there who merely recite Chan?
Who can lift their heads and look beyond the heavens? (Tieshan Ren)
Gleaming banners flash back and forth; how many who gaze from afar are filled with doubt?
At this moment, had one obtained the feet of Lord Fan, a single step would have flung open both doors of Hongmen. (Wuzhun Shanfeng)

Wenyuan’s cultivation does not fall into emptiness; from time to time he gazes upon and pays homage to the purple-gold countenance.
Although Zhaozhou’s staff is short, it cleaves asunder the myriad peaks of Mount Hua. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
Paying homage to the Buddha, one needlessly bumped into Zhaozhou; he instead took knowledge and views as enemies. Now the four seas are as level as the palm of a hand;
the clouds fly high and the waters flow on their own. (Zhaotang 1)
Knowing only to gaze upon and prostrate before the purple-golden countenance, one does not realize that the crown of the head has been struck by a thunderbolt.
All my heart and courage have been laid bare to others; those I have known remain as strangers to me. (Mong’an Chōng)
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is Zhaozhou? The Master said, "The east gate, the west gate, the south gate, and the north gate. Verse:
Within these words, the vital pivot is presented, striking face-to-face; The *śakrāloka* eye is cleared of all subtle dust. The gates of east, west, south, and north—
True. An infinite wheel-mallet cannot strike it open (Xuédòu Xiǎn).
At the four gates and portals lies Zhàozhōu; almost beneath the city walls, spears and halberds rise. Where now are the general’s war-horses?
Wild grasses and idle flowers fill the earth with sorrow (Zhàojiào Zǒng).
A golden mallet from within the sleeve strikes once and opens it wide; east, west, south, and north, not a speck of dust remains.
On the southern side of the Stone Bridge is the path to Mount Tai; I inform you, traveler, go back or come forth. (Puyongping)
The gate opens wide; enter Zhaozhou. Roam freely in the east, west, south, and north.
The dragon towers and phoenix pavilions remain as they were, yet one has lost the good path by which they came. (Lohan Nan)
The four gates stand wide open for those who come and go; with clear vision beneath one's feet, one reaches the very source.
Through the four or five hundred lanes of flowering willows and poplars, there rise two or three thousand towers of pipes and strings. (Yuantong Xian)
[Continued Collection] Old Zhaozhou has a single secret: open the four gates and reach the very source of the path. Upon entering the gate, it is bright and pure;
when exiting the gate, do not let it leak away. I shall explain for you this single thread: on the day of the New Year, it is a festival of Great Peace. (Huanglong Xin)
When a monk asked Zhaozhou, Zhaozhou replied: "If you receive a horse from one person, you should return an ox to another.

When people are level, they do not speak; when water is level, it does not flow. Where the favor received is deep, it is best to withdraw first; when the fulfillment of one's purpose is at its height, it is precisely the time to rest."
(Old Zhaozhou of the South, North, East,
and West / Sees people riding horses and also rides an ox / Seeking the path home beneath the clear wind and moon / Asks Kong Qiu before the gate of the Master. — Xiatang Yuan.

A monk once asked Zhaozhou, “Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses? The Master said, “It is like hitting a ball on a swift current. The monk then asked Touzi, “What is the meaning of ‘hitting a ball on a swift current’? Touzi said, “Every thought-moment does not linger. Verse: Hitting a ball on a swift current— The mind’s waves never cease; In every instant, there is no staying. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look at the infant’s face. If you can understand this, You will know the source of the myriad phenomena. If you cannot understand this, You will be lost in the sea of birth and death. Zhaozhou’s answer is like a flash of lightning; Touzi’s reply is like a clear mirror. If you can penetrate these two lines, You will see the ancient path clearly. If you cannot penetrate these two lines, You will wander in the dark. Do not seek it outside yourself— It is right here before your eyes. If you can grasp it in an instant, You will transcend the three realms. If you hesitate for even a moment, You will fall into the pit of views. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is the very lifeblood of the Zen school. Do not doubt it— It is as plain as the sun in the sky. If you can realize it now, You will be free from all delusion. If you do not realize it now, You will remain bound by ignorance. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. If you can understand this, You have attained the Way. If you do not understand this, You are still a common person. Do not look for it elsewhere— It is right within your own mind. If you can see it thus, You will be a true heir of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you do not see it thus, You are merely a follower of words. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. This is the final word. Do not doubt it. Do not hesitate. Just as it is—this is the truth. If you can practice it thus, You will attain liberation. If you do not practice it thus, You will remain in bondage. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. This is the essential point. Do not miss it. Do not overlook it. It is the very heart of the Dharma. If you can grasp it, You will be a true child of the Buddha. If you cannot grasp it, You are still wandering in the world of delusion. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. This is the ultimate teaching. Do not doubt it. Do not question it. It is as clear as the open sky. If you can realize it, You will be free from all suffering. If you do not realize it, You will continue to suffer. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. This is the final instruction. Do not forget it. Do not lose it. It is the very essence of Zen. If you can embody it, You will be a true master. If you cannot embody it, You are still a student. Therefore, I say: “Hitting a ball on a swift current— Every thought-moment does not linger. The six consciousnesses are without merit; let me pose a question. Masters of old have together discerned the source of this matter. Amidst the vast expanse, a ball is struck upon swift waters;
its point of descent never pauses—who can perceive it? (Xuedou Xian)
At first, the long infant plays with a water ball; the patch-robed monk follows the waves, never ceasing.
If one asks about Deshan’s execution of the true command, how does it compare to the question posed to Zhaozhou at that time? (Tianyi Hui)
What is called consciousness? It returns fully possessed of the six [consciousnesses]. Eighty-four thousand [dharmas] are utterly insufficient.
A newborn infant still prattles; it is like a ball struck by swift water, blocking the mouth with a seal. (Baiyun Cuan)
[Continued Collection] The morning sun busily strikes a ball; from birth, every thought-moment flows on without ceasing.
If one knows that once it falls to the ground, it leaves no trace, only then will one understand Yunmen’s “Six Non-Containments. (Cishou Shen)
A ball struck on swift water: moment by moment it does not linger. Before the six consciousnesses can be fully mastered, one first perceives the turning of the two eyes.
To perpetuate the lineage of this school is simply this; there is no need to seek further elsewhere. (Fóxìng Tàiyán)
A newborn child at first is merely a blank slate; yet the six consciousnesses are clever and the nature of the mind is skillful.
Like a ball struck upon a rushing stream, it rises and falls without anyone understanding. Since you are a pearl in the palm of the hand, you must become a treasure of the household.
Old Zhaozhou spoke thus—Fujian Qin.

[Added for inclusion] Once, a monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is your surname, Master? The Master said, “It is found in Changzhou. The monk asked, “How old are you? The Master said, “It is found in Suzhou.
The Verse says: The surname is found in Changzhou; The age is found in Suzhou. If you wish to know the true meaning, Look at the moon on the thirteenth day.
Suzhou has it; Changzhou has it. One must believe that these words come from the mouth of the patriarch himself. How could Zhaozhou, an ancient Buddha, have spoken in vain?
When the world is destroyed, he remains imperishable. If one can investigate the source and root herein, one will certainly face south and look at the Big Dipper. (Xuedou Xian)
In Changzhou there is one, in Suzhou there is one; they roar the lion’s roar with their tongues hanging out. The Mountain of Longevity is high and the Sea of Blessings is deep.
Eighty-one, nine times nine. If you can immediately turn the light back upon yourself, your name shall remain imperishable through ten thousand ages. (Fojian Qin)
In Changzhou there is, in Fuzhou there is not: the river wind turns fierce and the waves are coarse. There is no need to mark the boat to remember where the sword fell;
a single sail has already passed beyond Lake Dongting. (Chuan’an Jing)
Suzhou has it; Changzhou has it. Before you have reached Suzhou or Changzhou, you do not know that it exists. Once you have reached Suzhou and Changzhou, where exactly is it?
People today do not recognize the meaning of the ancients; they wander aimlessly and upside-down within the city walls. (Tuan’an Qi)
There is one in Suzhou and one in Changzhou; in the third month of the year, the *shébù* (partridge) cries in Jiangnan.
How laughable is this man who possesses years but lacks virtue—when pressed by others, he forces himself to make distinctions. (Tuingeng Ning).
[Added from another source] Zhaozhou asked a presiding seat-master (zuozhu), "What sutra are you lecturing on? He replied, "I am lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Master said, "May I ask about a certain passage of meaning? [The master] said, "Yes. The Master kicked into the air and blew once, saying, "What is the meaning of this?
[The master] said, "This meaning is not found in the sutra. The Master said, "You empty-talking, deceptive fellow! This is the fifth [case]."
Regarding the meaning of the *Hālāhala* (Bali) lifting the rock, it simply does not exist in the Way.
The verse says: With one kick, he causes the earth’s axis to overturn; With one breath, he turns the celestial pivot back again.
The lecturer does not understand the meaning of the *cundadāma* (the circular garland); In vain he leaves the mountain ahead and passes the mountain behind. (Guantang Jushi)
The meaning of "lifting the stone" has always differed; in the depths of the surging waves, he displays his spiritual powers.
His lofty banner does not rest on the reed-lined shore; in pairs and twos, they follow the morning breeze. (Ding of Daitang).
[Added to the Collection] Once, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "How should one apply the mind throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Master said, "You are driven by the twelve hours; I am the one who makes use of the twelve hours. He then added, "Brothers, do not stand here for long."
When there is business, deliberate upon it; when there is no business, sit beneath your robes and alms bowl and exhaustively investigate the principle.
When I was traveling on pilgrimage, apart from the two times for rice gruel and meals, these were the only occasions for miscellaneous mental activity;
outside of these, there was no other occasion for mental activity. If you do not act in this way, you will be far astray. The verse says:
A hundred years consist of thirty-six thousand days; each day has twelve periods from morning to dusk. Even if they were to kill this old monk, he would not care at all;
he does not know that amidst such clamor, who is there to witness? (Gushan Gui)

To cause one to be summoned at every hour of the day, only to be sent away again; relying on official authority and leveraging power to deceive others—vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis upon which to rely. (Jingshan Gao)
The bell announces the dusk, the cock heralds the dawn. Zhaozhou, why trouble yourself with idle vexation? He tears asunder the void into two sides;
from the incense burner in the ancient temple, a cluster of *zhicao* mushrooms emerges. (Xue’an Jin)
Peacefully settled in his native land, Old Zhaozhou was most elegant in his timing. "If there is wine today, get drunk today;
when tomorrow's worries come, worry about them tomorrow. (By Yan’an Xuan)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] While Zhaozhou was drawing water on the well-house at Nanquan, he saw Nanquan passing by. He immediately hugged a pillar and hung his legs out, saying, "Save me! Save me! Nanquan climbed the ladder and said, "One, two, three, four, five.

After a short while, the Master went back to pay his respects, saying, "Just now I thanked the Master for saving me. Verse: The well-house pillar hangs the feet; Nanquan ascends the ladder with a smile. One, two, three, four, five— How many times has the moon been swallowed by the tiger?

The old man’s words were like a thunderclap; The spring water flows clear and bright. If you can discern the meaning within this, You will know that the ancient path is not far. If you cannot yet see through it, Look again at the well-house pillar.
It is said:
"Nanquan and Zhaozhou employ the most profound [secrets]. Later people fail to understand them and instead continue to search for them.
Examine closely their words of coming and going; the two men stand side by side, hand in hand. (Fenyang Shao).

Zhaozhou creates it himself and undergoes it himself; Nanquan comes from outside to rescue him. Even if one’s reckoning were perfectly clear, it would still be walking on a private path. (Yuedang Chang)
It cannot be painted nor can it be sculpted; atop the tower, he hangs his body and cries out for rescue. Where Nanquan strikes, there is a profound reason;
a single stroke of elegance is like brocade. A-he-he! One, two, three, four, five—a tiger bites a fierce tiger.
(Magnificent is this thought.
How could such casual arrangements be in vain? Upon level ground, waves surge as if to submerge the heavens. Once more, strike the ladder several times;
thus, one avoids letting the arrowhead fall into the Yellow Springs. (Fóxìng Tài).

The Hall has always favored meritorious deeds; why, then, does the attendant harbor doubt? Zhaozhou reveals his very heart and liver;
when questioned, it remains as pitch-black as ink. (Zhaotang 1).

Summoned before the throne, he first responded with "Yes. He did not realize that the consciousness of karma was vast and boundless. Although his merit has already been accomplished, what can be done?
It was simply that from the beginning he did not emit light. (Gushan Gui)
What a magnificent hall of merit! It is entirely the work of past Buddhas, their bodies adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. They did not have it carved from sandalwood.
Day after day of incense smoke, night after night of lamps—when you look at it, it is truly nothing more than dried radishes (Jingshan Daowu).
[Added for inclusion] Once Zhaozhou arrived at Linji’s place, he was just beginning to wash his feet. Linji asked, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, “It happens to be the time when this old monk is washing his feet. Linji stepped forward and listened intently.
The Master said, “If you understand, then understand; why do you keep prying and pecking? Linji shook his sleeves and left. The Master said, “Thirty [blows].”
I traveled as a wandering monk for many years. Today, I have mistakenly provided a commentary for others. The verse says:
At the place where one washes their feet, there is no further arrangement to be made. When listening intently, it is not a matter of mere grasping or chewing.
As for the two elders, Zhaozhou and Linji—when they meet, what need is there to labor over providing a commentary? (Gushan Gui)
One man’s eyes resemble drumsticks; another’s head is like a wooden ladle. These two old men know no shame;
to this day, there is nowhere to put them. (Jingshan Gao)
Linji and Zhaozhou were the patriarchs of the Chan forest; meeting them unexpectedly was like being struck by a blow.
To encounter a wandering monk of the present day and call him "two idle monks" (Xue’an Jin).

[Added for inclusion: When Zhaozhou saw a monk approaching, he turned his face to the wall and wrote Sanskrit characters. The monk spread out his sitting mat, performed three prostrations, and the Master turned his body away.
The monk folded up his sitting mat and departed. The Master said, "How painful! How painful! The monk let out a great laugh.
The verse says:
To whom does the cry of "Suffering upon suffering" address itself? The essential trigger is a crossbow of a thousand-jun weight. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven strikes the Imperial Bell;
the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all break into dance. (Dianniu You).
Suffering within suffering, suffering within pleasure—who says gold is like dung?
The Old Teacher Xianggu rolled the ball; Bimao struck down and caught the rat. (Ying’an Hua)
"Suffering within pleasure, pleasure within suffering. This monk from Zhaozhou lacks realization in both cases.
Even if one were to suddenly penetrate the very source, it would still be like washing soil with soil (Fozhao Guang).
Not failing to perceive that which is manifest before one’s eyes is the foremost tally; when the occasion arises, a punch or a kick is not given lightly.
A scorched brick strikes and freezes through to the bottom; a red-eyed man bumps into a firebrand. (The room is opened.)
[Added from another source] Zhaozhou arrived at Yunju. Yunju said, "You are so old and aged; why do you not seek a place to stay?
The Master said, "Where could I possibly stay? Yunju said, "There is the site of an old temple ahead.
The Master said, "If that is the case, then you, Reverend, should stay there yourself. The Master then went to Zhunyu. Zhunyu said, "You are so old and aged..."

“I am not looking for a place to stay,” he said. The Master asked, “Where could you possibly stay? Nan-yü replied, “Old as I am, you do not even recognize my dwelling place. The Master said, “After thirty years of riding horses, today I have been thrown by a donkey! The Verse says: A lifetime of riding horses, Today met with a donkey’s kick. The old fellow does not know his own home; He has lost his way. If you wish to see the true man, Look at him where he stands. If you can discern this, Then you will understand the meaning of the verse. If you cannot discern it, You must seek a teacher. Do not let the days pass in vain; Seek out a true friend. If you meet such a person, You will surely attain the Way. If you do not meet such a person, You will wander in birth and death. Therefore, I urge you all: Do not be negligent. When the Master descends from the meditation seat and stands, the spirits wail and the ghosts weep. When the Master ascends the meditation seat and sits, the dragons coil and the tigers lie.
With one blow of the mallet, they are split in two; yet when picked up, they are originally but a single break. (Original Awakening, One).

[Added for inclusion] Once, when a scholar said to Zhaozhou, "The Master is an ancient Buddha," the Master replied, "The scholar is a new Tathāgata. The Verse says: The ancient Buddha is the scholar; The new Tathāgata is the Master. If you wish to know the true meaning, Look at the two of them together.
The palace of the Broad Cold Palace is pure and free of dust; you have already encountered the Master who has opened the Eight Characters.
There is no need to pluck the vermilion cassia branches bit by bit; simply uproot it along with its tree at once. (Nansou Long)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is it like when there is a difference of a hair’s breadth? The Master said, “Heaven and earth are separated by a vast distance. The monk said, “What is it like when there is not a difference of a hair’s breadth?

The Master said, “Heaven and earth are separated by a vast distance. The Verse says: A hair’s breadth of difference— Heaven and earth are suspended apart. No difference of a hair’s breadth— Heaven and earth are suspended apart. How could one ever fathom this? It is the Great Matter of the Buddhas. If you wish to understand it clearly, Look at the face of the Great Master Zhaozhou.
A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are divided. No hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are divided. Whether divided or not divided, both are definitive.
If you can simply pluck the willow flowers with a confident hand, you must understand the wind arising from the cypress before the courtyard. Zhaozhou’s barrier has a fine bearing.
On the path of Caoqi there is no trace. (Changling Zhuo) A single road is as straight as a bowstring.
The message of peace has been delivered; all nations bring tribute, and the fires of war have ceased across the four seas.
(Closing the Room / Opening the Door). [Added from another collection.

A monk once asked Zhaozhou, "When one encounters a person who has attained the Way on the road, one does not respond with speech or silence. I wonder, what should one use to respond? The Master said, "A man comes from Chen Prefecture;

he cannot bring news of Xu Prefecture. The Verse says: When meeting a man of realization on the road, One does not answer with speech or silence. If you ask what is used to respond, "A man comes from Chen Prefecture, He cannot bring news of Xu Prefecture."
The bow is drawn full yet misses its mark; the sword is brandished long yet leaves no trace.
How laughable—that place where the sun and moon do not reach—is a separate heaven and earth within this very midst. (Daopei Xing)
A patient who has consumed poison seeks out a skilled physician. The physician instructs him to take the very medicine that caused the illness to cure it.
Once the illness is gone and the medicine has returned to its original state, only one with eyes upon their tongue can discern the difference in flavor. (Fóxìng Tái, 2)
In this world, there are those who flee from their forms out of fear of shadows; they rush to the courts to lodge complaints, laboring their spirits in vain.
If one knew that form and shadow are fundamentally non-dual, one would sit facing the high hall, gazing at the autumn moon’s orb.

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk once asked Zhaozhou, "Where has Nanquan gone after his passing? The Master said, "He became a donkey for the eastern neighbor and a horse for the western neighbor.
The Verse says: A donkey in the east, a horse in the west— Who can fathom this old fellow? If you wish to see him clearly, Look at the clouds drifting across the sky.
Having shed the donkey’s head, he now bears the horse’s head; from the eastern house to the western house, there is no end to his toil.
I ask you, how much sorrow do you have? It is just like a river of spring water flowing toward the east. (Lan’an Shu)
[Added for inclusion] Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying: "In this place, what is called the Buddha-dharma is difficult when said to be easy, and easy when said to be difficult.
Elsewhere, it is easy to recognize but difficult to see; here with this old monk, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize. If you can understand this, [you have attained it]."
He roams freely throughout the world. The verse says: Knowing and not knowing;
seeing and not seeing; explaining as easy and explaining as difficult—it is like oil entering flour. (Fenyang Yizhuo)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection: As Zhaozhou was approaching the end of his life, he instructed a monk to take a fly-whisk and present it to the Prince of Zhao, saying:

"If he asks where you obtained this, simply say: 'This is what this old monk used throughout his entire life and has never exhausted. The verse says: When the Great Master was about to pass away, He entrusted a whisk to a monk to give to the Prince. If asked whence it came, one should say: "This is what the old monk used until his very last breath."
To enjoy for a lifetime, it should be inexhaustible; yet how many stalks are there in all? Entrusted to King Zhao, it remains for a thousand ages;
let the north and south compete with one another as they will. (Baoning Yong)

[Added to the Collection] A monk once asked Zhaozhou, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, “On the winter solstice, the first yang arises. The Verse says: On the day of the winter solstice, the first yang emerges; At the moment of the new moon, the full moon appears. If you wish to know the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, Look at the face of the old woman selling cakes.
The willow color is tender like fresh gold; the pear blossoms open like white snow. If you can understand the seasons, at the winter solstice, the first yang arrives. (Yuánwù Qín)
Iron trees bloom with tens of millions of flowers; stones sprout two or three shoots of bamboo. The clay-carved Vajrapāṇi opens his mouth and laughs:
tomorrow is the winter solstice, and the first Yang energy arises. (Fujian Qín)
The willow color is tender as fresh gold; the pear blossoms are fragrant like falling snow. If one but knew the power of spring, its splendor would be truly extraordinary. (Lóngmén Yuǎn)
At the winter solstice, the first yang arises; heaven and earth are connected by a single thread. How pitiable are the countless people who do not recognize their mother’s face. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Furong in Fuzhou (heir to Guizong). One day, the Master took his leave of Guizong. Guizong asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going back to the Ling Mountains. Guizong said, "You have been here for many years;
now that you have packed your things, come and let me speak a bit of the Buddha-dharma for you. Having finished packing, the Master went up [to see him].
[Zong] said, "Go. The Master said, "Come closer. The Master then drew near. [Zong] said, "The weather is cold; take care on your journey.
Upon hearing these words, the Master suddenly forgot his previous understanding. The verse says:
An eighty-year-old woman learns to paint her eyebrows; with a foolish heart, she wishes to compare herself to her youth.
One morning, when the mirror on the stand is shattered, she finally realizes that everything she has done before was wrong. (Cishou Shen)
[Added for inclusion] One day, Fuyong went to visit his fellow practitioner, Master Shixing.

As the Master ascended the hall, he took up his staff with his right hand, leaned it against the left side, and after a long silence, said: "If this matter were not in the hands of my elder brother Fuyong..."
Having related the great difficulty in full detail, he then descended from his seat. The verse says:
Exhausting my old spirit, I have prepared the cups and dishes with unusual care. Who would have thought that at a village tavern, it is difficult to persuade those who dwell in the imperial towers?
(Xiyuan Hui). Chan Master Zhītōng of Wǔtái Mountain (a successor of Guīzōng):

When the Master was first in the assembly of Guīzōng, he suddenly cried out one night, "I have attained great enlightenment! The multitude were startled by this. The next morning, they went up [to see him].

The assembly gathered in the hall. Zong said, "A monk who attained great enlightenment last night—come forward. The Master stepped forward and said, "I, this one. Zong asked, "What principle have you seen that you claim to have attained great enlightenment? Try to explain it. The Master replied, "An abbess was originally made by a woman. Zong marveled at this. The Verse says: The abbess was originally made by a woman; A single phrase, and the entire world is overturned. If you can understand this matter, Then you will know the meaning of "great enlightenment. If you cannot, you are still stuck in the dark. Do not look for it in words or phrases.
