"In the future, you must not let me down. At that time, a monk came forward, bowed, and said, "I, [Name], shall never dare to let the Master down. The Master said, "You have already let me down. He added, "I have told you clearly, yet you still do not understand; how much less could you ever conceal it? The Verse says: The old man’s words were like a thunderclap; He struck the monk right where he stood. If you can grasp it in this very moment, You will see the ancient path clearly revealed. If you hesitate for even a single thought, You will miss the point by a thousand miles. Do not seek it in the past or the future; It is right here before your eyes. If you try to grasp it with your mind, You will only increase your confusion. If you try to express it in words, You will only fall into error. If you wish to avoid being deceived, Just look at the face of the present moment. If you can see it thus, You will naturally transcend birth and death. If you cannot see it thus, You will continue to wander in the three realms. Do not doubt this for a moment; This is the true Dharma-eye. If you can see it thus, You will be free from all delusion. If you cannot see it thus, You will remain bound by ignorance. Do not seek it elsewhere; It is right within your own heart. If you can realize it thus, You will attain the Great Enlightenment. If you cannot realize it thus, You will remain a common mortal. Do not doubt this for a moment; This is the ultimate truth. If you can see it thus, You will be one with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you cannot see it thus, You will remain lost in the mundane world. Do not doubt this for a moment; This is the true teaching of the Buddhas. If you can see it thus, You will be liberated from all suffering. If you cannot see it thus, You will continue to suffer in saṃsāra. In studying the Way, one must first find the point of entry; once you have entered, do not let it go to waste.
Even when facing the Way with clear vision, one may still be deluded—how much more so when one is obscured by words? (Original Awakening I)
[Added for inclusion] Muzhou asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "The old monk has been shouted at by you.

The monk shouted again. The Master said, "After three shouts and four shouts, what then? The monk was speechless. The Master struck him and said, "You empty-headed swindler! Verse: Muzhou’s question cuts through the clouds; The monk’s shout is like a flash of lightning. When the Master asks, "What after three and four shouts?

The monk falls silent—no words to be found. A blow lands upon his head; He is exposed as a hollow, deceptive fellow. If one can discern the meaning here, One enters the gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The two shouts and the three shouts—the master who employs them knows the shifting of the occasion. If one says they are like "riding on a tiger's head," both become blind men.
Who is this blind man? He picks it up and shows it to the whole world. (Xuedou Xian)
The man from Muzhou carries a wooden board; he knows how to use it, but not how to calculate. Before others, he wins five hundred;
at home, he spends one thousand. (Puan Yu).
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Muzhou, "What is it like when one bows high to Śākyamuni and does not bow to Maitreya?
The Master said, "Yesterday someone asked that; I have already sent him away. The monk said, "Master, you must suspect that I am not sincere."
The Master said, "The staff is not here; I shall give you thirty blows with the handle of the broom for now.
Nantang Xing said, "For a monk, it is not considered out of place to bow high to Śākyamuni and not prostrate before Maitreya; yet this must be one's fundamental duty.
Only through the hammer and tongs of a master can one know who is genuine and who is false. Why? Thus he composed a verse:"
To emerge from the crowd, one must be a man of heroic spirit; to overcome the enemy, one must be a lion’s cub.
If one lacks such an eye for selecting a Buddha, what is the use of even a thousand years?
The stern command of the General has been issued; the eight wildernesses and the four seas must be cleared and purified.
He draws forth his sword-spirit that rivals the Ox and Dipper constellations, sweeping away all turbid dust to reveal the Great Peace. (Tiantong Jue)
He kills people without batting an eye; when it comes to saving others, he must act. He speaks of reality, not of emptiness; only when the *sheng* is full does it become a *dou*.

He bows high to Śākyamuni but does not prostrate before Maitreya; though he was driven out after being struck with a staff, it still cost him effort. When a drop of water produces ice, do you know it or not?
Someone recognizes that throwing a brick can draw forth a jade. (By Yuet Tang Chang)

How many people, with their unwholesome roots, see only the branches on the treetop growing ever longer? (Changling Zhuo)
Muzhou loved only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip; this monk did not see the squareness of the chisel’s head.
Even if one could turn over hundreds of thousands of scriptural treasuries, such offerings as these would still be considered commonplace. (Gushan Gui)
A single breath turns the entire Great Canon: sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, provisional and real. The boundless, wondrous meanings shine forth brilliantly;
yet originally, not a single character was recognized. (Jingshan Gao)
A casual question, yet it shall endure for a thousand ages; from this point on, it was propagated throughout the monastic communities.
How laughable that Muzhou’s formless transmission—this steamed bun must first be tasted by the hungry one. (Lan’an Shu)
Question: "If you overturn a mountain torrent, the answer is like toppling a peak. When the wild sheep emerges from the grass, it hangs upon its horns.
How can even a clear-eyed monk fathom this? Whether a foot is short or an inch is long, let it be as you judge. (Touzi Shu)
A single word for a swift man; a single lash for a swift horse. Let the prisoner rest, for it increases wisdom; ten thousand miles and eight thousand leagues.
(Muan Yong). Fine jade requires no carving; beautiful words require no ornamentation. Within three months in a smoke-filled village, there is a distinct spring of its own. (Xianan Guan).
[Added for inclusion] A monk once asked Muzhou, "I do not ask about removing one layer with another;
but what is it like when one does not remove one layer with another? The Master said, "Yesterday I planted eggplants; today I plant winter melons."
The Verse says:
Layer upon layer, all gone, returning to the ordinary; Spring warmth, gentle breezes, and days gradually lengthen. Outside the door, the birds’ songs are soft and fragmented;
Rock-flowers lie in profusion across the mountain cottage. (Zidehui)

The Taoist ascending the altar wears light feathered robes; though his power of incantation may be exhausted, the Dharma turns ever new. With his thumb he rends asunder the darkness of heaven and earth;
when the serpent’s head falls, ghosts and spirits are struck with awe. (Xiatang Yuan)
Donning the straw raincoat and tilting the bamboo hat atop a thousand peaks, he leads water to irrigate vegetables before the Five Elders.
Within lies a melon field where it is difficult to fit one's sandals; Muzhou would have retreated to the sidelines. (Nanyan Sheng)
Yesterday I planted eggplants; today I sow winter melons. With a single cry of the *Hemanzi*, the moon falls together with it—into whose house? (Xia’an Wu).
[Added for inclusion] Muzhou asked an official: "In the *I Ching*, it says that the common people use it daily yet do not know it.
Tell me, what is it they do not know? The official said, "I do not know. The Master said, "Truly you do not know."
The Verse says:
To pour it out and yet remain unaware— An iron hammer without holes, Hurled straight at one’s face. Even Buddhas and Patriarchs find it difficult to peer into. (Kentang Chong)

When Caoshan was traveling on pilgrimage, he asked: "What is the Dharmakāya Lord, Vairocana? The Master said: "If I were to tell you..."
"The Way is indeed something distinct. Cao Shan recounted this to Dongshan. Dongshan said, "What an excellent *huatou*! It simply lacks a follow-up statement.
Why not go back and ask him: 'Why do you not say it? Cao Shan then went back and offered the preceding words.
The Master said, "If I were to say, 'I did not say it,' that would silence my own mouth. If I were to say..."
"Way! It immediately makes my tongue falter. Cao Shan returned and related this to Dongshan, who deeply approved it.
He offered this verse:
"The old riddle-master of Wushan, His school’s style is steep and absolute. If someone asks about the Master Vairocana, Opening his mouth is truly distinct."
The teeth possess the mechanism of biting the barb; in heaven there is no second moon. Soft speech is like a diamond; *upāya* (skillful means) is birth and extinction. (Nantang Xing)
Vairocana is the Lord of the Dharma-body; his entire body is his mouth, yet it is truly difficult to utter a word.

When he draws back his tongue and remains mute, only Dongshan is permitted to grant silent approval. Were he not to grant such approval, even a cat would know how to catch mice. (A shout to the hall.)

[Added from the Supplement] Wushi once waited for an opportunity to knock on the door. When the Master opened the door, Xuefeng grabbed him by the chest and asked, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage?
The Master spat at him and said, "You wild fox spirit! He then pushed him out and shut the door. Xuefeng said, "I only wanted to recognize my elder brother.
The Verse says: The gate was opened; he seized him by the chest. A single word of spit, and he was cast out. Though the old man’s intent was to test his kin, How could one fail to see the wild fox?
Once begun, it must be finished; there is a reason for the shifting roles of host and guest. A scorched brick strikes one who is frozen to the marrow;
a red-eyed man bumps into a firebrand. (Songyuan Yue)
The lofty and rigid gatehouse is peerless in antiquity; Though Master Zeng wishes to enter, he finds no way at all. For his sake, I open it wide with eight characters:
Tender green covers the fields, with rice seedlings filling every plot. (A Note on the Bamboo House)
[Added from another source] Wushi went to visit Xuefeng by knocking on the door. The Master asked, "Who is it? Xuefeng said, "A phoenix chick. The Master said, "What for?
Xuefeng said, "To come and devour Old Guan. The Master opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak!
Xuefeng hesitated, and the Master immediately pushed him away and shut the door. After Xuefeng established his own monastery, he addressed the assembly, saying: "If at that time I had..."
"You have entered the gate of the 'Old Contemplation. Where, you lot—this crew of wine-dregs eaters—are you groping?
Xuedou said, "This ungrateful and undutiful fellow—what connection has he to it?
Had you not been able to enter at that time, would I have told you to enter? Now that you grope and cannot find it, you bring disgrace upon Xuefeng as well."
Under the Gate of Old Guan, the verse says:
The phoenix chick has fully developed its wings; Yet under the gate of Old Guan, it stumbles by chance.
Suddenly, in a cold place, it recalls its old debts; It returns to seek advantage elsewhere. (By Nun Wuzhuo Zong)
[Added from the *Yinzhou*] While Wushi was drawing noodles, a monk came to pay his respects. The Master drew the noodles and showed them to him; the monk then departed.
That evening, the Master asked the Head Seat, "Where is the newcomer who arrived today? He replied, "He left right away. The Master said, "It is so, it is so.

the monk then departed. At evening, the Master asked, "Where is that monk who came just now? The junior attendant said, "He has already left. The Master said, "He got only a single peg. Xuangjue said, "Where did you see him lacking a single peg? The verse says:
A thatched cottage with a wooden gate, secluded and even more remote. Who would have expected a traveler to pass this way?
Preparing a decoction of mugwort as a formal offering, he knows no shame; he still flatters others with empty words. (Duanqiao Lun)

The precious sword of Fengcheng has been buried for a long time; A single beam of cold light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox constellations.
Had it not been for Zhang Hua’s discernment of its true nature, It would have remained needlessly submerged for a thousand ages. (Cishou Shen)
Summoned back from the realm of brush and ink, the flower of awakening bloomed last night in Guilin.
Its hidden fragrance leaked forth to convey the message, dispersing as the talent for seasoning the imperial cauldron among men. (Zide Hui)
Floating clouds and lingering mists, both dim and hazy; I have traversed a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags.
Suddenly called back from a dream of frosty night, I raise my head and see the moon directly in the sky. (Wan’an Rou)
[Added for inclusion] Prime Minister Pei asked a monk, "What sutra are you studying? The monk replied, "The *Sutra of the Silent Youth*.
The official asked, "How many fascicles does it have? He said, "Two fascicles. The official said, "Since it is 'silent,' why are there two fascicles?
The monk remained silent. Guisan of Silla provided this alternative response: "If one speaks of silence, it is not merely two [fascicles]."
Volume. The verse says:
Once he dropped his official tablet outside Shishuang’s mechanism; Again he assisted coarse conduct reaching the Tang heavens.
Using only the hand that casts the line across the four seas, Shrimp, crabs, fish, and dragons are all strung upon a single thread. (Xutang Yu)
[Added for inclusion: Prime Minister Pei entered Da'an Temple and asked the various virtuous elders, "In what regard was Rāhula foremost?
They replied, "He was foremost in his secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*). The Prime Minister did not agree with this and proceeded to ask, "What Zen practitioners are there in this place?
At that time, Longya was planting vegetables in the rear garden; the Prime Minister then invited him to come and asked, "In what regard was Rāhula..."
"Who is the foremost? Ya replied, "I do not know. The Master then bowed and said, "A tattered rag wrapping a pearl.
He then offered this verse:
"The foremost in secret practice, His discernment is rare indeed. Possessing the eye that discerns the Dharma, He truly does not know. (Huanglong Xin)
What is considered foremost? Not knowing what is most intimate. A true pearl wrapped in rags—though one were to offer the entire city, it could not be exchanged for it. (Yuepo Ming)
When Venerable Yanyang of Xinxing in Hongzhou (whose name was Shanxin and who succeeded Zhaozhou) first visited Zhaozhou, he asked:
"What is it like when one brings nothing at all? Zhaozhou said: "Put it down. The Master [Yanyang] said:
"Since I am bringing nothing at all, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou said: "If you cannot put it down, then carry it away. At this, the Master...
Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. While residing on the mountain, a snake and a tiger constantly followed him, and he would feed them directly from his own hands.
He composed this verse: Not a single thing can be brought forth; It cannot be borne upon one’s shoulders. In an instant, beneath these words, I knew my error; Within my heart, there is boundless joy.
Having cast away all malice, even snakes and tigers become friends. A pure breeze has blown for several hundred years;
even to this day, it has not ceased. (Huanglong Nan)
Shifting from high to low, one wields power and authority; the gates of liberation open, yet how pitiable is the lack of faith!
Without obtaining the King of Emptiness’s true and wondrous secret instruction, one is led astray and dragged along by sounds and forms. (Zhenjing Wen)
It does not hinder one’s progress to yield the first move with subtlety; realizing one’s own mind was coarse, one feels shame for having struck one’s head.
When the board is broken and the axe-handle by the waist has rotted away, one washes clean the ordinary bones to roam together with the immortals. (Tiantong Jué)
"Without bringing a single thing, I teach him to let it go; suddenly awakened to non-arising, he casts away all worldly concerns.
(Master Min, the Ancient Buddha)
Exerting all one's strength, one cannot let it go; applying effort, one cannot bear its weight. One might think there is nothing at all, yet it is originally one's own.
Upon seeing what is one's own, the heart is filled with great joy; from this point on, the family estate flourishes, traversing ninety thousand li in a single stride.
(Lóngmén Yuǎn). [Continued Collection] Not bringing a single thing forward; unable to lift it with both hands. To directly take responsibility for it—this is entirely one's own. (Fódēng Xún).
A sudden strike reveals the opportunity; it is no ordinary thing. When the finest hair is exhausted, it is as heavy as a mountain. One hears the heart-rending melody as if listening in person;
there is no need for flowing water or mournful winds to play it. (The Poison-Coated Whip)
Slices of sincere heart—few know them; a mouth full of frost, causing particular doubt. To those students of the Way throughout the Five Lakes, I offer this report:
do not let these two eyebrows go to waste. (Yue’an Guo)
Zhaozhou says, "Let it go. Suddenly, flowers bloom on the tip of the pestle. Though there is not a single thing, he puts all practitioners to the test. (Xuetang Xing)
Suddenly he administers a needle to the vital point where medicine cannot reach. At that moment, there was nowhere for his whole body to settle. He laughed heartily and entered the realm of Yan Yang;
there, with snakes and tigers as neighbors, he cannot be sought out. (Mianjie).
Yanyang carried a dog’s head; its stench and filth were such that people feared it. For what reason did Old Zhaozhou pay the price for mutton? (Wild ox, level).
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Master Duofu of Hangzhou (heir to Zhaozhou). A monk asked, "What is the single grove of bamboo at Duofu?

The Master said, "One stalk, two stalks, leaning. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Three stalks, four stalks, bent. The Verse says: One stalk, two stalks, leaning; Three stalks, four stalks, bent. If you wish to know the meaning of Duofu, Look at the bamboo in front of your eyes.
One stalk, two stalks leaning; its intent as venomous as a snake. Three stalks, four stalks crooked; without doubt, one enters hell.

If you recognize the error the moment the words fall, you will return home with an empty heart, having passed the imperial examination. How laughable is the old man of Jiangshan, who for no reason has entered the wild weeds.
(Ying'an Hua): One stem, two stems, slanting;
sparse shadows stir dragons and snakes. The mind suspects the birth of dark specters; diseased eyes see empty flowers in the sky.
"Three stems, four stems, all bent; return to me this grove of bamboo. At times it draws in the pure wind; fallen leaves fill the mountain valleys.
If you understand it thus, then even a single grove of bamboo brings great merit. If you do not understand it, then three stems, four stems, all bent.
(No talent for Chan.)

One day, seeing an attendant carrying an alms bowl toward the hall, the Master called out to him. The attendant responded, "Yes? The Master asked, "Where are you going?
The attendant replied, "I am going to the hall for the midday meal. The Master said, "Do I not know that you are going to the hall for the midday meal? The attendant said, "Aside from this..."

"What other way is there to speak of it? The Master said, "I am simply asking you about your own fundamental matter. [The monk] said, "If the Master asks about my fundamental matter, I am actually going to the hall for the midday meal.

The Master said, "You do not fail in being my attendant. A verse says: What other way is there to speak of it? I ask only of your own fundamental matter. If you ask about the fundamental matter, I am truly going to the hall for the meal.
You are not mistaken in serving me as an attendant.
Father and son go hand in hand through the grass; they gallop like shooting stars and roll like lightning, with a roar like a sudden thunderclap.
They deceive countless heroic spirits, who mistake their saddles and bridles for the goal and spend their lives in error. (By Xingan Shou)

Be most careful not to follow others; they do not understand. This great following of words spreads to the ends of the earth.
Within the true pure nature, a single thought arises, and already there are a thousand differences and ten thousand divergences. (Beitapu Zu)
Lan’an’s disciple, Dasui, followed his teacher. When people asked him, "Does he follow his teacher? Dasui replied, "He follows.

Looking back, he could not rest or settle his mind; he gave rise to divergent views and fell into doubt. Fenyang [Zhao] has opened the celestial path for you: though there be ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, they all return to the One Way. (Fenyang Zhao)
Standing amidst the fires at the end of an eon, he poses a question; even the patch-robed monks remain stuck at two layers of barriers.
Piteous indeed—following that single phrase as it departs, they travel back and forth alone across ten thousand miles. (Xuedou Xian)
Wherever he goes, wherever he goes—thousand-armed Great Compassion cannot restrain him. He comes and goes amidst the flames of the kalpa-ending fire;
though his eyes be of copper and his pupils of iron, no one can find his trace. (Zhengjue Yi).
Destruction and non-destruction are neither internal nor external; there is not a hair’s breadth of separation between them. They are encountered in the ordinary course of life (Daowu Zhen).
To follow him along is also quite groundless. The golden mallet in one’s sleeve is not easily seen. Having finished the questioning, one knows not where he has gone;
the white poplar tree’s wind carries the chill of the tomb ridges (Fohui Quan).
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth, where is the great trichiliocosm? Whether it is destroyed or not destroyed—this "lacquer bucket" is not yet clear.
Would you truly follow him elsewhere? To be thus deceived is indeed excessive. If one were a person of this caliber, they would never arrive at a mistaken understanding. (Fayun Xiu)
To follow step by step is "great following. Blowing on the left side and then blowing on the right—this mere empty puffing of breath will not free you from conceptualization.
Why not instead keep it to warm your belly? (Baoning Yong).
The tongue, whether destroyed or not, has no bone; when looking straight into the face, the eyes protrude. The Great Companion still remains within the kalpa-fire;
the world is parched and vexed with idle clamor. (Baizhang Yuanwen).
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is destroyed, the nostrils before one’s face remain forever present.
It is only because of following another’s single word that one loses the leather bag at one’s waist. (The kindness of Kṣitigarbha).
Swaying between ruin and preservation, they suspect one another; at Jiange and Longshu, they wander in vain. Who else possesses the legs of Master Fan?
With a single step, the two gates of Hongmen fly open. (Cishou Shen)
The kalpa-fire blazes forth, destroying all; yet the blue sky and bright sun shine ever more brilliantly. The prince sleeps drunk, lost in a spring dream;
he does not perceive the warbling of the oriole or the drifting of willow catkins. (Fozhi Yu)
Amidst the billowing stench of smoke and fire, iron caltrops fly forth. If you do not understand this while facing the light, you will lose the opportune moment right before your eyes. (Fóxìng Tái)
Destruction and non-destruction; the end of speech and the end of words—the tip of the tongue bites itself through, and one feels a pang of self-pity.
Great Suizhou and Touzi were ultimately not two different things. Traveling a myriad miles in toil, he went and returned all alone. (Chu’an Fang).
[Continued Collection] One never knows the trap that ensnares the tiger; one simply follows the current and falls east or west. Dasui was naturally a master who holds the net;
letting go and drawing in was his way to test them. (Yuanzhao’s Edition)

The six directions overturn and come crashing upon one’s face; for a moment, one dons coarse hempen cloth to mingle with the dust. To use the wind to fan the fire is a trivial matter, yet it draws the wandering traveler who refuses to turn back.
Whether things are ruined or not, whether one follows or does not follow—it is all in vain to force the needle and the awl through what one hears and sees.
The Three Hundred and Sixty Thousand Acres of Taihu Lake: when the moon speaks from the heart of the waves, to whom can it be told? (Tongzhao Feng).
Clearly there is no separate dharma; who says that the seal lies in the south? A single phrase follows him away; across a thousand mountains, the *nàsēng* (patch-robed monk) hastens.

The crickets cry in the cold as they chirp upon the steps and leaves; the ghosts bow at night before the lamp in the shrine. Having finished my verse by the solitary window, I pace back and forth, my regret beyond measure.
(Tang Jingzun). Ruin and non-ruin are two colors on one canvas; fundamentally there is neither right nor wrong—what need is there to speak of hatred or love? Like clouds passing across the vast sky.
Completely free from all hindrance. Do you not see? The monk’s bowl-bag: having received it, one carries it out in the sun to dry (Fujian Qin).
When it is worn out, one lets it go; why then refuse to rest? Failing to understand the essential meaning, one needlessly seeks a turning back.
(Lóngmén Yuǎn): When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, this demonic phantom—the karmic debt of a hundred lifetimes—remains.
If a follower of Chan asks whether it is destroyed or not: "Last night, the stone man fought over prostrating. (Nántáng Xīng).
Mouths bit with iron, backs burdened by saddles—there is no constancy in this; Dragging plows and pulling harrows, they do not decline their toil.
Greedily seeking life, they go about in petty haste; Who cares that years have passed and white hair abounds? (Jiandang Ji)
Singing and responding amidst the flames of the kalpa-fire; drifting with the waves, all is in vain. Though one’s innermost heart is laid bare, no one understands;
take up the straw sandals and cover the tortoise—enough! (Shigan Sei).
Beside Dasui Hermitage there was a tortoise. A monk asked, "All sentient beings have skin wrapping their bones;
why does this sentient being have bones wrapping its skin? The Master picked up his straw sandals and covered them over the tortoise's back. The monk was speechless.
The Verse says:
Like the six limbs of the tortoise already revealed, Cease playing with your eyes before others. A single straw sandal covers it all;
Even until now, you have not yet awakened. (Beitang Zu)
The place of questioning is not as intimate as the place of answering; it is difficult for even a speck of gold-dust to enter the eye.
The single road to Chang’an is no more than a short distance, but how many people can pass through the Tongguan Pass? (Fohuiquan)
Clearly, it is a mass of bone upon the skin; the layered lines of the hexagrams are even more worthy of contemplation.
Having picked up his straw sandals and covered them all over, Dasui was nonetheless deceived by this monk. (Baizhang Yuanwen).
Exposing the feet and hiding the head—how truly strange! Who would say that for a thousand years this is a numinous tortoise? When the rain pours down, it does not know how to flow away;
when meeting a floating log, when will this ever happen? (Bao-ning Yong)
Once, with skin and bone, he questioned Dàsui; yet at that first blow, he remained further in doubt.
How pitiable are the countless who seek traces by sound, failing to realize the moment when the antelope hangs its horns from a tree branch. (Zhàojiào Zǒng)
A little tortoise outside Daisui Hermitage. A monk asked: "How is it that bone is wrapped in skin? "Covered by straw sandals, no one understands.
White clouds and flowing water linger together. (Dizang’s grace).
Skin wraps the bone, and bone wraps the skin; fortune and misfortune merely cause oneself to be confused by needles and awls.
With straw sandals covering [the feet], one returns alone; through the ages, who has recognized Dasui? (Puyong Ping).
A clear reputation for a thousand ages follows one who is great; the sharp edge of his wit stands like a cliff, utterly difficult to fathom.
Failing to transcend both the ordinary and the holy in a single stroke, he merely says, "I will take my shoes and cover over the tortoise. (Heshan Fang).
Lan’an’s successor, Dasui, followed his teacher: One stroke right at the head—do not doubt it further. The great earth and mountains and rivers are all covered over;
let the patch-robed disciples apply their needles and chisels. (Min Gufo)
Bones wrapped in skin, skin wrapped in bones—Old Man Dàsuì has no nest or lair. When those of superior capacity hear this, their laughter does not cease;
those of middling capacity give rise to doubt all at once. (Lóngmén Yuǎn)
Skin wraps the bone, and bone wraps the skin. It is clearly explained; why then do you harbor further doubt?
If you do not yet understand how to pick up the straw sandals, it would be better to go elsewhere and find a turtle. (Fóxìng Tài)
Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they are produced only by relying on conditions. A tortoise does not know how to climb a wall;
straw sandals follow the feet of a person. (Fodeng Xun)
[Continued Collection] To study the Way, one must cause the true eye to open; do not conjecture with the mind of wild interpretations.
If one fails to take off their shoes, the Master above will be difficult to understand, thereby causing them to come here specifically with their bags in hand. (Tiantong Jue)
Beside the Wooden Chan Hermitage dwells the old man Dingguang. Neither copper nor iron, formless and unconditioned;

he possesses the strength to support the heavens and the majesty to uproot the earth. He has the hand of an archer who shoots down a vulture and the mechanism of one who bites through a steel arrowhead.
His mouth is like the great ocean and his eyes are like his eyebrows—who in the human world or the heavens knows him? (Nantang Xing).
Bones wrapped in skin, and skin wrapped in bones. A Great Companion (Dàsuí) is released, soaring like a falcon across the vast heavens. Looking up toward the east, west, south, or north is in vain;
one does not realize they have already passed beyond the kingdom of Silla. (Wuzhun Fàn)
Do not stubbornly insist on distinguishing between skin and bone. When you obtain the six viscera, simply have the six viscera.
With a single sandal, everything is thoroughly covered; this monk has nothing left to contemplate. (Cishan Ying).
A numinous tortoise emerges from beneath the hermitage for a thousand years; upon its rounded shell, the hexagrams are layered thick.
Covered by straw sandals, it has neither head nor tail—just listen to others as they determine fortune and misfortune. (Hengchuan Gong)

[Added for inclusion] Dàsui asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to pay homage to Samantabhadra at Mount Emei. The Master raised his whisk and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here.

The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and then prostrated. The Master called to his attendant, "Give this monk a portion of tea. The verse says: The whisk is brandished; the two sages are present.
A circle is drawn, and he departs with a bow. One cup of tea is offered to the guest; The entire assembly is brought together in a single moment.
The light flashes from the tip of the staff; the alms bowl is wrapped in cloth, its surface sour with age. Shouldering it and carrying it on his back, he goes out the gate;
truly, no one dares to detain him. (Bounyeong Yong)
Below Mount Daishui, paths crisscross; aged bamboo and verdant vines grow everywhere.
Having grown accustomed to being a traveler across the four seas and five lakes, one must continue on even at the third watch when there is no moon. (Cishou Shen)
Those who understand the Dharma are cautious; those who deceive their enemies perish. To distinguish milk in water, one must be a king of geese (Tiantong Jue).
A single bright moon shines upon the Xiao and Xiang rivers; no longer does he meet anyone to ask about his hometown.
Naturally accustomed to being a traveler at the ends of the earth, he lets the monkeys cry until people's guts are broken (Shangfang Yi).
He thrust the fire into the cowshed; turning his body, he looked out from without. A thousand points of white plum blossoms;
how cold the sound of spring rain! (Yuedang Chang)
[Added from another source] Daishui asked a monk, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Drawing a winnowing basket with red earth.
The monk asked, "I do not understand the principle of this; how is it so? The Master said, "The winnowing basket has lips; the rice cannot leap out."
The Verse says: With red earth one paints a winnowing fan; Round and complete, without a single crack or seam. Even with the Buddha-eye one cannot see it; The Sea God does not know its price.
Shovel the soil and toss up the dust—it is nowhere to be found; Mountains are high, the sea is vast, and the white clouds are deep. (Nantang Xing)
A winnowing basket has a rim; the rice cannot leap out. All the monks in the world are bare-boned. You must still turn back the uppermost barrier.
The ten directions of the world are as black as lacquer. (Ying’an Hua)

The wheat ripens before the mountains; I inform you of this. Those who can discern the true source of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are rare.
Do not follow the old Chan master of Zhu Jing, who returned with an empty boat under the bright moon. (Xiangtian Village)
The great artisan is not "skillful"; the great Confucian scholar does not "study. Every movement spontaneously accords with the square and the circle; every action is perfected as ritual and music.
How laughable are the diviners in the countryside, who labor in vain to bore through the shells of tortoises! (Wuzhun Shanfeng)
[Added from another source: While burning a slash-and-burn field, Dashi suddenly saw a snake. The Master prodded it with his staff toward the fire and said, "Ho!
This physical form still refuses to let go. Die here; it is like finding a lamp in the darkness."
At that time, a monk asked, "At such a moment as this, is there still sin or not? The Master said, "When the stone tiger roars, the valleys and mountains resound;
where the wooden man bellows, the iron ox is startled. The Verse says: When the stone tiger roars, the valleys and mountains resound; Where the wooden man bellows, the iron ox is startled.
At the beginning and end of the kalpa, the Dharma is weak and Māra is strong. Elder Dingguang has an iron backbone; with the classics as warp and the martial arts as woof, he secures the borders.
Blue heavens, clouds dispersed—the Patriarchal Wind is cool; the Buddha-sun shines, longer than the days of Emperor Shun. (Nantang Xing)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Lingshu Rumín of Shaozhou (successor of Changqing An). A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "A thousand-year-old field has eight hundred owners.
The monk asked, "What is a thousand-year-old field with eight hundred owners? The Master said, "The dilapidated house has no one to repair it.

Verse: A thousand-year-old field has eight hundred owners; The dilapidated house has no one to repair it. If you wish to know the house style of Lingshu, Look at the old man’s face as he laughs aloud.

The coming occasion is profoundly discerned; there is unfolding and there is rolling up. The mountain behind the desk is moved aside, and the needlework is added once more. A thousand-year field has eight hundred owners;
to take it up directly is still crude and muddled. The dilapidated house has no one to repair it; who will go to set up the shards of tile and the roots of the rafters?
Do you not see? The sweet melon is sweet all the way to its stem; the bitter gourd is bitter even to its roots. (Yuedang Chang)
Lingshu was once asked by a monk, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master remained silent.

Later, when he passed away, they wished to establish a stele for his life and conduct and sought to select this very dialogue to be engraved upon it. At that time, Yunmen was serving as the head seat.
A monk asked, "How does one inscribe upon the monument the place where the former master remained silent? Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying, "Master. The verse says: Master, Master, Master.
Knowing, Knowing, Knowing. Threes and threes, twos and twos, they pass through Liaoxi. A pair of red apricots are exchanged for a quince.
(Langya Jue). When Lingshu first responded in secret, his literary brilliance was already fully manifest. Later generations have not seen the old Yunmen;
they vainly attempt to measure him in a thousand ways with a single word. (Foyin Yuan).
The single word "Master" is vast and towering; it alone determines right and wrong within the world. In the end, water must flow toward the sea;
in the final analysis, clouds must seek the mountain to return. (Baiyun Cuan)
Master Lingshu, the head seat of Yunmen, knew only how to set up a stele, failing to realize his words had fallen into error.

I, the mountain monk Zhikai, shall point this out for him: "Those who know the lamp is fire are as numerous as hemp seeds; but those who believe the fire is the lamp—how many can there be? (Zhikai Qing).
The Master’s words and the disciple’s response are known to the author; Shaoyang’s brilliance shines uniquely through the ages.

Chan Master Lingyun Zhiqin of Fuzhou (heir to Changqing An). Initially at Mount Guiyang, he attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms.
He composed a verse which says: "For thirty years I have sought the sword-wielder; / Time and again the leaves fall and the branches sprout.
/ Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, / To this very day I have had no further doubts. Mount Guiyang...
He said, "Awakening through conditions leads to ultimate realization; there shall never again be any falling back or loss. One must skillfully protect and maintain this.
A monk brought this up to Xuansha, who said, "How profoundly true! How profoundly true! Yet I dare guarantee that you, my elder brother, have not yet reached the bottom.
The assembly was puzzled by these words. Xuansha asked Dizang, "I have spoken thus; how do you understand it? Dizang said, "Not."

many youths are already white-haired elders.

Fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, as numerous as hemp seeds; yet alone is Lingyun acknowledged as a true master.

In the warmth of spring, peach blossoms bloom red on every tree. Lingyun’s path remains the same through the ages. Xuan Sha leaves behind words for the monastic community to inquire about;

Where do these two masters go when they do not walk side by side? On the fishing boat is Xie Sanlang. (Fushan Yuan)
Having seen the peach blossoms, one speaks of them as being beyond doubt; noble ambition has always been his very nature. If you ask Xuan Sha, his words have not yet reached the ultimate depth:
"The incriminating goods before you, you know them yourself. (Yunfeng Yue)
In the second and third months, the scenery is harmoniously warm; from far and near, every peach tree is red.
Though the patriarchs have attained awakening, they have not yet reached the ultimate depth; even now, they continue to laugh at the spring breeze. (Huanglong Nan, No. 2)
The dragon and the elephant meet; they are beyond the common world. One comes and one goes, revealing the distant and the near. People of this age do not realize the essential meaning within;
they pluck leaves and seek branches, only increasing the dust of the traveler.
At that time, Zilu asked about the ford at the pass. The world is vast and full of great men;
if meeting and encountering one another is like this, there will be spring after spring, year after year. (Cuiyan Zhen, 2)
The master of the sword-school is certainly not mistaken; throughout the vast monastic forests lies Xuan Sha. When a single speck of dust is raised, one knows the essential point:
to the east of the Eastern Sea dwell tens of millions of households.
In the warmth of spring, peach blossoms open, still bearing the dew. Upon seeing them, Lingyun awakened to the numinous mind.
Xuan Sha’s definitive realization has been transmitted through the ages; who can resolve all doubts with impartial judgment? (Jingzhao Zhen)
When the peach blossoms bloom, suddenly the brow is raised; that even Xuan Sha has not yet reached the ultimate is truly marvelous.
After being tossed by wild winds many times, they remain as before—ten thousand branches like fire. (Fohuiquan)
In the second month, when the spring courtyard is clear after rain, A few branches of small peach blossoms bloom in crimson.
Everyone sees the white rainbow vying for beauty; For what reason did Lingyun alone not doubt it? (Fayun Xiu)
Lingyun happened to see peach blossoms; in thirty years he finally reached home. Why did Xuansha not approve?
A new sprout grows from a withered root (Yang Wuwe).
After Lingyun attained enlightenment, what was it like? If one has not reached the ultimate, no one can discern him.
At the foot of Mount Hua for a thousand ages, who would have known Pan Lang riding his donkey backward? (Baiyun Yuan).
Suddenly we meet beneath the ten-thousand-year-old pine; The wind roars as it uproots the trees and rattles the branches. It is laughable that, come evening, there is no place to find them;
Lofty and steep, they remain amidst the clouds with the rain. (Bao-ning Yong)
From Kunwei he brings forth flawless jade; from the waves of Chishui he gains the night-shining pearl.
Throughout antiquity and today, who has been able to discern them? It is Xie Sanlang on his fishing boat. (Cheng Kumu)
How marvelous! Once one has seen the peach blossoms, One no longer doubts amidst the myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences.
Only Xuansha’s words have not yet reached their full depth; Among his descendants, how many are true sons? (Zhenjing Wen)
All wriggling and breathing beings share the same nature; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all cognizant companions.
An ancient said, "The yellow oriole sings as if it were conversing with the peach blossoms about their old hearts. (Yunju Yu)
When peach blossoms are seen, all doubts vanish. Why, then, was Xuansha not so? Throughout ancient and modern times, the monastic communities have been in great turmoil.
One who wishes to drive a fine horse must brandish the whip upon the road. (The Three Patriarchs)
Old Lingyun has exhausted his life’s work; the news has been transmitted to the Xia family.
Without having reached the ultimate source of this essential point, let the power of spring naturally cause the flowers to bloom. (Wuishan Xiu)
Lingyun’s reputation has been celebrated for a thousand ages; yet upon examination, it turns out he was not yet a master.
The fragrant grass fills the garden with the fullness of spring—how can one speak only of awakening through the peach blossoms? (Dizang En)
How laughable that the spring breeze leaks its secret: the peach blossoms newly bloom upon last year’s branches.
On the Luo River there is a fisherman who laughs until he kills himself at Lingyun’s words, “I have no doubt. (Foguo Bai)
When spring arrives, every thing is in full splendor; how enviable is Lingyun, the true master! Upon seeing a single peach blossom, his mind and world were utterly transcended;
the Old Barbarian [Bodhidharma] needlessly crossed the shifting sands himself. (Yungai Chang)
Lingyun’s eyes were cleared of all cataracts; Xuansha concealed his blade within his sleeve. Taking hands, they ascended directly to the peak;
with a single laugh, heaven and earth were overturned and the void was emptied. (Fuxin Cai)
Lingyun saw it and was free from all delusion; he walked alone throughout the world with nothing left to compare. I dare say you, elder brother, have not yet reached the bottom;

Money lost in the river is fished from the river; once picked up, one may act with total freedom throughout the world.
Having purchased the land of the Southern Mountain along with the clouds, one plows at will, sowing shallowly and tilling deeply. (Fuxincai)
The Venerable Juzhi of Jinhua in Wuzhou (he was a successor of Tianlong).

When he first resided at his hermitage, there was a nun who, wearing a bamboo hat and carrying a monk’s staff, circumambulated the Master three times and said, "If you can speak the Way, I shall take off my hat. She asked this three times.
The Master had no reply. The nun then departed. The Master said, "It is already somewhat late; why do you not stay for a while?

The nun replied, "If you can speak the Way, then I shall stay. Again, the Master had no reply. After the nun had gone, the Master sighed and said, "Though I possess the physical form of a man, I lack the capacity of a man.
It would be better for me to abandon this hermitage and travel to various regions to seek instruction."
He then sought out his acquaintances and departed. That night, a mountain deity told him, "You need not leave this place;
a flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva will arrive to preach the Dharma for you. More than ten days later, Master Tianlong indeed arrived.

The Teacher welcomed him with prostrations and related the previous events in detail. Tianlong raised one finger to indicate the truth, and the Teacher attained great enlightenment. From then on, whenever students came to consult him...

A single finger from Tianlong awakened Juti; at that very moment, there was no private self, and nothing was not equal. Though ten thousand things interact and a thousand differences arise, how could they be described as distinct?
It directly causes the present and the past to be without even a needle or a chisel [of distinction]. (Fenyang Shao)
To respond to the profound love of Old Kūṭi: Since the universe has been empty, who else could there be? Once upon a time, one cast a floating log into the vast ocean;
there, amidst the night waves, it encountered a blind turtle. (Xuedou Xian)
An old, decrepit finger-joint of Koṭi; several autumns have passed beneath Mount Jinhua.
To this day, at the place where he sat upon the rock in meditative stillness, he still toys with his restless spirit and refuses to rest. (Foyin Yuan)
A man dies without breath, no different from the dead; suddenly meeting a celestial dragon, he is abruptly restored to life.
The Zen of a single finger-tip is inexhaustible in its application; the thousand hands of Great Compassion expend much effort. (Bye-hyeon Jun)
How easy is it to respond to the pivot of question and answer? Without money, it is hard to cultivate fine elegance.
When there is something on one’s mind that cannot be spoken, one can do nothing but hurriedly point a finger. (Foguo Bai).
Sudden enlightenment: A dragon and a tiger at a single finger-tip; the Buddhas and Patriarchs as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all of one kindred.
Even if Śāriputra were to deploy his torrential eloquence, ten billion Sumeru mountains would be gathered within a single mustard seed. (Min Gufo)
Do not seek with the mind outward; within this, there is a source for the message. To report the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West:
it lies right here on the single finger of Jueyi. (Fujian Qin)
The Great Master of the Old Lineage held up his finger; throughout his life he used it with the utmost elegance.
Xuansha broke it off, yet no one understands—year after year, it remains cold and stale. (Longmen Yuan)
Mats, curtains, and thatched doors stand at the entrance; who would say that a village dwelling is secluded?
When rain disperses and clouds clear, the mountains and peaks are revealed; a golden hook hangs upon a coral branch. (Huizhao Yu)
A single finger-joint of Jue: eat your fill and then rest. A hundred thousand strings tied around the waist:
riding a crane up to Yangzhou. (Jingshan Gao)
[Continued Collection] "One Finger from Kūṭi—know this for yourself! A hawk born this morning soars toward the heavens.
Without the strength to lift a tripod or pull up a mountain, it is no easy matter to ride a black steed for a thousand li. (Langya Huijue)
The Zen of Old Man Jue-zhi rests upon his pointing finger; for twenty years it has been used without exhaustion.
Truly there exists the world-transcending art of the Way-man; no vulgar things are to be seen before one’s eyes. What he has attained is exceedingly simple, yet his application is vast and wide.

Within the ocean of lands of the great trichiliocosm, he drinks from the tip of a single hair. Infinite phoenixes and dragons fall into whose hands? Reverently, Master Ren grasps the fishing rod. (Tiantong Jue)

Truly liberated from the dust and wind of the world, there is none his equal; he does not rely on arms and armor to craft a grand design. That rivers run clear and seas are tranquil has been the case since time immemorial;
it is simply that people of this age are no true men. (The Poison-Coated Whip)
The "Single-Finger Zen" of Jueyi has become a proverb throughout ancient and modern times. Having shattered the Gate of Ghosts, the pillar is found to have no cracks. (Shui’an Yan)
One step higher than the last; one stride wider than the last. Born within five hundred years, he points out this path.
This path—wherein the Ten Sages and Three Worthies are all at a loss. (Yuelin Guan)
The beautiful lady has risen from sleep and is too weary to comb her hair; she takes up a golden hairpin and inserts it, then leaves it at that.
For the most part, her natural flesh and bone are so excellent that even without applying rouge and powder, she remains elegant and graceful. (From *Bao'en Yanyou*).
[Supplement] There was once a youth named Juti who, whenever he saw someone asking a question, would also raise his finger.
People said to the Master, "The Master’s youth also understands the Buddha-dharma; whenever anyone asks him something, he always raises his finger just as the Master does.
One day, the Master secretly tucked a knife in his sleeve and asked the youth, "I have heard that you understand the Buddha-dharma, is this true? The youth replied, "Yes."

The Master asked, "What is the Buddha? The boy pointed with his finger. The Master cut off the boy's finger with a knife. The boy cried out and ran away. The Master called to the boy; the boy turned his head back.

The Master asked, "What is the Buddha? The boy raised his hand, but no finger was there. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. The verse says: The finger is the Buddha; The Buddha is the finger. Cutting off the finger, He sees the Buddha. Raising the hand, the finger is not seen; In that moment, he attains liberation. If you wish to know the Buddha, Look at the boy’s hand.
A single finger-joint of Jue; a single hair plucked from nine oxen. The Flower Peak reaches the heavens in its azure green;

the Yellow River flows from its very depths. Cut off the finger! Quickly turn your head back! Before the green bamboo hat, there are infinite matters; beneath the green grass-cloth robe, everything ceases at once.
(Shantang Chun): Juezhī left the old heavenly dragon at a loss; brandishing a sharp blade alone, he tested the young boy.
With a mere lift of his hand, Guli split the myriad peaks of Mount Hua asunder. (Wumen Kai).
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Liao Ran of Mount Moshan in Ruizhou (a successor of Dayu).
Once, Guankxi asked, "What is Mount Moshan? The Master replied, "It does not reveal its peak. Guankxi asked, "Who is the master of Mount Moshan?
The Master replied, "Neither male nor female. Guankxi then shouted, "Why do you not transform away? The Master said, "I am neither a spirit nor a ghost."
A ghost—what could it possibly transform? The verse says:

"Mount Moshan does not reveal its cloud-piercing peak; from ancient times to the present, its loftiness stands before our eyes. It is also said that fundamentally there are no marks of male or female;
were it not for you, who could discern the lotus in the fire? (Zhenjing Wen).
Neither male nor female, solitary and serene; the true body majestic and grand—who could possibly reach it? Not a single word is transmitted, yet the eyes of a thousand sages behold it.
The wind stilled in the nine heavens, the moon curves its arc. (Self-Attained Radiance)
Neither male nor female in appearance, the Master of Mount Moe stands majestic through the ages, forever revealed in solitude.
Is he seen in this perpetual solitude? His pure fame resounds throughout the world. (Moon Forest Contemplation).
The Fourth of the Fifth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch (The First of the Fourth Generation under Qingyuan):
Chan Master Xuanjian of Dingshou (Dezhou). He was the son of the Zhou family from Jianzhou.
While in Shu, he frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and was thus known as "Zhou the Vajra. He subsequently took up the *Commentary of Qinglong*.
He traveled out from Shu and reached the road to Liyang, where he went directly to Longtan. Arriving at the Dharma Hall, he said, "I have long heard of Longtan;
yet now that I have arrived, neither the pond nor the dragon is to be seen. The Master [Longtan] replied, "You have personally arrived at Longtan.
The Teacher was speechless and subsequently took up residence there. The Verse says:
The vast and deep abyss receives all streams; in vain one holds fragrant bait and casts a golden hook.
Wind and clouds swirl together as thunder and lightning stir—how can you not marvel that the Dragon King does not show his head? (Baoning Yong)
One goes personally to the Dragon Pond but does not see the dragon; the dragon of the Dragon Pond is not within the pond. Under the blue sky and bright sun, clouds and rain arise;
for a thousand ages, people alike have laughed at Old Master Ye (Foguo Bai).
Going personally to the Dragon Pool, the dragon is not seen; this wondrously accords with the realization of the profound mystery by those who have awakened first.
A thatched hut is nestled upon a solitary peak, where one sits in stillness facing the cold moon hanging in the azure sky. (Lohan Nan)
The dragon pool is not seen, for the dragon does not appear; having personally reached the dragon pool, one meets with a single blemish. In a flash he returns, his fangs like swords;
from the tip of the staff, blazing flames are cast forth. (Changling Zhuo)
[Continued Collection] A blood-basin mouth with swords for teeth—exhausting the world’s pivotal mechanisms is not enough to boast of.
Having personally arrived at Longtan, the dragon did not appear; this time, one has lost the flowers before one's eyes. (Xinwen Ben)
The dragon is not seen in the deep pool; one must give a living response upon actually reaching the dragon’s pool. Do not act like those who merely echo empty sounds and transmit hollow echoes.

To sit and wait for a rabbit at a stump is to lose the capacity for adaptive transformation. Know this adaptive transformation: when the cup is dashed to the ground, the saucer shatters into seven pieces.
(Duan’an Yan): When the abyss is not seen, the dragon does not appear; the whole body is already within the Hall of the Empty King. Returning from a dream, one suddenly hears the dawn oriole singing;
the spring breeze has blown away all the peach petals. (Huanshan Ning).
One day, Deshan was attending Longtan until late at night. Longtan said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not go out?
The Master said, "I take my leave," and he went out. He then returned and said, "It is dark outside. Longtan lit a paper lamp and passed it to him.
As the Master reached out to receive it, Longtan blew it out. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What have you seen?"
"What is it? the Master asked. [The monk] replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.
On the following day, when Tanzhi ascended the seat, he said to the assembly, "Among you there is a man whose teeth are like sword-trees and whose mouth is like a blood-basin;
he cannot be turned back by a single blow of the staff. In the future, atop a solitary peak..."
"Establishing my Way depends on where you go," [the Master] said. The teacher then took the commentaries and sub-commentaries, piled them before the Dharma Hall, and holding up a torch, he said:
"To exhaust all profound arguments is like placing a single hair in the great void; to exhaust all worldly pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss.
He then burned them. Thereupon, [the disciple] paid his respects, took his leave, and departed. The Verse says:
The mutual overcoming of light and darkness is not worth mentioning; to have even a hair’s breadth of understanding is not yet intimacy. When the paper lamp suddenly goes out, the eyes emerge;
the Great Tang is shattered, and there is not a single person left. (Baiyun Yuan).
At one time, a waterfall falls before the cliff; at midnight, the golden sun shines upon the palm of the hand.
Opening his mouth wide to display his spirit and resolve, with whom does he traverse the world together? (Baoning Yong)
The affairs of light and dark contrasted against one another are vast and obscure. Who knows that from behind the head, the divine light bursts forth?
All at once, it cuts through the myriad divergent paths; north, south, east, and west, one reaches one’s own native land. (Da-hong Sui)
When light and dark are distinguished, time is fixed in motion; where the firelight extinguishes, one sees its origin.
After Longtan cut off the source of words, the Buddhas and Patriarchs continue their insults from solitary peaks without ceasing. (Zhaojue Zong)
A whirlwind sweeps through, parting the misty haze; a thousand peaks emerge, their azure heights towering and majestic.
Startled monkeys and resentful cranes have long been cast away, yet at midnight before the mountains, they are called back home. (Wang Fangyi)
A single spark from the dragon’s pool was blown out; at that moment, his mind’s eye was too sharp and clear.
When even a speck of dust of the Buddhas and Patriarchs leaves no trace, how can a lame turtle gallop? (Gufo Min).
Golden bones and jade-like ridges—do not seek them in his house today. How many craftsmen of the awakened mind have there been from of old?
They have all taken up this very matter to continue the legacy of Vipaśyin. (Longmen Yuan)
The "spitting and pecking" kōan of Deqiao and Longtan; a mustard seed and a needle meeting in perfect accord with the profound mystery.
Seated wrapped in his head-cloth atop a solitary peak, he pays no heed to the green mountains as the clouds return of their own accord. (Lian of Tianning, Jingzhao Prefecture)
[Continued Collection] Mist rises from Longtan as the old dragon roars; it terrifies the white-marked beast of Nanshan. Without disturbing the waves, he seizes the turtle’s nose;
his head and horns stand out sharp, his spirit like a rainbow. (Nantang Xing)
One goes personally to the Dragon Pond but does not see the dragon; the paper lamp is blown out, and before one's eyes all is empty.
A single white staff stirs up heaven and earth, extinguishing the Dharma lineage of Bodhidharma who came from the West. (Fozhao Guang)
A hundred-knot tunic and a tattered head-wrap; year after year he fails the examinations and departs from the Divine Land.
Yet, because of a single arrow that pierced the willow, in his old age he comes to receive a fief as a guard at the imperial post station. (Luoyue Ying)
Opening the mouth, no teeth are seen; extending the hand, no palm is seen. At midnight, they suddenly meet;
the entanglement grows ten thousand feet long. (Xue’an Jin)
Coming from the south, I originally intended to shatter heterodox teachings; yet where the paper lamp is extinguished, it is difficult to clear away the confusion.
Treading upon a sledgehammer as hard as iron, one mistakenly mistakes a tortoise for a soft-shelled turtle. (Yuanquan Qionggu Liàn)
Having personally reached the Dragon Pond, he has already cast his hook in the dark. Who shares the night stroll through the Imperial Street?
The paper lanterns are extinguished as the smoke of war subsides; he sits firmly throughout the four hundred states of Central China. (Tianmu Li)
Meeting suddenly and unexpectedly, there is no need for further words. As soon as the foul mouth opens, one hears the local dialect. When the paper lamp is extinguished, there is the ultimate point:
the azure dragon is not permitted to lie in the green depths. (By Village Elder Xian)
Deshan took his leave of Longtan and went straight to Mt. Mui. Carrying his double-layered mat, he ascended the Dharma Hall, walking from west to east and from east to west.
Looking toward the abbot’s quarters, he asked, “Is there anyone here? Is there anyone here? Deshan was sitting there and paid him no heed.
The Master said, “No, no,” and then departed. Upon reaching the entrance, he said, “Even so...”
"This will not do; one must not be so casual. He then assumed his full dignified demeanor and entered again to meet him.

As soon as he stepped across the threshold, he held up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*) and said, "Venerable Master! The Master was about to take up his whisk when the student gave a shout and swept out of the room with his sleeves.

He penetrated the truth. He then offered this verse:

How many can truly attain perfection? Run swiftly past; do not let it slip away.
Sitting amidst the grass atop a solitary peak—where tigers dwell and deep forests where no man goes—only a hunter can reach such a place.
When the tiger sleeps, startled awake, it raises its eyes; with a sudden leap, the hunter escapes with his life. (Haiyin Xin)
Stealing the camp, cutting through the encampment, and entering the central army—his strategic ingenuity is already complete. Yet the golden mallet in his sleeve has not yet been struck;

Old Deshan was capable of waging a battle of Dharma; with a single shout, his voice and light roared like thunder and lightning. He rode the tiger’s head and gathered its tail;

[Continued Collection] Great function is not restricted by time; it is the standard of both past and present. To grasp the sting of a scorpion upside down and to stroke the whiskers of a tiger—were it not for a profound discernment of the underlying principle, how could one sit idly by and watch success or failure?
Where there is brilliance, the point pierces through the bag like a needle; where there is loftiness, the movement unfolds beyond the mundane world.

Mastery of both strategy and tactics, with bold and heroic spirit; he fears not the towering clouds of battle arrayed before him.
He calls himself a hand who tears down the banners at the gates, yet he cannot avoid being like a solitary peak submerged in a nest of weeds. (Wan Shi Kong)
Seven things follow him at all times; not even a single hair’s breadth is used. Once more he unfurls his spear and banner, and heaven and earth tremble.
Upon the summit of the solitary peak, cease further speaking of dreams. (Tuan-an Qi)
Whenever Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would strike him with his staff. A verse says:
Deshan’s staff—cutting through the distinction between sage and ordinary, the demons’ gall blanches. Skillfully employing expedient means, he pulls the tiger’s whiskers;
even the wrathful Nala is utterly shattered. (Haiyin Xin)
One blow leaves a mark upon every scar; its bitterness and pain are beyond description. Men of spirit abound in ambition, but how many truly recognize gratitude? (Da Hong En).
Prominently distinguishing the debates of the two-headed soldier, he once shattered Tongguan with a single blow.
Since the world has been at peace, he has wandered among men, known as Deshan (Baizhen Yuan).
Sudden rain and swift thunder strike; clouds arise as lightning follows. Though the General has his orders, how can they compare to the time of Emperor Yao? (Da Hong Sui)
With both hands he pushes open the seamless stupa; with one foot he kicks down Mount Sumeru.
Amidst the thunderclap of the blue sky, there is no protection—yet this master still seeks a "gate of Chan" (which is as dry wood).
A single white staff comes crashing down upon the head; blood splatters like flying stars, a pain most piteous.
The Patriarch has no place to evade it; even the summit of Mount Sumeru collapses. (Foguo Bai).
Deqiao’s discernment was clearly extraordinary; from the tip of his staff he struck out all subtlety. He caused the Buddhas and Patriarchs to act without fail;
it was just like a Wheel-Turning King grasping the myriad affairs of state. (Yun’gai Chang)
A single staff leans against the blue sky; it is transmitted separately outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Before even blinking an eye, one encounters eight hundred blows;
as soon as one attempts to open the mouth, three thousand blows are applied. (Zhang Wujin)
At that moment, he cuts off both the holy and the profane; upon his knees, cold light shines like snow.
Vast and boundless is the universe—within this skin, who has any blood? (Puyongping).

Severing the vital ford of birth and death, making no distinction between ordinary and sage, deluded or awakened—one blow shatters the gateway of the face, and naturally heaven and earth are revealed alone. (Fuxin Cai)
Entering the gate is a fine thing beyond dispute; when pressed, the red stream flows forth and they strike one another. It is not that this servant’s affection has grown thin;
it is simply that without money, one cannot be a good son. (Fodeng Xun)

Under the staff, brass does not equal gold. Deshan’s thoroughgoing, grandmotherly heart—later generations see only the surging waves, but do not see the depths of the Dragon King’s palace. (Gushan Gui)
Upon entering the gate, he immediately struck with the staff; his mastery was not at all slight. Following this and practicing accordingly, one becomes like sesame seeds being ground together.

Who can discern that which suddenly emerges before them? Only those who are masters of the monastic community may know. (Chuanfang)

Killing and giving life proceed together; ambrosia and poison are both reward and punishment—leave all such deliberations to others.

Deshan personally obtained the hand of the Master Ren; with one clear line, he cast two hooks.

The sword for slaying dragons is not yet to be brandished against snakes; how could a great hunter rely upon foxes and rabbits? Have you not seen how Zhuge Liang served as military strategist?
His methods of capture and release were known by few. With a million heroic troops at his fingertips, he would seize petty rebels and then release them again.
The soldiers sighed in wonder and their horses neighed repeatedly; countless youths sang of his great marvels. It was like this:
These four generals of heroic valor; their names heard, the banner of surrender has long been raised.
(Haiyin Xin) Who dares to debate when the Patriarch’s command is fully upheld? A mere hair’s breadth of movement falls into the strategic pass. This monk does not discern the proper occasion;
how many are there who forget their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma? (Kumu Cheng)
The General’s command sweeps away the dust and smoke; the Imperial Edict circulates, proclaiming its virtuous grace.
The young lord knows only to sing of "Intoxicated with Wine," yet at nightfall he is captured alive. (Bao Feng Zhao)
Horizontally grasping the Mohe sword, he dwells beyond the gate; who would dare to violate his heavy encirclement when facing the front?
How admirable is this monk from Silla—his total capacity for breaking the enemy shines with brilliance. (Min Gufo).
[Continued Collection] High and lofty, the Patriarch’s seal occupies the center of the world. Who would dare face him to determine fortune or misfortune?
Were it not for this monk from Silla, how could the pure breeze have been stirred for a thousand ages? (Daopei Zhe)
The great smith smelts the gold; a sudden peal of thunder startles the spring, causing grasses and trees to flourish and their brilliance to renew daily.

Without expending the slightest effort, he captures the celestial qilin. Possessing complete majesty, he masters both killing and giving life with ease. For a thousand ages his radiance shines forth like the icy wheel of the moon.

"Gee-liao!"—the tip of the tongue is three thousand miles away. (Yuánwù Qín)

Six Strategies and Three Tactics—military patterns and civil classics. The Korean monk has the "Bing" but lacks the "Ding. (Nantang Xing)

Seeing his cheek behind his head, no one dares to provoke him; with eyes beneath his brows, he gains the advantage. (Tiantong Ju)

The Chanyu prides himself on his skills surpassing those of others; when the minor general gave him instructions, it seemed as if they were genuine. Upon arriving there, he indeed achieved a small victory;
yet upon returning, he could not avoid having his entire body ensnared. (Seal of the Dharma-Imprint)
It is like a young parrot in a golden cage; its beak is like red jade, and it wears a green robe.
Though it has learned to speak the human tongue, when questioned, it is found to know nothing at all. (Fujian Qín).
[Added from another collection] Once, when a monk came to visit Deshan, the Master simply closed the door. The monk knocked on the door, and the Master asked, "Who is it?
The monk replied, "A lion. The Master opened the door; as soon as the monk entered and prostrated, the Master mounted him head-first and said, "You beast!"
"Where have you been coming and going for so long? The verse says: Seeing the rabbit, he releases the hawk;
because of the crooked, he strikes the straight. Before your feet have even crossed the threshold, you must immediately awaken with fierce resolve. (Muan Yong)
[Added from another source] Master Deshan ascended the hall. The entire assembly understood it completely; even the Buddhas of the three periods of time had their mouths hung upon the wall.

Yet there was still one person who laughed heartily, "Ha-ha! If you can recognize this person, your study of the Way is finished (alternatively, this is called a "mysterious word of perfect clarity").
Touzi Qian said: "Even though it is so, Deshan was very much like one who has hidden everything away."
The moon over the Btian sky still endures; the stars remain in the land of Han. He then offered this verse:
Two blind men enter a dark path, rugged and steep; When the sun sets, they rest by the reeds and find brief respite. How can they compare to the stone man sleeping through the midnight?

He need not wait for Shun to abdicate so that he may dwell in the forest. One must know that the blossoming of flowers has nothing to do with the wood; When walking without feet, it is already too late.
Touching upon every path: Yesterday morning the wind rose on the Chang'an Road; it was originally the state map presented from Kunlun.
Gathered in, it seizes the vital throat; wind-polished and cloud-wiped, the waters are cold and the sky is autumnal. Do not say that the scaled dragon lacks flavor.
Having fished out the moon over the Canglang River with a single cast. (Tiantong Jue).

Chan Master Liangjie Wuben of Dongshan in Junzhou (Successor of Yunyan). Once, he took his leave of Yunyan.

Yankuan remained silent for a long time and said, "It is just this. The Master hesitated. Yankuan said, "Dharma brother Jia, in undertaking this matter, you must be extremely careful. The Master still harbored doubts. The verse says: A hundred years hence, if someone should ask, "Can you still capture the Master's true likeness? The essence and measure are not achieved through effort, nor do they fall into the present. As the stars shift and the constellations change, how could they be like a wheel?
Though the dates of many years may be of no use, if one commits an offense, it must result in the total extinction of the lineage. (Zhengtang Bian)
Dongshan, while crossing a stream, beheld his reflection and attained great enlightenment regarding his former realization. He composed a verse which says: "By all means, do not seek it from others;
To do so would distance you from me. I now go forth alone, And everywhere I encounter him.
He is precisely myself right now, But I am not he. You must understand it in this way Before you can realize Suchness."
The Verse says:
Movement and stillness have always been together from the start; Turning one’s head, suddenly one encounters him.
Even if it were thus, it would still be laughable; To call it "Suchness" (tathatā) is yet another detour. (Benjue I)
The shadow in the water exists because the body exists; if the body were truly non-existent, the shadow would also be non-existent.
Just as one takes a step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole, the Vairocana manifests upon the tip of a single hair. (Wenyu Qin)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Later, while Dōngshān was making offerings to the portrait of Yúnyán, a monk asked him, "The former master said, 'It is just this.
Is it not so? The Master said, "It is. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "At that time, I nearly misunderstood the former master's intent.
The monk asked, "I wonder whether the former master himself knew [this] or not? The Master said, "If he had not..."
If you know there is, how could you resolve it by speaking thus? If you know there is, how could you be content to speak thus? The Verse says: How could one resolve it by speaking thus?
At the fifth watch, the rooster’s cry brings dawn to the home-grove. How could one be content to speak thus? For a thousand years, the crane grows old with the green pines.
The precious mirror shines brightly, verifying both the direct and the indirect; The jade mechanism turns its side, seeing both as they arrive. This is the Gate-Style.
