Chan Master Jingtong of Mount Huo in Jinzhou (a successor of Yangshan) first visited Yangshan.
As Yangshan sat with his eyes closed, the Master raised his right foot and said, "Thus it is, thus it is. The twenty-eight patriarchs of India were thus;
the six patriarchs of China were thus; the Master was thus; and Jingtong is also thus."

"Yes. Shanqi rose and struck him with four strokes of the rattan cane. From this, the Master called himself "The Great Zen Buddha under Mount Jiyun, Whose Four Strokes of the Rattan Cane are Renowned Throughout the World.

The Master once went to the place of Master Huoshan and introduced himself as "The Great Zen Buddha under Mount Jiyun, Whose Four Strokes of the Rattan Cane are Renowned Throughout the World," whereupon Huoshan summoned the *karmadāna*.
He struck the bell and departed with rapid strides (under Guizong there was also a great Chan master named Zhitong who resided at Wutai). The verse says:
Beneath Mount Jiyun, four creeping vines; how perilous they were, nearly breaking my waist then!
It is laughable that those who followed later called themselves fierce generals, knowing only how to speak empty words like Huo Qubing. (By Yanxuan Zun)
In the land of India and in China, all have reached a definitive seal; there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. Eyes askance and nose straight—rumors spread throughout the world;
one hearty bowl of leftover soup will keep one from hunger forever. (Baoning Yong)
There was a reason for raising his foot on the spot; four strokes of the rattan were not enough as recompense. He went further to the gate of Mount Huo;
though he possessed the capacity to perceive the occasion, he lacked true elegance. (Dizang’s kindness).
Beneath Mount Jiyun, four vines and weeds; the pass of Tongguan is shattered, leaving but one path. Like cranes and like clouds beyond heaven and earth;
like dragons and like phoenixes in the misty heights. (Yuantong Xian, 2)
Having chewed the rattan cane, one wanders at leisure; yet before reaching the secure barrier, one will not rest. Beating the drum and striking the bell are both but formal commands;
who else has the capacity to discern the occasion and adapt to change?
[Continued Collection] At Ziling Beach, the water flows as swiftly as a string. There, he catches yellowfish and shrimpy bream.
Holding them up in the marketplace, he repeatedly asks for a price; yet no one else would value them at even half a coin. (Fuxincai)
When a robber encounters a formidable opponent at home, his stolen goods are lost and he has no other recourse.
Though the mountain creeper pierces to the bone to force him into submission, it instead provides that fellow with a flower to adorn his face. (Oran’s Verse)
A thousand-year-old, ten-thousand-year-old withered stump; let iron pestles and bronze hammers strike it as they will.
For now, it stands amidst a heap of rotting mud. (Pah! (Byōyō Gen).
[Added from another source] Because a practitioner asked Huo Shan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? the Master bowed.
The practitioner said, "Why does the Master bow to an ordinary person? The Master replied, "Do you not see it said:
'I revere my disciples'? The Verse says:
Gold beaten into brass chopsticks; white jade carved into ivory combs. A black-lacquered Kunlun statue possesses many skills;
from the sea, one picks up a night-bright pearl. (Cishou Shen)
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Guangyong of Nanta at Yangshan in Yuanzhou (a successor of Yangshan). A monk asked, "What is the essential meaning of Caoxi?

The Master said, "A single lock enters the cold void. Verse: A single lock enters the cold void; The moon shines upon the autumn waters. If you wish to know the meaning of Caoxi, Look at the bright moon in the sky.
Layered peaks and towering ridges pierce the cold sky; the pagoda is locked in deep clouds, its majesty beyond measure. For a thousand ages the sound of pines comes with rhythmic cadence;
for ten thousand years the mountain stream flows on without a trace. (Touzi Qing)

A single phrase brings forth the myriad phenomena; Mahākāśyapa silently closed his heavy gates.
Had the patch-robed disciples opened their eyes even slightly at the beginning, they would have stuck their chopsticks in the incense burner and burned them as firewood. (Touzi Qing)
Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi of Hangzhou (who succeeded Yangshan) traveled to Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai.
Upon arriving at the Vajra Cave, he paid his respects. There he encountered an old man leading an ox who invited the Master into the temple. The man asked, "Where have you recently come from?
The Master replied, "From the South. The man asked, "How is the Dharma maintained in the South? The Master said:
"A monk of the Final Dharma Age observes the precepts but rarely. He says, 'How many disciples do you have? The Master says, 'Either three hundred or five hundred.
The Master then asks, 'How is the Buddha-Dharma maintained here? He replies, 'Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together.
The Master says, 'How many disciples do you have? He replies, 'Three times three before, and three times three after. At evening, [the Master] departed.
He then asked the old man, "May I stay for one night? The old man replied, "You still have a mind of attachment; you may not stay. The Master said, "Wenxi has no mind of attachment.
The old man asked, "Have you ever received the precepts? The Master replied, "I received them long ago.
The old man said, "If you have no mind of attachment, what need is there to receive the precepts? The Master took his leave. The old man then sent forth a youth.
As they were seeing each other off, the Master asked the boy, "What is the total of the three threes before and the three threes after?
The boy called out, "Venerable Sir! The Master responded, "Yes. The boy said, "How much is that? The Master asked again, "Where is this place?
The boy replied, "This is the Vajra Cave Prajñā Temple. The Master was moved with sadness and realized that the old man was Mañjuśrī.
"We shall not see you again. He then prostrated himself before the youth and requested: "I pray that you grant me a single word as a parting gift.
The youth spoke in verse: "No anger on the face is the offering; No anger in the mouth emits wondrous fragrance;
No anger in the heart is the true treasure— Stainless and undefiled, it is the eternal reality. Having finished speaking, the youth Cunda...
Both temples were hidden. The verse says:
The sacred monastery extends throughout the realm of sand; Mañjuśrī fills the eyes as he engages in conversation.
If one does not open the Buddha-eye beneath these words, One turns back and sees only green mountain crags. (Mingzhao Qian)
The Advisor asked, "How is it when dwelling in the South? He replied, "A group of three or five is not many. Jixiang (Shishuang Chuyuan) spoke of the intermingling of dragons and snakes;
the teaching of "three times three" was told to Heshang (Huangbo). Wuzhuo did not yet understand, so he sought further clarification;
Junpiti pointed to the place where the Immortal does not dwell. Looking at the name behind the Vajra, one sees nothing but desolate mountains—what can be done? (Fenyang Shanzhao).
A thousand peaks wind and turn, their color like indigo; who says that Mañjuśrī is here in conversation?
How laughable are the many crowds at Qingliang—three times three before and three times three after. (Xuedou Xian)
It is laughable that the first three and the last three were merely chattering back and forth at the outset; yet, because of non-attachment, they saw clearly.
From this point on, there is nothing left to investigate in Qingliang. (Foyin Yuan, 2)
Though the pavilions have plaques, they are entirely blank. I ask the顽童 (stubborn child) about their original construction: suddenly pointing to the Vajra [statue], he looks behind him;
in declining years, one is often mocked by ghosts.
In the past and present, there have been many such as these who, when questioned on various matters three times each, respond with a coarse and superficial understanding according to their capacity;
they carry their bowls and waist-packs about everywhere, seeking alms (zhuan bo). (Zhengjue Yi, No. 3)
Accumulated greenery covers a thousand peaks leaning against the half-vaulted sky; dragons, snakes, ordinary beings, and sages are intermingled therein. How many ordinary beings and sages are within?
Their number—three by three, before and after—is inexhaustible.
The temple plaque suddenly flashed at the tip of my finger; even the Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara could not behold it.
Since I first caught sight of the back of the Vajra, I have remained thus until now, acting as a wild monk.
Three times three before and after—how much is that? A great matter, radiant and brilliantly clear. Turning back, one sees no one who understands emptiness;
white clouds fill the eyes as one lies amidst the wild grass. (Daowu Zhen)
The Sage has always been beyond companionship; meeting and questioning him can never be contrived. Three by three, they illuminate past and present;
a single word, free from self-interest, shakes the nine realms. (Zhaojue Zong)
Three times three before, and three times three after—calculating and deliberating, one is ultimately unacquainted with it.
Amidst the lush, verdant grass within the misty landscape, where the partridges cry out—that is Jiangnan. (Dizang En)
Mañjuśrī answered three times, three by three; alone he drifted in a light boat across the South Sea. Amidst the heart of the surging waves, he beheld the movement of the water;
a single bright moon was reflected in the cold pool. (Yunxi Gong)
White clouds drift beyond the Green Mountain Gate; By the green waters of the stream, I see you off as you return home. Do not wonder why I urge you to drink again and again while we sit here;
Since we parted, I have rarely seen you, O Distant One of Longmen.
[Continued Collection] The principle of "Three Threes" is profoundly deep and mysterious. This old man shall strike a needle right between the teeth.
To inform the Zen followers, listen attentively: the boat follows the current, while the stone sinks. (By Prajñā-róu)
The three sets of three before and after do not lose their essence; they transcend far beyond the thousand sages, their number difficult to exhaust.
The diamond-hard skull is fully exposed at the back of the head; layer upon layer of green mountains lock the azure void. (Danxia Chun)
Asaṅga and Mañjuśrī are not easily encountered; when they meet, each inquires after the other’s family tradition. How many are there among the assembly at Qingliang?
Their numbers, three by three before and after, are inexhaustible. (Fundamental Enlightenment, One)

Girded with gold, he ascends Mount Taihang; all eyes of the bandits are struck with alarm. Had it not been for encountering those poisoned hands, who would have dared to burn incense in the night? (Yuedang Chang, 2)
Wide shoes for narrow feet; short sleeves for long arms. With staff and wooden block ever by one's side, one performs the play upon meeting the stage.
Three before, three after—suddenly piled all atop the shoulder pole. Only when arriving home does one set them down and inspect them.
At present, the package is exposed and shaggy;
three by three, before and after. I thank the Master for his guidance. Dragons and snakes leap about; tigers glare with fixed intent. I intend to observe them again and again.
What is there to discuss? Junti’s attempt to brandish his whip is but empty pretense; how could he withstand the trampling of the Elephant King?
(Touzi spreads his hands. Meeting on a common road, you are but dust in the eyes; bowing your head in worship, you obscure your true nature. Upon rising, you do not see Mañjuśrī.
Manifesting now, he shatters the Great Tang so that not a single person remains.
(Xiuyan Rui) Three before and three after—this cannot be taken up, nor can it be investigated. Furthermore, ask how many followers Qingliang has:
the moon shifts, and its reflection falls upon the cold pond. (Yuelin Guan)
In the Buddha-dharma, there is originally neither north nor south; why must one stand face-to-face to engage in profound discourse?
Although Mañjuśrī is indeed capable of such transformative skill, he has already been divided and scattered by you, falling short by two or three [steps]. (Yun accepts the auspiciousness.)
Asaṅga, invited by an old man, entered the temple with him. The man bade him sit and they conversed.
The old man called for his boy to serve tea, along with some butter and curd. Asaṅga partook of their flavors, and his mind was pleased.
The old man picked up a crystal cup and asked, "Is there anything like this in the South? Asaṅga replied, "No. The old man said, "What do you usually use then?"
"Drink some tea. The Master had no reply. The verse says:
The Great Being Mañjuśrī leaned upon a crystal cup, And asked, "In the South there is something marvelous. Wuzhuo suddenly said, "There is not this thing.
How many old *jiaoluo* (monks) has he misled? To this day, they still do not know the definitive truth. Raising his hand, he picked up the tea—no more.
"Using doubt" (Fenyang Shanzhao).
Since parting from the South and traversing the mountain paths, he has used crystal cups at every place where tea is served.
How is it that upon arriving at Qingliang Temple, when questioned, he originally knew nothing at all? (Zhengjue Yi).
One must not be separated from the South for even a moment. Why did Wuzhuo, on the contrary, say "there is nothing"? Send this message to future Chan practitioners:
when picking up the teacup to drink, do not be negligent. (Foyin Yuan)
[Continued Collection] A pair of crystal jewel cups are raised before you; though the flavor of the tea is thick, the dream does not awaken. Ask further: how many are in the group of three-threes?
Who can teach people not to distinguish between victory and defeat? (By Xiangtian Qing).
Sitting in meditation on Mount Wutai, my thoughts linger long; Under the bright sun and blue sky, one is deluded by ghosts.
The most painful thing of all is difficult to comprehend: When drinking tea from a crystal cup. (Xiangtan Yong)
[Added to the Collection] Wuzhuo went to visit Yangshan and immediately attained realization through a sudden accord of mind. Yangshan appointed him as the head cook (*diànzuò*).
Once, Mañjuśrī appeared atop the rice-pot; the Master struck him with his rice-stirring paddle and said, "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī;
Wenxi is Wenxi. Thereupon Mañjuśrī spoke this verse: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to end..."
Tianxiang: "To practice for three great kalpas yet be disparaged by this old monk.
The Verse says: "The Śakrāloka-eye opens at the crown of the head; Having awakened, there is no need for a teacher to come again. Knock down the rice-pot and stop reciting gāthās;
In practicing, one must believe that karma is the womb of calamity. (Xiangtianqing)
The Sixth Patriarch’s Lineage, Sixth Generation, Part Three (Qingyuan’s Lineage, Fifth Generation, Part One) [Added to the Collection].
Chan Master Juhui of Daguang Mountain in Tanzhou (Successor of Shishuang). Once, a monk asked him, "Is it that Bodhidharma was not the Patriarch?
The Master said, "He was not the Patriarch. The monk said, "If he was not the Patriarch, why did he come here?"
"Ma? The Master said, "It is precisely because you do not realize it. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after realization?
The Master said, "Only then will you know it is not the Patriarch. The Verse says:
The transmission of the flame at Shaolin is a marvel; on the night of the winter solstice, plum blossoms open upon branches after the snow.
Huangbo had a saying in years past: "In the Great Tang Empire, there are no Chan masters. (Danxia Chun)
The command of Shaoshi is fully presented face-to-face; when the occasion arises, failing to realize it is like crossing over to Silla.
Meeting a true friend atop the Qingfeng Tower, one stirs up dust and smoke—what can be done about it? (Zuan Jian).
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Jiufeng Daogyan of Ruizhou (successor of Shishuang). A monk asked, "The patriarchs have transmitted it from one to another;
what is it that they transmit? The Master said, "Śākyamuni was stingy, while Kāśyapa was wealthy. The monk asked, "In what way was Śākyamuni stingy?
The Master said, "He had nothing to give to others. The monk asked, "In what way was Kāśyapa wealthy? The Master said, "Within his own country..."
Mengchangjun asked, "Ultimately, what is it that is transmitted? How is it so? The Master said, "An old man of a hundred years divides his night lamp.
The Verse says: Within the silent light, the entire body appears; its noble uniqueness naturally transcends all categories. In a wealthy house, the son and servants especially receive their share.
Power. At night, the lamp-light illuminates the western neighbor. (Danxia Chun).
[Added from another source] Once a monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the student’s own self? The Master said, "Ask anyone else."
[The student] asked, "If one accepts it directly in this way, what then? The Master said, "Sumeru must once again bear Sumeru.
He spoke in verse:
"The cold and warmth of oneself are known by oneself; Who else is there to ask about the Ancestral Meaning that came from the West? Accepting it as a whole, it is the whole."
It is so. Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru rests Mount Sumeru.
(Shixi Yue). [Added by Zeng] Regarding the "Nine Peaks," a monk asked: "In India, one uses a wax figure as proof of having spent the summer retreat; many there attain the fruits of the Path.
I wonder how it is here? The Master said: "On his head he wears the midnight moon; with his feet he treads the yellow earth."
Jingdi asked, "Does this person still undergo transmigration? The Master said, "How could they avoid transmigration? He asked, "How does one transmigrate?
The Master said, "In this very life, you have already heard that the dragon has shed its bones. Verse: How could they avoid transmigration? In this very life, the dragon has shed its bones.
At midnight in the mountain hermitage, the moonlight is deep. Ten parts of clarity fall into the realm of achievement.
Pushing aside, one reaches the upward-opening aperture that pierces to heaven; Layer upon layer of misty peaks, where no person is seen. (Zidehui)

Leading a donkey to drink from the river, its nostrils blowing up waves; on the bank below, hooves tread upon hooves;
in the water, beaks follow beak. (Fang’an Xian)

[Added for collection] A monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the indestructible body? The Master said, "It is precisely this. The monk said, "I do not understand; I pray the Master will point directly to it. The Master said, "Just now, how much was there of crookedness? Verse: The indestructible body is right here before you; If you seek it elsewhere, you are far astray.
When the questioner asks about the unchanging, The Master points directly to the very thing. How much crookedness was there just now? If you can see through this, you have attained the Way.
The indestructible body is precisely the Correct; the Correct is precisely the indestructible body. How much twisting was there just now?
It pinches the tip of the nose until it stings. (Shixi Yue).
When Jiufeng [Zhixian] passed away following Shishuang’s transformation, the assembly requested the Head Seat to take charge as abbot. At that time, the Master was serving as the attendant;
he addressed the assembly and asked the Head Seat: "The late master said: 'Rest! Cease! Be cold and silent!
Like a single length of white silk! Like an incense burner in an ancient temple! Like a single thought spanning ten thousand years!'—what aspect of this did he clarify?"
[The Master] said, "If you can grasp this matter, you may remain as abbot; if you cannot, you may not. The Head Seat replied, "I understand the matter of the 'single color' (the ultimate reality).
The Master said, "If that is so, then you have not grasped the meaning of the former master. The Seat said, "Just bring some incense.
If you can go [attain realization] at the moment the incense smoke breaks, then you will grasp the meaning of the former master. If you cannot go, then..."
"No. The Master then burned incense. Before the incense stick had even finished burning, the head monk’s seat suddenly detached from him.
The Master patted the head monk’s back and said, "To depart while seated or to pass away while standing is certainly not lacking; yet you have not even dreamed of the meaning of our former master.
The verse says:
The Zhang family raised several sons. The eldest followed his father in managing the household estate. Among them was one son whose artistry was most refined;

his presence was like that of a king, and his majesty and virtue were extraordinary. Extraordinary! He would have trampled the vast ocean without a second thought for the black dragon, and he would have dispersed the white clouds without envying the bright moon. (Seal of Haiyin)
Shishuang chose his successor based on high talent; the Head Seat, greedy for the journey ahead, departed and did not return. He only loved that in a cold sky flames might arise;
how could he have known that withered wood would put forth blossoms? Attendant Qian is truly pitiable;
though he understood the Great Meaning of the former master, he could not avoid dragging his worn-out straw sandals for a long time. (Fohuiquan)
What matter in this world is most worthy of sorrow? A hole-less iron hammer from the beginning. The furnace and forge cannot melt it through;
let it be blown by the wind for a thousand ages. (Baoning Yong)
Those who vanish while seated or attain liberation while standing are as numerous as hemp seeds; how few, however, do not err upon this path!
Recalling the words of Shishuang, I find that even where there is no brilliance, all is brilliance. (Zhikai Qing)

A single expanse of empty space stretches through past and present. The horned dragon and the pronged qilin vie with one another over intimacy and distance. How many are there who know how to vanish while seated or be liberated while standing?
When the flowers bloom upon the iron tree, it is a spring of its own. (Kai Fu Ning)
With horns and shaggy fur, a body of a different species; cold ashes, withered wood, and dust in the eyes. Although this has never been the intent of the former masters, what can one do?
At the moment of departure, there is that one personal touch. (Danxia Chun)
The foremost person in the Hall of the Withered Tree; sitting idly watching success and failure, he wastes his spirit. Piteous is this matter of "one color" (myō-issoku);
until this very day, there has been no trace of the eye-tendon. (Bǎofēng Zhào)
Though one arrow may settle the Tian Mountains, it is difficult to strike out amidst a hundred-fold battlefield. Do not say that the incense offerings at the ancient shrine have ceased;
before the deity, there shall naturally be wine and trays. (Shangfang Yi)
The seat-holder has shed his birth-and-death; why would the attendant not accept him?
If one says that Shishuang clarifies "one color," it is like using a broom to paint a蛾眉 (a beauty’s brow). (Dizang En)
As the incense smoke drifts faintly on the breeze, the Head Seat sits in meditative absorption and passes away.
Were it not for the long-veteran and devoted attendant, who would have known the true "nose" of Shishuang? (Zhang Wujin)
An old fisherman on his single fishing boat sails freely amidst a thousand waves and ten thousand billows.
His children and grandchildren, unaccustomed to the violence of wind and tide, have fled into the reeds and do not look back. (Cishou Shen)
To cast it off was as easy as bending and extending one’s arm; the intent of my former master has been attained with intimacy.

For the sake of another’s grain of millet over many years, one loses the ten-thousand-bushel treasure within one’s own home. With the weight of brotherly affection, the attendant served with devotion;
how could the liver and gall of a lifetime be fully recounted? At the head of the Fragrant Grass Ferry, he took a light step; casually, his body now dwells in Apricot Blossom Village. (Fodeng Xun)
The single school of Shishuang was personally transmitted by Jiufeng. When the incense has burned out and he has departed, the true pulse is difficult to penetrate.
The crane in its moon-nest dreams of a thousand years; the person in the snow-house is lost in the function of "one color. Cutting off the ten directions, he still gets his forehead marked;
shifting one step secretly, watch the flying dragon. (Tiantong Jue)
Within the city of Nirvana, one is not yet a true kinsman; only those with horns and shaggy fur are truly so.
Everyone they meet says, "I am retiring from office," yet not a single person has ever been seen beneath the forest trees. (Da Hong Sui)
A single expanse of empty stillness, beyond all conceptualization or sentiment; white clouds disperse as colored mists spread across the sky. Travelers, do not blame me for hurrying on my journey;
I sit waiting upon this cold crag, where the strange grass turns green. (Yunyan Yin)
[Continued Collection] The stone man fears not the lion’s roar; atop the summit of Mount Sumeru he performs a somersault.
The vast ocean is exhausted at the third watch; the raw-iron Kunlun runs beyond the clouds. (Xuedou Zong)
Countless people have been brought back to life from death; those who die while still alive are rare from ancient times.
One only knows that withered wood returns to spring early, yet misses the moment when cold ashes flare up again. Attendant Qian is also a fool;
though he understands the meaning of the former master, he cannot avoid falling entirely into the tiger’s trap. (Yuánwù Qín)
Ten-thousand-fathom cold pools are clear to the bottom; on a frosty night at midnight, they are about to freeze over.
To fish, one must cast a golden-scaled bait; shift the reed-boat’s sail toward the bright moon. (Zhengtang Bian)

[The student] asked, "Is there such a person? The Master said, "There is. [The student] asked, "What is it like to be one who is not mad? The Master said, "Walking through the morning mist with eyes wide open. The verse says: Walking through the morning mist, the eyes do not blink; The whole world is vast and open. If you wish to know this person, Do not look for them within the ten directions.

The great musical pitch arises in the cold valley; its merit of universal salvation is complete and transcendent. The gardens transform into flowers and willows—why wait for the spring breeze? (Fang’an Xian)

How could the great mountain ever lack a single inch of soil? Yanruo was deluded by his own head, yet his madness has not yet returned. In seeking the Way, there is fortunately a phrase that provides strength;
suddenly at dawn on the road, the eyes have not yet opened. For now, remain outside the gate. (Shixi Yue)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Jiufeng, “What is the eye that fixes heaven and earth? The Master said, “Heaven and earth are within it.
The monk asked, “Where is the eye of heaven and earth? The Master said, “It is precisely the eye of heaven and earth.
The monk asked, “Why did you just now say heaven and earth are within it? The Master said, “If it were not so, [the eye would be] before the skull.”
He saw countless ghosts. (The *Wudeng Huiyuan* version differs slightly. The verse says:

When consciousness asks, he answers without confusion; when consciousness answers, he questions without confusion. Since there is a source for every question and answer, one clearly perceives it directly beneath.
Truly, when one clearly understands and breaks through this, one is not replaced by a skull. I exhort those who study the Way: examine and contemplate this with great care.
(Great Perfect Wisdom).
With one punch, he topples the Yellow Crane Tower; with one kick, he overturns the Parrot Isle.
When there is spirit, he adds to that spirit; where there is no elegance, he is elegant nonetheless. (Xutang Yu)
[Added for inclusion] A monk asked Jiufeng, "The ancients said, 'Based on the true, the false is established; through the false, the true is revealed.
Is this so? The Master said, "It is. The monk asked, "What is the true mind? The Master said, "That which is not mixed with food is it. The monk asked, "What is the false mind?
The Master said, "Grasping at conditions and giving rise to inversion is it. The monk asked, "Apart from these two paths, what is [the mind]?"
Regarding the "original substance," the Master said: "The original substance is not separate. [The student] asked: "Why is it not separate? The Master said:
"If one does not revere the Goddess of Merit, who would dislike the Woman of Darkness? The Verse says:
"Truth and falsehood; sifting gold from sand. Entering and leaving the same gate—old-time enemies. (Fang’an Xian).
[Added by Zeng] Jiufeng addressed the assembly, saying: "The eternally abiding Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished. A monk asked:
"If it is neither born nor extinguished, why do we cycle through the six realms? The Master said: "It is because of the mind. The monk asked: "By what..."
"What skillful means should one employ to realize the Dharmakāya? The Master said, "By uniting the empty mind with the principle of emptiness.
[The student] asked, "What is it like after realization? The Master said, "Let the three realms turn as they will; merely listen to the four modes of birth rush about. He spoke again:
"Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "Prostrate yourself. The verse says:
Refined gold must undergo a hundred smeltings; After a hundred smeltings, its color does not change. Turning toward the Way, value being without mind; Without mind, the Way is restored.
Deeper still, the autumn night moon; the incense burner in the ancient temple is but ashes. The Dharma-body possesses not a single thing;
the mountain peaks stand empty and towering. (Nantang Xing)
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Shizhu of Fengxiang Prefecture (he was a successor of Shichuang). While the Master was traveling, he arrived at Dongshan.
At that time, Master Qian uttered a statement, saying: "There are four kinds of people. One person has transcended the Buddhas and patriarchs, yet cannot take a single step.
Another person has traversed the path of the Buddhas and patriarchs, yet cannot utter a single word. Another person can speak..."
"One can practice; another says one cannot practice. "Which of these two is the true person? The Master stepped out from the assembly and said:
"The one who says that Buddhas and patriarchs cannot practice it simply has no tongue to permit such practice.
The one who practices beyond Buddhas and patriarchs yet cannot utter a single word about it simply has no feet to walk."
It is permitted to speak thus. When one person says that [the Way] can be attained through speech and can be attained through practice, it is simply a case of the lid fitting the box.
When another person says that it cannot be attained through speech and cannot be attained through practice, it is like seeking life by cutting off one’s own breath;
this is like the son of a barren woman carrying a cangue and wearing shackles. Shan said, "What about your own portion, Master? The Master said, "In my own portion, I stand out prominently."
Zhuo Ningzhang said, "As for 'The public official Minggongxiu on the sea,' how about that? The Master replied, "When illusory people meet, they clap their hands and laugh aloud.
The verse says: The public official Minggongxiu on the sea— How could he possibly be grasped? If you wish to see his true form, Look at the laughing man on the mountain peak.
The mud-ox at the bottom of the sea plows the white moon; the wooden horse in the clouds gallops through the clear breeze. The barbarian monk is too lazy to hold the bowl of the Western Heaven;
at midnight he boards a boat and crosses over to the eastern sea. (Danxia Chun)

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Jingxin of Yongquan in Taizhou (successor of Shishuang). A monk asked: "What is the matter that has been transmitted? The Master said: "The dragon spews forth water of eternal life;
the fish swallow inexhaustible bubbles. The monk said: "I ask the Master to clarify this further. The Master said:

"Beat the drum and turn the prow of the boat; the oars pierce the moon beneath the waves. Verse: The dragon spews forth water of eternal life; The fish swallow inexhaustible bubbles. Beat the drum and turn the prow of the boat; The oars pierce the moon beneath the waves.
Lingeringly, the crescent moon sinks into the cold waters; Resolutely, the three stars fall upon the emerald peaks. In days past, Yunyan once let it leak out:
The precious flower crown of the Prince of the Golden Wheel. (Danxia Chun)
[Supplement] Yongquan Xing was tending cattle at the monastery during the suppression of the Buddhist teachings by Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty.
At that time, two Chan guests, Qiang and De, encountered the Master riding a cow along the road. Not recognizing him, they remarked, "The hooves and horns are very distinct;
what can be done about the rider not being recognized? The Master spurred the cow away, and the two Chan guests subsequently took rest nearby.
While tea was being brewed beneath a tree, the Master returned and dismounted his ox. The two guests approached to pay their respects; the Master offered them seats and tea.
The Master then asked, "Where have you two Zen guests recently come from? They replied, "From over there. The Master said, "What is the matter with 'over there'?
One of the Zen guests lifted his tea bowl. The Master said, "This is still 'over here. What is the matter with 'over there'?"
"How is it? The two men had no reply. The Master said, "Do not say that those who ride oxen do not recognize what is good.
He then spoke this verse:
"The lush green grass stretches far—how could autumn ever change it? The cowherd boy and the white ox roam at their ease. For those on the path of difference, others find it difficult to perceive."
[Danxia Chun] saw him and said, "Riding a cow yet not recognizing the cow.
[Added from another source: Chan Master Zhiyuan of Yungai Mountain in Tanzhou (a successor of Shishuang). Once, a monk asked Shishuang: "When ten thousand..."
When all the doors were closed, he did not ask. "What about when ten thousand doors are all open?
Xuefeng said, "What about the matter within the hall? The monk had no reply. After half a year, he finally uttered a phrase:
"No one can receive him. Xuefeng said, "In speaking, you speak too much; you have only spoken eighty percent. The monk asked, "Master..."
Furthermore, how is it? Shuang said, "No one recognizes him. When the Master heard this, he prostrated himself and requested that Shuang provide an illustration.
Shuang was unwilling. The Master then took Shuang up to the abbot's quarters and said, "If you, Preceptor, do not speak..."

“Go strike the monk! Shuang said, “I have attained it. The Master prostrated repeatedly. Shuang said, “No one recognizes him. At these words, the Master suddenly attained realization. The verse says: The staff strikes, and the monk departs;
“I have attained it,” he declares. Prostrations follow one after another; “No one recognizes him”—at these words, he suddenly awakens.
In the ancient hall, the cliffs open to reveal the moon locking the pines; Frost, snow, and dew gather, their resonance inexhaustible.
Before the stars, a man lies in his chamber amidst a thousand peaks; Buddhas and patriarchs have no way to recognize this fellow. (Touzi Qing)
No one can grasp him; he presses upon Ma Xiangru. Indeed, he comes upon the bridge;
remember the inscription on the pillar-head. (Tiantong Jue, 2)
No one recognizes him; the chessboard and the drunken woodcutter—turning his head, the axe handle has rotted away, and even the great ocean has turned to dry land.
To "receive" and to "recognize"—who would then compare them by the smallest fraction? If you ask about the affairs within the hall, the affairs within the hall become ever more remote.
As for Yun’gai’s awakening—what then? *Suru suru.* (Zuian Yin).
[Added from another source] Chan Master Hongjian of Fushan in Fuzhou (successor of Shishuang). A monk asked: "If one brings the raw jade to the teacher, will you receive it?
The Master struck the incense stand with his hand. The monk bowed. The Master said: "Bowing."

"It is not non-existent. As for the matter within it, how is it? The monk then struck the incense stand. The Master said, "The tongue does not leave the mouth. *Verse:* It is not non-existent; How can one speak of it? The monk strikes the incense stand; The tongue does not leave the mouth.
The tongue does not leave the mouth; three times three makes nine. Calculating until one returns to the incense altar, both have fallen behind others. (Yuedang Chang)
[Added to the Collection] The Scholar Zhang Zhuo (met Shishuang). Because the Great Master Chan Yue directed him to study under Shishuang, Shishuang asked, "What is your surname?
He replied, "My surname is Zhang and my given name is Zhuo. Shishuang said, "Seeking for the clever, it is utterly unobtainable;

from where does the clumsy come? The scholar suddenly attained realization and presented this verse: "Brilliant and silent illumination pervades the Ganges sands; Ordinary and holy beings alike contain [it within them]."
The spirit dwells together with my house. When not a single thought arises, the entire body is fully manifest; as soon as the six sense organs stir, they are shrouded by clouds.
To sever afflictions is to increase one's illness once more; to strive toward True Suchness is likewise a form of deviation.
Flowing in accordance with worldly conditions without hindrance, both nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky. The Verse says:
Old and decrepit Shi Xiang was without inhibition; he once raised the pivotal phrase right before one’s face.
It was only because of his "old wife’s heart" on that day that it remains hanging from lips and teeth, silent and vast through the ages. (Fujian Qin)
He does not envy the transmission by oral proclamation; he has mistakenly taken the mountains and rivers for his own eyes.
Skill and clumsiness are both shattered at once, yet the severing of afflictions only increases the illness. (A laughable old man indeed.)

Advancing forward, there are precipitous cliffs three thousand *zhang* high; retreating backward, there are hanging cliffs numbering nearly ten thousand layers. Cherish and honor the Elder Zhang Zhuo of the Great Tang;
his iron hammer, though without a hole, dances in the spring breeze. (Bao Ye Yuan)
Chan Master Yuan’an of Luopu Mountain in Lizhou (a successor of Jiashan). Having long served as an attendant to Linji, he took his leave one day.
As Linji was ascending the hall, he said, "In the gate of Linji, there is a red-tailed carp."
Shaking its head and wagging its tail, it went toward the south; one knows not in whose pickle jar it will be drowned.
After the Master had finished his travels, he went straight to Jia Shan and pitched a hermitage there. For a year he did not visit Jia Shan. Jia Shan composed a letter and sent a monk to deliver it.
As soon as the Master received it, he sat down and tucked it away. When the monk extended his hand again to ask for it, the Master made no reply.
The Master then struck him and said, "Go back and report this to the Abbot.
When the monk returned and reported it, Mount [Shishuang] said, "If this monk opens the letter, he will surely come within three days; if he does not open the letter, this man cannot be saved."
The Master indeed arrived three days later. Upon seeing the Mountain Man, he did not prostrate; instead, he stood facing him with his hands joined at the chest.
The Mountain Man said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix’s nest is not of its kind; get out! The Master replied, "I have come from afar to seek your teaching."
"Please grant me one reception," the Master requested. Yunmen said, "Before my eyes there is no *śrāmaṇera*; here there is no old monk.
The Master then gave a shout. Yunmen said, "Stop, stop! Do not be so hasty and reckless. The clouds and moon are the same, yet the streams and mountains differ.
It may be that you, *śrāmaṇera*, can cut off the tongues of all people under heaven, but how can you make a person without a tongue [speak]?"

[The monk] tried to explain his words. The Master stood there reflecting for a moment. Shanshan struck him. From this point on, [the monk] took him as his teacher. Xinghua spoke on his behalf: "Simply know how to become a Buddha;
do not worry about sentient beings. The verse says: Simply know how to become a Buddha; Do not worry about sentient beings.
A companionless stone man enters the mountains at night; snow enshrouds his crimson crown as his green robe chills.
With a shout, he cleaves the summit of the three peaks from the very beginning of the kalpa, holding aloft the golden robe to gaze upon the sun (Touzi Qing).
Having drunk deeply, the realization is profound; returning to the orchid marsh, one seeks a kindred spirit. The clouds, moon, mountains, and streams have never changed;
through all time, who has been able to mirror this mind? (Kumu Cheng)
Attending to the master with towel and pitcher for twenty years, he now shakes his head and wags his tail as he leaves the forest springs. Strolling leisurely, he heads straight south;
having been steeped in the pickle jar, he can now sleep soundly. (Yunju You)
Shaking head and wagging tail, the crimson-scaled fish; thoroughly without dependence, he knows how to turn the body.
He has the skill to cut off the tongue, and his artistry is such that he pulls back the nostrils with wondrous penetration. Beyond the curtain of night-brightness, wind and moon are as bright as day;
before the cliff of the withered tree, flowers and water are ever in spring. A tongueless person, a tongueless person—when the true command is fully upheld, there is this one fresh phrase. Alone.
Walking through the center of the world with clear understanding, one may let the whole world rejoice as it pleases. (Tiantong Jue).
Once, when a monk asked Luopu, "It is said that making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as good as making offerings to a single mindless practitioner of the Way.
I wonder, what fault do the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have, and what virtue does the mindless practitioner possess?"
Deshan said: "A single sheet of white clouds spans the mouth of the valley; how many returning birds are utterly lost in their nests?
The verse says: "Shide is negligent and does not realize the dawn; Hanshan is indolent and knows not the way home. Before the sound, there is a single phrase of perfect resonance."
Beautiful! Beyond all things, the crescent moon shines upon the three mountains (Danxia Chun).
That which is Buddha has always involved effort; only when the mind is clarified does it accord with the Way. As for the blooming and falling of flowers, what cause do they have?
They all belong within the impartial workings of transformation (Kumu Cheng).
The eyebrows of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are curved; with nothing realized and nothing cultivated, their eyes are shrouded in delusion.
Treading upon the unthawed ice that reaches to the very bottom, they all at once mistake it for azure lapis lazuli. (By Fozhi Yu)
[Continued Collection] The old mountain stands towering, locked in cold mist. It is unwilling to lightly grant its heart for transmission.
At night, the Jade Maiden seeks the seal of no-words; the stone man points afar toward the clarity of the moon. (Zidehui)
[Added from another source: Once, a monk asked Luopu, "What should I do when I intend to return to my hometown? The Master said, "The house is broken and the people are gone;
where would you go back to? The monk said, "In that case, I shall not return. The Master said, "The remaining snow in the courtyard is melted by the sun;
who will sweep away the drifting dust inside the room? He then spoke this verse: "Resolute in my vow to return..."
Departing from the village, he boards a boat to cross the Five Lakes. As he raises his oar, the stars and moon vanish; as he halts his rudder, the sun stands solitary.

Unmooring the ropes, he leaves the shore of error; unfurling the sails, he emerges upon the path of rectitude. Upon arriving, his worldly home is utterly swept away, sparing him from being a fool within the house. The Verse says:
The road to the peaceful homeland is far indeed. My longing for return drifts on, beyond the reach of thought. When one lets go and arrives home, what is there to find?
A crystal palace locked away with empty flowers. (Danxia Chun)

[Added for inclusion] Once, a monk asked Luopu, "What is that which cannot be contained within the Great Canon of Teachings? The Master said: "The rain nourishes the three types of grasses; a single piece of jade is radiant by nature. The Verse says:

The rain nourishes the three types of grasses; A single piece of jade is radiant by nature. The Great Canon of Teachings cannot contain it; How could it be grasped by the mind? If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
Before Biepo Cliff, the dawn brings spring; the fragrant breeze occasionally gathers atop the peaks of Vulture Mountain. You must know that within the jade statue’s bottle lies a stupa;
there is another lamp that shines upon heaven and earth. (Touzi Qing)
[Added to the Collection] A monk asked Luopu, "When a single hair swallows up the vast ocean, what more can be said therein?
The Master replied, "In a household that possesses the White-Ze Map, there are no such monsters. Baofu spoke differently, saying: [The text ends here.]
If one’s home does not have the *Bai Ze* diagram, there will certainly be no such demonic apparitions. The verse says:
Though there may be thousands of acres of clouds before the crags, Within the door there is utterly no lamp at midnight. The perilous peaks stretch to the eye, ancient and modern dwellings;
In the evening sky, the slanting light shines upon the layered blues. (Danxia Chun)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Luopu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Where the green mists cover, one emerges and conceals the point; when the white moon shines, the azure pool has no reflection.

The Verse says: Where the green mists cover, the point is concealed; When the white moon shines, the blue depths cast no shadow. If you wish to see the Patriarch’s meaning, Look at the autumn waters in the bright moonlight.

The myriad flowers have not yet bloomed, yet the plum blossoms fall first; The ten thousand trees are withered and bare, yet the cypress grows all the more wondrous. Clouds are so thin they do not obscure the shadows of the moon filtering through;
Mist is so light it cannot reveal the branches that beckon the wind. (Danxia Chun)
[Added from another source] Once, when Layman Pang rose after prostrating, he said, "In midsummer it is scorching; in early winter it is slightly cold.
The Master said, "Do not speak erroneously. The Layman said, "I am an old man. The Master said, "Why do you not say it is cold when it is cold, and say it is hot when it is hot?
The Layman said, "What is the point of pretending to be deaf? The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows. The Layman said, "Then shut my mouth!"
"I have stopped my mouth and plugged up your eyes. The verse says: "Right now I have silenced my mouth;
clearly I have plugged up your eyes. From the beginning, Luopo and Master Pang have never emerged from Muzhou’s 'carrying a single board.
Directly confronting all at once, he brings forth the essence that illuminates past and present. Whether winter cold or summer heat, who can choose? (Ling)
[The source is from the *Qingyuan* (Yuanqing).

[Added by Zengshou. Once a monk asked Luopu, "Are the intent of the Patriarchs and the intent of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said, "The sun and moon revolve together in their brilliance;
whose house has a separate path? The monk said, "If that is so, then light and obscurity follow divergent ways, and matters are not of one kind."
Gai asked, "The Master said: 'Simply do not lose your sheep yourself; why must you weep at the fork in the road? The Verse says:
The moon sifts through pine shadows on high and low trees; The sun shines upon the pool’s heart, where heaven reflects above and below.
The brilliant light in the empty sky is not yet midday; The full orb of autumn night remains unknown as a circle. (Danxia Chun)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Luopu, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, “Clouds cover the solitary peak, yet the peak is not white; rain nourishes the stone sprouts, and the sprouts have just begun to grow. The Verse says: Clouds cover the solitary peak, yet the peak is not white;

Rain nourishes the stone sprouts, and the sprouts have just begun to grow. The ten thousand phenomena are all thus; How could there be any other principle? If you wish to understand the Great Way, Look at the clouds and the rain.
The dragons roar at the bottom of the sea as clouds and rain moisten the world; The tigers howl in the forest as the valley breeze clears the air.
Do not say that thorns grow along every path, For even in a poor household, there is little need for seeing off or welcoming guests. (Danxia Chun)
[Added for inclusion] Once, when the practitioner Gaxi came to visit Luopu, the Master asked, "Since we parted at Lixi, how many years have passed?
The practitioner replied, "The Master still remembers events from long ago. The Master said, "I am told that practitioners generally forget the passage of years and months.
The practitioner said, "The Master’s administrative duties are many; please allow me to observe you closely."

The Master said, "If you strike, strike; you are a man who understands Zen. The monk replied, "I am capable of receiving it. The Master said, "Dharma-teacher, your affairs on the mountain are many. Verse: Strike! Strike! You who understand Zen— "I am capable of receiving it," he said.
"Brother, your mountain duties are numerous," the Master replied.
Such news is most extraordinary; every branch of the moon-plant bears a far-reaching fragrance.
Last night, Chang’e displayed her ingenuity, embroidering mandarin ducks directly upon her eyes. (Danxia Chun)

[Added for Collection] A monk asked Luopu, "When many hands sift through gold, who is it that obtains it? The Master said, "The ancient treasure within the fist does not wait for one to sift through the sand. The monk said, "If that is so, then even with hands outstretched, one does not encounter it.

The Master said, "Do not mistake the cry of a crane for the song of a warbler. Verse: Many hands sift through the gold; Who is it that obtains it? The ancient treasure within the fist— It does not wait for sifting through the sand.
Even with hands outstretched, one does not encounter it; Do not mistake the cry of a crane for the song of a warbler.
Seeking gold—how could it depend on sifting through sand? Even touching the stones amidst the waves still requires effort.
When the incense pillar suddenly emits light at the third watch, at that moment, one knows not who can recognize it. (Danxia Chun)
[Added from another source] When Luopu was ill, on the first day of the twelfth month, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"I shall not remain long. Now I have a matter to ask you all: if you say this is it, you are placing a head upon a head;
if you say it is not, you are seeking life by cutting off your own head. The first seat replied: "The green mountains do not lift a foot."
"Under the sun, one does not pick out a lamp. The Master said, "What kind of time is this to speak such words?
At that moment, the senior monk Yanzong replied, "Apart from these two paths, I ask the Master not to question me further. The Master said:
[The Master] said, "I have not yet spoken further. [Hui]yan said, "From has not exhausted the Way. The Master said, "I do not concern myself with whether you exhaust it or not.
[Hui]yan said, "Since I, Yan, have been without an attendant, I have had no one to respond to the Master for me. The Master then desisted.
That night, he ordered an attendant to summon From and asked, "Ācārya, today you responded with great reason. You ought to embody this."
One grasps the meaning of the former master. The former master’s Way is this: "There is no dharma before one's eyes; the meaning lies before one's eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment;
it is not that which can be reached by the ears or the eyes. Now tell me: which phrase is the guest? Which phrase is the host?

When he had been selected, [the Master] handed him the bowl bag and said, "Yancong, you do not understand. Yancong replied, "I am indeed capable of understanding. The Master said, "Yancong truly does not understand," and shouted him out.

Then he said, "Suffering! Suffering! Xuanjue said: [Note: The provided text contains a fragment of a kōan concerning the transmission of the Dharma between Master Mazu Daoyi and his disciple Yancong. The dialogue concerns the nature of realization and the paradox of "understanding" versus "not understanding."]
Furthermore, tell me: is it because the Elder truly does not understand? Or is it because he fears seeing the alms-bowl bag sticking to him?
The verse says:
Baiting the clouds and hooking the moon at the clear ford, Old in years and solitary at heart, he has not yet caught a scale. A single song of the *Li Sao*, then he returns home.
Later, on the banks of the Muli River, there was the man who alone remained sober.
(Tiantong Jue) The matter beneath the paper robe does not require a womb; with hands let go from the precipice, he is but an infant in swaddling clothes.
At the assembly of Nirvana, the site of practice opens; the directly pointed, single transmission brings forth the Crown Prince. (Nantang Xing)

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Shao Shan Huanpu of Luojing (successor of Jia Shan). A monk asked: "What is the realm of Shao Shan? The Master said: "The howling of monkeys and birds through ancient and modern times; emerald hues shrouded in thin mist. The monk asked:
"Who is the person within the realm? The Master said: "Step back and look. Verse: Ancient and modern, monkeys and birds cry out; Emerald hues are enshrouded in thin mist.

If you ask who is within the realm, He says: "Step back and look! The whole world is the Buddha’s Dharma-body; How could there be any duality? If you can see it at once, You will know the source of the myriad phenomena.
The scenery of Shao Mountain is most excellent; Mist enshrouds its light, verdant hues. I wish to paint it, yet have not finished; Monkeys and birds call out one after another. (Shixi Yue)
[Added for inclusion] When Zun Bunan visited Master Shao Shan, they met at the foot of the mountain. Zun asked, "Where does the road to Mount Shao lead?
The Master pointed with his finger and said, "It goes toward the place where the Wuna Peak is green and dark."
Zun approached him, took hold of him, and said, "I have long heard of Mount Shao; is it truly so? The Master replied, "It is indeed so.
But what business do you have, O *ācārya*? Zun said, "I intend to pose a question; will you answer me?
The Master said, "Look at you—you are not made of gold teeth; how could you possibly draw a bow to shoot Wei Chi? Zun said, "The phoenix..."

"Directly entering the misty heights, who fears the wild sparrows in the forest? The Master said, "The great drum hangs before the hall; strike it as you wish, but try to display your family style like an old monk. [The student] said, "A single phrase transcends beyond the thousand sages. The Master said, "If you can speak such words, you may indeed be called a patch-robed monk. The student said, "I have already spoken. The Master said, "What did you say? The student said, "I have not yet spoken. The Master said, "If you have not yet spoken, how can you be called a patch-robed monk? The student said, "I am not a patch-robed monk. The Master said, "If you are not a patch-robed monk, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "It is for the sake of the Way. The Master said, "If it is for the sake of the Way, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To uphold the lineage. The Master said, "If it is to uphold the lineage, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To transmit the Dharma. The Master said, "If it is to transmit the Dharma, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To benefit living beings. The Master said, "If it is to benefit living beings, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To manifest the Buddha's work. The Master said, "If it is to manifest the Buddha's work, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To repay the four debts of gratitude. The Master said, "If it is to repay the four debts of gratitude, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To fulfill the three obligations. The Master said, "If it is to fulfill the three obligations, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To carry on the ancestral tradition. The Master said, "If it is to carry on the ancestral tradition, why do you wear the robe? The student said, "To maintain the monastic rules.
