The Master said, "If it is to provide a standard for future practitioners,
“Pine and ivy do not reach the height of the moon’s orb. The Master said, “Even if you were to emerge directly outside the realm of *Viyūha*, you would still be half a journey behind Śāoshan.
[The monk] asked, “Where does the fault lie? The Master said, “Such bold words are known only to people of this age.
[The monk] said, “If that is so, then true jade is distinct from within the mud; it brushes aside the dust of myriad activities. The Master said, “...”
“The disciples under Lu Ban merely display their cleverness. The student said, “If that is how a student acts, I wonder what the Master’s own intention is?
The Master said, “The Jade Maiden tosses her shuttle at night, weaving brocade in the western house. The student said, “Is this not the very style of our monastery, Master?
The Master said, “The plowman splits the jade-leak; this is not the work of a true master. The student said, “...”
This was still merely a matter of words. [Zun] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Lying across the body to face the universe—who is the person who puts forth their head?
Zun was speechless. The Master then returned to the mountain with him; as soon as the formal greetings were concluded—
The Master called him forward and said: "The *ācārya* possesses the spirit that pierces the heavens; this old monk has the stratagem to enter the earth.
The *ācārya* swallows the vast ocean in one gulp; this old monk carries Mount Sumeru on his back. The *ācārya* comes forward brandishing a sword; this old monk awaits him with a leveled spear.
Speak quickly, speak quickly! What is the single path that leads upward? [The student] said: "A bright mirror."

[The monk] stood at the dais and requested, "I pray that the Master will take one look. The Master said, "I do not look. [The monk] asked, "Why do you not look? The Master said, "The water is shallow and there are no fish;

it is a vain labor to cast down the hook. Zhenzuo was speechless. The Master then struck him. The verse says: The water is shallow and there are no fish; Toiling in vain, he casts down the hook. The old man’s staff strikes the head; The golden-haired lion roars.
Moving with the times and adapting to change, following the fortunes and setbacks of all things—whose among the wild geese and cranes can distinguish the male from the female?

Before the Marquis of Han met his destiny, his family style was that of a monk in coarse hemp robes. To roll up the Three Qin like a mat was not without plan; why labor to recall Kuai Tong’s words on loyalty and righteousness? (Fang’an Xian)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Shao Shan, "In a place where right and wrong do not reach, is there still a phrase? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is that phrase? The Master said, "A single mass of white clouds does not reveal its ugliness.

The Verse says: A single mass of white clouds does not reveal its ugliness; The ten directions are all covered by the bright moon. When the spring breeze blows over the green willows, The yellow flowers naturally fall. The ten thousand phenomena are all within this one phrase; How could it be grasped by the mind? If you wish to know the meaning of the ancient sages, Look at the clear sky above your head.
A single solitary cloud reveals no blemish; the white cloud-child leans against its green mountain father. The crane nestles in the numinous dew as dreams first return;
a new crescent moon like a half-hook rises over ten thousand households. (Zidehui)
Alone facing the vast blue sea, he cuts off the many currents; casually dancing the oars, he casts his golden hook. The white clouds do not reveal themselves as the misty waves stretch wide;
a single sound from the horizontal flute fills the heavens and earth with autumn. (Muan Yong)

[Added from another source] A monk asked Shao Shan, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Rootless grass on the summit; leaves rustle though there is no wind. The Verse says: Rootless grass on the highest peak, Leaves rustle though there is no wind.
If you wish to know the Master’s house style, Look at the weeds growing by the stream.
The solitary peak of Wondrous Summit is uniquely lush and oily; a celestial, numinous sprout that never touches the ground. Its verdant leaves sway of their own accord without a breeze;
its pure fragrance does not seek to rival the charms of springtime. (Danxia Chun)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk arrived to visit Shao Shan. As he rose after prostrating, the Master said, "A man of great talent hides his skill in a humble door. The monk stepped aside and stood there. The Master said, "He has lost the timber for a ridgepole.

The Verse says: A man of great talent hides his skill in a humble door; He has lost the timber for a ridgepole. If you wish to know the meaning of this matter, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
With palms joined, one must know that the ferry has already been crossed; to advance further still would only lead to drifting and drowning.
If dull copper were treated as gold bullion, it could only deceive those who lack eyes.
(Danxia Chun) Volume Twenty-seven, *The Linked Pearl Collection of Verses on the Ancient Cases of the Chan School*, Volume Twenty-eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou, Song Dynasty;
continued by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery in Shaoxing, Yuan Dynasty. *Anecdotes and Occasions of the Patriarchs* (Zushi Jiyuan).
The Fourth Patriarch of the Sixth Generation of the Sixth Patriarch (The Second Patriarch of the Fifth Generation of Qingyuan) [Added by Zeng]:
Chan Master You of Mount Tiangai in Fengxiang Prefecture (Heir to Jia Shan). He had a monastery named Wugou Jingguang (Stainless Pure Light).
He constructed a bathhouse. Someone asked: "Since it is called 'Stainless Pure Light,' why..."

He built a bathhouse, but the monks remained silent. Later, he invited the Master to represent them. The Master said: "On a night of bright moon in the third autumn month, this is no time for displaying fullness. The verse says:
Although the answer has exhausted the profound meaning, alas, the phrase that strikes the vital point remains unacquainted.
If you wish to realize the originally stainless nature, you must further enter the water to see the tall man. (Danxia Chun)
Chan Master Haihu of Taiyuan (a successor of Jiaoshan) was once invited by someone to provide offerings for Tripitaka Master Guanding.
After the seats had been arranged, the Master took his place on that very seat. At that time, the Dharma Master Yunshe asked:
"In what year did the Upādhyāya practice the Way? The Master said, "Come forward, Seat-Master. Zhaozhe approached.
The Master said, "As for Kātyāyana, in what year did he practice the Way? Zhaozhe was at a loss. The Master shouted: "Hah!"
This bed-wetting ghost. The verse says:
For the most part, these things are learned from others; for a lifetime, one vainly flaps their mouth in empty chatter.
If you wish to exhaustively investigate this patch of empty luminosity, it is not encompassed by any of the seven Buddhas, nor by those who came before them. (Danxia Chun)
Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo of Ezhou (a successor of Deshan). One day he went to visit Deshan;
as soon as he stepped across the threshold, he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it holy? Deshan immediately shouted. The Master bowed.
Someone reported this to Dongshan, who said, "If it were not for Master Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle. The Master remarked, "Old man Dongshan..."
Failing to distinguish between good and evil, he mistakenly applied names and phrases. At that time, I raised one hand while clutching down with the other.
The verse says:
"The old fellow Yantou—whom would he distinguish as ordinary or holy? Half monk, half layman; noble or base? For three coins, he takes one."
Black clam, black clam! By the riverbank they call out to each other to gather shrimp and clams.
(Fayun Xiu) A hare runs across the level plain; release the gray falcon. With one snap, it devours both eyes. A poisonous hand seizes it and carries it away for someone to buy;
alas, the weight has not yet been clearly determined. (Baoning Yong)
A single shout startles heaven and shakes the earth; the sea turns over and Mount Taihua opens wide and clear. Even Yantou’s courage failed him and his soul fled;
do not say that at that time he merely held up his hand. (Shushan Ru).
[Continued Collection] A master displays his skill without revealing his edge; he is accustomed to settling the male and female blades with a pair of swords.
Suddenly a thunderclap bursts forth, startling heaven and earth; the three peaks of Mount Hua stand inverted in the void. (Zantang Shen)
The great garuḍa strikes the wind; the azure dragon emerges from the sea. Raising the hand and clasping the hand; the sun rises and the moon sets.
When frost and snow are severe and solid, one recognizes the cold of the year. By the side of the double-six gaming board, one must cry out in acclaim. (Zuʼan Yin)
The first arrow was still light, but the subsequent arrows were deep; countless ordinary people have been submerged in the mud. Here, open wide the eye of heaven and earth;
brandishing the "blow-off-hair" sword, one may roam freely as one pleases. (Mukan Egen)
[Added for collection] When Yantou first visited Deshan, after he had spread his sitting cloth and prostrated, Deshan used his staff to thrust the sitting cloth down the steps.
The Master went down the steps, picked it up, draped it over his back, and departed to attend the hall.
Mountan said: "I do not approve of your letting go; I only approve of your gathering in. The Verse says:
A single movement of the strings reveals the melody; a leaf falling makes known the autumn. I do not approve of your letting go; I only approve of your gathering in.
Next year there will be new branches once more; the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease. (Dun’an Yan)
[Added for inclusion] Yantou addressed the assembly, saying: "The intent of my teaching is like a 'poison-coated drum.
When struck once, everyone who hears it, whether far or near, loses their body and forfeits their life. At that time, the Senior Monk Xiaoyan came forward and asked, "What is the poison-coated drum?
The Master pressed both hands upon his knees, leaned his body forward, and said, "Han Xin at the imperial court."
The Verse says:
"The Buddha-dharma is beyond recompense; leave it to you. In a mere breath, one is born or slain.
If you had taught Han Xin the wondrous secret, He would have naturally understood how to guard against Emperor Gao. (Nanyan Sheng)
Yantou was once asked by a monk, "What is it like when the ancient sail is not yet hoisted? The Master said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass.
Verse: It cannot be smashed by a hammer; It cannot be burned by fire. In heaven or on earth, where can it find rest? A-he-he! It is this!
What is it? Do not bite through; chew thoroughly. (Haiyin Xin) The ancient sail is not raised—this is Yantou.
The moon is cold, the wind high, as he lowers his straight hook. Who sees the donkey in the back garden eating grass?
Having shed its cage and unburdened its pack, it snores contentedly. (Dahong Sui)
In the back garden, two donkeys eat grass—one old, one not. Suddenly they charge up the mountain;
their encounter is perfectly timed. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
In the back garden, a donkey eats grass; do not seek it by following words. Leap up and ride upon its waist, traveling the road to Chang’an. (Gushan Gui)
The wind-signal does not come; the spring colors grow old. I recall instead the donkey eating grass in the back garden. A full moon in the sky is bestowed upon the traveler;
the wild guest’s path home by the stream is early. (Chu’an Fang)
[Continued Collection] A donkey eats grass in the back garden; how pitiable, this infinite aging in vain. At midnight, a blind man asks for his hometown;
he does not know he is on the Chang’an road. (Xuedou Zong)
In the rear garden, a donkey grazes on grass; reeds and flowers roll like flying snow. Before the frost, a pair of white geese—two solitary shadows fall upon the celestial pond. (Tudu’s Staff)
Before the ancient sail was hoisted, the donkey in the back garden ate grass. Days are short and nights are long;
the traveler must set out early. (Xue’an Jin)
Yantou was once asked by a monk, "After the ancient sail has been hoisted, what then? The Master said, "A small fish swallows a large fish. Verse:
Once the ancient sail is hoisted, what more doubt remains? In one's studies, as before, one is again deluded. The large and small fish are both one.
The sea—how can one contend with the bait on the hook being uneven?
(Fenyang Zhao). A small fish swallows a large fish; the direct path is too circuitous. Cease further questioning of the ancient sail; you shall encounter him everywhere.
(Jingshan Gao): A small fish swallows a large fish;
peach-wood talismans are nailed above the gate. No demons or malevolent spirits can enter; even the Buddha-dharma is eliminated.
(Gushan Gui). [Continued Collection] Once the ancient sail has already been hoisted, the small fish swallows the large-headed fish.
Although Li Guang may employ his divine arrows, from of old Zhang Zhiyan has understood cursive script. (Zhaotang Yi).
I ask a single word of Budong about the reed-sail: the great fish is swallowed by the small fish.
Only by directly transcending the lips and jaws beyond the ordinary can one finally believe that Yantou has no brain-pan. (Tianmu Li)

Yantou was once asked by a monk, "How does one discern the host amidst the dust? The Master said, "Oil contained within a copper sand-pan. (As recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*) He then spoke this verse:
Oil contained within a copper sand-pan; The host is discerned amidst the dust. If you wish to know the host, Look at the oil in the pan.
To distinguish the master amidst the dust is most difficult to clarify; among a thousand or ten thousand people, few are truly awake.
The bronze sand-pan and the oil have been pure from antiquity to the present; I pull out the nail in your eye for you. (Fenyang Zhao).
Discerning the master amidst the dust, his eyes are clear; seeking the direction all at once, he further applies the "eye-dot.
It is laughable that although Jīvaka may cause dizziness and nausea with his treatments, to this day no one travels between the north and south. (Foyin Yuan)

The dampness of the foundation stones means rain is about to fall; the clouds part and the moon shines bright. An old fisherman idly casts his line, stirring up a constellation of stars within the single pool. (Haiyin Xin)
A bronze sandal filled to the brim with oil; this is precisely the seal of Vairocana, gathered in its aftermath.
If one can further discern the master amidst the dust, in an age of great peace, every general shall be enfeoffed as a marquis. (Yunxi An).
The oil is pure within the bronze sandal; it reflects the ancient host amidst the dust. Send word to the Zen practitioner:
practice with fierce diligence, lest you let this present life go to waste. (Cao Tang Qing)

[Continued Collection] All day long he runs through the marketplace; within the marketplace there is truly much. One must laugh at those people of Wulao Lake, shaking out their ragged robes in poverty. (Daguai Zhi)
A bronze sandal filled to the brim with oil; fresh greens served with radish heads.
Just wait until the fifteenth day of the first month next year, when every household will have paper lanterns hanging at their doors. (Fujian Qin)
When the sandalwood gong is struck at the crown of the head, body and mind are both unseen. A gust of western wind arrives, and two or three fallen leaves drift down.
(The Poison-Coated Whip)
Returning from drinking at night in the village, three, four, or five of us fall prostrate in exhaustion. Rubbing our hands over the green moss, do not be angry that we startled you. (Sian Guan)
A bronze sandal filled to the brim with oil; the decrepit Yantou knows no shame.
Yet upon the eyelashes of a gnat, he flaunts his gallantry atop a tower. (Kongsou Yin)
A million brave soldiers enter Han’s pass; their majesty is like fierce tigers, their formation like mountains. With a single blade he straightway takes Yan Liang’s head;
were it not for Lord Guan, this would have been most difficult indeed. (Wujingche)
In the midst of the dust, Bianzhuzhi questioned Yantou: "How can one bring the mind and consciousness to rest?
One must see both the nostrils and the eyes; a copper sand-pan filled to the brim with oil. (Heunggwam Go)
[Added for Collection] Yantou asked Qinshan, "What is the true word? Qin replied, "Namo Buddhāya.
The verse says:
Responding to the occasion, he answered as the question arose; It is neither Chan nor the profound mystery. Later generations have needlessly translated it.
[He] went out. Then he translated the Sanskrit into Chinese (Tángyán).
[Retuìgēng Níng]. [Added by Zōngshòu]. Whenever Yàntóu was asked anything, he would simply let out a single sigh. A verse says:
The dragon lies asleep in the tranquil azure pool; the clouds gather and the bright moon becomes full. The Seven Stars shine with brilliant splendor—who can offer incense before birth? (Da-hong Sui)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Yantou, "What should one do when encountering a fierce tiger on the road? The Master said, "Press! The Verse says:
Yantou’s single press—empty space shatters asunder. Not transmitted from father to son; it is the wondrous secret of the immortals. (Pō’ān Xiān)
[Added from the Supplement] Yantou addressed the assembly, saying: "In general, when proclaiming the teaching, one must let the three phrases flow forth from a state of desirelessness.
This is merely the principle of the matter: biting off and biting on; wishing to leave but not leaving, wishing to stay but not staying.
At times one proceeds exclusively without leaving, and at times one proceeds exclusively without staying. The verse says:
For three coins, I bought a dredger; for years I have been dredging clams and dredging shrimp. Whether conditions are favorable or adverse, long or short—cease all such talk.
In whose house has the hearth-fire ever lacked smoke? (Xutang Yu)
Yantou encountered a period of religious purging and became a ferryman on the shores of Lake Ezu. He hung a wooden board on each bank;
whenever someone came to cross, he would strike the board once, and the master would call out, "Who is it?
If someone replied, "I wish to go to the other side," the master would then row out to meet them. One day, an old woman carrying a child approached him.

He said, "I do not ask about you presenting the oar and dancing with the paddle; tell me, from where did this child in the old woman’s hand come? The Master struck her. The old woman said, "I have given birth to seven sons;

six did not meet with one who understands them. This one alone is not even worth keeping," and she threw him into the water. The verse says: Presenting the oar and dancing with the paddle—this is not what I ask. Tell me, from where did the child in the old woman’s hand come?
The Master struck her; the old woman said: "I bore seven sons; six did not meet with those who understand. This one alone is not even worth keeping," and she cast him into the water.
In buying and selling, one must pay the full price. If even a single coin is short, one will surely be subjected to verbal abuse. Do not resort to such abuse;
for if it reaches the ears of those near and far, it will become a lasting scandal. (Haoyin Xin)
At that time, he displayed a family tradition distinct from the crowd; he had the skill to venture his body into the tiger’s den. Where he brandished the oar and struck, no stratagem could remain.
In the stillness of night, with whom would he sail upon the Five Lakes? (Third Patriarch).
Having abandoned one's own child, there is no further kinship. Cast off your hands and return home; cease seeking the ford.
A traveler upon the waves, wielding oars and dancing with the rudders—do not seek a ferryman at the riverhead. (Zhenru Zhe, 2)
In old age, there are neither burdens nor causes; sleeping alone in the lofty hall, there is but this single body.
Aside from the traveler mingling with the waves upon the river, who else could be such an unrestrained man?
"Alas! This old woman; she cannot help her own children. When rich, she complains that a thousand mouths are too few; when poor, she laments that even one body is too many. (Chuna Xiu)
The rhythmic movement of oars and paddles reveals a distinct intent; meeting upon the river, they speak of their journey. Having dropped off his own child, he returns alone;
the spring waters are deep and clear, filling the lake with azure. (Zhīhǎi Púróng Píng)
Waving oars and displaying paddles at the ancient ferryhead, the old woman meets [the traveler] and asks for his origins.
Who could bear to cast their own biological child into the heart of the river and not rescue them? (Shangfang Yi)
Casting the fishing line at the mouth of the E-yang River, he gathers clams and catches shrimp without regard for the time. Suddenly, an old woman asks him a question;
this has served as a heroic standard for the monastic groves for a thousand ages. Now, the fault lies with the heterodox teachers who meet him shaking their hands and discuss his "discarded child.
If you can understand that the intent is right before your eyes, do not believe the slanders of bystanders. (Fodeng Xun)
The formal custom of borrowing a path to pass through— Who would have known that ancestors would burden their descendants? The old woman, harboring resentment, cast [the child] away by the riverbank;
Yet she left behind a fine reputation heard throughout the four seas. (Wuyuan Guo)
Having abandoned one’s own child, what more is there to say? The moon in the heart of the waves seals the azure sky.
With but this single body, free from all entanglements, one sleeps when weary and sits when awake, following conditions as they arise. (Shushan Ru)

[Continued Collection] On the banks of the Eyang River, I cast my fishing line. When the season meets, the scarlet-scaled fish appear. Picking it up with a casual hand, I move freely in all directions;
following the waves and drifting with the current, I have no lingering attachment. (Dahui Zhi)

The only child, born of her own flesh, follows her step by step; she presents the oar and raises the paddle, pointing toward home. The old woman receives a beating, yet the pivot of the mechanism is revealed first;
the seas and mountains are overturned, shaking the four quarters of space. (Jiantang Ji)
A single-leafed skiff floats upon the vast and boundless; Paddling and rowing, it transcends the notes of *gong* and *shang*. Mountains, clouds, sea, and moon are all cast aside;
Thus winning for oneself the long dream of Zhuang Zhou’s butterfly. (Nun Wuzhuo Zong)
Meeting face to face, we hold hands atop the high peak. Looking out in all four directions, the heavens and earth are vast and empty.
A single song of the fisherman no one understands; the wind rises at the ferryhead, scattering the reeds. (Wuan Quan)
Paddling and rowing, he encountered a thief’s foot; three knocks upon the hull, and he captured him in person. With this single act, he cast everything away;
singing his oar-song, he returned as the wind and waves subsided. (By Master Park Hyeon-hyeon).

From the beginning, six have been unknown companions; one has cast himself entirely into the depths of the treacherous waves. Righteousness severed and sentiment forgotten, there is nowhere to seek him;
the ocean of three thousand worlds is cold and silent. (Tianmu Li)
At the ferryhead of E-zhu, the ghost-child reaches his limit; his entire skill was misplaced at the moment he struck the boat’s side.
How much better it would have been to offer another turn of phrase, to rescue the seventh son of the old woman. (Nansou Long)
Waving oars and displaying paddles by the shores of E-zhu, one examines people: why do they so painfully create karmic enmity?

When Bodhidharma was deluded, he was at Shaolin; people today do not understand that this is for the transmission of the mind. How admirable it is that the deluded encounter Bodhidharma:
after the three winters have passed, there is once again a new spring. (Tianyi Huai)
Tearing asunder past and present, he has submerged all conventional molds. When the occasion arises, he opens wide his blood-basin mouth;
from the tip of his toe he kicks out Buddhas as numerous as sesame seeds, leaving Li Si and Zhang San with no way to flee. (Huikang’s Verse)

[Added for inclusion] A monk asked Xuefeng, "When one is silent and without dependence, what then? The Master said, "This is still an illness. The monk asked, "What about after turning over? The Master said, "The boatman goes down to Yangzhou. Verse: Silent and without dependence—this too is an ailment. After turning over, the boatman heads for Yangzhou.
The waves on the river are vast; The moonlight upon the water is clear. If you wish to see the ancient path, Look at the clouds and mist rising from the mountain peaks.

In profound stillness and without reliance, the illness is deep; the Old Man of Snow applies the needle to the painful spot of yesteryear. With one call, he awakens the dreamer, and the spring dream shatters;
ten thousand mountains resound as one with the cry of the wooden dragon. (Zide Hui)
[Added for inclusion] Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "This matter is not obtained from verbal expressions; it is not obtained from the yellow scrolls [of the scriptures];
it is not obtained from the venerable elders of various quarters. From where, then, should it be obtained? You must also examine this with great care."
The Verse says:
A single drop of true pearl, crimson as the fermenting ale; With earnest persistence, you urged me two or three times.
In the end, wishing to exhaust the Master of Spring’s intent, I swallowed it all before departing on my horse. (By Xuan Shan Ning)
A monk once asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? The Master said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom.
The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it? The Master said, "It does not enter through the mouth. Later, this monk went to Zhaozhou and raised this story.
Zhaozhou said, "If it does not enter through the mouth, it must not enter through the nose. The monk then asked about the ancient...
"Master, how is it with the cold spring water in the mountain stream? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter. The Master asked, "What happens to those who drink it? Zhaozhou said, "They die.
Upon hearing this, the Master remarked, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha," and prostrating himself from afar, he thereafter ceased responding to questions.
The verse says:
In the ancient ravine, cold springs flow vast and boundless; Their branches and tributaries are clearly visible as they stream in secret. They do not enter through the mouth and have no flavor;
One must exhaust oneself in death to make them speak, yet they remain unknowable. (Yungai Chang)
Gloomy clouds gather, shrouding the snowy peaks; Venerable Zhao’s two eyes are a vivid green. No one has recognized his labors on the battlefield from of old;
He simply wishes to have his epoch-making merit re-evaluated. (Baofeng Zhao)
Even granting or seizing it back, he is an old master; rushing currents crossing the blade are as numerous as hemp seeds.
Deep within the ravine, no one can reach; those who drink only add more sand to their eyes. (Fuxincai)
[Continued Collection] When the Old Man Bao laughed at Guo Lang in years past, his sleeves were flaunted with such grandiosity before the crowd.
But when it came time for the Old Man Bao himself to dance, he remained as grandiose as ever—surpassing even Guo Lang. (Zhenjing Wen)
Zhaozhou’s Elephant Bone Cliff—peerless throughout all the world. Together we stroke the stringless zither; for a thousand years it has cleared the ears of men. The cold spring of the ancient ravine:
staring with fixed eyes, it does not enter through the mouth; those who drink forget the trap. To speak again would be bitter and lead to death;
to not answer questions is the same for both parties. Meeting face to face, the two families gather; they beat the drum and play the lute. Within this—
Who is it? A white crane enters the reeds. (Yuánwù Qín). At Xuefeng, the ancient stream’s spring is deep;
at Zhaozhou, the stone bridge’s water is bitter. If you know that different waters share the same source, then those who drink from them need not doubt or realize [the truth].
It does not enter through the nostrils; the white waves rise three tiers high. From this point on, he will no longer answer questions. How could this be?
Exempt from paying a high price. Within the adamantine circle, the thorny brambles; having penetrated this, one traverses the four quarters of the world at will.
(Fóxìng Tái). [Added by Zēngshōu] Xuěfēng said: "The world is one chi wide; the ancient mirror is one chi wide. The world is ten zhang wide."

An ancient mirror was one zhang wide. Xuansha pointed to the brazier and asked, "How wide is this? The Master replied, "As wide as the ancient mirror. Xuansha said, "The feet of you old monk have not yet touched the ground. A verse says: An ancient mirror, one zhang wide;
Xuansha points to the brazier. "How wide is it? he asks. "As wide as the ancient mirror," he replies. "The feet of you old monk," Xuansha says, "Have not yet touched the ground."
The world can align with the ancient mirror; yet to seek the mark within words is itself delusion. Where white clouds arise, the green mountains are exquisite;
at dawn, as before, the moon sets in the west. (Xiangtian Qing)
The worlds of the ten directions are a single mirror; looking at one’s form within the mirror is not yet the truth.
When you grasp the tip of your own nose and realize, "This is I," only then will you see the person of original nature. (Lan’an Shu)
[Added to the collection] Xuefeng heard of a monk who had built a hut at the foot of the mountain many years prior.
He did not shave his head and kept a long-handled ladle with which he drew water from the stream. At times, a monk would ask him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The host said, "The stream is deep and the ladle handle is long. Upon hearing this, the Master remarked, "That is truly extraordinary.
One day, taking a razor with him, he went to visit the host. As soon as they met, the Master raised the previous conversation and asked, "Was that the words of the hermitage master?
The host replied, "Yes. The Master said, "If you can say something [in response], I will not shave your head. The host then washed [the razor].
He knelt before the Master with his head bowed. The Master immediately shaved his head. The verse says:
When speaking, one does not avoid cutting out the tongue; When tending the furnace, one does not avoid the fierce fire. Working as one goes, one gains mastery over the household;

Reaching old age, one can sit steadily of one's own accord. The water is deep and the ladle handle is long; Scoop up the water to wash the head and shave it. Upon Xuefeng’s blade, the eye suddenly opens.
Open. Within the lapis lazuli hall there is no closing.

(Yuedang Chang) When Old Xue shows compassion and is willing to visit him, he distinguishes dragons from snakes upon the tip of a single hair. You must know that this does not involve the realm of verbal explanation;
it is a total, free-flowing expression of one who has emerged as a true master of the house. (Dongshan Yuan)
Xuefeng had been presented with a silver folding chair by the Military Commander of Min. A monk asked him, "The Master has received such offerings from the Great King;
how will you repay them? The Master pressed his hand against the ground and said, "Don't hit me too hard" (the modern corruption being "hit me lightly").
A monk asked Shushan, "What was the meaning of Xuefeng saying, 'Don't hit me too hard'? Shushan—
It is said: "A melon-pickle tucked in his hair; the tail hangs down, heels even. The Verse says:
"The Great King, with deep faith, sent a bed; He asked the Chan followers nearby, 'Are you too hasty? Lowering his hand, he spoke in a low voice, 'Strike sparingly';
In inferiority, there is total victory—who can discern this? (Dongshan Cong)
When asked how one repays the debt of gratitude to the Master, he raised his staff and withdrew it entirely, taking his seat at the vital ford.
If wind and waves stir at the prow of the boat, the flowing sands fill the eyes and no person is seen. (Fenyang Shanzhao)
He received a bull from one person and returned a horse to another; he bestowed kindness upon them and requited their favors with such refined elegance.
Today there are many who have received his grace, yet we do not know who among them is the one who returns that grace. (Zhengjue Yi).

Not knowing what with which to repay the grace of the sovereign, The wind rises over the rivers and lakes, leaving ripples in its wake. A single ancient sail, riding the inspiration of the moment, departs;
With whom does it travel as it passes through the Celestial Gate? (Baoning Yong)
[Continued Collection] This principle has circulated for seventy years; many have discoursed upon it, yet few have discerned it.
To step upon the ground is to cause one to strike oneself lightly; to recognize it as such leads, as before, to further delusion. (Prajñā-ruci)
Both sides of receiving a gift are illusions; when the moment arrives, why not spare your eyebrows and whiskers?
I know that beyond this there is no superior artifice—*tut*, you old blind donkey from Qinzhou! (Baoye Yuan).
Xuefeng was once presented by the King of Min with one tangerine and one orange each.
The king sent an envoy to deliver them and inquired, "Since these two are of the same color, why are their names different? The Master then returned them to him exactly as they had been sealed.
The King again hurriedly questioned Xuansha. Xuansha took a sheet of paper and covered [the question] over it. The verse says:
Mandarins and tangerines, the King of Min sealed with his own hand; brought forth, he asked directly to strike at the ancestral wind.
A tall man enters the water—clearly visible there; yet asking further of Xuansha, one does not penetrate. Fenyang opens the celestial path for you; the jeweled monastery and golden realm are azure.
The sky is clear (Fenyang Zhao). The Lord of Min offers two kinds of tribute;
Xuefeng returns them all at once with a single seal. The sentiments of those above and below are both perfectly harmonious;
there is no need to further divide what is already whole (Baoning Yong).
[Continued Collection] Do not doubt that the citrus will come; it would be as foolish as an iron ox being bitten by a mosquito.
Even King Min has not yet understood the Master’s intent—please let Xuansha drive another spike into him. (Yanshou Hui)
Clearly distinguish the tangerine from the orange; do not confuse them with clamor. Offer flowers and borrow water to discern the dragon from the snake.
A single sheet of white paper covers it all, sparing the world from raising arms in conflict. (Yezhu Chuan)
Ordinary colors have two kinds of names; paper covers cannot deceive the eyes of the multitude. At that time on the Snowy Peaks, it was immediately sealed and sent away;
yet King Min still had not ceased his doubts. (Hengchuan Gong)

[Added for Collection] Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "The entire earth is this gate of liberation. I hold out my hand to pull them in, yet they refuse to enter. At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "Master, you cannot blame me. Another monk said, "What is the use of entering? The Master then struck him. Verse: The whole earth is the gate of liberation; He holds out his hand, yet none will enter. One says, "You cannot blame me," Another asks, "What is the use of entering? The Master strikes— Who can bear to look upon it? The thousand sages are all at a loss; How many have attained the Way? The Great Matter is right before one’s eyes; Why do you seek it elsewhere? If you wish to see the Buddha, Look directly at your own face. The ancient mirror is bright and clear; It reflects the myriad forms. If you can see it clearly, You will not be deceived by others. If you do not see it clearly, You will fall into the pit of views. The ten directions are all empty space; The four seas are but one body. If you can understand this, You are a man of great capacity. If you do not understand, You are but a common person. Do not seek it outside yourself; Seeking outside is a mistake. If you can turn back and reflect, You will naturally attain peace. Do not be attached to words and phrases; Words and phrases are like floating clouds. If you can let go of them all, This is called true liberation. The Master’s staff is like lightning; A single blow shatters the heavens. If you can withstand it, You are a true heir of the Buddhas. If you cannot, You are but a ghost in the weeds. Xuefeng’s teaching is peerless; His legacy remains forever fresh. If you wish to follow his path, You must first cut off the root of doubt. Do not seek it in books or commentaries; Books and commentaries are but dead letters. If you can see into your own nature, You will realize the Way of the Buddhas. Do not be deluded by appearances; Appearances are like illusions. If you can see through them, You will transcend birth and death. If you do not see through them, You will remain in the cycle of suffering. The Master’s teaching is vast and deep; It is beyond the reach of thought. If you can understand this verse, You will know the heart of the Patriarchs. If you do not understand, You are but a blind man in the dark. Do not seek it in the past or future; Past and future are but names. If you can see the present moment, You will be free from all attachments. Do not be bound by forms or emptiness; Forms and emptiness are both delusions. If you can transcend both, You will attain the Great Enlightenment. If you do not transcend them, You will remain a wandering spirit. Xuefeng’s teaching is like the sun; It illuminates the world. If you can receive its light, Your mind will be bright and clear. If you do not receive it, You will remain in darkness. Do not seek it in the mountains or forests; Mountains and forests are but shadows. If you can dwell in the midst of the marketplace, You will be a true Bodhisattva. If you cannot, You are but a hermit in the wilds. Do not be attached to stillness or noise; Stillness and noise are both distractions. If you can be at ease in both, You will be free from all hindrances. If you are not at ease, You will be troubled by the world. Xuefeng’s teaching is peerless; It is the ultimate truth. If you can practice it, You will attain the Way. If you do not practice it, You will remain in ignorance. Do not seek it in the scriptures or treatises; Scriptures and treatises are but secondary teachings. Xuefeng rides a fine steed; Yunmen mounts a donkey. One kick, one tread, as they gallop side by side.
There is a road to Chang’an, though it is not that there is no road; when traveling at midnight, people do not know it. (Wenyu Qin)
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, what is this? It is presented directly before one’s face; almost missed! Not missed.
Let us lie down and sleep upon a heap of discarded chaff. (□□□).
[Added for Collection] One day, Xuefeng was tending the fire inside the Sangha Hall. Having closed both the front and rear doors, he cried out, "Help! Help with the fire!

Xuansha took a piece of firewood and threw it in through the lattice window; the Master immediately opened the doors. The Verse says: The fire is burning fiercely within the hall; Xuansha casts in a piece of wood. The Master opens the door; Who can fathom this? A single spark ignites the vast expanse; The whole world is ablaze. If you wish to know the source, Look at the face of the old man.
Dust flies from the great mountain; a gnat gives birth to a child. The child falls into the dust like an awl piercing mud. Using fire to extinguish fire; closing the door and then opening it.
Throwing firewood and having family disgrace seen outside. Swallowing the myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos in one gulp.
(Yuedang Chang)
A high fever from burning firewood warms the whole body; such joy is difficult to contain—a spring within the room.
Were it not for Master Xie coming to share the fire, who would have known there were those suffering from the cold outside the gate? (Shilin Gong)
[Added from another source] Xuefeng asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From Zhejiang. The Master said, "By boat or by land?
He replied, "I have not traversed either path. The Master said, "How did you get here? He replied, "What obstacle could there be?
The Master struck him and drove him out. Ten years later, the monk came again. The Master asked once more, "Where have you come from?"
A man came from Hunan. The Master asked, "How far is Hunan from here? He replied, "It is not separated.
The Master held up his whisk and said, "Is it separated by this? He replied, "If it were separated, I would not have arrived."
The Master again beat him and drove him out. After this monk settled elsewhere, he would insult anyone he saw who was associated with the Master.
One day, a fellow practitioner heard of this and went specifically to inquire: "Brother, when you arrived at Xuefeng, what words were spoken that caused you to insult him so?

A verse says: Wearing horns and holding up his head, he goes and returns again; In the snowy courtyard, twice I saw the battle banners unfurled.

Before the army, he did not fail the General’s command; Vainly there were heroes emerging from the nine realms. Though they emerged from the nine realms, there was a secure barrier; Without having pierced that secure barrier, one has not yet—
A worthy observation. "The eyes on the tip of the staff are like the rising sun; one must recognize true gold by examining it in the fire.
(Fodeng Xun) "I have heard that Mount Min abounds in venomous insects; though one employs a thousand methods and a hundred schemes, there is no way to avoid them.
Since there are already 'soul-hurrying ghosts' within the tomb, only when the life-force is returned to them does one finally find rest. (Xutang Yu)
While Xuefeng was performing communal labor, he was carrying a bundle of rattan himself. On the path, he encountered a monk and immediately threw it down.
As the monk reached out to pick it up, the Master gave him a kick and sent him tumbling over. Upon returning, he remarked to Changsheng, "I felt quite exhilarated just now after kicking that monk.
Changsheng said, "The Master must substitute for that monk and go to the Nirvana Hall yourself."

Deshan said, "Changsheng is much like a family member who dies in the east and the neighbors in the west come to offer their condolences. It would be well to give him a kick as well. Had it not been for the swift reeling in of the line, he would have nearly lost it to the herons. (By Shangfang Yi)
How great is the Old Man Xue, a hero among the Dharma! The firewood on his shoulder is presented face-to-face. If you do not recognize it before your eyes, he strikes you at once;
With a single kick of the whole body, the sack is overturned. Only when one understands does one know the burden is heavy because of the bundle of firewood;
Naturally it is heavy, and not light. Which mountain shall I report this to my fellow practitioners? A child must indeed be born of the same parents. (Fodeng Xun)

Xuefeng did not kill the monk who stepped on him; Changsheng did not raise the monk who supported him. Pity this bundle of withered, rotten vines;
they lie in disarray to this day, filling the earth with sorrow. (Xiyan Hui)

Father and son walk hand in hand into the old garden; Passing by the short fence, their bamboo hats hang down. In the thick mud there are thorns, yet no one sees them;
Only when they step upon them do they realize their feet have been pierced. (Lan’an Shu)
Xuefeng was once asked by Sansheng, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? The Master said, "I will tell you when you have emerged from the net.

Sansheng said, "A teacher of fifteen hundred people and yet you do not even recognize the point of the question! The Master said, "The affairs of this old monk’s abbotship are too many. Verse: The golden fish has passed through the net; What food does it take? If you emerge from the net, I shall speak.
Fifteen hundred disciples— Do you not know the very head of the matter? This old monk’s duties as abbot are too numerous.
The fish that swims through the net does not recognize the hook; greedy for wandering in the waves, it mistakes the floating head [of the bait] for sustenance.
To the one sitting on the high bank fishing with a lowered line in compassion—turn back the oars, gather in the line, and board the boat once more. (Fenyang Zhao)
A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net—do not say it lingers in the water. It stirs the heavens and the earth; it quivers its gills and lashes its tail.

A thousand-fathom whale rushes forth as great waves surge; with a single roar, thunder shakes and a pure breeze arises. As the pure breeze rises, who among heaven and earth knows how many such there are?
(Xuedou Xian): Zhang San sells his goods by raising the price high; Li Si returns and pays according to the market rate.
The transaction fails and they still make a fuss; Li Gong’s shop closes down all at once. (Haiyin Xin).
The aged fisherman sits upon his fishing platform; golden-scaled dragons surge forth, drumming the waves. The sea-gate is vast and empty as he casts his net;
with a single thunderclap, heaven and earth are opened. (Zhenjing Wen, 2)
Releasing and gathering, coming and going with freedom; that which is unbearable to grieve over is also fit for grief. Pity those who remain stuck in phrases and cling to words;
they argue over right and wrong until their hair turns white in vain.
A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net possesses a mechanism as swift as a flash of lightning. Do not say it lingers in the water or drags through the mud.
With a single strike of thunder amidst the blue heavens, where would the cascading torrents not overflow? (Zhenru Zhe)
Emerging from the net with clarity, he turns toward the Way and rests. Where wind and clouds meet, there is a reason for their coming.
Last night, thunder and lightning resonated in harmony; as before, they bring rain to moisten the nine provinces. (Yuantong Xian)
Seizing the waves and grasping the clouds, the momentum is as if to level the heavens; startling the void, the sudden rain pours like an overturned basin.
Had it not been for the releasing of the dikes at the Huai and He rivers, the tide-head of the nine bends would never have subsided. (Shangfang Yi)
Within the cave, there is no cloud; there is another heaven. Peach blossoms are like brocade; willows are like cotton-wool. The immortals do not concern themselves with winter or summer;
when the rocks crumble and the pines wither, it has been a year. (Wuzu Yan)
The Kun and the whale have already spread their sky-piercing wings; yet the sea-traveler still suspends his moon-fishing hook.
Disregarding the fierce, billowing waves that overturn the void, he sets sail on a single banner of favorable wind from the head of the turtle. (Fuxin Cai)
Fully dead within full life; fully alive within full death. One is a clumsy fellow; the other is a man from Fujian. (Jingshan Daoyuan).
The golden-scaled fish pierces the net, intending to swallow the boat; it has long been surging against the waves, flowing upstream. Yet it is caught by an old fisherman who idly casts his line;
following the waves and drifting with the current, it wanders aimlessly. (Gushan Gui)
[Continued Collection] The noble falcon soars toward the heavens; the cold rooster crows while still asleep. Shedding all traces of the nest, there is no partiality in speed or slowness.
Cutting off the life-root at the point of urgency, yet relaxing one’s hands and feet right before the opponent. When a drop of water freezes into ice, one fails to recognize the source;
plotting within the tent, one’s capacity is as vast as the ocean. Do you not see? The golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net has a new livelihood. The affairs of the abbot are many—laugh!
Taking a life (Chōtō Shō). Appearing and disappearing at the tips of the hundred grasses;
roaming beyond the three realms. In vain they spread nets across the heavens; in vain they cast hooks to catch giant turtles.
Shaking his scales and lashing his mane, he stirs heaven and earth. With bulging eyes and upraised head, he spouts forth great waves. A rain of blows falls as shouts drive the clouds away;
who would consent to settle their merit through strife? (Yuǎnwù Qín).
Zhang the Monkey is white; Li the Monkey is black. Hard as cotton, soft as iron. Meeting on the road, two masters of the same house.
Linji was not yet a thief who steals in broad daylight. (Duan’an Yan)
Silla’s staff and Suining’s bowl—what monk of the lineage does not possess these? When viewed as a single whole, they are pitch black;
who could possibly weigh them down to the finest fraction of a grain? (Xutang Yu)

Still not yet crossed over the sea of birth and death; conveying words and transmitting messages across thousands of leagues. With one blow, the carp of the Eastern Sea is struck down;
the deluded person is instantly awakened from their madness. (Nun Wuzhuo Zong).

Raising the staff, I strike for him; yet when a person of the highest caliber arrives, I let them pass without striking.

[Added from the Supplement] Chan Master Jiǎn of Gāotíng in Xiāngzhōu (he succeeded Dēishān). Initially, while across the river, he saw Dēishān from afar;

(Caodong) Chan Master Daoying of Yunju in Hongzhou (he was a successor of Dongshan).
Once, while a monk was reciting a sutra inside his room, the Master asked through the window, "What sutra is the Venerable One reciting? The monk replied, "The Vimalakīrti Sūtra. The Master said:
He did not ask about the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. "What sūtra is he reciting?"—by this question, the monk was able to enter [the state of realization].
The verse says:
"He does not ask about the *Vimalakīrti*, so what is he reciting? A Korean hawk flies through the clouds; The staff-head strikes, yet there is no majesty."
Ling: "Sighing over Pao-tso T’uo of Mount Song (Fo-hui Ch’üan), what he was mindful of was actually the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
Every time he brought it up, he became more refined. The parrot cannot return to its native land;
for the most part, its speech is too distinct. (Yang Wu-wei)
Question: The sutra does not ask about mindfulness; it is Vimalakīrti who possesses it. Is the bottom of this mindfulness clearly seen?
If one wishes to enter the ocean of dharmas as numerous as motes of dust, a single word suffices to expound them—there is no need for many. (Master Tianzhang of Yuezhou).
Following the wind, one was about to reach Yangzhou, when the wind shifted and the current flowed against the bow. Steering the rudder relied entirely on the strength of the three elders;
yet in an instant, they reached the shore—there is no need for worry. (The Dharma Hall is like this.)
[Continued Collection] The height of Mount Sumeru cannot be seen to its peak; the depth of the great ocean cannot be seen to its bottom.
One searches for it in vain amidst the tossing soil and rising dust, only to turn one's head and bump into one’s own ground. (Nantang Xing)
Yunju was once asked by a monk, "What is it like when the water is cut off and the wheel is stopped? The Master said, "The millstone does not turn.
He then offered this verse:
Yunju has words; the mechanism is severed. It does not turn—now you must reflect back upon it yourself. Cutting through iron, closing the gate, and stopping delusion.
Explanation: A single garden blooms with a hundred flowers; the blossoming and fruiting arise from within it.
From the ground, the stalks emerge and grow toward the azure sky. (Fenyang Shao)
Cutting off the water, the wheel stops; the talk is already complete. Borrowing the mother-in-law’s skirt to bow for New Year’s greetings.
Later generations do not see the Old Master of Yunju; they often speculate on both sides of the stone. (Foyin Yuan)

[Continued Collection] While stopping the wheel by cutting off the water, this state—my teacher knows it, yet he does not awaken to it. I shall briefly reveal a single word to bring about realization:
if one does not turn [the wheel], how could there ever be a stopping? (By Prajñā-róu).
[Added for inclusion: Yunju addressed the assembly, saying: "Twenty years ago, when I was staying at Sanfeng Hermitage, the Elder Xinghua from Weifu came and asked me:
'May I borrow a question as a preliminary probe? What do you think?
At that time, my faculties were dull and I could not provide an answer; I simply set down a question for him."
His head was extraordinary; he did not dare to fail him. Xiyun said, "I suspect the Abbot cannot answer this question.
It would be better to bow and withdraw. Looking back now, I think at that time it would have been unnecessary even to say, "Why bother?

Why must it be so? Why must it not be so? Continuous and dense—confronting the situation directly.
If there is anyone who can provide the final word, I grant that you have personally seen the two venerable masters (Dahui Zonggao).
Why must one necessarily rely on golden knives and jade rulers? That which is sweet is like bitter gall, and that which is bitter is like honey.
For twenty years, there has been no place to clear this grievance. Ehi! (Biefeng Yin).
Why need one concern whether things are square, round, curved, or straight? When the eyebrows and eyes are distinct, how could they fail to be discerned?

(Seal of the Most Profound Abode).
Why must it be so? Why need it not be so? Continuous and dense; face-to-face, seizing the opportune moment. Official horses kicking one another. (No-attainment Compassion).

The antelope hangs its horns from the peak of Mount Ou; the hunting dogs are bewildered, finding no trace.
Yet it is the old man by the side of Stone Bridge who, three thousand miles away, understands how to meet him. (Zhengjue Yi)
The antelope’s tracks vanish; six times six is thirty-six. A poor child finds ancient coins; a lean horse eats withered grain.
I tell you, seeker of the profound mystery: listen to this song of non-arising. Last night fire burned the void; today I leap forth to bathe in the water.
(Caotang Qing): The hunting dog, lost from its track, still cowers in fear; with no breath remaining, where can it be pursued?
Suddenly meeting him within the city of Zhaozhou, it remains as ever: six times six is thirty-six. (Qingchun).
[Added for inclusion] Yunju was asked by a monk from Silla: "What is it that makes it so difficult to speak of?
The Master said, "What is there that is difficult to speak of? The monk said, "Please speak of it. The Master said, "Silla, Silla. The verse says:
A Silla Monk’s Question and Answer: The Flying Cavalry General was full of martial spirit;
Seizing the spear and mounting the bandit’s horse, He brought the conflict to an end without further blade. (Suraam Chong)
This very thing is not this; it is entirely apart from this. Walking level-footed across the azure heavens, the high mountain is looked up to with reverence.
Encompassing all before one’s eyes, there is no need to vie for more; the myriad phenomena of the forest are but flowers in the eye. To strike a blow upon one's own body—Silla, Silla! (□□□).

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Yunju, "Ultimately, how should one be as a member of the monastic community? The Master said, "It is good to dwell in the mountains. The monk bowed.

The Master asked, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "Ultimately, for a member of the monastic community, amidst the realms of good and evil, birth and death, and favorable and adverse conditions, the mind remains unmoving, like a mountain. The Master then struck him, saying, "You have brought shame upon the former sages."
"I have lost my children and grandchildren. He then asked a monk standing nearby, "How do you understand this?
The monk bowed and said, "For a member of the Sangha, after all, the eyes do not look upon the colors of black and yellow, and the ears do not listen to the sounds of strings and flutes.
The Master said, "I have betrayed the former sages and lost my children and grandchildren. Huanglong Nan said, "How would you say it?"
If you can grasp a single phrase, you will not have brought shame upon the former sages nor lost your own descendants.

If you can speak it, then at every place the green mountains are none other than a site of enlightenment (dōjō). If you cannot speak it, there are cold and heat that shorten your lifespan, and there are ghosts and spirits that envy your fortune. The verse says:
Lofty and towering, ten thousand fathoms wide; no path exists on any side for passage. Since antiquity, the light of the two wheels has never reached here.
At night’s deep, the old king enters the western peak. (Touzi Qing)
Gazing in the four directions at the towering peaks and dense green shadows, the pines and wind harmonize with the rain to sound like a lute.
To dwell in the mountains, one need not flee from sounds and colors; when the hundred birds return, where shall they be sought? (Composed by Kumuk).
For the monastic community, dwelling in the mountains is ultimately best. A girl with cropped hair grows white-headed too soon. Walking through the moonlight, one passes the pines atop the ridge;
one’s traces reach the grass beneath the white clouds on the crag. Solitary and still is the foundation of an ancient temple before the peak;
at every household gate lies the road to Chang’an. Together we see the geese fly south in the eighth month; do not let this old man of the Great Peace go in vain. (Fujian Qín)

Spring comes; the stone man gazes at the distant mountains. The oriole sings among flowers and trees as the blue waves remain tranquil.
One must know that the auspicious pine on the cliff beyond the clouds Welcomes the wind for a thousand ages, enduring the cold of the year. (Touzi Qing)
[Added from another source] When Yunju was nearing the end of his life, he asked his attendant, "What date is it today? The attendant replied, "Today is the third of the month.
The Master said, "Thirty years hence, simply say, 'It is just this. Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away in peace.
The verse says:
This blind fellow, facing peril, knows no shame; Asking others for breath, he borrows their throat. Pitifully, he speaks of the third day of the month;
He is alive, yet buried head-deep in a mire of filth. (Bao Ye Yuan)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Yunju was asked by a monk: "If there is no place of learning at all, how does one establish oneself? The Master said, "There is no place to establish oneself. The monk asked, "What need is there for Buddhist activities?
The Master said, "It is not the same as Xinghua. The Verse says: No place to establish oneself; Buddhist activities are effortless. Not the same as Xinghua.
Moss covers the halls as the mist clears and purple qi swirls; the courtiers bow before the imperial dais and retire in the age of Yao.
The Phoenix Pavilion does not harbor guests from Peach Blossom Spring—how could it compare to the golden light that gazes upon the heavens of Han? (Touzi Qing)
[Supplement] Yunju was once visited by Cheng Rui, the Regional Inspector of Jingnan, who sent a high-ranking general into the mountains to present offerings.

The general asked, "The World-Honored One had secret words, which Kāśyapa did not conceal. What are these secret words of the World-Honored One? The Master called out, "Minister! The man responded, "Yes?

The Master said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said: "Secret words are not hidden; The essential meaning is right here. If you wish to know the Buddha’s intent, Look at the Minister before you."
If you do not understand, this is the World-Honored One’s secret language; if you do understand, Kāśyapa will not conceal it. The verse says: Kāśyapa does not conceal it;
he lies across his body alone and bears it himself. The meaning of the words is clearly present; from ancient times to the present, it is revealed in all its grandeur.
(Buddha-eye far-reaching, 2).
The World-Honored One’s esoteric words are difficult to conceal; Kāśyapa’s descendants see them as mere dust. For ten thousand autumns and ten thousand springs, all is dark and vast.
The scorched-tail tiger was originally a tiger.
Chan Master Caoshan Benji (who succeeded Dongshan) of Fuzhou was asked by the monk Qingrui (the name is now erroneously written as Qingxue, which is incorrect):
"I, Qingrui, have failed myself; I beg the Master for rescue. The Master said, "Venerable Qingrui, come forward.
Qingrui approached, and the Master said, "The white-housed wine of Quanzhou—three cups and yet you say it has not even wetted your lips. (*Wudeng Huiyuan*)

[The monk] falsely claimed he was a poor, destitute tax collector and begged the Master for relief. The Master called out, "Tax Collector *Ācārya*! and the man responded, "Yes. The Master said, "Qingyuan’s white family wine—after drinking three cups, you still say it hasn't even touched your lips.

Xuanjue asked, "Where did he give him wine to drink? The Verse says: The call and response were like thunderclaps; The wine was drunk, yet no trace remained. If you wish to know where the wine was given, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
Qingrui was solitary, poor, and too coarse of mind; Cao Shan took him by the hand onto the path of success. Three cups of wine from the Bai family moistened his lips;
after he was drunk, adding more cups seemed as if there were none left. (Foyin Yuan)
Qingyuan’s Bai Family Wine: Three cups have not even touched my lips; Seventy-two blows shall be lightly pardoned, But one hundred and fifty blows—hardly can I let you go. (Dizang’s grace)
A house full of gold, yet he refuses to touch it; alas, he willingly harbors resentment and remains solitary and poor. For no reason at all, he drinks three more cups of wine;
after becoming drunk, his staggering laughter is enough to kill people with mirth. (Nanhua Bing)
[Continued Collection] A Persian merchant trading by sea enters the Great Tang. First, he secretly buries precious treasures; then he comes forward to stretch out his hand and seek from others.
Alas, how can he deceive those who are experts in the trade? (Kentang Chong).
Three cups of clear poverty are a light recompense; ten thousand miles from Cao’s Gate, he emerges from Zhengzhou. He chops away the pillar in the moon with all his might;
yet the spring wind, causing such disturbance, does not cease at last. (Tiantong Jing)
Zhang’s jar and Li’s jar each have their own ailments. Red-eyed one bumps into a firebrand;
a scorched brick strikes the frozen bottom. (By Puguang Xian).
Caoshan habitually uses Baijia wine; he sets it before people and pours it out to the very dregs.
The travelers from the ten continents and the clouds and waters fall drunk, yet you, O Kalyāṇamitra, still do not wake up. (Wanshan Ning)
Ganmu encounters the marketplace and probes its depths; with eyes that distinguish dragons from snakes, he discerns the distant from the near.
When two humpbacked camels meet upon the road, there is no one in the world who can judge them with impartiality. (Tuigu Yun)
Tonggong Tang and Tie Fenghua—everyone hates them and everyone fears them. They are not people from Mingzhou;
they must surely speak the dialect of Suzhou. (Wuzhun Shanfeng)
[Added from a later collection] Once, when Jingqing asked Caoshan, "When the principle of ultimate emptiness is ultimately formless, what then?
The Master said, "The principle is indeed so; but as for the phenomenon, how is it? Jingqing said, "It is just like the principle and just like the phenomenon.
The Master said, "You may deceive Caoshan alone, but what about the eyes of all the Buddhas? Jingqing said, "If there were no eyes of the Buddhas, how [could one know]?"

The Master said, "I have realized something that is not like this. The Teacher said, "In official matters, even a needle is not permitted; in private affairs, carriages and horses pass through freely.
The Verse says: "Not like this—how groundless! Caoshan willingly allowed himself to be deceived by Jingqing. As for suchness, principle, and phenomena—who understands them?"
Ultimately formless, it is also a great difficulty. It is also a great difficulty. Everyone, all you sages, look before your very eyes.
(Fang’an Xian) Before the vast chaos was yet divided, there was no distinction between the distant and the near; ultimately, it is impossible to differentiate between phenomena and principle.
At midnight, it is perfectly luminous yet remains unrevealed—the iron Kunlun Mountain behind the Diamond King’s head. (Xueyan Qin)

[Added for inclusion] A monk asked Caoshan, "The student is sick all over; I beg the Master to treat me. The Master said, "I will not treat you. The monk asked, "Why will you not treat me? The Master said, "I will let you seek life and find no life;

seek death and find no death. The Verse says: The whole body is illness— Who can cure it? If you try to seek life, you cannot find it; If you try to seek death, you cannot find it. When you have neither life nor death, Then you see the Buddha-nature. If you wish to know the meaning of this, Look at the man on the mountain peak.
Since birth and death can no longer be sought, the myriad ailments of the faculties and their objects have all ceased. From this point on, all is empty and revealed alone:
a single orb of the moon in the clear autumn (Xuedou Zong).

[Added for Collection] A monk asked Caoshan, "A student brings his uncut jade to the Master; I pray the Master will polish it. The Master said, "I do not polish it. The monk asked, "Why do you not polish it?

The Master said, "You must know that Caoshan is a master craftsman. The Verse says: A single word from the Master’s mouth, Like a sword cutting through the air. If you wish to see the true man, Look at the one who does not polish.
Embracing the raw jade, he comes to the master with deep intent; on a narrow path, they suddenly meet.
Who would have known that the master’s hand does not toil at carving? He splits apart the myriad peaks of Mount Hua. (Xiaoweng Kan).
[Added from another source] Once, when the Wayfarer of the Paper Robe came to visit Caoshan, the Master said, "Are you not the Wayfarer of the Paper Robe?
He replied, "I dare not say so. The Master asked, "What is the matter beneath the paper robe? He replied, "As soon as the single cloak is hung upon the body..."
"Everything is exactly as it is. The Master asked, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? The man stepped forward, responded with an "Amen," and then stood there naked.
The Master patted him on the back and said, "You only know how to go like that; why do you not know how to come like that?
The man suddenly opened his eyes and asked, "When the one spiritual true nature does not rely upon the womb, [how does it manifest]?"
"How is it? The Master said, "Not yet wonderful. [The monk] asked, "What is wonderful? The Master said, "Do not borrow from others.
Having said this, he paid his respects and passed away. The Master presented a verse, saying: "The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous, the formless body;
Do not falsely seek intimacy through intellectual views. When thoughts differ, one is obscured from the profound essence; When the mind deviates, it does not dwell as a neighbor to the Way."
Sentiments cause the myriad dharmas to sink into the realm before one; consciousness, with its many facets, loses the original truth.
If you can fully understand and realize these words, you will clearly see that you are the person of old, free from all affairs. The Verse says:
Wrapped in hemp and bound in paper like an infant; a blue lotus blooming within the fire. A single point of numinous light endures for a thousand ages;
the solitary lunar orb borrows a womb. (Nantang Xing, 3)
Exhausting the body and toiling the bones, one knows not of spring; attaining the meaning and forgetting the words, one immediately transcends the mundane.
Without relying on a womb and without borrowing from others, the golden crow emerges from the sea and the moon leaves the clouds.
The matter beneath the paper robe does not rely on a womb; letting go at the precipice, one is but an infant in swaddling clothes.
At the assembly of Nirvāṇa, the site of enlightenment opens; the single transmission and direct pointing brings forth the Crown Prince.

[Added to the Collection] A monk asked Caoshan, “What is it like when the bright moon is suspended in the sky? The Master said, “He is still a man standing on the steps. The monk said, “I ask the Master to lead him up the steps.

The Master said, “Come see me after the moon has fallen. The Verse says: The bright moon is suspended in the sky; He is still a man on the steps below. When the moon has fallen, come and meet me; Then you will know the meaning of the Buddha’s Way.
The bright moon hangs in the sky, yet has not entered the pass; falling flowers and flowing water have no concern for one another.
This clear, single phrase transcends both the mundane and the sacred; when light and objects are both forgotten, who can perceive it? (□□□).
Standing in the bright moonlight, he poses a question; ascending the steps, he becomes increasingly coarse and vague. One must wait for the moon to fall before meeting again;
there is another spiritual light that makes one’s gallbladder shiver with cold. (Zai-an Xian)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Once, when Jingqing asked Caoshan, "What is it like when moss grows upon the path of the mind? The Master said, "It is difficult to find such a person.

Jingqing said, "I do not understand where this person goes. The Master said, "They only know that moss grows upon the path of the mind; they do not know where they go. The Verse says: The path of the mind is overgrown with moss;
How can one find such a person? They only know the moss upon the path; They do not know where they go.
Moss grows upon the heart’s surface; where has it gone? The family of the Xies is not at home on the fishing boat.
Ten thousand acres of reeds fill the vast expanse of water and sky; White birds settle deep, turning and circling as they please. (Zidehui)
Moss grows upon the heart’s diameter, its departure unknown. The mouth resembles the nose; the eyes resemble the brows. Far, far beyond the kalpas, the boundaries are vast.
The bright moon and the reeds—though similar, they are not identical. (Closing the room, opening it.)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Caoshan, "When snow covers the thousand mountains, why is the solitary peak not white? The Master said, "You must know there is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary.

The monk asked, "What is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary? The Master said, "It does not fall into the colors of the myriad mountains. Verse: Snow covers the thousand peaks, yet the solitary crag remains unwhite; One must realize there is the extraordinary within the extraordinary. How is it the extraordinary within the extraordinary? It does not fall into the hues of the myriad mountains.
Snow covers the thousand mountains, obscuring the paths; the solitary peak remains unwhite, towering and majestic.
Though the young lords of the Five Tombs may swell with pride, the wild old man meets them without a frown. (Pak Ong-hyeom)
They cannot be mixed; their kinds are not uniform. The six lines wind and turn to reveal the double *li* hexagram.
At night deep, looking down upon a thousand mountains white—none who are not people of its midst would know this. (Moon over Shixi).
In these words, both sides carry a profound mystery; they exhaustively discern and rectify everything within speech.
Alas, this solitary royal highway is neglected, lost in the vastness before the bright moon. (Jue'an Xiang)
[Added for inclusion] Caoshan asked Jinfeng Zhi, "What have you been doing? He replied, "I have been building a house. The Master said, "Is it finished yet? He replied, "This side is finished.

The Master said, "What about that side? He replied, "I shall inform the Master on the day the work begins. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. The Verse says: The house is finished, yet the work continues; The path is clear, yet the traveler still wanders. When the day comes to report the beginning, The Master’s seal is already upon him.
The whirling adze that creates the wind is the marvel of Master Shi; the towering pines and cypresses rising from the ravine possess the form of great beams for pillars and rafters.

Discerning the measure within the school, knowing the opportune moment beyond it—here and there, every step is flawless. Moving across the plate without fixed course, they are like radiant, falling pearls. (Yungeng Jing).

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Caoshan, “What is it like when one sits upright and perfectly still? The Master said, “One cannot see the body. The monk asked, “Is there still any function? The Master said, “The very moment you speak of sitting is itself function.

One must not shift mountains or block the sea; speaking of Chan or speaking of the Way is not what constitutes function. Verse: When sitting upright and perfectly still, The body cannot be seen. If you ask whether there is still function, The moment you speak of sitting is itself function.
Do not shift mountains or block the sea— Speaking of Chan or speaking of the Way Is not what constitutes true function.
Do not say that the principle of unity is one of empty vacuity; if you claim it is empty vacuity, you will lose your very body.
It is as if the eyebrows were to ask the eyes: how could the dark pupil see its own iris? (Benjue I)
