What can be said of the cold hues upon a thousand peaks? Snow piled upon frost, the ice so thick and slippery.
If one were to encounter the warm laws of music blown by Zou Yang, the flowers on the crags would surely not wait for the harmony of spring. (Yang Woei-wei)
A thousand peaks gather cold hues, heaped with azure; raindrops fall upon rock-flowers, shining bright before the eyes.
If you ask for the essential meaning within this, do not mistake the cry of a crane for the song of a warbler. (Benjue I)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Xuedou, “The mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the stream water is as clear as indigo.
Why is it that within the student’s own sphere, one does not understand? The Master said, “Staring with eyes wide open inside a withered tree.
The monk said, “If that is so, then one discerns the field by its sprouts, and recognizes the person by their words. The Master said, “Thirty blows of the staff—wait for another time.”
The Verse says:
A single withered blade of grass, vainly used to hide one's shame; A bright mirror facing the window, illuminating every hidden corner.
With a face full of embarrassment, he takes a step back; Before such radiant clarity, there is no way to avoid it. (Baizhang Yuan)
[Added for Collection] Xuedou’s Verse on the Two Gates of Changing the Tracks: "The kalpa-fire once blazed forth; the wooden man shed tears first. How pitiable is Master Fatu!
Everywhere he lost his pavilions and towers. One, the ancient adept De-yun, how many times did he descend from the peak of Mt.
Miaofeng? He calls out to that deluded sage, carrying snow together to fill the well. (2) Before the Patriarchs and Buddhas were born...
Previously, the drum smeared with lethal poison was already struck; who now would delight in hearing it? Please try to resolve this contradiction.
(3) It winds and turns, winding and turning again; let the true gold cease its hundred refinements. Having lost Vaiśālī, there is no one who knows how to look at the arrow. (4) The verse says:
Kāśyapa listened to the zither and rose to dance; Yuanming heard the bell and frowned. Ceasing his plowing in a cramped room, he sat upright;
through half the window, the cold sun shone radiantly. (Xutang Yu)

The wind sweeps away the floating clouds until they are gone; the azure sky is utterly free of a speck of dust. Mountains and rivers are both before one’s eyes—what need is there to ascend a high terrace? (Gelu Tan)

[Added for collection] Xuedou’s verse says: Three parts of one’s life have already passed; The single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished. Vexed by daily pursuits, one rushes toward birth and death; When called back, one does not turn—what can be done? Verse: Three parts of one’s life have already passed;
The single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished. Vexed by daily pursuits, one rushes toward birth and death; When called back, one does not turn—what can be done?
Karmic consciousness is vast and boundless; there is no foundation upon which to rely. *Du!* Alas, you deluded fellow! To go on just like this—(Kengtang Chong).
A scale-weight split by a saw, a stone pillar fried in oil. Held up with both hands: reward those who have merit—(Qian’an Ren).
Wu Chancai said: "Old man Xuedou is coarse and clumsy; he is blunt and uncouth.
Even if you were to study him for another thirty years, you still would not understand Zen. Nevertheless, though this is so, the land is vast and the people are few;
let us try to provide a commentary on this. He then spoke in verse:
The three eyes of Maheśvara are blinded; north, south, east, and west, the paths cannot be distinguished. Leaves fall from a thousand forests, yet no one sweeps them up;
alone at the pine gate, he stretches his legs and sleeps.
[Added for Collection] While Xuedou was seated with Chief Censor Li, a scholar and a Daoist arrived at the monastery. Chief Censor Li asked, "Among the three teachings, which is the most noble?

The Master stood with his body slightly turned to the side and his hands folded. Chief Censor Li said, "You have a mouth; why do you not speak? The Master replied, "It is difficult to speak in the presence of the Master.

The Verse says: The three teachings stand before one like mountains. The moon shines clearly upon the water. If you wish to know the meaning of the ancient sages, Look at the face of the man from Shu.
Before the Five Elders Peak lies the foundation of an ancient observatory; the Old Lord was originally one with Śākyamuni.
In times of hardship, we can only share the same incense and lamps; do not listen to others' slanders or praise. (Nantang Xing)
[Added to the Collection] A monk asked Xuedou, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Surrounded on all four sides by mountains.
The Verse says: A mad dog chasing a clod; a blind donkey chasing a herd. I permit only myself to know it; I do not permit others to understand it. (Nanhuabing)

[Added from another collection] A monk asked Xuedou, "What is one who is above all Buddhas? The Master said, "White clouds cover the green mountains. The monk asked, "Is this not where you, the Master, act for the sake of others?

The Master said, "In the clear water, the lotuses grow in vain. The Verse says: White clouds cover the green mountains; In the clear water, the lotuses grow in vain. If you wish to know the person above all Buddhas, Look at the autumn moon shining on the river.
Layer upon layer of snow peaks, deep and lush like emerald lattices; A wind arises from the cold ridges, binding thick clouds together. Last night the vermilion phoenix soared toward the Milky Way;
At dawn, it listens as the woodcutters pursue the flocks of wild geese. (Touzi Qing)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Xuedou asked Dalong: "Neither the speaker nor the silent one is it. The Verse says:
The three armies do not move, yet the banners flash; Upon the battlefield of dragons and snakes, one observes the stratagems.
It makes one long remember General Li, As a solitary eagle soars through ten thousand miles of clear sky. (Feng of Fuan)

Suddenly, the iron mace strikes like a swift wind; all the flowers before one’s eyes vanish. (Baizhang Yuan).
He smashed the skulls and pounded out the joints of the bones; before those with clear eyes, he exposed his own ugliness and clumsiness. (Muan Yong). [Added by collection:
Chan Master Congyi of Tianping in Xiangzhou (he was a successor of Qingxi Jin). When the Master arrived at Xiyan, he would often say to himself:
"Let alone people who understand the Dharma of the Buddhas—there is not even a single person to be found who can raise a koan. Upon hearing this, Xiyan...
[The Master] remained silent. On another day, as the Master was ascending the Dharma Hall, the Abbot summoned him from the side.
The Master raised his head; the Abbot said, "Wrong. The Master stepped forward three or two paces; the Abbot said again, "Wrong. The Master approached further;
the Abbot said, "Those two previous 'wrongs'—was it the Senior Monk’s fault, or was it the old fellow Ximing’s fault? The Master replied, "It was Congyi’s fault. The Abbot [laughed].
He said, "Mistake! Mistake! Then he said, "Venerable Elder, stay here for the summer retreat; let us deliberate together on these two mistakes. The Master refused and departed.
Later, while residing at Tianping Mountain in Xiangzhou, he would frequently cite the previous dialogue, saying:
"When I was traveling as a mendicant, I was blown by a malignant wind to Ruizhou. There was an elder there, the West Court Abbot, who examined me..."
"Two errors have already followed one after the other. Stay here for the summer retreat; let us deliberate together.
I do not say that it was an error at that time. Had I known it was an error when I first set out for the South, I would have known it then.
Shoushan Nian said, "According to Tianping’s understanding, he has not yet seen Xiyuan in his dreams. Why?
The old story remains. The verse says:
"The Chan practitioners love frivolity; Though they fill their bellies with inquiry, it proves useless. How laughable, how laughable! Old Tianping!"
"Who would have thought that at first I regretted traveling on foot? A mistake, a mistake! Xiyuan’s pure breeze suddenly melts away. He further said:
"Suppose a monk were to come out and say, 'A mistake!'—Xuedou’s mistake, how does it compare to Tianping’s mistake? (Xuedou Xian).
Letting down the cable to launch the boat; sticking to old rules while tuning the strings. Distant water cannot save from a nearby fire;
a short rope cannot reach the deep spring. Tianping Laotaohu was careless; for his two mistakes, he regretted his travels. The vast earth stretches on, filling people with sorrow.
Without the sinews in one's eyes, one remains poor for a lifetime. (Yuanwu Keqin)
He calls out and I respond; he spits and I peck. Hearing as if not hearing, taking error for error.
The diamond eye has been exchanged for a *huangzi* bead. Whether one understands or does not understand, it is all entirely an error. (Fujian Qin).
The two are brought together, yet in the end they do not unite; consequently, the paths of north and south diverge.
Later, one exhausts every word of explanation and distinction—half is thinking of you, half is resenting you. (Yunna Qing)

(Cao-Dong) [Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Jingxuan of Taiyang in Yingzhou (successor of Liangshan Guan). A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style? He replied, "A full pitcher cannot be emptied; the great earth has no hungry people.
The Verse says: A full pitcher cannot be emptied; The great earth has no hungry people. If you wish to know the master’s house style, Look at the clouds and mist rising from the mountain peaks.
What need is there to distinguish the beautiful jade of Mount Jing? There is no use picking up the dark pearl from the Red Water.
Wangxiang was heartless, yet the Yellow Emperor valued him; Bian He possessed wisdom, yet the King of Chu detested him. (Danxia Chun)
[Added from another source] Tàiyáng Xuán asked Liángshān, "What is the formless site of enlightenment?
Shān pointed to Guānyīn and said, "This is a painting by Wú Dàozǐ. As the Master was about to offer a word in response, Shān hurriedly asked, "This one has form;
which one is formless? The Master attained realization and prostrated himself. Shān said, "Why..."
"Is it not right to speak even a single phrase? The Master said, "I would not decline to speak, but I fear it would take up too much paper and brush.
Daoshan smiled and said, "This very phrase shall be inscribed upon a stele. The verse says:
The path ends at a precipitous cliff; he asks an old mountain man. The man points elsewhere, saying: "To the west of the crags, on the eastern ridge.
As he prepares to advance, mist descends and the mountain mists grow heavy. Turning his head, he suddenly beholds the crimson sun. (Touzi Qing)
Ultimate emptiness is signless and transcends names and forms. What is established is subtle; what is painted is coarse. To speak of it is not to refuse ascending the paper.
The bearded monk from the Western Heaven has no mustache or beard. (Zhi Hongjian).
(Chanyuan) [Supplement] National Teacher Deshao of Mount Tiantai (who succeeded Chanyuan) addressed the assembly, saying: "The green creeper winds its way straight up to the summit of the cold pine;

the white clouds linger lightly, appearing and disappearing within the great void. All dharmas are fundamentally at ease; it is only man who makes a fuss. Verse: The green creeper climbs the cold pine; White clouds drift through the vast sky.
All phenomena are inherently still; It is only man who creates the clamor.
These [words] are the manifestation of compassion for you; his tongue drags the ground as his voice rolls like thunder. Vines and tangles fill the earth, with no one to prune them;
once again, the spring wind leaves everything in disarray. (By Zhuwu Jian)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] National Teacher Shao addressed the assembly, saying: "The summit of Tongxuan Peak is not of this human world;
outside the mind there is no dharma—before one's eyes are the green mountains. A verse says:
Outside the mind, there has never been a single dharma; yet the National Teacher’s point of view was not yet intimate.
If one says that the green mountains filling the eyes are it, by clinging to them, the dust of the eyes arises once more. (Wuyinjian)
[Added for inclusion: Chan Master Taiqin Fading of Qingliang in Jinling (he was a successor of the Fa’yan lineage).
The Master asked a monk, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The monk said, “Neither east nor west. The Master did not approve. The monk then asked [the Master]:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Neither east nor west. The monk then grasped the essential point and composed a verse:
"The Patriarch's intent in coming from the West is neither east nor west; Monkeys and birds, in the depths of spring, embrace the trees and cry out. How many travelers pass by in vain lamentation!"
Gazing afar, the green mountains rise solitary and high, while the white clouds hang low.

(By Baoning Yong) Neither east nor west—a single phrase held in its entirety. Soft as cast iron, yet hard as soft mud. Needles have been cast, yet one is still unskilled at reading the water in the bowl;
the film has been scraped away, yet the golden lancet is used once more. Clouds lock the ancestral mountain, the path home cut off; turning one's head, one laughs at Du Fu.
The Cuckoo Cries (Kentang Chong).
[Appendix] Monk Yunju Qi was serving as the Librarian (Zhizang) within the assembly of Master Faideng. One day, Faideng said to the Master:
Someone asked me about the meaning of [the Master’s] coming from the West. I answered him, "Neither East nor West. How do you understand this, Librarian?
The Master replied, "Neither East nor West. Dēng said, "Even understanding it thus, how can you attain it?
[The Librarian] said, "Dàozǐ simply says so; I wonder what your own venerable intention is, Reverend Sir? Dēng said, "That family of their own..."
"The child and grandchildren are present. The Master suddenly clarified its essential meaning with this verse: "Receiving beings and benefiting life is most exquisite;
External offspring are ultimately unworthy. Each house has its own children and grandchildren; When brought forth, they are used exactly as needed."
The Verse says:
"The family has its own descendants; The ancestral fields and gardens are not loved.
In a single kṣaṇa, the livelihood of a lifetime— Bought at the eastern end, sold at the western. (Dahong En)
When someone asks about the meaning of the Patriarch who came from the West, Master Deng replies: "It is neither east nor west; his own descendants already exist.
For the most part, people follow the words and thereby become lost themselves. (Benjue I)
Chan Master Xuance of Baoen Monastery in Jinling (he was a successor of Fayan).
Initially, he asked Qingfeng, "What is the student’s own self? Feng replied, "The child of fire comes seeking fire. Later, he visited Fayan.
Yanguan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Qingfeng. Yanguan asked, "What words did Qingfeng speak? The Master recounted the previous dialogue.
Yanguan asked, "How do you understand this, Senior? The Master said, "'The element of Bing-Ding belongs to fire,' yet he seeks fire further;
it is like seeking oneself by means of oneself. Yanguan said, "Even if you understand it thus, how can that suffice?"
The Master said, "I am just like this; I do not know how you, Reverend, are. Baizhang said, "Ask me, and I will tell you. The Master asked, "What is the student’s own self?

Baizhang said, "A child of the fire element comes seeking fire. At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. Verse: The child of the fire element comes seeking fire; The fire is already there within his own hand. If he had not been able to recognize it himself, How could he have known it was right before his eyes?
At first he weighed eight *liang*; then he weighed it again and it was exactly half a *jin*. In whose hand does the zero-point of the scale rest?
To contend over a mere hair’s breadth is truly strange! (Baizhang Yuan).
Seeking fire under the stems Bing and Ding, one finds it within one’s own person; The Dharma-eye travels the ancient path of Mount Qingfeng. Reaching the end of the water, one knows the limit;
Sitting and watching the clouds rise, one sees one’s whole life. (Zhaojue Zong)
Seeking fire in the directions of Bing and Ding, he asks Qingfeng; how can one endure this hound chasing after clods? Fortunately, Qingliang applied the essential point to break through it;
with a single clap of thunder, he was transformed into a dragon. (Dahong Su).
The question is clear and the answer is direct; at Blue Peak, the eight characters open the gate wide.
Every single thing is a possession of my own house—why must one ask for the way again when standing at the crossroads? (Fodeng Xun)
[Continuation] The Boy Bingding comes seeking fire. He asks again: "The blazing flames scorch the face-gate.
The Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future—do not depart from within this as they turn the wheel of Dharma. (Yiyu Chuan)
"The lad Bingding comes seeking fire. Since Bingding in the south also belongs to the element of fire, what can the Master who brandishes his sword do?
This is merely the thought within your own mind. (Wan’an Yan)
Once again, I have stumbled drunk before the Jade Tower; my hair is disheveled, my hairpins askew, and my speech and laughter are wild. Most grievous is that place which breaks one’s heart:
borrowing my neighbor’s robe to bow in greeting for the New Year. (Wan Shan Ning)
What was seen before was not real; what is seen now is not false. After three transcriptions, "wu" and "an" become "ma. (From the *Bǎoyèyuán*).
Chan Master Dàoqián, the founder of Yongming in Hangzhou (who succeeded Fayan), first visited Fayan.

Fayan asked, "Aside from your formal inquiries and requests for instruction, what sutra are you studying? The Master replied, "The *Avataṃsaka*. Fayan said, "The General and the Particular, the Same and the Different..."
[The student] asked, "To which category do the six aspects of formation and destruction belong? The Master said, "All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are fully endowed with the six aspects.
[The student] asked, "Does emptiness also possess the six aspects? The Master had no reply. [The student] said, "Why do you not ask [me]?
The Master then asked in return, "Does emptiness possess the six aspects? [The student] said, "Emptiness. Thereupon, the Master attained enlightenment. [The student] asked, "How did you do it?"
At a gathering, the Master said, "Empty. Yan nodded in agreement. The verse says: "Empty, empty—no front or back.
Picked up, suddenly it becomes two pieces. Carried to the corner of Nanping Mountain, Few have seen it through ten thousand autumns.
Do you wish to see it? (He strikes a circular shape with his whisk and says: The golden crow flies upon the crystal."
Crystal Hall. (Duanqiao Lun). *The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases in the Chan School*, Volume Thirty-Seven.
*The Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases in the Chan School*, Volume Thirty-Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Baoen Guangxiao Chan Temple in Chizhou, Song Dynasty;
continued by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Temple during the Shaoxing era of the Yuan Dynasty. *Ancestors’ Occasions for Inquiry* (Zushi Jiyuan).
The Eleventh Generation after the Sixth Patriarch, Part One (The Tenth Generation after Nanyue) (Linji): Chan Master Chiming Chuyuan of Shishuang in Tanzhou (Successor of Fenyang).

A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Water flowing from high ground. The Master himself composed a verse on this: Water flows from high ground; The moon shines upon the water. The old man’s face is revealed; The child’s heart is clear. The wind blows through the pines; The clouds part to reveal the sky. If you wish to know the Buddha, Look at the water and the moon.
Water flowing from a high plateau—how truly marvelous! Even a Zen practitioner who does not understand this will have his eyes go numb.
If you have not yet clarified the phrase regarding mud and water, the lanterns and the pillars are all laughing.
Cimeng causes water to gush forth from the high plateau; Zen monks from all under heaven run like smoke.
They hear only the clear sound coming to their ears, unaware that it flows and falls before some distant peak. (Zhengjue Yi)
Water flows from the high plateau; the wind turns the waves like silver. I unroll my brush to compose this brief verse, to speak as a reminder upon the sash within a dream. (Cuiyan Zhen)
It breaks through the roots of clouds and hurls forth rocks; cold and clear, it falls from the towering heights for a thousand ages.
Without yet clearly understanding its intent to flow toward the sea, listen as the thunder shakes the earth deep in spring. (Wuwei Shanxiu)

High plateaus where waters gush forth under the clear dawn sky; responding to questions as they arise—how could this be mere chance? The patch-robed monks do not know where they have drifted and fallen;
they seek out withered trees amidst the smoke of broken mountain streams. (Dizang’s Grace)

[Continued Collection] Piercing through clouds and bursting through rocks, he does not shrink from toil; in general, his departure and arrival are sublime. How could mountain streams and ravines retain him?
In the end, he returns to the great ocean to become its waves and tides. (Xueyan Qin)
Water flows from the high plateau, its waves lashing against the heavens. In the four quarters and above and below, all dust and smoke have ceased.
Clearly, this is a truly excellent message; yet it seems few people of this age reach that realm. (Gao Feng Miao)

The heat departs and the cold arrives; spring follows autumn. The setting sun goes west as the waters flow east. Where now are the warhorses of the general?
Wild grasses and idle flowers fill the earth with sorrow. (Xiatang Yuan)
Four or five hundred lanes of flowers and willows; two or three thousand towers of pipes and strings.
Even if there were empty fields to occupy, they would not be for planting flowers or kicking the breath-ball. (Huantang Ren)
The home mountain points out that the way is not far: ten thousand fathoms of towering peaks pierce the azure heavens.
A single sheet of white cloud spans the mouth of the valley; how many returning birds lose their nests? (Shui’an I)
A single spear and a lone horse emerge from Fenyang; truly, he proves his commander’s prowess. A basin of water and straw sandals lie across the chamber;
he slays men without ever meeting a blade’s edge. (Wuji Pai)
The lanterns and whips pass through the midst of a hundred flowers; how much elegance and refinement there is! The unexamined scholar peeks at them with longing eyes;
what can he do with the old sorrows filling his breast? (Lun of Duqiao)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] When Ciming was among the assembly, he went to Master Zhi’s quarters. As Zhi sat there opening a small box and taking incense into his hand, intending to burn it, the Master asked, "How do you burn it?
Zhi then placed it into the incense burner to burn. The Master said, "You clumsy fellow! You’ve gone off like that again. The Verse says:

When the incense smoke rises, the fragrance fills the ten directions; The old man’s nostrils are pierced through. If you wish to know the source of this matter, Look at the face of the one who has no eyebrows.
A thousand people and ten thousand travelers walk a single path. How many move their bodies without moving a step? Facing one another, they take up incense burners to offer upon the altar;
yet these clumsy fellows go on just as they are. (Baizhang Yuanwen).

[Added for inclusion] Once, when a monk asked Ciming, "What is the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas? the Master said, "The silver moon first emerges from the sea; where would it not be clearly visible? Verse: The silver moon first emerges from the sea; Where would it not be clearly visible?
If you can see it right now, Then you will know the ancestral style of the Buddhas.
The silver hare emerges from the sea, its light shining without partiality. Everywhere it is clearly manifest—who could it be? There is no need for further greetings upon meeting;
let it be scorched by the sun and fanned by the wind. (Gao Feng Miao)

[Supplement] On a winter day, Ciming posted this character on the Sangha Hall: 𠕋 (composed of two circles, two twos, three, and the "ji" radical; below it, the "san" radical with a "tian" radical and the "shui" radical). Beneath it, he wrote:
"If one recognizes this, one is never apart from the four modes of deportment. When the Head Seat saw it, he said:
The Abbot dismissed the evening session today. When the Master heard this, he laughed. He then offered this verse:
"Before the Hall of the Buddha-Selecting, a brilliant blaze; Clearly manifest is a Daoist’s sword.
Truly, as the Head of the Hall dismisses the evening session, The words of the Chief Seat reveal a divine vision. (By Nanyun)
Painting below, painting above; painting short, painting long. Clearly revealed and broadly deliberated—how does this compare to the "Great Yellow" (rhubarb) produced in the capital? (Yuetting Chung)

With a cloth bag for a pillow, one attains the freedom of deep sleep; let others’ things clamor and chatter as they will.
Wearing coarse clothes and eating plain food, one has no further concerns; who cares whether the sun rises over Fusang? (Haiyin Xin)
[Added to the Collection] Because a monk asked Ciming, "What is the Immovable Honored One? the Master said, "It cannot be lifted.
The Verse says:
The Immovable Honored One cannot be lifted; Vast and boundless is the universe—who can fathom it? Upon the clear autumn river, the night moon is bright and serene.

The egret flies into the reeds. (Gao Feng Miao). [Added from another collection. Once, when a monk asked Ciming, "What is it like when one travels on foot and meets no one? the Master said, "The ripples of the fishing line on the water. The verse says: The egret flies into the reeds. A solitary fisherman sits alone in his boat. The autumn moon shines upon the clear waves; The night wind blows across the vast sky. When the mind is empty and the body is still, One naturally enters the realm of the Buddhas and patriarchs. If you do not understand this at once, How can you avoid being deceived by the weeds? The aged and decrepit Ciming points the way for the lost; his fishing line ripples the water, manifesting myriad functions.
People of this age greedily gaze at the white reeds, failing to see the sand gulls flying across the shore. (Shitenn Kū)

[Added for inclusion] Ciming asked Yangqi, "When Mazu saw Master Xiangruo, he attained enlightenment immediately. Tell me, where exactly did his delusion lie? Yangqi replied, "To attain enlightenment is easy;

to remain deluded is difficult. The verse says: To awaken is easy, But to remain deluded is hard. If you seek the source of the mind, You will find it nowhere at all. The ancient mirror is bright and clear; How could there be any darkness? If you wish to see the moon, Do not look at its reflection in the water.
To awaken is easy; to remain deluded is difficult. If one does not penetrate it down to the finest hair, a mere inch separates one from a thousand mountains.
Talking of food will never satisfy one’s hunger; only by putting on clothes can one ward off the cold. I recall the words once spoken at Mount Wutai:
"Three times three before, and three times three after. (Yuánwù Qín)
For a patch-robed monk, awakening is easy, but remaining deluded is difficult; countless fishermen have lost their fishing rods.
It is still tolerable to turn iron into gold, but to turn gold into iron is utterly senseless. (Biefeng Yin)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Ciming was once asked by Prince Li: "I have heard that there is a golden-haired lion in Xihe; is this so?
The Master said, "From where did you, Prince, receive this news? Prince Li let out a shout. The Master said, "A jackal howling. Prince Li shouted again.

The Master said, "The lion's roar. The Verse says: The golden-haired lion roars, The jackal howls in response. If one can distinguish them clearly, One will not be deceived by the sounds of the wild foxes.
The wind blows against, and the wind blows with. With iron eyes and copper pupils, who dares to peer?
The moon in the empty realm of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool—only after dredging it again and again shall one finally know it. (Gao Feng Miaoyan)
[Added from another collection] Ciming asked Senior Monk Xianying, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Where were you during the summer retreat?
He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Where were you last summer? He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Where were you the summer before that?
He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "And where were you the summer prior to that? He replied, "Why [do you ask]?"
[The Master] acknowledged the remark. The Master said, "I am unable to examine you myself. Let the servant in the storehouse examine you;
meanwhile, have a cup of tea prepared to moisten your parched lips. The Verse says:
A scorched brick strikes one who is frozen to the marrow; Red-Eye bumps into a firebrand.
As long as the General possesses a fine reputation, why need he be enfeoffed as a Marquis of Ten Thousand Households? (Shitian Xun).

An eighty-year-old old man wearing embroidered boots, treads open the deep cavern with a laugh; bystanders point him out, forgetting to return home.

"One mu of land; three snakes and nine rats. The goods are priced correctly; the money is full amount. (Yinkong Sǒu).
[Added from another source] Chan Master Huìjué of Lángyá Mountain in Chūzhōu (successor of Fényáng) ascended the hall and said:
"All of you who have spent the summer retreat here with me—I shall point out five kinds of illnesses for you. First, you must not head toward the myriad..."
1. Depart from places where there is not even an inch of grass. 2. Do not dwell alone on a solitary peak. 3. Do not draw bows or set arrows. 4.
Do not seek refuge outside of phenomena. 5. Do not stagnate in the realms of birth and death. Why is this?
If one is obstructed in even one of these areas, it is difficult to save oneself. If one is unimpeded in all five, one is called a true guide. You all—
"O people, if you travel to various regions and encounter a master of clear vision who acts as a true practitioner, convey this message to me, so that the ancestral wind may not fall into ruin.
As for those who are merely ordinary followers, they should simply cease their efforts.
Why do you display all manner of finery in a land where the body is stripped bare? I suspect you are utterly ignorant of the times. The verse says:
The cricket treads upon both ends of its trap. The mute man has a dream and laughs to himself. Laughing until dawn, to whom could he tell it?
A crow understands how to cry out like a qilin. (Zhengtang’s Discernment)
Langya pointed out five kinds of illness; though the world’s skilled physicians find it difficult to prescribe the medicine, I shall smash them all for you right here and now.
To prolong one’s life, why need one rely on the nine-reversion elixir? (Muzhou of Shaoshi)

Seeing existence and non-existence; turning the hand back and covering with the hand. A man from Mount Langya does not fall behind Gautama.

The scale-weight, sawn apart, has no seams or cracks; it is blown by the wind and scorched by the sun from morning until night.
Although one is not permitted to engage in random deliberation, let it be freely lifted up and carried throughout the world. (Baizhang Yuanwen).
Sawed apart like a plummet, stars fly and lightning whirls; pulled from the left and pulled from the right, it falls into seven or eight pieces.
Sometimes it lands on the ground, obstructing people’s passage; though the Great Compassionate One with a thousand eyes cannot see it (Buddha-huiquan).
The saw-cutting scale-weight is entirely like iron; Old Guyu once spoke too much. The water flowing down the ravine is far too busy;
the clouds atop the ridge peak are never at rest. (Gushan Gui)
When asked, "How is it, Buddha? the Master immediately replied: "A scale-weight split with a saw; beyond words, he ferries the deluded across. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] Grasping the golden whip, he strikes the iron ox; he roams at will throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Meeting him upon the banks of the Ganges sands, he nods his head in silent understanding without a word. (Baoning Yong)
"Sawing apart a scale-weight" is from a poem by Old Du [Dù Fǔ]. "The fragrant rice, pecked at by parrots;
the azure paulownia, where the phoenix has grown old in its branch. (Huáyù, the Head Seat Xuàn).
The blood from the sawing of the scale-weight drips drop by drop; has the root of doubt regarding birth and death been severed?
This is no mere child’s play. (Pak-ung Hyeon)

The complete mechanism of killing and giving life is presented face-to-face. Everyone gathers together to eat a ladle of congee.
Later generations do not understand this meaning; they merely wander aimlessly about picking up firewood. (Songyuan Yue)
Suffering within pleasure, pleasure within suffering; the Great Tang beats its drums while Silla dances. Hanshan burns fire, his head covered in ash;
he laughs instead at Fenggan for riding a tiger backward. (Shi’an Si)
Hard as cotton, yet soft as iron; those who drink water must beware of choking.
How laughable—the old fool at the riverbank, who until now has been practicing cleverness only to end up clumsy. (From *Kuchan Jing*).
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Quanju of Fahua Monastery in Shuzhou (a successor of Fenyang). He arrived at the place of Master Langye Huijue.
Langye asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The Master replied, "The Two Zhe regions. [Langye] asked, "By boat or by land? The Master replied, "..."
A boat arrived. [The Master] asked, "Where is the boat? The Master said, "Underfoot. [The Guest] asked, "How do you express the phrase that does not involve traversing the journey?
The Master struck him once with his sitting cloth and said, "Fabricated elders are as numerous as hemp and millet.
He then shook out his sleeves and departed. Xuefeng asked the attendant, "Who was this person? The attendant said, "Jian."
The Senior Monk (Shangzuo) said, "Could this be Master Ju, my junior uncle? My late teacher instructed me to seek him out.
He then went down to the guest quarters and asked, "Senior Monk, could you be Master Ju, my junior uncle? Please do not take offense for having disturbed you just now.
The Master then gave a shout and asked again, "When did you arrive at Fenyang, Elder? The monk replied, "I arrived at such-and-such a time."

The Master said, "I have long heard of your reputation in Zhejiang. It turns out your understanding is merely like this; how then can your fame spread throughout the world? Xie then prostrated himself and said, "It is my fault. The verse says: Fame spreads far and wide, yet it is but a name;

The mind is vast and boundless, yet it is but a single thought. When the clouds part and the moon appears, the whole world is bright; When the wind blows and the waves rise, the ten directions are stirred. If you wish to know the ancient Buddha’s true meaning, Look at the mountain peak where the spring flows clear.

When they revile one another, there are no kind words; when they strike one another, there are no gentle fists. How much better it is when the wind is calm and the waves are still, with the bright moon filling the boats upon the river. (Da Hong En)
Having seized the black pearl, he immediately returns; the little-rooted sons of Mara are all filled with doubt and suspicion.
He picks it up and hurls it into the vast waves; casting off their hands, everyone, come back home! (Jingshan Gao)
The fisherman is carefree, drifting east or west as he pleases. He plays the reed flute crosswise, its melodies uneven. When the night is still and the moon is bright, the fish do not bite;
he lies down in his small boat and drifts into the Wuling Creek. (Mengan Xin)
Water does not wash water; gold is not bartered for gold. One obtains a horse by mistaking its coat color; one delights in the lute by tuning its silk strings.
From the binding of cords and the drawing of trigrams, such were the many affairs performed; yet they utterly lost the true simplicity of Pangu’s heart. (Xinwen Ben)
Walking alone on the official road where no one else is present, one’s own official pass is perfectly clear.
The traveler who secretly traffics in private salt by the roadside crouches in the grass for the rest of his life. (Gushan Gui)
There is host and guest; there is ritual and music. As for gain and loss, right and wrong—how can one grope for them?
The moment one gropes, the unsurpassed *amṛta* becomes poison. Do you not see? When the Great Garuda spreads its wings, it covers the Ten Continents;
yet the creature that throws itself against the window merely chirps in vain. (Shi’an Shao)
Beating the great drum, one clamors through the red dust; with blades and spears covering the ground, one sheds the physical body.
Entering the crisscrossing patterns wherever they may be, silver mountains and iron walls are the thoroughfare. (I-an Quan).
Hearing a name is not as good as meeting the person; meeting the person is not as good as hearing the name. There is not even two ounces of gold in this place;
the common folk sell three sheng of wine. (Shiguyu)

[Added from the *Zengshou*] A monk asked Fahua, "The matter of birth and death is great; I pray that you, Master, will save me. The Master said, "I have lost my boat in Lake Dongting. The Verse says: The matter of birth and death is indeed great, Yet he asks for rescue from the Master.
He has lost his boat in Lake Dongting— How can he ever find the shore?
The boat is lost within Lake Dongting; the barefoot Persian sleeps at the bottom of the water. All the people of the world cannot call him awake;
the spring breeze blows him into the village of apricot blossoms. (Xue’an Jin)
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Daoguo Yuanquan of Bajiao Hermitage on Mount Nanyue (he was a successor of Fenyang). He went to visit his fellow student Ciming.
Ciming asked, "White clouds hang across the mouth of the valley; from where has the man of the Way come?
The Master looked to the left and right and said, "Where did the fire come from last night that burned out the ancient tomb? Ciming said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master—
He made the sound of a tiger. Ming struck him with his sitting mat, but the Master caught it and pushed Ming onto the meditation seat.
Ming again made the sound of a tiger. The Master laughed heartily and said, "I have seen more than seventy virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra), yet none were like this."
"Today at last I have met a true master. The verse says:
The question was like a needle within cotton; The answer was like a thorn in the mud. Two tigers roar with fierce ferocity; Each has sharp fangs and claws that strike terror.
Seated upon the head of the azure peak, He cuts off the path right before one's eyes. Even if you were to bring forth the Secret Demon (Bimbara), [he would still strike]!
The forked path is narrow and the grass deep, making it difficult to advance. Meeting yet not encountering; yielding yet not yielding.
The four sevens and two threes gaze upon one another with their eyes. Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. (Yafu Valley).
When the two armies clash in battle, the banner-staffs stand upright and the drums lack mallets. Not a hair’s breadth is violated of the General’s command;
each holds fast to their own single-legged mechanism. (Xiatang Yuan)
A scholar and a warrior met by chance; they spoke at length, each hero being different. Together they went to Chang’an to pay court to the Holy Sovereign;
their names shall ultimately reach the Sage’s ears. (Xu Tang Yu)
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Tiansheng Haotai of Anjishou (Successor of Fenyang). A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "A black-lacquered holy monk. The Verse says: A black-lacquered holy monk, His face is like a mirror; If you wish to see the Buddha, Look directly at this very person.
The Holy Monk is black-lacquered; truly a rare wonder. Do not defile him with pigments and colors.
When people fail to show reverence by joining palms and burning incense, Hanshan and Shide smile while knitting their brows. (Haiyin Xin)
[Added by Later Editors] Chan Master Fayan Yuanjian of Fushan in Shuzhou (successor of Xieyan Xing). A monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master said: "A pile of bones rising from level ground. The Verse says: Level ground rises as a heap of bones; No one can discern its source. If you wish to see the Patriarch’s face, Look directly at this very moment.
Tender grass lines the winding path; mountain springs carry their azure currents. Wen Zeng sought the waters of the Wei; Zhuang Zhou was ashamed to serve as an official. (Touzi Qing)
A heap of bones rises from level ground; in the third spring, the earth-shaking thunder rolls. One hears only that they have gone a thousand miles away;
not a single person is seen returning. (Benjue I)
A heap of bones rises from level ground; the golden-haired lion roars. Who knows this flavorless discourse? It blocks the mouths of the multitude.
(The grace of Kṣitigarbha).
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Fushan Yuan was asked by a monk: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed? The Master said:
"An eighty-year-old old man rolls a brocade ball. The monk said: "If so, then a single phrase suddenly opens the lineage of the Patriarchs."
"The Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) rank foremost, shaking the entire forest [of the lineage]. The Master said: "Li Ling was originally a minister of the Han dynasty.
Touzi Qing said: "The water is deep and the fish hide; the leaves have fallen and the nests are sparse. He further offered this verse:
Rootless grass within the moon; withered tree flowers before the mountain. The wild geese return after the desert passes; whose house is the sound of the mortar and pestle falling?
Ancient halls are covered in moss; the Milky Way and the handle of the Dipper hang low. The golden cock has just announced the dawn; the jade maid ascends the steps late.
(Tianning Lian of Jingzhao Prefecture):
The lion yawns and opens its mouth; it can grasp its golden mane and shake it out. When it rolls over, it tosses a brocade ball;
the hundred beasts flee in a frantic rush. (Zuyin Ming).

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Fushan Yuan was asked by a monk, "What is the one path that leads upward? The Master said, "In the first month of spring, it is still cold. The Verse says: In the first month of spring, it is still cold; The path of the patriarchs is not far. If you can understand this within a single phrase, You will see the moon reflected in the water.
In the first month of spring, the cold still lingers. From head to toe, there are ten thousand kinds and a thousand varieties. Last night, the void fell to the ground;
the gentle breeze settled upon the balustrade. (Biefeng Yin)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Yang Wenyong Yi, Palace Secretary of the Song Dynasty (who studied under Guanghui Lian). His courtesy name was Dainian. While serving as the regional governor of Ruzhou, he first went to visit Guanghui.
Upon being received by Guanghui, the official immediately asked: "A cloth drum is struck at the front of the hall; who is the one who knows this well? Guanghui replied:
"The wind that brought you here has been thoroughly discerned. The official said: "If that is so, then when Zen guests meet..."
[The Master] merely snapped his fingers. He said, "A gentleman may be eight [in stature]. The Master responded, "Yes, yes. [The Master] said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated.
During a conversation at night, Huì asked, "Director of the Imperial Library, with whom have you ever discussed the Dharma?
The Master replied, "I once asked Chan Master Liáng of Yúnyán, 'When two great tigers bite each other, what then? Liáng said, 'One...'"
Heshang He said, "I simply keep watching; I do not know if speaking in such a manner will suffice.
Hui said, "It is not so here. The official said, "Please, Master, offer another turn of phrase.
Hui made a gesture with his hand as if pulling a nose and said, "This beast is still leaping about! At these words, the official was suddenly liberated from all doubt.
There is a verse that says: An octagonal millstone runs through the void; A golden-maned lion transforms into a dog.
If you wish to hide your body within the Northern Dipper, You must join your palms behind the Southern Star. The commentary says:
The Inner Secretary clings to the Southern Dipper and leans upon the Northern Pole; with vast wisdom he turns the celestial gates and reverses the earth’s axis.
How silent and vast—throughout the ages, who can truly know him? A severed string must be joined only by *luangjiao* glue. (Shiyan Lian)
The white stone is sharp and clear; it contains within it a beautiful jade. When the Way of the noble person is obscured, the noble person finds joy therein.
(Xutang Yu). [Added] Yang Wengong asked Guanghui: "I have heard the Master say that all sinful karma arises from wealth and treasures, and you advise people to distance themselves from them.
How much more so for the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, who rely on wealth as their..."
[The Master] said, "In governing states, one gathers people through wealth. Within the teachings, there are two kinds of giving: that of material wealth and that of the Dharma.
How can you encourage people to distance themselves from material wealth? Huì said, "The iron cage atop the flagpole. The Master said, "The stallion at Haitan is as large as a donkey.
Huì said, "A chicken of Chu is not a phoenix of Mount Dan. The Master said, "Two thousand years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
Year. A bhikṣu with little shame and modesty. The verse says: A yakṣa’s head and a bodhisattva’s face;
a ghost pounding grain and the Buddha leaping over a wall. Sharing the same gate and door yet not knowing one another;
surpassing past and present, yet lacking even an inch of merit. A lamp-wick, a *zhī* plant, a broken stone, and a person’s foot; Bian Que and Lu Yi compete for mastery.
(Or the essence of the hermitage).
One man’s teeth are like sword-trees; another’s mouth is like a blood-basin. One punch receives a kick in return; one kick repays a punch.
Raising high the eye of Mahesvara on the crown of the head, it does not hinder one from personally treading upon the ultimate barrier. (Shi’an Shi).
"Skillful smiles, so radiant; beautiful eyes, so gazing; with the plain as the ground for the brilliant patterns.
This is precisely what is meant by the Elder Da-nian and Master Guanghui (from *Baoye yuan*).

The breeze is gentle and the sun warm; spring is at its peak. The willow colors are like gold, and the shadows of the flowers are thick.
Entering the old site of my former travels in Peach Blossom Spring, One peak locks another in succession. (By Baiting Yong)
The remainder of the eleventh generation after the Sixth Patriarch (the tenth generation after Qingyuan) [Yunmen]:
[Supplementarily Recorded] Chan Master Yunju Xiaoshun of Nankang Commandery, popularly known as Old Man Shun (he was a successor of Dongshan Cui).
After leaving Dongshan, he traveled to Wuchang to beg for alms. His first stop was the home of Layman Liu Gong, whose noble conduct was revered by his contemporaries;

whatever he intended to grant or withhold, none failed to follow his lead. At that time, the Master was young and, unaware of the Layman’s extensive training, treated him with some degree of casualness.
The Layman said, "I, an old man, have a question. If our minds accord, then I shall open [the gate]."
The Commentary states: When [the official] did not reach accord, he requested the Master to return to the mountain. He then asked, "How is it when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished?
The Master said, "Black as lacquer. [The official] asked, "How is it after it has been polished? The Master said, "It reflects heaven and reflects earth.

The official gave a long bow and said, "For now, I ask you, Great Master, to return to the mountain," then brushed his sleeves and entered his residence. The Master returned dejectedly to Dongshan. Dongshan—
When asked the reason for this, the Master recounted the matter in detail. Mount said, "Ask me, and I shall tell you. The Master repeated his previous question.
Mount said, "It is not far from here to Hanyang. The Master then offered the latter part of the phrase.
Mount said, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower lies the Parrot Isle. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; his spiritual acuity was unassailable.
The Verse says:
Black clouds at noon shroud the clear void; White rain overturns the sky, erasing the painted landscape. When the rain has passed and the clouds are gathered, the mountain colors are pure;
Zhaozhou hangs his gourd on the eastern wall. (I-an Kwon)
Before the Yellow Crane Tower lies Parrot Isle; the mind of Yunju does not dwell upon the hook’s tip. A small boat sails steadily across the clear green Yangtze River;
with one great laugh, the mist and rain vanish. (Iron Ox Seal).

[Added from the Supplementary Collection: Chan Master Chenghao of Yuzhan in Jingmen Commandery was commonly known as "Hao the Cloth Pantaloons" (a disciple of Beita Guang). On the first day of winter, he ascended the hall and said: "The movement of the sun's shadow shifts; my cloth pantaloons are a brilliant red.

Do not wonder that they have not been washed—there is nothing else to replace them. He then offered this verse: Verse: The movement of the sun's shadow shifts; My cloth pantaloons are a brilliant red. Do not wonder that they have not been washed; There is nothing else to replace them.
To boast of wealth and honor is to be impoverished even by selling oneself cheaply; while murder may be excused, lack of propriety is difficult to tolerate.

(Wuzu Fanzhen) [Added from another source]. Chan Master Yihuai of Tianyi in Yuezhou (a successor of Xuedou), having accepted the invitation to Shan Mountain, ascended the hall for his inaugural sermon:
"Twenty years ago, I yearned for and admired this mountain; today, I am truly glad that the karmic conditions have converged."
Before this mountain monk had even reached this mountain, his body had already arrived here;
yet by the time he actually arrived, Shanshan was already within his own body. The verse says:
Shifting the body and changing the step, the old man’s robe is worn thin. How many know him who does not spare his own eyebrows?
If today you clarify the events of that day, the sun is warm in Jiangnan and the partridges cry. (Cishou Shen)

[Tianyi] ascended the hall and said: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its reflection sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no thought of retaining the reflection.
If you can act in this way, only then will you understand how to walk among those of different species.
There is no need to shorten the crane or lengthen the duck, nor to level the mountains or fill the valleys. When let go, there are a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses; when gathered in—"
"Clasping and grasping with earnest devotion—when employed, one dares to compete in wealth with the Eight Great Dragon Kings;
when not employed, it is not worth even half a penny at all. *Chan* (Consider). The Verse says:"
The cry of the wild goose resonates high as cold clouds drift by; its shadow falls upon the chilly river, yet it knows not of itself.
The river water is without sentiment, and the goose is without intent; even as they move among different kinds, it is thus. (Benjiao I)
A lone wild goose cries out in the vast autumn sky. The Persian offering jewels has a nose like a hook. The wind sweeps white clouds back to distant peaks;
At twilight, the moon hangs from the tips of the willow branches. (Wan’an Rou)
[Added from the Supplement] Tianyi Ju. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Fayan said:

If you can penetrate these two points of failure, only then will you behold Gautama. (Benjue I)

"Before the Age of Awesome, a single arrow pierces through two layers of mountains. [The monk] asked: "What is the matter that is transmitted?"
The Master said, "Now, by means of the moon over Huai, I have obtained the spring light of Yingyang. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then one enters the water and sees the tall man.

Jade flowers bloom upon coral branches; the wind carries their pure fragrance throughout the nine realms.
Do not say that heaven and earth are devious; Shaoyang once saw Muzhou come. (Danxia Chun)
(Dharmacakṣus) [Added by Zongshou]: Chan Master Huiji Yongming Yanshou Zhijue of Hangzhou (he succeeded National Teacher Guishan Shao). A monk asked:
"What is the wondrous purport of Yongming? The Master said, "Add more incense. The monk said, "Thank you for your instruction.
The Master said, "I am glad you have no connection [to it]. The monk bowed. The Master presented this verse:
If you wish to know the purport of Yongming, Look at the lake before the gate. When the sun shines, radiance arises; When the wind comes, waves stir. *Commentary:*
It is said:
"The lake before the gate reflects the opening of its countenance; facing one another, it presents a platter held out in full.
This is indeed Yongming’s teaching without superfluous words: when the wine is rich, it does not depend on many cups. (Xiangtan Yong)
[Added for inclusion: When two monks came to visit Master Zhijue, the Master asked the head monk, "Have you been here before? He replied, "I have.
The Master then asked the second senior monk, "Have you been here before? He replied, "I have not. The Master said, "One has gained; one has lost.
After a short while, an attendant asked, "Regarding those two monks just now, I do not understand which one it was that [gained]..."

"One has gained it; the other has lost it. The Master asked, "Do you recognize these two monks? The man said, "I do not recognize them. The Master said, "In the same pit, there is no different soil. The verse says: One has gained it; the other has lost it. If you wish to know, look at the two monks.
When the Master asked about their recognition, He said, "In the same pit, there is no different soil."
"Arrived or not arrived? One gain and one loss. It is either arsenic or rock honey; how can you eat it when there are no eyes upon the tip of your tongue?

Just as the attendant was about to inquire for the definitive meaning, do not blame those in the same pit for having different soil—before the lightning has subsided, a thunderclap crashes down. (Chijue Chong)

Chan Master Yuan’an (d.u. of the Upper Hall at Rui鹿 Temple in Wenzhou (who was a successor of National Teacher Miaoxi) once studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage, "When cognition and vision establish cognition, this is the root of ignorance;
when cognition and vision are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa," the Master read it by breaking the phrasing as follows: "Cognition and vision establish / Cognition, which is the root of ignorance."
To know that there is no seeing—this very seeing is *nirvāṇa*. Upon this, he attained realization, which remained unaltered for the rest of his life.
At that time, he was called An Lengyan. As he was about to pass away, he spoke this verse:
This is not a matter carried from the mountain peaks; how could it have been transmitted from beneath Mount Kukkutapāda? Since time immemorial, the sages and worthies have all been like this;
it is not I who am fashioning it for you today.
The spring grasses are emerald green; the spring waters have verdant waves. As I see you off at the southern ford, my grief is beyond measure.
(Yanxi Wen). One of the twelfth generation under the Sixth Patriarch (the first of the eleventh generation under Nanyue) [Linji]:
Chan Master Huinang of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture (who succeeded Ciming Yuan). He would constantly question the monks in his quarters:
He said, "Every person has their own karmic conditions for birth. Where, Elder, are your karmic conditions for birth?
Just as they were at the height of this exchange of questions and answers, he reached out his hand and asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
He then asked about what the masters they had visited in various quarters had attained, whereupon he lowered his feet and asked, "How are my feet like a donkey’s feet? (Thirty)
In his later years, he presented these three questions. Among scholars, none were able to grasp their essential meaning.
Even when someone offered a response, the Master never once expressed approval or disapproval. The monastic community designated them as "The Three Barriers of Huanglong.
The Ancient Buddha Yuan Tong Min of Mount Lu said: "Formerly, I saw the Head Seat Guangbian holding the three barriers written by hand by National Teacher Nan."

When my hand and the Buddha’s hand are raised together, let the Chan practitioner directly realize it. Without moving a blade or raising a banner, the Way is manifested right where one stands.

Transcending the Buddhas and surpassing the Patriarchs—my feet and the donkey’s feet walk side by side; at every step, one treads upon the Unborn. Only when you realize that the clouds have withdrawn and the sun has rolled up will you know that this Way extends in all directions.

Where the conditions for birth are severed, the donkey’s hoof is extended; when the donkey’s hoof is extended, the Buddha’s hand opens. To report this to the students who travel the Five Lakes:
pass through each of the three barriers one by one.
Clouds disperse over the Yangtze River, and the waters flow on vast and deep. Suddenly a wild wind arises and the waves rise high.
Failing to recognize the profound mystery of the fisherman’s way, one is tossed about by the wind and billows amidst the surging seas. (Jingfushun, 3)
The Persians of the South Sea entered the Great Tang; there were those who could distinguish gems and thus engaged in trade, sometimes meeting with low prices and sometimes with high.
As the sun reached the western peaks, its shadows grew long.
The Old Monk Huanglong had a saying regarding his "karmic affinity. This mountain monk has inherited his lineage; today I shall raise it for you.
I raise it for you: the cat is uniquely adept at catching mice.
As soon as the Buddha’s hand opens, the ancient mirror shines bright; the myriad phenomena cannot conceal their subtle forms. Morning after morning, day after day, it rises from the east;
how many travelers ask about the direction of Bing and Ding? (Zhaojue Zong 3)
When the donkey’s hoof extends, it shakes the wheels of the earth; red dust is scattered across the bottom of the great ocean. Only the green cypresses at the edge of the courtyard remain;
once a year passes, and once again comes spring.
He asked where his karmic conditions had led him from; upon arriving home, the Chan guest was free from even a speck of dust.
He has already roamed through the ocean of Vairocana’s lands—there is no need to speak of Mount Emei or Mount Wutai.
"What is my hand like compared to the Buddha’s hand? Who can discern their beauty or ugliness by turning them over?
If one is not the offspring of a lion, a jackal merely opens its mouth in vain. (Zhenjing Wen, 3)
My feet are like a donkey’s feet; hidden and manifest, a thousand differences and ten thousand errors. If you wish to open the diamond eye, look at the good and evil right before you.
Every person has their own place of karmic affinity; yet if you fixate upon it, you will lose your way as before. The clouds disperse across the vast sky, and the moonlight shines bright.
Open it! East, west, south, and north, follow the Master.
My hand is the Buddha’s hand; who does not possess it? Use it clearly and directly; why must you run about wildly? (Wuwei Xiu, 3)
My feet and the donkey’s feet tread upon the high and the low. After the rain, the moss is green; when the clouds part, the sun gleams.
When asked about the place of my birth, there is no doubt regarding that place of birth. My words are direct and my mind is free from ailment; who would debate right and wrong?
The Dharma Cloud Chan Master Weibai of Fokuo Monastery in Tokyo arrived at the dharma seat of National Teacher [Fayan] at the beginning of the Xining era.

He remained there for nearly two years until the Master passed into parinirvāṇa. Nevertheless, he entered the Master’s quarters to inquire about the Way, and the Master revealed his lifelong three turning-words to the disciples of the world.
Having recently had the opportunity to consult with him several times, I have observed his seal [of realization].

Regarding the *Xingyulu* (Recorded Sayings of Xing): within it, there are instances where [the Master] either picks up a phrase or offers a verse, yet its underlying intent remains unfathomable. Alas!

Less than thirty years have passed since he departed this world, yet those who propagate errors and delusions transmit such things as these. How truly lamentable! Consequently, I have composed these verses.
One who knows the Master may partake in the same flavor. The verse says:
Master and guest meet, displaying the family style; Question and answer are distinct, arrow meets blade point-for-point. Stretching out a hand, he asks you: "Is it like the Buddha’s hand?
Iron gates and golden locks, ten thousand layers thick.
I traveled everywhere to consult masters and probe the profound mysteries; by chance we met and spoke of the wonders of the Way. When I extended my legs, he asked about the donkey’s legs;
what I had realized throughout my life was once again filled with doubt.
Do not be surprised that we meet yet do not recognize one another; a master must discern the source of the matter.
Having fully discussed the winds and moon of one’s native land, it is difficult indeed to answer when asked about the circumstances of one's birth.
"What is my hand like? It is like the Buddha’s hand—rare in the heavens and among men.
Even if one were not to act in such a way, it would still be like placing shackles upon a collar. (Haixin, III)
"My feet are like a donkey's. To serve the patch-robed monks, I have plucked them away. In years past, my illness was not yet healed;
now, once again, I have encountered a virulent poison.

If you ask about the source of one's life—whether it be the true or the conventional—the moment the source of life is severed, one falls into the unconditioned (*asamskrta*). How can one avoid these two paths?
So it is. An eighty-year-old old woman learns to paint her eyebrows.
My hand and the Buddha’s hand. Eighteen, nineteen. The clouds disperse and the moon becomes full. The deluded person runs through the night. (Zhandang Zhun III)
My feet and the donkey’s feet—let this one point pass. Pang’s old winnowing basket, Qingping’s wooden ladle:
the karmic conditions of every person. Northern Vinaya, Southern Chan; Daowu dancing with his ritual tablet, Huating rowing his boat.

At the gateway of the profound mystery, there is much spirit and vigor. Without grasping a single inch of iron in hand, nor employing a single steed of the army, the eight barbarian tribes and the four frontier peoples are all brought to peace through effortless means.
Reclining in exhaustion beneath the mulberry trees as the spring sun slants, one wanders contentedly, unaware of what age this may be.
(Universally Fusing and Leveling).
What is my hand like? It is like the Buddha’s hand. From the beginning, it has had a robe but no sleeves.
Sometimes, idly appearing before others, I do not realize that both elbows are exposed. (Shangfang Yi; 3)
What are my feet like? They are like donkey’s feet. When the cold comes, one must wear socks; do not let them tread upon mud and water, lest you lose your shoes all at once.
Every person has their own karmic affinity (*jīvyatā*); why must everyone seek Liangyuan? If you ask where this old monk was born, [it is] the *lǜzhī* (lychee).
The fragrance fills the Southern Garden.
How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? A furnace, bellows, tongs, and hammer—a metal broom—once smelted the body of purple-polished gold;
its light radiates upon the Seven Stars and the Ox and Dipper constellations. (Nantang and the Three).
My feet are like those of a donkey; amidst the flashing of white blades and red banners, I sit and cut off the hundred battlefields. I skillfully contend with the *Liubao* and *Sanlue*.
Every person has their own karmic affinity for life—seeing, hearing, looking up and down, and moving about. They bear upon their heads the sun and moon within the world, and hold in their hands...
Regarding authority beyond the threshold:
"What is my hand like? It is like a Buddha’s hand. Picking flowers and breaking willows according to one's capacity, one suddenly finds oneself grasping the head of a snake;
one cannot avoid being bitten by it. (Yuánwù Qín, 3)
"My feet are like a donkey's feet; Zhaozhou’s stone bridge is but a mere footbridge. Suddenly, as if a leather ball were kicked up, the three mountains and five peaks collapse.
Everyone has their own karmic connection, yet they crouch with no ground upon which to drill and investigate. If the eyelids burst open, one must beware of him.
The bottom of the bucket is pierced through;
Buddha’s hand and donkey’s feet are one's own karmic conditions. Huanglong never said such words.
Even if you understand it in this way, I do not yet dare to grant my approval lightly. I report this to you, monks from the four seas: first of all, do not misquote it. (Longmen Yuan)
The Buddha’s hands and the donkey’s feet arise from conditions; wherever they land is itself the universe.
Within the infinite, layered pavilions, there is no door for one who enters by a mere snap of the fingers. (Fosincai, 3)

The donkey’s feet are born from the Buddha’s hand; strike through the pivotal lock of the highest realm. Having cast off the mud-splattered cloth trousers, one directly attains the "Pass with Empty Mind.
The donkey’s feet and the Buddha’s hand—these I now pluck away for you as a single entity. Sitting at ease, one brings about Great Peace. The fierce general!

Vainly boasting of one's schemes and stratagems—knocking at the gate, how could one be a true man? When the donkey’s hoof finds its affinity, whom does it ask? The Buddha’s hand is fully extended, yet there is nowhere for it to be used;
the foundations of peace and prosperity flourish abundantly for each. (The Dharma-hall is thus.)
[Continued Collection] What is my hand like? It is like the Buddha’s hand. The Southern Dipper and the Northern Dipper are in the heavens above. What are my feet like? They are like a donkey’s feet.
All past affairs have been forgotten. Every person has their own karmic affinity; each one has square feet and a round head.
Standing on the banks of Dayu Rapids, the solitary moon reflects its shadow upon the deep cove. If you cannot understand it, even seeing it is difficult. A single song of the fisherman descends.
Yuantan (Baiyang Shun): "What is my hand like? It is a Buddha-hand.
Under Huanglong’s nose there is no mouth. What was seen at that time was coarse and vague;
to this day it remains a hundred clumsy and a thousand ugly things. (Zhengtang Bian 3)
"My feet are like a donkey's. Mañjuśrī saw it directly; it is a fine crystal tea bowl—do not hide it from one's own face.
Every person has their own karmic affinity (*janmanidāna*); from of old, their transgressions have filled the heavens. Whether it be plowing with oxen or pulling a harrow, or else...
In the cauldron and the boiling oil—what is my hand like? It is a Buddha-hand. The monks of the world have no mouths;
even if they were to suddenly spring up and depart, it would still be running within a ghost cave. One cannot deny it. (Zhang Wugou, 3)
"My feet are like those of a donkey, and they are further stuck together by rice-glue. I have turned my body upward directly toward Tuṣita Heaven;
I have already been struck by the 'rat-poison' of another, and I cannot vomit it up."

Every person has their own karmic affinity for life. Beneath the Iron Ring Mountains for thousands of years, when the three calamities burn up to the fourth dhyāna heaven, this fellow still remains by the side. He has achieved the work of killing.
"What is my hand like? It is like the Buddha’s hand. How laughable that Zihu raised a dog only to run into a striped tiger;
he has surrendered his life to it in a single bite. (Shi’an Shao, 4)

"What are my feet like? They are like donkey's feet. To even consider this is to know you are greatly mistaken. You step forward wishing to drink the *amṛta*, yet it is as if you have already encountered its poison.
Every person has their own karmic affinity; it is not merely a matter of barbarians or the Central Plains. A large radish emerges from the government office of Zhenzhou—this is Zhaozhou.
To see Nanquan face-to-face:
"The Buddha’s hand, the donkey’s hoof" is one's original condition; "one's original condition, the donkey’s hoof, the Buddha’s hand.
When Lord Li falls drunk on the street, it is originally Lord Zhang drinking wine. The "old woman’s Chan" of Huanglong Mountain is just like the ugliness of a newlywed bride from Heyang.

"What is my hand like? It is like the Buddha’s hand. Twenty-eight, perfectly fitting; nineteen. Calculating from the end of the year to the beginning of the year, there is not a single coin within the house. (Iam Gwon, No. 4)
"What is my foot like? It is like a donkey's foot. Stepping upon Zhaozhou’s narrow bridge, it startles Kāśyapa to frown;
Mañjuśrī, in turn, strikes Wuzhuo.
Every person has their own karmic affinity (*jāti-pratyaṃśa*). A man of spirit has a bearing that pierces the heavens. If you are one who disputes fields and contends for land, I—

To call death "like sleep" is a case of a Buddha’s hand and a donkey’s feet arising as conditions; it has been widely transmitted throughout the vast forests of the monastic community. Even if one were to pierce through it all at once, one would still not avoid the distance of eighty thousand miles.
What does my hand resemble? It resembles the Buddha’s hand. With palms joined, I face south to gaze at the Big Dipper.
The Hare pushes the bright moon up the thousand peaks, drawing Cold Mountain to open his smiling mouth. (Xue’an Jin, No. 4)
"What are my feet like? Like donkey's feet! Hurry home; the sun is setting. Since ancient times, Chang'an has been as level as a mirror;
for no reason at all, I have stumbled drunk upon the Yellow River."
Every person has their own karmic affinity; it is neither here in the East nor there in the West. Striking the coral tree, every branch is beautiful;
scattering the mercury beads, every grain is round.

The Buddha’s hands and the donkey’s feet arise from conditions. A Persian from the South Sea sails upon an iron ship; fine gold and beautiful jade are piled in heaps for sale, yet in the end, they have never been worth a single coin.
A Buddha’s hands and a donkey’s feet are easy to see; the most difficult point is one's own birth-condition (*jìngyuán*). Huangmei was not Zhou’s son;
at seven years of age he transmitted the robe and immediately understood Chan. (Hengchuan Hongguo)

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fasheng of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Chizhou during the Song Dynasty.
Continued Collection of the Patriarchs’ Occasions for Enlightenment by the Śramaṇa Puhui of Tianyi Wanshou Chan Monastery during the Yuan Shaoxing Era;

[Supplement] When Huanglong Nan first visited Letan Cheng, Yunfeng Yue directed him to see Ciming.
Having settled at Fuyan, Master Xian appointed him as the Secretary. After Xian passed away, it happened that Ciming succeeded to the abbacy.
One day, he went to visit the abbot. The next morning, Ming said, "You have studied under Yunmen Chan; you must surely be well-versed in his essential meaning.
For instance, regarding Dongshan’s three blows of the staff—was it appropriate for him to receive them or not? The Master replied, "It was appropriate.
Ming said, "From dawn until dusk, the cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies—all are due to receiving those blows. He then had the Master prostrate himself. Ming asked again, "Zhao..."
The Master said, "I have thoroughly scrutinized and exposed you, Old Lady of Mount Tai in Zhoudao. Now tell me, where exactly was it that he scrutinized and exposed the old lady?
The Master broke into a sweat and could not answer. The next day, the Master went to the room again. Baoming scolded him incessantly.
The Master said, "Is scolding the compassionate gift of the Dharma? Baoming replied, "You take it as scolding."
When Huìné would not answer, the Master [Zhaozhou] finally attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "An eminent elder who stands out from the groves, Old Zhaozhou;
The old woman’s discernment has its origins. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; Travelers, do not let the road be your enemy.
Míng nodded in approval. He then spoke this verse: [Verse omitted per instructions.]
Mistake! Mistake! A fierce dragon in the sea of play, a soaring crane reaching the clouds. Old Ciming was without attachment; within his laughter, he repeatedly revealed the sacrificial rope.
When the Buddha’s hand is once extended, sun and moon darken; from this point on, the great river is filled with wind and waves. (Shilin Gong)
How can stagnant water nourish a dragon? It must ultimately reach the great ocean to stir up the stinking winds.
Heaven ordained that in a single instant of wind and clouds, it was sent forth amidst the mist and rain of Mount Tai. (Zhuwu Jian, II)
There are those who deserve the staff and those who do not; when one stands before the furnace, the quicksilver and silver flow away.
Had it not been for the severing of the path on Mount Tai, the resentment of the cloud peaks would remain unredeemed for a thousand ages.

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] A monk asked Huanglong Nan: "What is it like when there is neither going nor coming? The Master said: "The three peaks of Mount Hua stand upside down. The monk asked: "What is it like when there is both going and coming? The Master said: "The wind blows the willow catkins, rolling them like a ball.

Verse: The three peaks of Mount Hua stand upside down; The wind blows the willow catkins, rolling them like a ball. If you can see through this at once, Then you have attained the Way of Huanglong. If you hesitate for even a moment, You will fall into the pit of the Three Realms.
If you wish to know the meaning of the Patriarchs, Look at the willow catkins as they roll.
A woman from Xisha with skin like ice and snow, her makeup skillfully applied as she paints her brows;
though a bystander’s brush may powerfully transmit her likeness, how can she truly be seen outside the door? (By Benji Guan)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] When Huanglong Nan was residing at Huangbo, he would frequently raise these cases in his quarters: "Reciting hymns atop the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bed. None of the assembly could provide a response that accorded with the truth.

One day, the Head Seat Sheng said, "A fierce tiger sits in the middle of the road. Thereupon, the Master withdrew from Huangbo and stayed with Sheng. The Verse says: A fierce tiger sits in the middle of the road; The bell tower and the bed foot are one. When the time comes for the true meaning to be revealed, The whole world is but a single sound.
Reciting hymns atop the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bed’s feet. A fierce tiger crouches across the road; people of the time all fail to understand.
When the flowers of Huangbo bloom, they will do so of their own accord. In Mingzhou there is a certain "Dull Bagman" (Zhao Tang).
Directly out, directly in; facing him, one does not recognize him. What more could one expect? Why such a desperate urgency? (Jingshan Gaofeng):
A fierce tiger sits blocking the road; a roaming fish passes beneath its paws. I do not follow the old Master Zihu, who would simply strike Liu Tiemo.
(Gushan Gui). [Supplemented by] Huanglong Nan.
Because Heyishan Pu studied under him, and Pu was well-versed in the sutras and śāstras, he was known as the "Tiger of Meaning" throughout the two Sichuan provinces.
The student asked the Master, "Ānanda asked Kāśyapa: 'Beyond the transmission of the golden robe by the World-Honored One, what else was transmitted?
What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "When you, Venerable One, left Sichuan, did you ever go to Yuquan?
Fupin replied, "I went there. The Master asked again, "Did you stay there for any time? He replied, "I departed after only one night. The Master said, "Wisdom!"

"This is the Dharma-assembly of Guanyin at Daochang; we have established a karmic connection through offerings. How could it matter how long you stay? Fupin remained silent for a long while, then again addressed the Master as before.
The Master bowed his head. Fupin hurried out and said in great astonishment, "The tiger of righteousness from the two rivers cannot withstand a single spit from this old man. The verse says:
Huanglong’s single spittle cuts off all hesitation; it makes the onlookers laugh to death and yet evokes pity.
The beautiful maiden has already returned to the celestial void, while the foolish lad still nestles by the fire. (Duan’an Yan)
