A three-legged donkey prances about, pawing the ground. I urge all travelers to open their eyes: if you see him amidst the grass, you will surely lose your life;
it is because his kicking and stamping are most distinct. (Baizhang Yuanwen)
The front step is high and the back step is low; head moving, tail shaking—three hooves. He rides through the bustling market as people move east and west.
In Hunan, there is yet another Subhūti. (Baoning Yong)
A three-legged donkey trots about, prancing its hooves; a swift steed chasing the wind cannot catch up.
Having trampled through the illusory city, there is no place to be found; the Elder of Hunan applies the whip once more. (Fujian Qín)
A three-legged donkey prances about, its hooves kicking up dust; at every step, lotus flowers grow beneath its feet. How laughable are those who search for it amidst the weeds;
they do not know that the spring oriole is warbling from the fragrant tree. (Fóxìng Tái)
This three-legged donkey is truly excellent; let it roam freely in the back garden to graze on grass.
If you casually lead it out before others, it will kick over the blind old monk of Hunan. (Gushan Gui)
Yangqi’s one-headed donkey has only three legs; Pan Lang rides it backward home and tumbles, killing Huang Fancho. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
[Continued Collection] A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves; it goes straight through the ten-thousand-fathom pit of Vipaśyin. The clouds atop the ridge peak are never at rest;
the water flowing down the ravine is far too busy. Elder of Hunan, who can understand this?
The traveler is even beyond the green mountains. (Liangshan Yuan).
A three-legged donkey trots along, prancing its hooves; In the south of the two rivers, autumn is once again hot. In the northwest, one fears the early cold of wind and frost;
I shut my door, sorrowfully watching the willow petals fall. (Wan’an Yan)
First pulling the rake, second leading the plow; on level fields and shallow ground, we follow one another for now.
Just when hunger strikes and there is no fodder, they let loose their horns and wander east and west. Old Yangqi, old Yangqi—everyone says he has always been skilled at prancing his hooves.
(Benefiting the Upper Realm).
When the lame donkey with three legs prances on its hooves, one does not know it unless one personally rides it; the purple-golden body cannot be moved by the load.
A bamboo switch is truly superior to cold tongs and hammers. (Wandering with the Ox).
When the Dharma appears, deceit arises; when a buttress is built, it invites an arrow. As for this three-legged donkey—who has seen him face-to-face?
If you have seen him face-to-face, then Śākyamuni Old Man is Nala’s face (Fozhao Guang).
A three-legged donkey trots along, prancing its hooves; it stirs up a clear breeze that chills to the very bone. It tramples through Vairocana’s light until the shadows are severed;
there is no need to stir waves upon level ground. (Yue’an Guo)
Yangqi’s one-headed donkey has eyes that flash like lightning; it tramples all people underfoot—what need is there to speak of three legs?
(Yun’an Qing of Jingshan).
A single arrow shoots down the wild geese at the edge of heaven; a thousand, ten thousand people gaze upon it with fixed eyes.
They do not know from where this arrow comes; when has the Elder of Hunan ever seen it? (Zhong’an Kong)

[Added from another source] Yangqi was once asked by a monk, "What is the meaning of Shaolin’s wall-gazing? The Master said, "The Western Heavens do not understand the language of Tang. The Verse says: The Western Heavens do not understand the language of Tang; The wall-gazing at Shaolin was not for the sake of words. If you wish to know the intent of the Patriarch, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
The heavens are high and the earth is distant, yet they are not difficult to see; the waters are broad and the mountains are layered, yet they are not hard to describe.
For ten thousand ages, the eight winds have never been able to enter; those from the West do not understand the language of Tang. (Baiyun Yuan).
The man from the Western Heaven did not understand the language of Tang; he sat upright and majestic before Mount Shaoshi.
He was only justly struck by Bodhiruci until his teeth were knocked out; even now, he has no way to explain his reasoning. (Fóxìng Tái)
The people of the West do not understand the language of Tang; the thunder of a drought shakes through the great trichiliocosm.
For nine years he faced the wall, yet no one understood; the jade hare and golden crow whirl within the fire. (Wuan Quan)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Once, Yangqi was holding a memorial vegetarian feast for the anniversary of Ciming’s death.
As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master placed his two fists over his head before the portrait, drew a line with his sitting mat, and struck a circular mark.
He then burned incense, withdrew three paces, and performed a "woman's bow. The Head Seat said, "Stop making such strange antics! The Master replied, "Head Seat..."
The Master asked, "What about the one sitting here? The second monk replied, "Preceptor, please stop making such a fuss. The Master said, "A rabbit eating an ox's teat.
The second monk stepped forward, drew a circle in the air, burned some incense, then withdrew three paces and performed a woman’s bow.
As the Master stepped forward to assume a listening posture, the monk hesitated; the Master struck him with his palm and said, "This..."
Even a lacquer bucket acts in a chaotic manner. The verse says:
Yangqi listened to the situation and sealed a thousand differences; from ancient times to the present, he has caused people to love him as a master craftsman.
As long as one holds the Three Seals of the Patriarch, there is no hindrance to twisting things strangely in a manner as tangled as hemp. (Guitalu Jushi)
A single puppet carved from wood, half divine in form and half demonic. When the singing and drumming cease, the sky is not yet dawn;
a lingering cold moon still hangs upon the sparse lattice windows. (Vast Hall of Folly)

[Added from the Supplement] A monk asked Yangqi, "What is it like when one pushes through the clouds and sees the sun? The Master said, "One who comes from the east sits in the east. The Verse says: Pushing through the clouds, the sun appears; Eastward he comes, eastward he sits. In the vast expanse of the great void, He alone is the true master.
Yao and Shun draped their robes and the myriad states came as guests; Pushing through the clouds to see the sun, there was no need for further words. Those who come from the East sit in the East;
Grass and trees are once again moistened by fresh rain and dew. (Baizhang Yuan)

About to depart with the "black pearl," one encounters a great merchant; the golden platter is moved, and its luster remains. There is no need for a single word to discuss its high value;
taking it by the hand, one returns home to share many smiles. (Baizun Yuan).
Let us ask: what is there in the human world so busy? One should take these spring affairs to report to the spring light.
Even if one were to get drunk before the flowers day after day, an entire season consists of but ninety days. (Zhengtang Bian)
Hu Zhangsan draws his bow with his back turned; Hei Lisu turns his body to brace his arrow.
Even if it were the ancient General who bites the arrowhead, he would have his skull pierced through from front to back. (Biefeng Yin)
One probes the water with a staff to know its depth; one knows a horse’s strength by the distance of the road; and one discerns a person’s heart over the long term.

When a son is unfilial and a father is unkind, when one is reverent yet lacks propriety, or affectionate yet distant—unless one enters the startling waves, it is difficult to encounter the fish that satisfies one’s desire. (Yeshu Creek)
The cat’s entire skill lies in its blood-drinking; the tiger prepares the raising of corpses for slaughter. There is nothing to be done about the uncle;
the secret of climbing trees is not transmitted. (Nanyan Sheng)

Horses turning back and oxen retreating—how could this be worthy of praise? A thorn stuck in soft mud; this is the mark of a true practitioner. With a single stroke of the frosty blade, one’s spirit is fully realized;
sitting thus, one settles dragons and snakes for a thousand years. (Wuan Quan)
[Added for Collection] Yangqi asked a monk, "The clouds are deep and the path is remote; from where have you come with such a lofty stride? The monk replied, "The heavens have no four walls.
The Master said, "How many straw sandals have you worn out? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "What about one shout, two shouts?
What then? The monk said, "Look at this old monk! The Master said, "My staff is not here; sit for a moment and let us eat."
Tea. The verse says:
With lofty steps, from where have you come, fishing for elephants and rhinoceroses? Turning back, you carry not even a trace of mud.
Suddenly, a shout rises a thousand fathoms high; Looking back beyond the kalpas, who can know it? (Guītáng Jūshì)
[Added for inclusion] A monk asked Yangqi, "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil. When a patch-robed monk attains the One, what can he do with it?

The Master said, "The mouth of the alms bowl points toward the sky. Verse: Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil. When a patch-robed monk attains the One, He holds his bowl upright, facing the heavens.
The time when the almsbowl turned toward the base of heaven: the worlds of the ten directions were but a single lump of iron. Shao-lin faced the wall in vain for many years;
this only adds more grit to the eyes of the patch-robed monks. (Baiyun Yuan).

When a patch-robed monk is pressed once, the mouth of his alms-bowl opens wide. Throughout the world, Yangqi [Yixian] is like one who hopes for plums to quench thirst. (Songyuan Yue). Yangqi’s golden circle and the chestnut burr—swallowing or leaping over them, the circumstances remain the same.
To swallow the entire great ocean in a single gulp, there is no longer north, south, or the West. (Zhaotang 1)
The Vajra Ring, the *kṣavaka* thorn, Xuan Sha’s three kinds of illness, and Shigong’s single drawn bow—I shall explain these directly for you:
Silla lies to the east of the sea. (Jingshan Gaofeng)
The Old Man of Yangqi’s secret for locking the mouth: A ten-thousand-li long wall of solid iron.
When the Zen traveler who chops at the sign arrives, the golden hammer strikes without moving and the skull splits open. (Gushan Gui)
What difficulty is there in swallowing a chestnut burr? To be told to spit it out again brings a pang of sorrow. Having swallowed and spat it out, do not chew it to pieces;
the light of the Southern Dipper shoots forth as the Northern Dipper grows cold. (Zhengtang Bian)
Suddenly, behind the elbow, there arises a loose and dangling cord; before the wind, all at once, a chaotic crossbar is spread out. Nanda’s eight arms are left in vain lamentation;
at the third watch of the night, one walks in broad daylight. (Tiantong Jing)
Last night, fresh thunder broke forth; the venomous snake left its den. One who usually keeps its mouth shut now spurts fresh blood upon being stepped on. (Oran’s Verse)

[Added from another source] When Yangqi entered the monastery, after he had finished ascending the seat and descended, Jiufeng Qin seized him, saying, "Today I have joyfully found a fellow practitioner.
The Master asked, "What is this matter of being a fellow practitioner? Qin said, "Jiufeng plows the ox;
Yangqi drags the harrow. The Master said, "At such a time as this, who is in front—Yangqi or Jiufeng?"

[The student] stood before him, diligently attempting to deliberate [on the meaning]. The Master pushed him aside and said, "I thought we were fellow practitioners; it turns out you are not. He then offered this verse:
First he drags the harrow, second he pulls the plow; In the level fields and shallow grass, let us follow along for now. But when hunger strikes, there is no fodder.
Unleashing his horns, he goes east and west. Old Yangqi, old Yangqi! Everyone says he has always been skilled at prancing.
(Shangfang Yi). Yangqi’s left eye is half a catty; Jiufeng’s right eye is eight taels. This pair of unperforated iron hammers remains to this day.
[This case] cannot be resolved. (Wúxiàngfàn).
The remainder of the twelfth generation under the Sixth Patriarch (the eleventh generation under Qīngyuán) [in the Cáo-dòng lineage].
【Added by Subsequent Editors】 Zen Master Dàokǎi Fúróng of Tiānníng in Tōngjīng (who succeeded Tóuzǐ Qīng). A monk asked: "At midnight..."

It is clearly revealed that at dawn nothing is disclosed. What is this undisclosed matter? The Master said: "The boat is full, yet empty; the fisherman sleeps among the reeds under the moon. The Verse says: The boat is full, yet empty;
the fisherman sleeps among the reeds under the moon. The myriad phenomena are all here, yet not one is seen. If you wish to know the Buddha’s meaning, Look at the autumnal waters of the West River.
In the land of flowing stars and waters, lamps burn through the night; the moon’s reflection on the river is as bright as a mirror.
Manifestation and concealment are impartial, yet no fixed position can encompass them; to stir even slightly is to fall into partiality or correctness. (Danxia Chun)
[Added for inclusion] Fuyong Kai ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-body is subtle in principle and profound in expression; it gives rise at once to the afflictions of beginning and end.
You worthy ones, is there a Dharma-body existing apart from this illusory body? Or is this illusory body itself the Dharma-body?
If you understand it in such a way, you are entirely relying on others to form interpretations; you are mired in ignorance."
Two branches. Fayan had not yet attained it; Tongming did not see it. A monk asked Jia Shan, "What is the Dharma-body?
Shan said, "The Dharma-body has no form. [The monk asked again,] "What is the Dharma-eye? Shan said, "The Dharma-eye has no flaw."
Therefore, Master Wuye said: "There has not yet been a teacher like me. Suppose someone were to ask this old monk, "What is the Dharmakāya?
A sheep would simply lie down where it is dry. "What is the Dharmacakṣus? A donkey would simply urinate where it is damp.
Furthermore, if someone were to ask, "How is the Dharmakāya? [The answer is: "Buying a hat to fit the head. How is the Dharmacakṣus? [The answer is: "..."
The eyes, pits, hollows, and mounds—if one were to examine them closely, Jia Shan’s teaching would simply not be profound;
it is like worldly objects within the inner chambers that one cannot let go of, causing the gates of emotion to remain firmly shut and the shackles of consciousness to be difficult to open.
If I, this old monk, do not reveal this directly today, how shall those who come after know it?
Return! I exhort you all: do not seek the Truth; you must only cease your views. When all views are exhausted, the thick mists will no longer arise.
Then, natural wisdom will be clear and penetrating, and there will be nothing else. Do you all understand?
After a long silence, he said: "There is fire within the pearl; you must believe this. Do not go to the heavens to ask about the sun. He then spoke in verse:
"When the Way accords with the ordinary, there is no room for heterodoxy. Why must the practitioner traverse hardships? From now on, do not trust Sun Bin."

[Added by Zengshou] Fuyong Kai was asked by a monk: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed? The Master said: "The golden phoenix perches at night on a shadowless tree; the mountain peaks have just appeared when the sea clouds obscure them. The Verse says: Whose song does the Master sing? [Added] Chan Master Shouduan of Baoyun in Shuzhou (a successor of Yangqi) addressed the assembly, saying: "This matter is like being at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff.

Today, Fahua, without moving a single hair’s breadth, shall lead you all to the very bottom."
[He] threw down his staff. The verse says:
When intending to cast off the body from a perilous place, Who could deliberate upon it without knitting their brows?
Without moving a single hair, one reaches the very bottom; The eyelids open wide, covering Mount Sumeru. (Xutang Yu)

[Added from another source] Baiyun ascends the hall and presents a koan for the assembly’s edification. After a long silence, he says: "The mouth is fit only for eating rice. He then offers this verse: Verse: The mouth is fit only for eating rice; The hands are fit only for holding a bowl. If you wish to know the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, Look at the old man on the mountain peak.
Baoyun cites an ancient precedent; it is truly extraordinary. One’s mouth is capable of eating rice, yet few people know this.
All you venerable Chan masters, do not hesitate: once full, one naturally forgets a hundred hungers. (Duan’an Yan)
[Added from another collection] Baiyun ascended the hall. Seeing that the assembly had gathered, he held up his staff and asked, "Does the great assembly understand?
He then struck the ground with the staff and said, "Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow; half are for thinking of you, and half are for resenting you."
The Verse says:
How many times have you been drenched by water and dragged through the mud? Old in years and solitary at heart, you do not realize it yourself.
The traveler does not return, leaving only empty longing; A stream flows on, with falling flowers drifting along. (Wuan Quan)

[Added for inclusion] Baiyun was once asked by a monk: "The old year has passed and the new year has arrived; what is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? The Master said: "The eyebrows are above the eyes. Verse: The old year has gone, the new year arrives; How can there be any transmigration?
The eyebrows are above the eyes— This very thing is the meaning of non-transmigration.
Having finished fishing, I return home and do not moor my boat; as the moon sets over the riverside village, it is precisely the time for sleep.
Even if a wind should blow me away all night long, I shall remain by the shallow waters amidst the reeds. (Yuetting Chung, No. 2)
Falling leaves have already followed the flowing water away; the spring breeze has not yet allowed the hundred flowers to bloom.
The face of the green mountains remains as it was, stretching across the day in contrast to the setting sun.
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Renyong of Baoning in Jinling (a successor of Yangqi) addressed the assembly, saying:
"Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, yet he never uttered a single word.
Upagupta’s room was so full that the tally sticks overflowed, yet he never ordained a single person. Bodhidharma did not dwell in Shaoshi, and the Sixth Patriarch did not reside [at Caoxi]."
Caoshan said: "At Caoxi, who is the descendant and who is the one first awakened? Since it is thus, they have no sores of their own; do not wound them.
He struck his knee and looked at the assembly, saying: "How joyful! The world is at peace. The Verse says:
The smoke rises warm and the earth is rich with moisture as farming begins; a single furrow breaks the spring plowing after the fresh rain.
The plains and fields stretch far and wide, green beyond measure; wild grasses and idle flowers grow in their proper succession. (Xutang Yu)
Baoning Yong addressed the assembly, saying: "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Clouds arise beyond the railing; clouds drip before the eaves.

The mountain stream is as clear as indigo; the mountain flowers bloom like brocade. If you do not investigate the source at this very moment, you must wait until the future to question Maitreya. The verse says: Clouds rise beyond the railing, Drops fall before the eaves. The stream is deep blue, The flowers are like brocade.
If you do not examine the root now, You shall wait for the future to ask Maitreya.
Spiritually lucid, it does not involve past, present, or future. The entire triple world is but a single point of mind. Beyond the railing, the spring breeze and spring butterflies dance;
before the gate, the willow trees and morning orioles sing. (Danxia Chun)

Yangqi said, "This is because the Bi-bu official’s great vow is profound and vast, seeking to benefit all sentient beings. The layman said, "Not yet."
Shen asked, "How is it so? Qiji showed him the way with a verse, saying: "Manifesting in the body of an official, The compassionate vow is widely propagated and deep.
For the sake of people, he points out the place again: Beneath the staff, blood flows profusely. At this, Gong had an awakening. He composed a verse, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]

The Fourteenth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch (the Thirteenth Generation under Nanyue) (Linji Lineage) [Added by Zongshou]:
Chan Master Fayan of Wuzu Mountain in Qizhou (he succeeded Baiyun Yuan). Initially, he visited Master Fushan Yuan.
One day, Yuan said to the Master: "I am old; I fear you will waste your time in vain. You may..."
He went to rely on Baoyun. Although this old man was junior to him in age, Xuedou had not yet met him in person;
however, having seen his verse on the story of Linji’s three blows, he knew that Baoyun possessed a capacity beyond ordinary men and would surely be able to resolve his great matter.
The Master wept as he took his leave and traveled to Baoyun’s place, whereupon he raised the dialogue concerning the *maṇi* jewel asked of Nanquan for inquiry. Baoyun said:
He rebuked him. The Master attained realization and offered this verse of immediate resonance: "A plot of vacant land before the mountain;
With palms joined, I earnestly questioned the patriarch: How many times have I sold it only to buy it back? Out of love for the pines and bamboo, which draw in the pure breeze.
Yun specifically granted his certification. The Verse says:
Before the mountain, fields are sold and bought; amidst the pine and bamboo, one deeply pities the pure breeze.
It is laughable to boast of wealth and nobility within a dream; once awakened, it is not worth even half a coin. (Duan’an Yan)
Dying, he gave me his earnest instructions; I saw the white clouds. A cup of gall-poisoned wine was poured to the full.
Had I been told not to drink and returned empty-handed, there would have been no way for my fields and lands to sink into oblivion. (Zhuyue Jian, No. 2)
In a sudden gale and torrential rain, his tracks were lost; he crashed into the net of Mount Fushan.
Even if Baiyun could have pulled him out, he would still have been nothing more than a wood-seller.
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Wuzu Yan said: "For over ten years I have traveled as a pilgrim, studying under dozens of virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra).
I thought I had reached a definitive understanding; yet when I arrived at the assembly of Fushan Yuanjian, I could not even open my mouth.
Finally, I came to Baiyun, where by biting into a single iron pastry, all a hundred flavors were revealed."
Sufficient. Now tell me, how would you express the single phrase regarding the "filling"? The cockscomb flowers bloom, enchanting the early autumn; who can dye their purple silk tips?

Sometimes the wind stirs and they lean against one another, as if vying incessantly before the steps. The Verse says: The cockscomb flowers bloom, enchanting the early autumn; Who can dye their purple silk tips? Sometimes the wind stirs and they lean against one another, As if vying incessantly before the steps.
White clouds and iron dumplings—difficult for a patch-robed monk to bring to his mouth. Suddenly, if he can bite through them, he lets out a great lion’s roar. (Yue’an Guo)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Wuzu Yan was serving as the miller in the assembly at Baiyun Mountain.
One day, Baizhang came down to the mill and said, "Miller, do you know one thing? The Master replied, "I do not.
Baizhang said, "Recently there were several Zen guests who came here from Mount Lu; they all claimed to have attained realization. When I asked them to speak about it, they were able to explain it."
There was a reason for this. He cited the causal conditions for him, and [Yunju] understood it clearly; he could also apply the words of the Teaching appropriately.
After a long silence, Yunju said to the Master, "The Head of the Monastery is simply not yet there. What do you say? Upon hearing this, the Master felt uneasy in his heart;
for seven days and seven nights, he could not digest anything. It struck right at the core of his being. Then—
He thought to himself, "I have already awakened to it; I can explain it and I can clarify it. Why then am I still not 'there'?
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, he finally understood. All that he had previously cherished was cast away at once.
He then went to report this to Duan, who rose up and danced for joy. Foyan Yuan said: "When I served my former master..."
The Master, citing this causal occasion, said to [Name]: "In studying the Way, you must let go all at once before you can attain peace and happiness.
He then asked the assembly, "Do you see this? and spoke in verse:
If you can let go, you are truly liberated and carefree. If you cannot let go, it is like an ox pulling a plow.

How laughable are the ancient masters of all quarters, beating drums and preaching Zen without end—without end! Not being startled or afraid is truly marvelous; they know how to walk upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.
Without speaking, they naturally transmit it throughout the world. Well done, great brother!
[Added for inclusion] Master Wuzu Yan was asked by a monk: "The entire Tripitaka is a 'cutting foot' (a suffix). I wonder, what word does it cut? The Master said: "Bolanang. Verse:
The entire Tripitaka is a cutting foot; What word does it cut? "Bolanang"— The sound of the wind blowing through the pines.
Above the lips there must surely be the markings of a leopard’s skin; upon the tip of the tongue lies the very heart of the imperial capital. (Tell me, what characters are these?
Since ancient times, even the most sagely have not recognized them; how could ordinary people of the mundane world ever understand them? (Shi’an Shui).
The entire Great Canon of Teachings is merely a foot-note. Dongshan cut through it and attained *prajñā*;
the resentment coiled within his breast could no longer be contained, and suddenly he manifested a rainbow ten thousand fathoms long (namely, Dahui Zonggao).
The belly is overturned and the entrails come forth; how many times have you ever mastered the Chinese and Sanskrit tongues? Before words and after phrases, know the essential point:
lotus blossoms bloom one by one upon dry land. (Bieshan Zhi)
The texts of the Great Canon serve as the radical for the character "qie" (pronunciation guide). The meaning of *praṇidhāna* is most profound and subtle;
among the disciples of Confucius, none recognize it. The blue-eyed barbarian monk nods his head in the dark. (Yuan of Dun’an)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Master Wuzu Yan was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The mouth is the gateway to calamity. Verse:
A phrase right before one's eyes, A path clearly behind the arrow. The man wearing boots eats the meat; The barefoot man chases the rabbit.
(Jingshan Gao): The mouth is the gateway to calamity;
like lightning flashing and thunder rolling. Sāgara emerges from the sea, shaking heaven and earth. (Gushan Gui).
"What is the Buddha? "The mouth is the gate of calamity. "A single coin is not worth its weight. "Selling it to the buyer.

A human ghost-messenger arrives with a talisman to take him away; the flower-crown upon his head is already fading.

A Kunlun child cast from raw iron: light-headed, heavy-footed, and large-bellied.

(By Huaisu Guang).

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Huìqín Fójian of Tàipíng in Shūzhōu (he succeeded Wǔzǔ Yǎn). A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Eating rice and biting upon grit. The Verse says:
Eating rice and biting upon grit— The Buddha’s meaning is not far off. If you wish to see the Buddha’s face, Look at the man before you.
While eating, he bit into a grain of sand; his third tooth was hidden away. Once the spring breeze had passed, even his staff blossomed with flowers. (Cishou Shen)

I am not as good as you. The Master’s doubts grew deeper, so he went to consult the Head Monk Yuanli for a definitive resolution.
He took his seat. Bowing, he led the Master’s ear with his hand and circumambulated the brazier several times, speaking as he walked:
"You have understood it well yourself. The Master said, "I hope you will grant me an awakening; why do you mock me so?
Liangjie said, "Only when you attain realization in the future will you understand the twists and turns of today. The Verse says:
I am not as you; when Bodhidharma stood at the gate, two of his teeth were missing. Throughout the hall, there is the boundless wind of white artemisia;

I am not like you; it is laughable that a thousand flowers bloom upon the tip of a pestle. Though Sudhana wandered through a hundred cities in vain, when has he ever trodden upon his own ground?

[Lóngmén] added for inclusion, addressing the assembly: "A thousand explanations and ten thousand expositions are not equal to seeing one face in person.

The old woman selling fans shields herself from the sun with her hand; this is a single style of Chan that flows from the head of the house.
Tell this to the travelers on the road who have not yet returned: why must you go outside to eat the *pōzhā* fruit? (Yuepo Ming)
[Supplement] Later in life, Dàhuì remained at the Gǔ Yúnmén Hermitage, where students gathered in great numbers. After some time, he entered Fúmián and built a thatched hut on Yángyù in Chánglè.
Within his quarters, he would take up a bamboo stick and question his students: "To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back [on the truth]. One may neither utter a word nor remain silent."
Thirteen people attained the Dharma by following him.
The verse says: Yunmen raises up his bamboo staff; ordinary and holy beings hide their tracks and conceal their traces. Outside the Diamond Gate, anger arises;
inside the wooden horse stable, faces turn red. (Nun Wuzhuo, No. 2)
Yunmen held up his bamboo whisk. As soon as one engages in thought, one has missed it; merely deliberating on "back" or "touch," the old man has already fallen into verbal error.
At Jingshan, there is a bamboo whisk; directly beneath it, there is no other principle. It passes straight through the Buddha Hall, the kitchen, and the three sheds.
The eyes and ears of a patch-robed monk (Fuzhou Qingliang Tan):
A three-foot bamboo snake with a mouth reeking of raw flesh; it once swallowed thirteen men of exceptional talent.
Dust covers the four walls, and the lamp within its cage is blacked out. Old tail scorched yellow, its eyes glaring with rage (Zhuyu Jian).

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Mingbian Zhengtang of Daochang Monastery in Anji Prefecture (he succeeded Longmen Yuan). In his quarters, he asked students: "Why does an earthworm transform into a lily? The verse says:
A single thread of silk, Woven into a thousand layers. When the time comes, it will naturally unfold; How could one ever know its length? [End of Verse]
Ten autumns have passed since I stayed in a guest house in Bingzhou; my heart yearns for Xianyang day and night.
Without cause, I crossed the Sanggan River once more, and now I remember Bingzhou as my true hometown. (Cen Yuanji)

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Foguo De Guang of Yuyang in Mingzhou, surnamed Zhu’an (a successor of Dahui). Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty summoned him for an audience.
The Master cited the verse by Lingyun, “Even until now, I have no further doubts,” and asked, “Wherein lies his state of having no doubts?

The Emperor replied, “Leading an iron ox with empty hands. The Verse says: Even until now, I have no further doubts; Empty-handed, he leads an iron ox. If you wish to see the true man, Look at the one who stands before you.
In the leisure between ten thousand affairs, he explored the Chan school. How could the Six Dragons find rest along the way?
Empty-handed, he led his ox past the Celestial Gate; the Purple Palace lies deep within Mount Miaogao. (Guital Jushi)

What was the outcome of six years of diligent toil? I ask the King: do you remember it or not? Though one may know it directly, it is difficult to evade;
in the end, one cannot accept being smeared over. (Beijian Jian, 2)
Borrowing my mother-in-law’s robe to bow for her birthday; the commentary edition says this is a Zen that cannot be grasped with a spoon.
Raising the Jade Dragon to thunder like a clap of lightning—the morning star still shines in the Ninefold Heavens.
Question: When in the heavens one turns left; Answer: When on earth one turns right. In Great Peace there are no signs; the eyes at the head are wide.
The Snowy Mountains loom high, reflecting the Golden Hall. (Awakened Perfect Clarity).
Great roots, great capacity, and great cultivation— In a fleeting turn of the pivot, one transcends to the ultimate source. Throughout ten billion years, there is but a single Buddha;
The Snowy Mountains have never separated the Dragon Palace. (Shi Yanlian)

[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Shui’an Shi-yi of Jingci Temple in Lin’an Prefecture (heir to Fozhi Yu). In his quarters, he asked a monk: “Why does the bearded man of the Western Heaven have no beard?
The verse says: The bearded man of the Western Heaven has no beard; It is because he was born in the West. If you wish to know the reason for this, Look at the moon reflected in the water.
One must not speak of dreams before a fool. Beardless where there should be a beard; the alert and the dazed (no gate opens).
The cowherd has lost his tattered raincoat; long years have passed since it was lost, and those who see it are rare.
Picking it up, he drapes it over the fence-top, drawing the crows to circle and fly about the tree. (Dull Hall, Steadfast.)
The Eighteenth Generation after the Sixth Patriarch (the Seventeenth Generation after Nanyue) (Linji Lineage) [Added by Zeng]:
Chan Master Yanchong Kentang of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture (Dharma heir of Wan’an Yan). He addressed the assembly, saying:

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Chan Master Yian Youquan of Huazang Monastery in Changzhou (he was a successor of Wuan Quan). Once, he sat in meditation through the night until dawn.
When the粥 (congee) server arrived, he forgot to spread out his alms bowl. A neighboring monk touched it with his hand, and the Master was awakened to realization.
He composed a verse, saying: "A pitch-black K'un-lun man holds a fishing rod; The ancient sail is hoisted high as he descends the surging rapids. Among the reeds..."
Playing with the bright moon within its own shadow, he enticed the blind turtle onto the fishing boat. The Verse says:
Clouds deepen, the river ends, and the sail is drawn alone. A pity that the neighboring monk dragged him back on board.
Only then can one believe the matter of the Perfectly Bright One’s snap of the fingers; it turns out these words do not transmit anything false. (Guantang Jushi)
[Added from the Supplement] Chan Master Huchu Shiti (Successor of Cishan Yuan), of Pujie Chan Temple on Mount Jiao in Zhenjiang Prefecture.
Once, Administrative Commissioner Ge Xinzhai asked him: "When a husband and wife are fighting, their son serves as witness.
Now tell me, does he bear witness for the father, or does he bear witness for the mother? The Master said: "The small emerges, and the great encounters it."
He then uttered this verse:

Eight-armed Nātha with three eyes, Beating the drum with twin mallets as he turns the prow; The giant turtle swallows it all at one gulp, the vast ocean is exhausted— The wind clears across the universe, throughout the four hundred provinces.

Majestic is the sixteen-foot countenance of purple-gold; amidst the arena of a hundred performances, there is transformative penetration.
When the short man looks upon it, his eyebrows stand erect; the iron hammer, having no hole, dances in the spring breeze. (Ge Lu Tan)
[Added to the Collection] Chan Master Xutang Zhiyu of Jing Mountain in Lin’an Prefecture (successor of Yun’an Yan). He gave this turning word:
"Why is it that those whose own eyes are not yet clear take empty space to wear as trousers?

Why is it that they draw lines on the ground to create prisons and cannot pass through them? Why is it that those who enter the sea to count its sands direct their attention toward the point of a needle?"
With his feet raised above his head. The verse says:
Sewing up the void, counting every grain of sand; Drawing lines upon the needle’s point is one’s livelihood. Changing heads and faces, no one sees it;
How many times has the spring breeze blown the flowers down? (Xianji Yun)
Understanding how to take empty space as trousers and a shirt—though one may draw a dungeon on the ground, escaping it remains difficult.
With both feet poised atop the point of a needle, one still speaks of the year’s cold against the spring breeze. (Ge Lu Tan)
The lineage of Master Louzi is not clearly known.
Once, while passing through the marketplace, he happened to stop for a moment beneath a wine shop as he adjusted his socks and sash.
He heard someone upstairs singing a song that went: "Since you have no heart, I shall simply let it rest. Upon hearing this, he was suddenly [awakened].
He attained great enlightenment. From this time on, he was called Lóuzi (Master Lou) (from the *Lengyan Jing Shuowen* by Chan Master Changqing Huan). The verse says:
Singing songs on the tower, his speech is elegant and refined; Since you have no mind, I shall also rest. I strike the heart of the slave-girl.
Matters of this world, with all their lifelong affections, are but cold and hollow sounds (the "deep compassion" of Cishou).
Yet, by chance, I heard a pure song rise from a high tower: "If you have no mind, I shall let it rest. At once, the wild mind can be suddenly stilled;
from now on, as one expounds the Dharma, one will not lose sight of the head (the One Original Enlightenment).
Since you have no mind, I shall also rest; this mind has neither joy nor sorrow. When hunger comes, eat; when weariness comes, sleep.
Let the falling flowers follow the current as they drift away. (Baofeng Ming)
【Continued Collection】If you have no heart, I shall also desist. Within the phoenix curtains, I am loath to raise my head. My servant asks after this profound meaning;
I laugh and point to the moon through the gauze window—it is truly autumn. (Bǎohuājìng)
Passing by the flower-strewn streets and wine taverns, I suddenly heard a song that stirred my parting sorrows.
A sharp blade has severed the crimson thread; if you have no heart for me, then I shall rest as well. (By Hantang Ren)
[Added for Collection] Master Dushun’s Verse on the Dharmakāya: The ox of Huaizhou eats the grain; (Ciming adds: "In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

(Ciming says: "A donkey grows horns. Zhuan’an says: "Everyone in the world seeks a physician. To cauterize the left shoulder-blade of a pig... (Ciming...)
It is said: "Painting a tiger results in a wildcat. Zhuan-an said: "Like roasting the left shoulder-blade of a pig.
The verse says: These are the Dharma-body verses of the ancient worthies; they are like sleep-talking or boiling hot fat. If you wish to learn to sing the *bāgē*, you must be naturally clever.
(Daowei Zhi): A single rain, a single cloud, and the wind is not yet harmonious; spring is consumed within this state of unease.
The peach blossoms have already followed the flowing stream in secret, leaving Master Liu to suffer much in his desolation. (Xinwen Ben)
It is both laughable and pitiable: the ears are originally but two pieces of skin. (Songyuan Yue). [Added from another source:
The King of the Yuezhi heard that the Venerable Jīvaka of the kingdom of Kaśmīra possessed great renown.
Accompanied by his ministers, he went to that country to pay his respects and inquire about the Dharma. Once the King had finished his formal salutations, he invited him...
The Master said, "When Your Majesty arrived, the path was auspicious; now as you depart, it is just as it was when you came.
The King then sighed in admiration and submission. The Verse says:
Utterly simple, utterly easy, most honored and most noble. Coming and going, it rests upon the crowns of a thousand sages. Neither mundane nor supramundane.

The Wayman said, "I am able to refute any statement whatsoever. Aśvaghoṣa then pointed to the king and said, "The current realm is peaceful and prosperous, and Your Majesty enjoys long life;
I request that you refute this. Thereupon, the non-Buddhists were defeated and humbled.
The Verse says:
The six masters raised their weapons improperly, claiming, "What can we not do to you?
They silenced the ninety-six schools, yet could not extinguish a single verse of the Song of Great Peace. (Original Awakening, One)
Once there was an elder who did not speak a single word to his disciples throughout an entire summer retreat. A monk sighed to himself, saying, "I have spent this whole summer in vain.
I do not dare hope for the Master to preach the Buddha-dharma, but it would be enough just to hear two words of the True Cause.
Upon hearing this, the elder said casually, "Dharmācārya, do not lament so quickly. As for..."
"The primary cause—there isn't even a single word for it. Having said this, he tapped his teeth and remarked, "Just now, I spoke thus without reason.
An elder living in the adjacent wall heard this and said, "What a fine pot of soup that has been defiled by two mouse droppings! The verse says:
Throughout an entire summer, he harmonized a single pot of soup. Even at the Fuyan hermitage, they would not yet allow him to compete for equality.
Do not say that his stains went unseen; the Chan elder next door possessed but a single eye of clarity. (By Zhengjue Yi)
Throughout the long summer, there was no other pursuit; I prepared a single cauldron of harmonized soup. Its flavor was quite fragrant, yet it left stains upon the firm ground.
The mouth is the gateway to calamity; the tongue is the axe that fells one’s own body. One has been burdened with three catties of iron, all because of gazing upon the rusted shackles.
(Ci Shou Shen). [Continued Collection] Cold, clear mountain streams weep in the autumn ravines; having just realized the nature of the vast ocean, one sets sail upon it.
It is said that Xu You once washed his ears; how pitiable that Chao Fu went further and whipped his ox! (Xu Tang Yu).
The Chan Master Yushan of Chaling in Tanzhou had never traveled as a wandering monk (*yújiǎo*).

Once, when a transformation-monk (*huàshì*) from Mount Lu arrived and they discussed matters of the Chan school, [Yushan] was instructed to contemplate the following: "A monk asked Fadeng, 'How does one advance further atop a hundred-foot pole?
Fadeng replied, 'Ugh! For three years he did so. One day, while crossing a bridge on a donkey, he gave it a kick.
As he was stepping onto a bridge plank, it gave way and he fell. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse, saying:

"I possess a divine pearl, a single one, Long obscured and locked away by various defilements. This morning, the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers."
For this reason, he no longer traveled abroad. A verse says:
Having advanced further from the top of a hundred-foot pole, A single step upon the mountain stream bridge leaves no trace of mountains or rivers.
From now on, he will not emerge from the banks of the Tea River; His chanting and laughter are nothing other than *lālīla*. (Baiyun Yuan)
【Continued Collection】Advancing further, he steps upon the bridge and breaks it through. Where the void bulges, the water and sky are concave.
How many throughout ancient and modern times have suffered such a tumble? Not like this one tumble of yours, O *śrāmaṇera*. (Beijian Jian)
Tripping over the stream bridge, both eyes go dry; By mistake, one takes fish-eyes for bright pearls.
Even if dust were cleared away and light were born, It would illuminate mountains and rivers, yet no dream could be seen. (Wunian Fan)
Picking up a bright pearl, his mouth opens in a smile; he says that when the dust is cleared, it turns back into dust.
If one lacks the capacity to accept this directly, one fails the donkey for its single leap. (Jishi Peng)
At the top of the hundred-foot pole, the talk is most intimate; once the bridge is crossed, not a speck of dust remains. Finding life within death, the pearl is revealed;
I am content to be the one who follows behind the donkey and the horse. (Wumen).
The place where the donkey loses its footing on the mountain stream bridge; the moment one advances further atop the hundred-foot pole.
At that instant, from crown to heels, everything is completely transformed—yet it remains nothing other than Layman Yü (Shixi Yue).
A single stumble results in total disorder; the path through the tea fields turns increasingly circuitous. Yet one takes a mud pellet to be a night-shining pearl. (Ge Lu Tan)
[Added for Collection] Once, two head monks met after ten days had passed. The senior monk asked, "Where have you been all this time?
The junior monk replied, "I was in the hermitage building a seamless pagoda. The senior monk said:
"I, so-and-so, also wish to construct one. May I borrow the model from you, elder brother?
The hermit replied, "Why did you not say so sooner? It has just been borrowed. The verse says:
A seamless stupa-like object; both hands cannot lift it. Borrowed by someone, it has not been found until this day.

It happened that it was borrowed by someone else. Do not say the neighbor is inhospitable; it is a seamless circle where even a brush cannot find rest.
One merely smears on a couple of layers of mist and clouds. (Gong of Shilin)

At present there is no other path; with a trusting hand, one chops out the square and the round. The eyebrows lie across the eyes;
the nostrils hang from the large head. (Kongsou Yin)
The year ends and the king grows old; at night, paper money is burned. It is difficult to find a boat going downstream that will carry one across.
The deluded do not know their own arrival at the shore; they merely follow the shifting of cold and heat in vain. (Yuan of Dun’an)
Question comes and answer goes; there is a source. A single phrase encompasses the entire great chiliocosm. When the year ends and the time is spent, what is the ultimate matter?
The old Wang of the eastern village burns paper money at night. (By Jianweng Jing)

On the country roads in the spring breeze is the gallant man. He spends the money he receives as it comes into his hands. When his goods suddenly match [the price], he happens upon exactly what he needs. (Xueyan Qin)

[Added for inclusion] An ancient worthy was asked by a monk: "What serves as the boat and rudder for birth and death? The worthy said: "When the year ends, one does not burn paper money. The verse says: When the year ends, one does not burn paper money; For what purpose would one seek a boat? If you wish to cross the river of birth and death, You must first understand the nature of the mind.
The year ends without burning paper money; the rat's burrow is pierced by a snake. Even if one attains profound realization, they face each other across the Western Heaven. (Cao Yuan-sheng)

[Added for collection] An ancient worthy was asked by a monk: "What is it like when the year has ended and the time is exhausted? The Worthy said: "Every household looks upon the wild fox cubs. The Verse says: Every household looks upon the wild fox cubs; The year is spent, and the time is exhausted. If you wish to understand the meaning of this, Go ask the old woman at the well.
Every household looks upon the wild fox cubs; The iron flute is held crosswise and blown in a chaotic melody. Having finished blowing, they know not where they have gone;
The evening sun has already hung low behind the willow branches in the west. (Songyuan Yue)
Every household looks upon the wild fox cubs; though many see them, those who truly recognize them are few. A hundred monsters and a thousand sprites have all been cleared away;
the spring breeze has already reached the ten-thousand-year branch. (Huisou Guang)

[Added from another source] An ancient worthy asked a monk, "Why do you not read the sutras? The monk replied, "I do not know how to read. The worthy said, "Why do you not ask someone else? The monk extended his hand and asked, "What kind of characters are these? The worthy was speechless. The verse says: A single word, like a jewel, is difficult to obtain;

If one does not encounter it, one will never see it. The monk’s question was truly profound; The ancient worthy could not respond. The true meaning lies within the palm of the hand; Who can discern its essence? If one can see it without opening the eyes, One will surely attain the Way.
The precious sword within the sleeves grinds the stars and constellations; the numinous talisman behind the elbow illuminates the eight directions.
Once the pivot before one’s eyes is turned, let the world below remain vast and boundless. (Shuan-an Yan)
Standing like a crane, crawling like a snake, its momentum never ceasing; the Brahmī script of the Five Indias makes the ghosts and spirits wail.
None among the disciples of Confucius can recognize it; the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and nods his head. (By Saryak Hui)
[Added from the Supplementary Collection: Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty once dreamed of a divine being who exhorted him to give rise to the *bodhicitta*.
The following day, he asked his court ministers, "How does one give rise to the *bodhicitta*? The assembled ministers were unable to answer. Xuedou [Yi] spoke on their behalf:
"Truly something rarely heard in all antiquity. Biefeng Yin answered on their behalf: "The words of Your Majesty are like fine silk; they emerge [from the source]."
Like a silk thread. The verse says:
How does one give rise to the wondrous mind of Bodhi? Responding to ten thousand occasions throughout the day, it is fundamentally never at fault.
If you turn your head and take a fleeting glance, the great chiliocosm is the Imperial Court. (Songyuan Yue).
Ten thousand *li* sing of the Sage’s transformation; with gentle breezes and timely rains, woodsmen and farmers rejoice.
Had it not been for the three cries at Mount Song, who would have known this true peace beyond all signs? (By Shuangshan Yuan)
To give rise to the bodhicitta is not difficult; it lies within a single thought-moment of the sovereign. Transmitted from sage to sage, all follow this same principle;
may the enduring reign of the state remain as secure as Mount Tai. (Xin’an Chou)

[Added from the Supplementary Collection] Emperor Taizong asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Woyun Hermitage. The Emperor said, "In the depths of Woyun, one does not face the court; why then have you come here? The monk had no reply. Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "It is difficult to escape the ultimate transformation. The Verse says: The imperial decree reaches even the clouds; How could he remain hidden in the deep mountains? If he had not been moved by the Sage’s transforming power, He would never have left the mountain peaks. The Emperor’s question was like a thunderbolt; The monk’s silence was like a dead tree. Xuedou’s verse is truly peerless; He brings out the monk’s hidden meaning. The Emperor asked about his recent travels; The monk replied with the name of his hermitage. The Emperor then questioned him further: "Why have you come here? The monk was speechless and could not answer. Xuedou spoke for him: "Difficult to escape the ultimate transformation. ten thousand *li* of Yao’s heaven are but a single speck of cloud. (Beijian Jian)

Two thousand years since our parting at Vulture Peak; that we meet again in this sagely age could not be by mere chance.
Gently scooping up clear spring water to wipe my aged eyes, I push aside the clouds and mist to behold the blue sky. (Sokcheomyeok)

They replied, "From the place of Master Mazu in Jiangxi. The Commander asked, "What kind of skillful means does Master Mazu possess? They said, "If one speaks of it—"
"Mind is Buddha. He was then ushered out. Two other monks arrived and asked the same question as before.

Postscript to the Comprehensive Collection of Linked Verses on Ancient Cases of the Chan School:
The blue lotus flashes its gaze; the golden hue smiles subtly. The lineage of transmission began here and was secretly established; at Shaolin, the flowers bloomed, and Shen Guang [Huikong] appeared.
Sealed and received, the lineage is thereby further illuminated. Although the branches and lineages differ, their functional application is without duality.
Sometimes they employ concession and withdrawal to shatter the profound locks of the ancients; sometimes they use opening and closing to reveal the spiritual pivot for later students.
When the Great Function manifests, not even a speck of dust can stand. The four propositions alone transcend the realm of words; all phenomena...

Vanishing before sound, [this work] is the jade-bell of the Chan school; it links like pearls within the ancestral domain. Although its circulation has reached afar, its selection has not been entirely pure.

Even those with discernment still criticize it, let alone those who come later. Master Huì of Lú-ān in Qiántáng stands solitary and transcends the mundane; his accumulated practice perfumes his heart.

Having struck the ancestral mechanism from afar and deeply soaked himself in the flavor of the Dharma, he has gathered these karmic conditions to supplement previous omissions and compose verses on ancient cases.

Entering this newly published work, one may comprehend both the preceding and the subsequent, and illuminate both the ancient and the modern; how vast is the effort invested here! I have respectfully dispatched my pure companions to personally seek the postscript.
Though I am ashamed that my view through the narrow tube [of a straw] reveals but a tiny portion, I have briefly moistened my brush to satisfy this request.
Written by Xiling of Mount Jing in the late summer of the Wumwu year of the Yan’you era.
Within the Chan school, there are one thousand seven hundred koans, which are termed "ancient and modern" and also called "superfluous things.

To speak of them is to defile one's lips and teeth; yet to set them aside is to have no way to avoid them. Every phrase rolls like jade and turns like pearls; every word melts like ice and crumbles like tiles.
Though the masters of successive generations have offered verses upon them, they could not help but be like painting snakes with extra feet. Master Baoyue—
Compiled previously by [the author], it was later further collected by Master Luan. The evidence of the offenses is clear and requires no further investigation.
There is, however, one point of ambiguity therein; a monk with true insight will surely be able to discern it. On the Double Ninth day of the year Ding-si of the Yan-you era.
Respectfully inscribed by Chūpō, the mountain-dweller of Lingyin.

This *Lianzhu Songgu Tongji* (Comprehensive Collection of Linked-Bead Verses on Ancient Cases) has been transformed from its original and rendered increasingly magnificent; its phrasing is intricate and its expressions sharp, emerging more and more as one reads.
It is like bees in their hives brewing honey from a hundred flowers, or ants threading a nine-curved pearl with their silk. Those who consume this honey shall surely reflect upon its source.
The Bee. Those who cherish its pearls long for its ants. I have made this statement, whereupon a guest stepped forward and said:
"If one were suddenly to encounter someone who does not eat honey, does not prize pearls, and has no taste for words or texts—what would be the purpose of this collection?
I replied: "One who is afflicted by an illness cannot be made ill by that very illness. The guest withdrew in shame. Thus was it written in the spring of the Zhizhi era at Tiantong.
Inscribed by Yunxiu.
